article_title: Reading Plus®
citation: What Works Clearinghouse. (2010). WWC Intervention Report: Reading Plus®. U.S. Department of Education. http://www.readingplus.com/
title: Three-part session structure combining perceptual warm-up, adaptive silent reading, and contextual analysis activities
description: Within a typical 45-minute session, students engage in visual perceptual warm-up activities, scaffolded silent reading activities that "dynamically adjust content-level difficulty, degree of repetition, duration of reading, rate, and style of presentation," and contextual analysis activities building word knowledge and inferential abilities. Program length varies from 9 weeks (3–4 times per week) to 30 weeks (5 times per week).
requirements: Computer-based assessments determine each student's independent silent reading rate and level before assignment to an intervention path
target_learning_goals: Reading fluency
Comprehension skills
Vocabulary mastery
examples: Competency with 25 comprehension skills is tracked during scaffolded silent reading, and students are assigned appropriately leveled offline skills lessons targeting identified deficiencies
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse. (2010). WWC Intervention Report: Reading Plus®. U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/419

article_title: Reading Mastery (English Language Learners)
citation: WWC Intervention Report: Reading Mastery SRA/McGraw-Hill. (2006). What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Reading Mastery lesson design: fast-paced scripted lessons with modeling, guided practice, and individual practice
description: Reading Mastery lessons are 'designed to be fast-paced and interactive,' using 30- to 45-minute lessons with seven to nine short activities spanning multiple content strands such as phonemic awareness, letter-sound correspondence, sounding out words, word recognition, vocabulary, oral reading fluency, and comprehension. The overarching teaching routine repeated throughout the curriculum is composed of modeling new content, providing guided practice, and implementing individual practice and application. Lesson scripts guide teachers, and signals and group responses keep students involved and on task and control lesson pacing.
requirements: Lesson scripts act as a guide for teachers; delivery assistants received 10 hours of preservice training and were observed weekly in the first month and twice a month thereafter to ensure program standards.
target_learners: Beginning readers in grades K-6, including English language learners
target_learning_goals: Explicit, systematic beginning reading skills across phonemic awareness, decoding, vocabulary, fluency, and comprehension strands
examples: A typical lesson includes seven to nine short activities that encompass multiple strands of content.
key_sources: WWC Intervention Report: Reading Mastery SRA/McGraw-Hill. (2006). What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc

article_title: Red Light, Purple Light! (RLPL)
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2022). Red Light, Purple Light. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Implement Red Light, Purple Light as short circle-time sessions twice weekly over eight weeks with trained teachers
description: In the studies contributing to the WWC report, the program was delivered in low-dosage, repeated circle-time sessions rather than as a separate curriculum block. Teachers implemented sessions "for approximately 20 minutes during circle time," and "The Red Light, Purple Light sessions took place twice a week for 8 weeks." Teachers implementing the sessions received a 3-hour in-person training and a developer-provided kit of materials; comparison teachers received no program training.
requirements: A half-day (3-hour) in-person training from the developer, plus a training manual and a materials kit.
constraints: The evidence comes from Head Start centers in the Pacific Northwest with children from families below the poverty threshold; effects on other populations are not established in this report.
target_learners: preschool children in Head Start classrooms
target_learning_goals: self-regulation skills supporting school readiness
examples: Both qualifying studies used cluster randomized designs in which teachers were assigned to receive the training and implement the sessions or to continue with business as usual.
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2022). Red Light, Purple Light. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/725

article_title: Read Naturally — Students with Specific Learning Disabilities
citation: Read Naturally®. (2010). WWC Intervention Report: Read Naturally®. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.readnaturally.com
title: Three-component fluency-building strategy: modeled reading, repeated timed reading, and student-teacher progress monitoring
description: All four Read Naturally® products share a common fluency-building strategy with three components: "modeling of story reading, repeated reading of text for developing oral reading fluency, and systematic monitoring of student progress by teachers and the students themselves." Students listen to and read along with a fluent recording, do 1-minute practice readings toward a speed goal, then complete a teacher-scored pass timing; they graph scores from initial to final readings and across successive stories so both teacher and student track progress.
requirements: Sequenced texts at the student's reading level
audio recordings of fluent readers
teacher time for pass timings
graphing tools for progress monitoring
constraints: Designed as a supplement to core language arts instruction, not a replacement
target_learners: elementary, middle, or high school students
target_learning_goals: oral reading fluency
self-monitoring of reading progress
examples: The report describes students choosing a story, recalling what they know about the topic, reading aloud while the teacher identifies missing words, and graphing words read in one minute
key_sources: Read Naturally®. (2010). WWC Intervention Report: Read Naturally®. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.readnaturally.com

article_title: Reading Recovery — Grade 1 Beginning Reading
citation: Reading Recovery®. (2013). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report, Beginning Reading. Updated July 2013. http://www.readingrecovery.org
title: Interactive individualized lesson structure combining reading, letter/word work, and story writing
description: Each Reading Recovery lesson follows a recurring structure: "reading familiar or novel stories, manipulating letters and words, and writing and assembling stories." Lessons are "interactive between the teacher and student, with the teacher carefully monitoring each student's reading behavior," and teachers tailor instruction to accommodate each student's needs. This pattern combines text reading, orthographic work, and composing within a single one-on-one session, with continuous teacher observation guiding what each lesson contains.
requirements: A trained teacher who carefully monitors each student's reading behavior and tailors lessons to individual needs
constraints: Implemented as one-on-one pull-out tutoring for first-grade struggling readers, 30 minutes daily over 12–20 weeks
target_learners: First-grade students struggling in reading and writing
target_learning_goals: Reading and writing strategies
Literacy skills
examples: Lessons are discontinued when students demonstrate the ability to consistently read at the average level for their grade—between weeks 12 and 20 of the program
key_sources: Reading Recovery®. (2013). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report, Beginning Reading. Updated July 2013. http://www.readingrecovery.org

article_title: Repeated Reading
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2014). Repeated Reading: WWC Intervention Report, Students with Learning Disabilities. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Repeated reading as a flexible practice with seven variable implementation parameters
description: The report describes repeated reading not as a fixed protocol but as a practice whose implementation teachers can vary along seven parameters. As printed, "Teachers can vary" the criterion for progression to the next passage (minimum number of reads or a minimum reading rate of 85–100 words per minute), the instructional settings (teacher-directed, with same-age or cross-age peers, in groups, independently), the purpose, the materials (narrative texts, expository texts, poems, chants, songs, student- or class-written text), the modalities (silent with a tape, aloud with a model, choral, to a peer, to oneself), the length of the passage read, and the feedback provided on reading errors.
requirements: A teacher who selects passages and sets a progression criterion such as a minimum reading rate of 85–100 words per minute
constraints: The reviewed evidence covers individual delivery with a teacher in grades 5–12; the report does not rate effectiveness for the other configurations it lists
target_learners: students with learning disabilities in grades 5–12 with inadequate reading fluency
target_learning_goals: oral reading fluency
reading comprehension
examples: Settings range from teacher-directed one-on-one to work with same-age or cross-age peers, groups, or independent practice
Materials may include narrative texts, expository texts, poems, chants, songs, or text written by the student or class
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2014). Repeated Reading: WWC Intervention Report, Students with Learning Disabilities. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/576

article_title: Reading Recovery®
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2023, June). Reading Recovery® Intervention Report | English Language Arts Topic Area. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Reading Recovery training cascade: university-affiliated teacher training sites, teacher leaders, and certified teachers
description: Reading Recovery® sustains implementation through a three-level training infrastructure. Teacher training sites in public schools, affiliated with partnering universities, house teacher leaders who train teachers. Teacher leaders complete a yearlong training of graduate coursework and supervised practicums, and are expected to "provide initial training for up to 15 teacher candidates and provide ongoing support for 40 to 60 Reading Recovery® teachers or teachers in training annually." Teachers complete a yearlong graduate-credit training and must maintain registration by teaching at least eight students per year and participating in ongoing professional development.
requirements: Teacher leaders hold a master's degree and teaching credentials and complete a yearlong certification training
Teachers must be certified, experienced early elementary teachers and complete a year of training with graduate credit
Teachers must maintain registration by teaching at least eight students per year and attending ongoing professional development, typically no less than six sessions per school year
constraints: Neither contributing study provided details about the Reading Recovery® teacher training sites or the training of teacher leaders
Registration lapses after 1 year if teachers do not maintain the requirements
target_learners: Grade 1 students with low literacy achievement in districts implementing Reading Recovery®
target_learning_goals: Early literacy intervention delivered with training fidelity
examples: Based on survey results from one study, teacher leaders met 87% of the implementation standards, including attending 73% of training sessions and 98% of professional development sessions
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2023, June). Reading Recovery® Intervention Report | English Language Arts Topic Area. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/730

article_title: Reading Mastery
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2010). WWC Intervention Report: Reading Mastery (Adolescent Literacy). http://www.mcgraw-hill.co.uk/sra/downloads/Reading%20Mastery/Reading%20Mastery%20Signature%20Edition%20Brochure.pdf
title: Reading Mastery lesson pattern: modeling, guided practice, and individual practice within scripted 30–45 minute multi-strand lessons
description: A typical Reading Mastery lesson lasts 30 to 45 minutes and includes "seven to nine short activities that encompass multiple strands of content, such as phonemic awareness, letter-sound correspondence, sounding out words, word recognition, vocabulary, oral reading fluency, or comprehension." The repeated teaching routine proceeds through modeling new content, providing guided practice, and implementing individual practice and application. Lesson scripts guide teachers, and signals and group responses keep students involved and on task while controlling lesson pacing.
requirements: Lesson scripts act as a guide for teachers
Signals and group responses are used to keep students involved and on task, and to control lesson pacing
target_learners: Elementary students in grades K–6, including struggling readers
target_learning_goals: Decoding, word recognition, vocabulary, oral reading fluency, and comprehension
examples: The program typically spans one academic year with daily lessons of this structure
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2010). WWC Intervention Report: Reading Mastery (Adolescent Literacy). http://www.mcgraw-hill.co.uk/sra/downloads/Reading%20Mastery/Reading%20Mastery%20Signature%20Edition%20Brochure.pdf

article_title: Reading Plus
citation: Reading Plus — Evidence Rating Summary. (2024). https://www.readingplus.com
title: Supervise Reading Plus use with qualified classroom teachers, reading teachers, literacy specialists, or well-prepared paraprofessionals
description: The page specifies that Reading Plus does not require specialized staffing beyond existing school roles: "Classroom teachers, reading teachers, literacy specialists, and well-prepared paraprofessionals are qualified to supervise the use of Reading Plus." This makes implementation feasible within ordinary school staffing structures, provided supervising adults are prepared through the program's training and support system.
requirements: Supervising staff must be classroom teachers, reading teachers, literacy specialists, or well-prepared paraprofessionals
Completion of the program's instructor-led training (two hours in the study)
target_learners: Students in grades 3-12+ using Reading Plus
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Vocabulary
Reading efficiency
Reading motivation
examples: In the evaluation study, classroom teachers supervised Reading Plus students after completing two hours of instructor-led training.
key_sources: Reading Plus — Evidence Rating Summary. (2024). https://evidenceforessa.org/program/reading-plus/

article_title: REDI (Research-Based, Developmentally Informed)
citation: REDI (Research Based, Developmentally Informed). (2024). Program description page, Evidence Rating: promising. http://www.pathseducation.com/
title: Pairing social-emotional learning with interactive storybook reading and phonological awareness activities in preschool
description: REDI's instructional design combines an SEL curriculum with structured early-literacy activities: "an interactive storybook reading and retelling approach, along with phonological awareness training and alphabet center activities." The pattern pairs self-regulation and emotional-control teaching with language and print activities in the same preschool day.
requirements: Classroom teachers trained in both the PATHS curriculum and the literacy activities
constraints: Evaluated in Head Start preschool settings with disadvantaged students
target_learning_goals: executive functions
school readiness
early literacy
examples: The one REDI study randomly assigned Head Start centers to REDI or control conditions and measured TOPEL and EOWPVT outcomes at the end of the preschool year.
key_sources: REDI (Research Based, Developmentally Informed). (2024). Program description page, Evidence Rating: promising. https://evidenceforessa.org/program/redi-research-based-developmentally-informed/

article_title: Reading Edge
citation: The Reading Edge. (2008). https://www.evidencebasedprograms.org/programs/the-reading-edge/
title: Team-based cooperative reading with team recognition based on average member scores
description: The program organizes reading instruction around small cooperative teams whose members prepare one another for individual assessments. "Teams are recognized based on the average of all members' scores on these assessments," which makes each student's preparation valuable to teammates. This recognition structure pairs cooperative practice with individually administered assessments rather than group products.
requirements: 4-5 member teams
individual assessments of reading skills
a recognition mechanism tied to team average scores
target_learning_goals: reading skills built through peer support and individual accountability
examples: Students engage in partner reading, story retelling, story-related writing, word mastery, and story-structure activities to prepare themselves and their teammates for individual assessments.
key_sources: The Reading Edge. (2008). https://www.evidencebasedprograms.org/programs/the-reading-edge/

article_title: Sample Size Guide
citation: Mikia Manley, Virginia Knechtel, Gregory Chojnacki. (2023). Sample Size Guide. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/sample-size-guide
title: Engage a research partner to set sample sizes for validation-phase studies
description: Because rigorous effectiveness validation requires study-specific statistical planning, the guide recommends that organizations treat its general guidance as a starting point rather than a prescription. It states that in Phase 3 and Phase 4, "organizations can use this guidance as a starting point but should work with a research partner to determine the specific sample size needed for their study", pairing self-service tools with expert methodological support.
requirements: Access to a research partner with methodological expertise for Phase 3 and Phase 4 studies.
constraints: The guide's own sample size guidance is explicitly insufficient on its own for determining the specific sample size of a Phase 3 or Phase 4 study.
target_learners: students who are Black, Latino, and/or experiencing poverty
target_learning_goals: validating effectiveness of educational solutions
examples: The guide directs Phase 3 and Phase 4 users to work with a research partner to determine the specific sample size needed for their study.
key_sources: Mikia Manley, Virginia Knechtel, Gregory Chojnacki. (2023). Sample Size Guide. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/sample-size-guide

article_title: Enhancing the Generalizability of Impact Studies in Education
citation: Tipton, E., & Olsen, R. B. (2022). Enhancing the Generalizability of Impact Studies in Education. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance (NCEE 2022-003). https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/
title: Report information on the generalizability of study findings so readers can judge applicability
description: This principle holds that impact studies should disclose information about how findings generalize, because readers need this to judge applicability elsewhere. The guide names "reporting information on the generalizability of the study findings" as a key step researchers can take, completing the sequence from target population definition through sampling, recruitment, and adjustment.
requirements: Researchers must collect and document generalizability-relevant information during the study
target_learning_goals: reporting generalizability information to research consumers
examples: The guide lists reporting generalizability information among its key steps for impact study design
key_sources: Tipton, E., & Olsen, R. B. (2022). Enhancing the Generalizability of Impact Studies in Education. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance (NCEE 2022-003). https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/

article_title: The Community Ecocycle in Place-Based Systems Change: A Tool for Funder and Community Reflection and Action
citation: Meg Long, Wanda Casillas, James Liou. (2021). The Community Ecocycle in Place-Based Systems Change: A Tool for Funder and Community Reflection and Action. Equal Measure and Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Funder reflection on community developmental phase should precede and shape place-based investment
description: The article's guiding principle is that funders should first use the tool "to consider the dynamic, natural, and necessary developmental phases through which communities move" before committing investment approaches. Because communities' assets and needs differ by phase, reflection on phase is positioned as a necessary precursor to action, making investments more likely to fit community circumstances.
requirements: Access to the Community Ecocycle tool and engagement with the community to determine its phase
constraints: Applies to place-based systems change investments specifically
target_learning_goals: Aligning funding decisions with community readiness and developmental stage
examples: The tool's first stated use is funder consideration of communities' developmental phases
key_sources: Meg Long, Wanda Casillas, James Liou. (2021). The Community Ecocycle in Place-Based Systems Change: A Tool for Funder and Community Reflection and Action. Equal Measure and Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/the-community-ecocycle-in-place-based-systems-change-a-tool-for-funder-and-community-reflection

article_title: Leading the Change: A Comparison of the Principal Supervisor Role in Principal Supervisor Initiative Districts and Other Urban Districts
citation: Ellen B. Goldring, Laura K. Rogers, Melissa A. Clark. (2020). Leading the Change: A Comparison of the Principal Supervisor Role in Principal Supervisor Initiative Districts and Other Urban Districts. Mathematica, Vanderbilt University, and the University of Utah. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Redefine principal supervision from administration and compliance toward developing principals as instructional leaders
description: This principle holds that the principal supervisor position should be overhauled from a traditional focus on administration into a role centered on developing principals. The report describes the PSI's aim "to help districts overhaul a position traditionally focused on administration, operations, and compliance to one dedicated to developing and supporting principals to be effective instructional leaders." The PSI districts' changes in caseload, training, and aspirant programs reflect this redefinition.
requirements: Districts must reorient supervisor job expectations, caseloads, and training toward instructional leadership support
constraints: Evidence here comes from a comparison of six PSI districts with other large urban districts, not from an impact evaluation
target_learning_goals: Supporting principals' development as effective instructional leaders
examples: PSI districts reduced supervisor caseloads, added role-specific training, and offered programs for new and aspiring supervisors
key_sources: Ellen B. Goldring, Laura K. Rogers, Melissa A. Clark. (2020). Leading the Change: A Comparison of the Principal Supervisor Role in Principal Supervisor Initiative Districts and Other Urban Districts. Mathematica, Vanderbilt University, and the University of Utah. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/leading-the-change-a-comparison-of-the-principal-supervisor-role-in-principal-supervisor-initiative

article_title: English Learners in Chicago Public Schools
citation: de la Torre, M., Blanchard, A., Allensworth, E.M., & Freire, S. (2019). English Learners in CPS: A new perspective. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Report academic performance for all students who began as English Learners, not only active ELs, to give an unbiased picture of EL progress
description: The report argues that accountability and public reporting should follow a consistent group of students who began school as ELs, including former ELs, rather than the changing active-EL subgroup. It states "The best way to understand the average performance of the EL students... is to look at all students who began their schooling as ELs together." This regrouping showed performance of never-EL and ever-EL students was very similar. The report also suggests early identification of students with low first-grade ACCESS scores for additional support.
requirements: Longitudinal data linking students across years so the same cohort can be followed regardless of current EL status
constraints: Results apply to students continuously enrolled from kindergarten; the report states its results would not apply to recent immigrants entering in later grades, whom it hopes to study later
target_learners: English Learners in elementary and middle grades
district and school decisionmakers reporting EL outcomes
target_learning_goals: English proficiency
academic achievement across attendance, test scores, grades, and high school readiness
examples: The report regrouped 2018 eighth-grade ELA PARCC data to show former ELs passed at 31.5 percent versus 25.9 percent for students never classified as ELs
The report compared three kindergarten cohorts continuously enrolled through expected eighth-grade year
key_sources: de la Torre, M., Blanchard, A., Allensworth, E.M., & Freire, S. (2019). English Learners in CPS: A new perspective. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu

article_title: Still Crazy after All These Years
citation: Payne, Charles. (2005). Still Crazy after All These Years: Race in the Chicago School System. Consortium on Chicago School Research, University of Illinois at Chicago. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: External partners and reform programs should respect and draw on local educators' knowledge rather than imposing models
description: Payne argues school reform programs fail when developers treat local professionals as mere implementers. Quoting superintendent James Lytle's interview, "Nearly all of them are disdainful in their attitudes toward local educators," and Lytle's "McDonald's approach" analogy, Payne likens reformers to colonists who explain all failures in terms of local limitations. He further argues, citing Delpit, that universalist models devalue knowledge nonwhite professionals hold from culture and locality.
requirements: Reform designs must leave room for local professionals to contribute "over and above the model design."
constraints: Payne notes teachers of color can also exaggerate how much relevant knowledge they have; claims of special insight must be examined for self-service.
target_learners: urban school staff and educators in demoralized, high-poverty schools
target_learning_goals: building school capacity for improvement through respectful external partnership
examples: Payne's account of elite-educated interns who had to unlearn institutional arrogance and signify "I just work there" to work effectively in black institutions in Chicago.
key_sources: Payne, Charles. (2005). Still Crazy after All These Years: Race in the Chicago School System. Consortium on Chicago School Research, University of Illinois at Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/still-crazy-after-all-these-years-race-chicago-school-system

article_title: Research and Evaluation in the Chicago Public Schools
citation: Laurence Stanton and John Q. Easton. (2002). Research and Evaluation in the Chicago Public Schools: A Plan for the Future. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/research-and-evaluation-chicago-public-schools-plan-future
title: Locate the research and evaluation department so it reports directly to the chief executive to support independence and honest information
description: The report recommends that DRE "maintain its relative independence within the CPS by reporting directly to the CEO." Interviewees and committee members agreed that direct reporting "increases the likelihood that information and knowledge will inform district pol- icy" and that separating DRE from the departments operating the programs it evaluates "supports DRE's inde- pendence and its ability to be honest."
requirements: Department leadership with standing to deliver unwelcome news; separation from the operating departments it evaluates
constraints: The report notes the inherent difficulty of providing the system's leadership with news that it does not want to hear
target_learners: District and school leaders who use research to inform policy
target_learning_goals: Accurate information about program strengths and weaknesses to support mid-course adjustments
examples: Since October 2001, DRE reported directly to CEO Duncan rather than to the Accountability Office to which it previously reported
key_sources: Laurence Stanton and John Q. Easton. (2002). Research and Evaluation in the Chicago Public Schools: A Plan for the Future. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/research-and-evaluation-chicago-public-schools-plan-future

article_title: Annual CPS Trend Review, 2000
citation: John Q. Easton, Todd Rosenkranz, Anthony S. Bryk. (2001). Annual CPS Test Trend Review, 2000: Elementary School Test Score Trends in Chicago Public Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. http://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Report test score trends by age groupings rather than grade groupings to keep the comparison group constant when retention policies change
description: This data brief diverges from official CPS reporting by grouping students by age rather than grade, because large-scale grade retention changes grade composition over time and can inflate higher-grade scores. The authors state they "report student scores by age groupings rather than grade groupings" to distinguish retention effects from changing test score trends, keeping the comparison group constant across years.
requirements: Age must be defined consistently with school entry requirements, as the brief does by assigning students to age groups by birthday within the academic year.
constraints: The brief applies this specifically in the context of CPS retention policies beginning in fall 1997, primarily in grades three, six, and eight.
target_learning_goals: Accurate system-level monitoring of academic achievement trends
examples: The brief shows fifth-grade trend interpretation became unreliable as retained third graders moved through grades, motivating the age-based grouping.
key_sources: John Q. Easton, Todd Rosenkranz, Anthony S. Bryk. (2001). Annual CPS Test Trend Review, 2000: Elementary School Test Score Trends in Chicago Public Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/annual-cps-trend-review-2000

article_title: The Chicago Annenberg Challenge
citation: Dorothy Shipps, Karin Sconzert, with Holly Swyers. (1999). The Chicago Annenberg Challenge: The First Three Years. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Privately funded reform organizations must build a distinct identity and locally rooted legitimacy to influence public schooling
description: The report distills the Challenge's dilemmas into three overlapping influence requirements: identity, legitimacy, and legacy. To be influential, it argues, a reform organization "must distinguish its vision of school change in clear terms that permit it to have a meaningful identity in a crowded field of organizational change agents," and must "develop resource ties and cultural and political support from among the existing institutions in the city so that it develops its own locally rooted organizational legitimacy." The report warns that seeking legitimacy risks stretching the organization's theory of action beyond current plans.
requirements: A clear, distinct vision of school change; resource ties and cultural and political support from existing local institutions
constraints: Pursuing local legitimacy risks compromising the founding theory of action by stretching beyond current plans; strategic flexibility is constrained by early grant decisions and a changing institutional environment
target_learners: civic, business, political, and education leaders shaping urban school reform
target_learning_goals: building organizational influence for large-scale, privately funded school improvement
examples: The report concludes that the Challenge's pursuit of policy influence while remaining faithful to its initial vision may restrain its long-term reform legacy to one less deep and thorough than hoped
key_sources: Dorothy Shipps, Karin Sconzert, with Holly Swyers. (1999). The Chicago Annenberg Challenge: The First Three Years. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/chicago-annenberg-challenge-first-three-years

article_title: Charting Reform
citation: Susan Ryan, Anthony S. Bryk, Gudelia Lopez, Kimberley P. Williams, Kathleen Hall, Stuart Luppescu. (1997). Charting Reform: LSCs - Local Leadership at Work. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Require and expand training for all incoming Local School Council members
description: The report endorses mandatory, expanded training for incoming council members, finding that even under voluntary training most members received preparation in core areas yet a substantial minority felt underprepared. The authors write that the 1995 legislative provision to expand training "and require it for all incoming LSC members seems well-founded," because 40 percent reported not receiving enough preparation to do their job well. Training is most useful when tailored to the particular council, as principal-provided training was.
requirements: Training must cover essential areas: LSC roles and responsibilities, principal evaluation, the School Improvement Plan, and the school budget.
constraints: The article notes less common training topics included analyzing achievement data, good educational practices, and school and community partnerships.
target_learners: parent and community members serving on Local School Councils
target_learning_goals: governing a local school: principal evaluation, school improvement planning, and budget oversight
examples: The survey found most members received training from the principal, school reform groups, and the Board of Education, with principal-delivered training rated most useful.
key_sources: Susan Ryan, Anthony S. Bryk, Gudelia Lopez, Kimberley P. Williams, Kathleen Hall, Stuart Luppescu. (1997). Charting Reform: LSCs - Local Leadership at Work. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/charting-reform-lscs%E2%80%94local-leadership-work

article_title: Achieving School Reform in Chicago
citation: Consortium on Chicago School Research. (1991). Achieving School Reform in Chicago: What We Need To Know — A Research Agenda. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Research serving school reform must address multiple audiences and function as community education
description: The Consortium grounds its agenda in the conviction that a responsive research agenda must address public officials, school-based decision makers, and citizens broadly, since important decision making now occurs in individual school communities. It argues that the most effective research does not simply support administrative control but helps identify new concerns and offers concepts for discussing problem situations. Research reporting should therefore encourage a broad-based public conversation about educational issues.
requirements: Information must meet the quality test of deepening understanding and stimulating discourse about the aims and means of education
constraints: Good research is a slow and difficult process, so an infrastructure must be created in advance of the questions that will arise
target_learners: citizens of Chicago, public officials, principals, teachers, parents, and community members
target_learning_goals: public understanding of school reform progress and educational improvement
examples: The Consortium adopts a pluralistic policy, seeking open access to information and the ability of diverse groups to act on that information
key_sources: Consortium on Chicago School Research. (1991). Achieving School Reform in Chicago: What We Need To Know — A Research Agenda. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/achieving-school-reform-chicago-what-we-need-know

article_title: Kindergarten Redshirting: What Families Should Know
citation: Kindergarten redshirting: What families should know. (2026). NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/should-kindergartners-be-redshirted-costs-likely-outweigh-academic-benefits/
title: Advise against redshirting for most children, reserving it for children with significant developmental delays or major behavioral or emotional regulation struggles
description: The fact sheet's guidance for families weighing redshirting is that "For most children, the answer is likely no," while identifying a narrower group more likely to benefit. It names two exception groups: children with significant developmental delays and children who majorly struggle with behavioral or emotional regulation. The recommendation rests on the balance of short-lived academic benefits against costs such as childcare expense, dropout risk, and earnings effects.
requirements: Families should weigh the short-lived academic benefits against the costs the fact sheet lists before deciding
constraints: The fact sheet states the recommendation applies to most children and identifies exceptions rather than a universal rule
target_learning_goals: kindergarten readiness and school entry timing decisions
examples: The fact sheet lists children with significant developmental delays and children who majorly struggle with behavioral or emotional regulation as more likely to benefit from redshirting
key_sources: Kindergarten redshirting: What families should know. (2026). NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/kindergarten-redshirting-what-families-should-know/

article_title: High Dosage Tutoring for Academically At-Risk Students
citation: Davison, M., Postell, S., Isaacs, J., & Hashim, A. K. (2024). High dosage tutoring for academically at-risk students. Research brief. https://www.nwea.org
title: Remove barriers to access when designing high dosage tutoring programs
description: Among the implementation factors the brief identifies for effective high dosage tutoring, it highlights "new components like removing barriers to access." This principle directs program designers to treat access barriers as a design consideration on par with scheduling, group size, and personnel, so that at-risk students can actually participate in tutoring services.
requirements: Programs must consider and include access-related components alongside the other implementation factors for tutoring to be implemented effectively.
target_learners: Academically at-risk students facing barriers to accessing tutoring
target_learning_goals: Equitable participation in tutoring and accelerated academic growth
examples: The brief lists removing barriers to access among the factors that must be considered and included to implement high dosage tutoring effectively.
key_sources: Davison, M., Postell, S., Isaacs, J., & Hashim, A. K. (2024). High dosage tutoring for academically at-risk students. Research brief. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/high-dosage-tutoring-for-academically-at-risk-students/

article_title: English MAP Reading Fluency technical report
citation: NWEA. (2024). English MAP Reading Fluency Technical Report. https://www.nwea.org
title: Report oral reading rate, decoding accuracy, and comprehension separately rather than subsuming accuracy into WCPM alone
description: The report cites research "that accuracy scores are useful in instructional decisions, but that this use is lost when they are subsumed into the WCPM score alone." Following Valencia et al. (2010), it argues that rate, accuracy, prosody, and comprehension each contribute to predicting passage comprehension, and states "MAP Reading Fluency is modeled by this more robust approach." Accordingly, the assessment reports decoding accuracy and comprehension alongside oral reading rate to generate an individualized reader profile of strengths and needs.
requirements: Audio playback is needed for teacher rating of prosody where of interest
constraints: Complex comprehension tasks are typically a poor fit for oral reading administration since they often require revisiting the text for analysis
target_learners: primary-grade students still building passage comprehension skills
target_learning_goals: accurate individualized diagnosis of oral reading strengths and needs
examples: The Oral Reading Fluency report shows SWCPM, decoding accuracy, and passage comprehension scores, and teachers can play back the audio recording for further evaluation
key_sources: NWEA. (2024). English MAP Reading Fluency Technical Report. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/english-map-reading-fluency-technical-report/

article_title: An investigation of item parameter invariance using focused calibration samples for MAP Growth
citation: Wei He, NWEA Psychometric Solutions. (2021). An Investigation of Item Parameter Invariance Using Focused Calibration Samples for MAP Growth. NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Existing MAP Growth item parameter estimates can be reused in new assessments that administer items more closely aligned to student grade level
description: This principle holds that when focused calibration samples produce difficulty estimates comparable to original all-grade estimates, existing item parameters remain appropriate for new grade-aligned test designs. The report concludes that "the existing item parameter estimates are still appropriate if used in the new MAP Growth assessments that intend to administer items more closely aligned to the grade level of the student." Items showing different estimates across samples are routed to further content and psychometric review. The standard calibration procedure's minimum sample size of 1,000 and average of at least 2,000 are cited as likely contributors to the observed invariance.
requirements: Calibration sample sizes should remain large; the report cites the Rasch literature suggesting estimates are similar once sample size reaches 250, and the standard MAP Growth procedure sets a minimum of 1,000
constraints: Items whose estimates differ across calibration samples require further content and psychometric review before reuse
The report notes item parameter estimate accuracy can be affected by various factors beyond sample size, some of which may not be known to practitioners
target_learners: K-12 students taking MAP Growth assessments in math, reading, science, and language usage
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of student achievement on the RIT scale across grade levels
examples: Study 1 recalibrated items using on-grade-only samples; Study 2 used target-grade plus two adjacent grades; both found estimates comparable to the original all-grade calibrations
key_sources: Wei He, NWEA Psychometric Solutions. (2021). An Investigation of Item Parameter Invariance Using Focused Calibration Samples for MAP Growth. NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/an-investigation-of-item-parameter-invariance-using-focused-calibration-samples-for-map-growth/

article_title: Transforming education through COVID-19 recovery and learning acceleration: research findings, policy recommendations, and lessons from the ground
citation: Michael Conner, PhD, Beth Tarasawa, Deb Delisle, Janet Murguía, Chris Minnich, Marc Morial. (2021). Transforming education through COVID-19 recovery and learning acceleration: research findings, policy recommendations, and lessons from the ground. NWEA Research webinar. https://www.nwea.org
title: Treat the post-pandemic moment as an opportunity to reimagine education and build more equitable systems
description: The webinar positions pandemic recovery not merely as restoration but as a chance for systemic redesign toward equity. The page states that "we can use this critical moment in education to reimagine education and build more equitable systems that provide all children with an excellent education," tying recovery spending to longer-term equity goals.
requirements: Coordination among policymakers, education leaders, and advocacy organizations during the recovery period
constraints: Tied to the specific post-COVID recovery context and the availability of federal recovery funding
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to an excellent education
System-level transformation
examples: The webinar pairs NWEA trend research with policy recommendations from equity-focused organizations

Transforming education through COVID-19 recovery and learning acceleration: research findings, policy recommendations, and lessons from the ground. NWEA Research webinar. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/transforming-education-through-covid-19-recovery-and-learning-acceleration-research-findings-policy-recommendations-and-lessons-from-the-ground/

article_title: The relationship between test-taking disengagement and performance on MAP Growth retests
citation: Wise, S. (2019). The Relationship Between Test-Taking Disengagement and Performance on MAP Growth Retests. (The Collaborative for Student Growth at NWEA Working Paper). https://www.nwea.org
title: Retest disengaged students, but first focus on increasing their motivation so engagement improves
description: The article recommends that educators retest students who showed rapid guessing, because disengaged students who re-engage on retest are likely to show sizable gains and produce more valid scores. It stresses that "Simply retesting will accomplish little if engagement does not improve", so increasing the student's motivation before retesting is central to the recommendation.
requirements: The student's motivation must be addressed before retesting so that engagement actually improves
constraints: Educators should be cautious if they do not retest students showing high levels of rapid guessing, since those scores threaten the validity of test score interpretations
target_learners: K-12 students taking MAP Growth assessments who show rapid guessing
target_learning_goals: Valid measurement of what students know and can do
examples: Analysis of over 100,000 tests retested within one day showed disengaged students who rapid-guessed less on retest tended to see gains sometimes exceeding 10 RIT points.
key_sources: Wise, S. (2019). The Relationship Between Test-Taking Disengagement and Performance on MAP Growth Retests. (The Collaborative for Student Growth at NWEA Working Paper). https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/the-relationship-between-test-taking-disengagement-and-performance-on-map-growth-retests/

article_title: Effort analysis: Individual score validation of achievement test data
citation: Steven Wise. (2015). Effort analysis: Individual score validation of achievement test data. Applied Measurement in Education, 28(3), 237–252. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/effort-analysis-individual-score-validation-of-achievement-test-data/
title: Measurement professionals have a responsibility to identify invalid scores to individuals making achievement inferences from them
description: This principle holds that measurement professionals should actively flag invalid scores — those "materially distorted by non-effortful test taking" — to the individuals who make inferences about student achievement on the basis of those scores. The article recommends this as a professional responsibility so that score users are not misled by scores biased by low test-taking motivation.
requirements: Measurement professionals must be able to apply effort-related individual score validation to identify which scores are invalid before reporting them
constraints: Applies to scores distorted by non-effortful test taking; the article does not claim it covers all sources of invalidity
target_learners: K-12 students whose achievement test scores are interpreted by educators
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of student achievement from test scores
examples: The article recommends that measurement professionals identify invalid scores to individuals who make inferences about student achievement on the basis of those scores
key_sources: Steven Wise. (2015). Effort analysis: Individual score validation of achievement test data. Applied Measurement in Education, 28(3), 237–252. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/effort-analysis-individual-score-validation-of-achievement-test-data/

article_title: Continuing the educator micro-credential movement
citation: Center for Teaching Quality (CTQ) and Digital Promise. (2017). Continuing the educator micro-credential movement. https://digitalpromise.org/microcredentials
title: Make micro-credentials feasible by taking something off teachers' plates rather than adding them on top of existing professional development
description: The report argues micro-credentials "cannot just be dropped on top of the existing system of traditional, workshop-oriented professional development." Educators need dedicated time to develop and practice competencies and to collect and submit evidence, which has implications for district structures such as professional development and professional learning communities. A Charleston County teacher who completed a CTQ micro-credential on collective leadership is quoted: "It is very important for us to take something off teachers' plates. We cannot just add this without subtracting something else." The report adds that the new system must be reflected in formal policies such as teacher contracts and collective bargaining agreements.
requirements: District structures such as professional development time and professional learning communities must provide time for developing, practicing, and evidencing competencies
constraints: The report notes, citing National Board research, that teachers in high-need schools, because of lack of administrative support and adequate time, are less likely to participate in the National Board Certification process — so working conditions can make a significant difference in engagement
target_learners: K-12 classroom educators, especially those in high-need schools
target_learning_goals: Engaging in competency-based professional learning through micro-credentials
examples: Early adopters CTQ worked with in South Carolina and Tennessee were enthusiastic but wondered what would be taken off their plates so they could fully engage
key_sources: Center for Teaching Quality (CTQ) and Digital Promise. (2017). Continuing the educator micro-credential movement. https://digitalpromise.org/microcredentials

article_title: Designing for Technology Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory
citation: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory. (2016). https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Build regular reflection opportunities into adult learning experiences
description: Drawing on experiential learning theory, the report holds that "time and space for reflection helps learners absorb and make sense of the experience." It recommends quick discussions with peers or coaches, journaling, mind mapping, and discussion groups, tying reflection to learners' everyday lives so new information is processed in smaller chunks and sticks.
requirements: Provide time and space for reflection throughout the learning experience, "including self-reflection, group reflection, and peer reflection."
target_learners: adult ESL and basic education students
target_learning_goals: making sense of learning experiences
consolidating new information
examples: Instituto del Progreso Latino's Cyber ESL program blends in-class and online learning with "a one-on-one coaching session for students via Skype," which staff report makes a big difference in learner confidence.
key_sources: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory. (2016). https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/bb3f892f-a74d-4da1-8086-0334fd227316

article_title: Learning Analytics for Early Identification of At-Risk Students and Feedback Intervention
citation: Wei Dai, Jionghao Lin, Flora Ji-Yoon Jin, Yi-Shan Tsai, Namrata Srivastava, Pierre Le Bodic, Dragan Gašević, and Guanliang Chen. (2025). Learning Analytics for Early Identification of At-Risk Students and Feedback Intervention. Journal of Learning Analytics, 12(3), 102–125. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2025.8735
title: Regularly update at-risk prediction models with data from new cohorts to maintain reliable performance
description: Because predictive models for identifying at-risk students lose accuracy when transferred to new cohorts, this principle recommends periodic retraining. As the article's Notes for Practice state, "these models should be regularly updated using data from new cohorts" to maintain reliable performance across diverse student populations. The study's own post-hoc evaluation illustrates the risk it addresses: source-semester-trained models scored lower AUC on the target semester than models trained and tested within the target semester.
requirements: Availability of trace and academic data from each new cohort to refresh the training set.
A pipeline (Ed and Moodle data extraction, feature engineering, model evaluation) that can be rerun each semester.
constraints: Comprehensive historical data for model retraining are often limited in real-world educational contexts, which is why generalizable models matter.
target_learners: Undergraduate students in large higher-education courses
target_learning_goals: Early and accurate identification of students at risk of failing
examples: The study applied source-semester random-forest models to the target semester without retraining and observed lower cross-semester AUC (0.72 and 0.78) than for models trained and tested within the same semester (0.98 and 0.96).
key_sources: Wei Dai, Jionghao Lin, Flora Ji-Yoon Jin, Yi-Shan Tsai, Namrata Srivastava, Pierre Le Bodic, Dragan Gašević, and Guanliang Chen. (2025). Learning Analytics for Early Identification of At-Risk Students and Feedback Intervention. Journal of Learning Analytics, 12(3), 102–125. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2025.8735

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Reading Partners
citation: Reading Partners: Program Description and Evidence Rating. (2013). https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: Three-part consistent tutoring session structure: tutor read-aloud, targeted skill introduction, student read-aloud practice with feedback
description: Each tutoring session follows a consistent structure with three phases. First, "The tutor reads to the student, stopping to ask comprehension questions." Second, "The tutor then uses specific materials to introduce specific reading skills." Third, "the student reads aloud to the tutor and practices the new skill," with the tutor providing "feedback and coaching following prompts built into the curriculum." This gives volunteer tutors a scripted, repeatable lesson routine.
requirements: Curriculum with built-in prompts and specific materials for introducing specific reading skills
target_learners: Grade 2-4 students reading below grade level
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension and specific reading skills
examples: Tutor reads aloud with comprehension questions, introduces a skill with specific materials, then hears the student practice the new skill aloud with feedback
key_sources: Reading Partners: Program Description and Evidence Rating. (2013). https://www.evidenceforessa.org

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Reading Recovery
citation: Reading Recovery. (2020). Evidence for ESSA program review. https://www.evidenceforessa.org/programs/reading-recovery
title: Pair intervention teachers with a district-employed teacher leader providing initial training and ongoing professional development
description: Reading Recovery requires teachers to "affiliate with a Reading Recovery teacher leader who is employed by a school district and provides initial training and ongoing professional development to teachers." One teacher leader may work with about 42 teachers, from one or multiple districts. Teachers complete a yearlong graduate-level course for university credit; teacher leaders complete up to five graduate courses at a registered university training site.
requirements: Teachers must successfully complete a yearlong graduate level course taught by a teacher leader for which university credit is received
Teacher leaders must successfully complete up to five graduate level courses offered over two semesters at a registered university training site
constraints: Reading Recovery should not be a teacher's assignment for the entire school day
target_learners: kindergarten or primary-grade teachers, Title I teachers, intervention specialists, ELL or special education teachers, literacy coaches and administrators
target_learning_goals: delivery of one-to-one beginning reading intervention
examples: One teacher leader may work with about 42 teachers, who may all be from one school district or from multiple school districts.
key_sources: Reading Recovery. (2020). Evidence for ESSA program review. https://www.evidenceforessa.org/programs/reading-recovery

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Reading Recovery
citation: Reading Recovery. (2020). Evidence for ESSA program review. https://www.evidenceforessa.org/programs/reading-recovery
title: Plan intervention staffing around expected need of 20-30% of the first-grade population and part-day teacher assignments
description: The review advises that "a useful estimate to plan staffing is to expect between 20-30% of the first grade population to need Reading Recovery." Teachers deliver four individual 30-minute lessons daily in addition to other school roles, and "Reading Recovery should not be a teacher's assignment for the entire school day." Staffing depends on level of need and may change year to year and vary school to school.
requirements: Teachers able to teach four individual 30-minute lessons each day in addition to their other roles
constraints: Staffing depends on level of need in a school and may change slightly from year to year and vary from school to school
target_learning_goals: beginning reading
examples: Teachers work with four students individually for two and one half hours each school day, about 8-10 students over the school year, and in some other instructional role for the rest of the day.
key_sources: Reading Recovery. (2020). Evidence for ESSA program review. https://www.evidenceforessa.org/programs/reading-recovery

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Reading Corps
citation: Reading Corps program description and evaluation summary. (2024). https://www.readingcorps.org
title: Multi-level coaching model supporting tutor fidelity
description: Reading Corps tutors are supported by "a multi-level coaching model that includes site-based and external coaches". The school-appointed Internal Coach provides on-demand support and "monthly coaching and feedback that focuses on ensuring high fidelity to the program", while an assigned Coaching Specialist provides additional regular coaching to both tutor and school staff and "supports all data-driven decision-making practices".
requirements: An Internal Coach identified by the school partner, providing 6-9 hours per month per tutor.
A Coaching Specialist provided by Ampact in addition to headquarters staff.
target_learners: Kindergarten through grade 3 students served by tutors
target_learning_goals: Fidelity of implementation of evidence-based literacy instruction
examples: Coaching supports data-driven decisions such as eligibility, graph interpretation, and exit decisions.
key_sources: Reading Corps program description and evaluation summary. (2024). https://www.readingcorps.org

article_title: Teacher-Delivered Behavioral Interventions in Grades K-5
citation: Lane, K. L., Baldy, T., Becker, T., Bradshaw, C., Dolan, V., Dymnicki, A., Freeman, B., Holian, L., Lemire, S., McIntosh, K., Moulton, S., Nese, R., Payno-Simmons, R., Porowski, A., & Sutherland, K. (2024). Teacher-Delivered Behavioral Interventions in Grades K–5 (WWC 2025001). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance (NCEE), Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://whatworks.ed.gov/
title: Remind students to engage in expected behaviors (precorrections), rated moderate evidence
description: Recommendation 2 focuses on reminding students of expected behaviors before they have difficulty, using precorrections of varying intensity that fade over time. The guide's introduction states that "Recommendation 2 and Recommendation 3 focus on practices to remind students to engage in expected behaviors and to acknowledge students when they demonstrate those expected behaviors." Table I.1 assigns this recommendation a moderate level of evidence.
requirements: Reminders should be supportive and action-oriented, and faded as students succeed
constraints: Rated moderate evidence: there is some evidence meeting WWC standards, but there may be ambiguity about whether improvement is the direct result of the practices or replicable with a diverse population
target_learning_goals: Engaging in expected behaviors instead of challenging behavior
examples: The guide provides examples of precorrection types, a precorrection hierarchy, least-to-most precorrections for handwashing, and fading precorrections.

L., Baldy, T., Becker, T., Bradshaw, C., Dolan, V., Dymnicki, A., Freeman, B., Holian, L., Lemire, S., McIntosh, K., Moulton, S., Nese, R., Payno-Simmons, R., Porowski, A., & Sutherland, K. (2024). Teacher-Delivered Behavioral Interventions in Grades K–5 (WWC 2025001). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance (NCEE), Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/WWC/PracticeGuide/31

article_title: Using Research in Ed-Tech: What Does Research-based Product Development Mean?
citation: Digital Promise. (2015). Using Research in Ed Tech: The what, how, and why of research-based product development. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Review learning research broadly and critically before prototyping ed tech products
description: Before building a product, developers should ground design decisions in the learning sciences literature. The guide states: "Before prototyping products, ed tech companies should review research broadly and critically", pointing to tools such as Google Scholar, ERIC and its thesaurus, and Digital Promise's map of education research. It recommends considering research areas including pedagogy/instruction, curriculum studies, psychology, assessment, and cognitive science, and pairing each finding with an application example from companies such as GlassLab Games and BrainPOP.
requirements: Access to scholarly search tools (Google Scholar, ERIC) and to summaries such as review journals and distillation resources like Harvard's Usable Knowledge
constraints: Research findings may not transfer to the product's setting: the guide notes that if research "has only been done in large preschools with teachers, then the findings may not be applicable to your product"
target_learning_goals: designing products grounded in research on how people learn
examples: GlassLab Games designed Ratio Rancher around research on students' additive-strategy errors with proportions; BrainPOP's Make-a-Map was shaped by research on concept maps and knowledge retrieval
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2015). Using Research in Ed Tech: The what, how, and why of research-based product development. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/f25f7b43-06d9-4732-908b-7409f79b0a91

article_title: Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through 8
citation: Preparing Problems for Classroom Instruction. (2012). Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through Overview, U.S. Department of Education funded practice-guide presentation. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Review required mathematics concepts and explicitly teach specialized mathematics vocabulary (including multiple-meaning words) before problem solving
description: The guide advises teachers, when deciding whether to use a problem, to "review with the class the mathematics concepts required to solve it," noting the review is more beneficial the longer it has been since the concepts were addressed and especially for struggling students. It also says it is important "to explicitly teach academic language and review the meaning of specialized mathematics vocabulary, such as divisor or hypotenuse," and to distinguish multiple-meaning words like area, table, root, and volume in mathematical use, which is particularly essential for English language learners.
requirements: Advance problem preparation time to identify the required concepts and specialized vocabulary.
constraints: The benefit of concept review grows with the elapsed time since the underlying concepts were last addressed; explicit vocabulary teaching is described as particularly essential for English language learners.
target_learning_goals: Readiness to solve mathematical problems requiring known concepts and precise mathematical vocabulary
examples: Reviewing divisor or hypotenuse meanings, and distinguishing mathematical uses of multiple-meaning words such as area, table, root, and volume.
key_sources: Preparing Problems for Classroom Instruction. (2012). Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through Overview, U.S. Department of Education funded practice-guide presentation. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/16

article_title: Catching up or falling behind: Measuring middle school achievement trajectories for college readiness
citation: Angela Johnson, Megan Kuhfeld, and Greg King. (2020). Catching up or Falling Behind: Measuring Middle School Achievement Trajectories for College Readiness. EdWorkingPaper No. 20-233, Annenberg Institute at Brown University.
title: Monitor individual student performance regularly and consistently against college readiness benchmarks to enable timely intervention
description: The article recommends that schools continuously track students' on-track status relative to benchmarks throughout middle school rather than relying on annual state tests. As the authors argue, individual student performance should be measured regularly and consistently relative to a set of benchmarks to ensure timely provision of instructional intervention. Analyzing achievement relative to on-track benchmarks requires very little computation and the interpretation of results is straight-forward, making the approach easy for schools and districts to implement.
requirements: Regular, consistent measurement of individual student performance relative to a benchmark set (e.g., MAP Growth ACT benchmarks)
Benchmarks that link middle school scores to later college readiness criteria
constraints: The benchmarks capture one aspect of college readiness and are not deterministic of eventual college enrollment and success
The authors do not advocate using benchmarks to group and label students for academic tracking; multiple indicators such as course grades and attendance are recommended
target_learning_goals: Academic college readiness in math and reading
examples: Schools monitor as students move on-track, fall off track, or sustain their status, and respond by targeting programs and services accordingly; support services should be offered to boys and Black and Hispanic students on the margin of college readiness
key_sources: Angela Johnson, Megan Kuhfeld, and Greg King. (2020). Catching up or Falling Behind: Measuring Middle School Achievement Trajectories for College Readiness. EdWorkingPaper No. 20-233, Annenberg Institute at Brown University. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/catching-up-or-falling-behind-measuring-middle-school-achievement-trajectories-for-college-readiness/

article_title: The achievement gap or the engagement gap? Investigating the sensitivity of gaps estimates to test motivation
citation: James Soland. (2018). The achievement gap or the engagement gap? Investigating the sensitivity of gaps estimates to test motivation. Applied Measurement in Education 31(4), 312-323. https://www.nwea.org
title: Use achievement gap data only when estimates are accurate and unbiased, since gaps inform conclusions about education and societal issues
description: The article argues that because gap estimates are heavily relied upon in U.S. practice and policy, estimate quality is a precondition for valid inference. It states that "having estimates that are accurate and unbiased is necessary to making sure appropriate conclusions are being drawn about education and societal issues broadly." The principle directs users of gap data to attend to estimate accuracy and bias before drawing conclusions.
requirements: Gap estimates should be checked for accuracy and bias before being used to support conclusions about education or societal issues
target_learners: K-12 students whose subgroup achievement gaps are measured
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of achievement gaps for education policy and practice
examples: The article cites uses of gaps data such as research on why women participate less in quantitative college majors and Black-White gaps shedding light on societal progress in addressing inequities
key_sources: James Soland. (2018). The achievement gap or the engagement gap? Investigating the sensitivity of gaps estimates to test motivation. Applied Measurement in Education 31(4), 312-323. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/the-achievement-gap-or-the-engagement-gap-investigating-the-sensitivity-of-gaps-estimates-to-test-motivation/

article_title: Identifying Resource Inequities
citation: Taylor, T., & Bowman, A. (2024). Identifying Resource Inequities. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED593369.pdf
title: Six-category taxonomy of educational resources beyond funding
description: The document organizes educational resources into six categories for review: fiscal resources; human resources; time organization and structure; equipment, materials, and supplies; programs and services; and community collaboration and partnerships. For each category it provides resource examples, inequity examples, and review considerations. The document notes "This is not an exhaustive list, but it contains many resources that touch upon most normal operations in our educational institutions."
requirements: Decision-makers at LEA and school level to reflect on how their decisions might impact students
constraints: The list is explicitly not exhaustive
target_learners: All students affected by district and school resource decisions
target_learning_goals: Identifying and addressing resource inequities across all operational areas of educational institutions
examples: Table 1 lists inequity examples such as funding formulas accounting for average salaries rather than actual cost of highly qualified educators, and newest teachers having old, mismatched furniture
key_sources: Taylor, T., & Bowman, A. (2024). Identifying Resource Inequities. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED593369.pdf

article_title: Identifying Resource Inequities
citation: Taylor, T., & Bowman, A. (2024). Identifying Resource Inequities. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED593369.pdf
title: Review both fiscal and non-fiscal resources, drilling down by account codes to find spending gaps
description: The document recommends that determining the type of resources to include, "including fiscal and non-fiscal, is at the heart of the RAR." Fiscal review should examine expenditures via per-pupil expenditure reports and revenue allocations, with drill-down by program, object, and function account codes. Beyond funding, reviews should cover human resources, time, materials, programs, and partnerships.
requirements: Access to per-pupil expenditure reports required by ESSA and revenue allocation data including carryover amounts
constraints: The document states the resource list it provides is not exhaustive
target_learners: All students in LEAs and schools under review
target_learning_goals: Identifying funding sources with spending gaps and inequitable resource allocation patterns
examples: Drilling down by account codes enables leaders to determine what funding sources have spending gaps and identify trends in carryover
key_sources: Taylor, T., & Bowman, A. (2024). Identifying Resource Inequities. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED593369.pdf

article_title: The Essential Playbook for Family Engagement in Middle School
citation: Wallace, M., & Paredes, M. (2024). The essential playbook for family engagement in middle school. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Build relational trust as the foundation of school-family partnership, especially at transition points
description: The playbook holds that "Central to the school–family partnership is relational trust," defined as mutual respect, personal regard, competence, and integrity, involving open communication, reliability, and shared commitment to student well-being. Building relational trust is described as pivotal for keeping families connected during the elementary-to-middle and middle-to-high school transitions.
requirements: Open communication, reliability, and a shared commitment to student well-being among students, families, and educators
constraints: Described as especially crucial during early adolescence and school transitions
target_learners: middle school students and their families
target_learning_goals: maintaining family connection and investment in children's education across school transitions
examples: The playbook's real-world strategies, such as porch visits, explicitly aim to establish trust and ease transition anxieties
