article_title: Reframing Outcomes of Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education in Mathematics
citation: Rebecca Colina Neri, Jahneille Cunningham, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Reframing Outcomes of Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education in Mathematics. WestEd brief.
title: Reframe achievement gap data using six critical criteria rather than gap-gazing
description: The brief argues that gap-gazing — "the all-out focus on achievement disparities, primarily between White students, students of color, and other marginalized groups" — narrows conceptions of learning and equity to achievement and produces stereotypes of marginalized students. It recommends keeping achievement gap data but reframing it through six criteria, each with guiding questions in Figure 1, so gap data is contextualized, systemic, and paired with data on nondominant outcomes and spaces of excellence.
requirements: Achievement gap data should be situated in historical, sociopolitical, and longitudinal context and presented as a systems problem
constraints: The brief warns gaps are often misunderstood as purely technical problems solvable by fixing an instructional strategy, when they are rooted in histories of injustice and systemic racism
target_learners: marginalized students, students of color, and their families in mathematics education systems
target_learning_goals: educational equity in mathematics
mathematical identity development
critical examination of achievement disparities
examples: Figure 1 pairs each criterion with questions such as how the gap has manifested over time, how the system produces the problem, and what students and families say about how they experience it
key_sources: Rebecca Colina Neri, Jahneille Cunningham, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Reframing Outcomes of Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education in Mathematics. WestEd brief. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673572

article_title: Reimagining Excellence: A Blueprint for Integrating Social and Emotional Well-Being and Academic Excellence in Schools
citation: Reimagining Excellence: A blueprint for integrating social and emotional well-being and academic excellence in schools. (2021). https://selcenter.wested.org
title: Seven-dimension blueprint for integrating equity, well-being, and academics in learning programs
description: The blueprint organizes program quality into seven overarching dimensions — equity, responsive relationships, climate and culture, instruction, instructional materials, professional learning, and leadership — each with specific indicators of success. It states that "The blueprint has seven overarching dimensions of quality that apply to all programs, and each dimension has specific indicators of success." The dimensions build upon each other, beginning with equity, and are interconnected with common themes and practices throughout. It applies to the full range of program formats, using in-person, remote, and hybrid as its distinguishing terms.
requirements: A multidisciplinary leadership team embeds itself in the blueprint as a whole and forms committees to lead specific improvement efforts, collaborating often rather than taking a divide and conquer approach
constraints: The blueprint explicitly does not provide guidance for reopening approaches focused primarily on remediating learning gaps to boost academic performance
target_learners: All K-12 students in in-person, remote, or hybrid learning programs
target_learning_goals: Academic excellence integrated with social and emotional well-being and equity
examples: School leadership teams use the blueprint's dimension-by-dimension goals and indicators to plan reopening and continuous improvement efforts
key_sources: Reimagining Excellence: A blueprint for integrating social and emotional well-being and academic excellence in schools. (2021). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED613077

article_title: Reimagining Excellence: A Blueprint for Integrating Social and Emotional Well-Being and Academic Excellence in Schools
citation: Reimagining Excellence: A blueprint for integrating social and emotional well-being and academic excellence in schools. (2021). https://selcenter.wested.org
title: Prioritize responsive relationships as a prerequisite for learning, engagement, and well-being
description: The blueprint holds that "In order to effectively teach, learn, and thrive, humans must first feel physically and emotionally calm and settled and feel socially and emotionally connected through safe and responsive relationships." It therefore treats high-quality relationships as a prerequisite for student, teacher, leader, and family learning, engagement, and well-being, emphasizing interactions that are equitable, sensitive, and responsive to student and family identities. It notes these interactions are particularly critical in remote and hybrid environments where stakeholders are separated by distance and time.
requirements: Develop, implement, and monitor plans, policies, structures, and systems that support frequent, high-quality relational interactions among staff, between staff and students and families, and among students
A committee of diverse stakeholders that meets quarterly to establish a vision for prioritizing responsive relationships
target_learners: Students, teachers, leaders, and families in in-person, remote, and hybrid programs
target_learning_goals: Learning, engagement, and well-being supported by safe and responsive relationships
examples: Recommended structures include involving families in determining the timing, tone, and type of family-teacher connection, restorative practices and peer mediation, and protected time for professional learning communities
key_sources: Reimagining Excellence: A blueprint for integrating social and emotional well-being and academic excellence in schools. (2021). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED613077

article_title: The Toolkit before the Toolkit: Centering Adaptive and Relational Elements of Restorative Practices for Implementation Success
citation: Trout, L. (2021). The toolkit before the toolkit: Centering adaptive and relational elements of restorative practices for implementation success. [Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd]. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Four-element framework for restorative practices implementation: adaptive, relational, structural, and technical
description: The brief organizes restorative practices implementation around four interacting element sets. Adaptive elements are 'mindsets, paradigms, values, and belief systems, which lay the groundwork for any technical elements'; relational elements are intentional actions that build relationships and social capital; structural supports are infrastructure such as 'funding, people, time, discipline and other policies, and equity'; and technical elements are the concrete practices and toolkits. The guide treats the first three as precursors that make technical toolkits succeed.
requirements: Leaders and educators must attend to adaptive, relational, and structural elements alongside the technical elements for authentic, sustainable implementation
constraints: The brief states that aligning the elements is 'a journey, not a destination' and that results take years
target_learning_goals: School climate and community transformation
equitable whole-person outcomes
examples: Part 1 covers adaptive elements, Part 2 relational elements, Part 3 structural supports, and Part 4 lists technical guides and toolkits
key_sources: Trout, L. (2021). The toolkit before the toolkit: Centering adaptive and relational elements of restorative practices for implementation success. [Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd]. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED615970

article_title: The Toolkit before the Toolkit: Centering Adaptive and Relational Elements of Restorative Practices for Implementation Success
citation: Trout, L. (2021). The toolkit before the toolkit: Centering adaptive and relational elements of restorative practices for implementation success. [Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd]. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Restorative practices as an adaptive paradigm rather than a program placed within existing school structures
description: The brief argues restorative practices should be understood not as a packaged program but as a paradigm — a worldview in which 'strong relationships are the conditions for learning and academic success' — within which educators shift the structures of schooling themselves. It contrasts this with the traditional paradigm in which academic learning is the priority and relationship-building detracts from it. The guide's oil-versus-food-coloring metaphor illustrates that a paradigm diffuses through and changes the system, while a program added to an opposing system is never fully absorbed.
requirements: Individuals must internalize restorative principles and shift their own mindsets and values for the paradigm to take hold
constraints: The brief notes restorative practices operate 'often antithetically with the traditional paradigm of our education system,' creating implementation tension
target_learning_goals: Relationships and community as conditions for learning
equitable discipline and whole-person outcomes
examples: A comparison table contrasts traditional and restorative mindsets across paradigm, safety, time, power, teaching, discipline, and misbehavior
key_sources: Trout, L. (2021). The toolkit before the toolkit: Centering adaptive and relational elements of restorative practices for implementation success. [Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd]. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED615970

article_title: The Toolkit before the Toolkit: Centering Adaptive and Relational Elements of Restorative Practices for Implementation Success
citation: Trout, L. (2021). The toolkit before the toolkit: Centering adaptive and relational elements of restorative practices for implementation success. [Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd]. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Restorative justice tenets: harm to relationships rather than rule infractions, centered on people, trust, voice and agency, and equity
description: The brief defines restorative justice as 'a theory of justice [that] views crime, conflict, misbehavior, broken rules, and the like as harm to relationships, as opposed to infractions of societal laws,' aiming to center those harmed and create accountability that heals and prevents future harm. It traces the philosophy's origins to indigenous communities worldwide rather than its late-1970s Western criminal-justice emergence. Four guiding tenets are enumerated: centering people and relationships, trust, voice and agency, and equity.
requirements: Restorative justice is anchored by an inherent trust in people, communities, and their capacity to resolve their own conflicts
constraints: Within the restorative paradigm these relational elements are 'essential conditions for learning,' not add-ons
target_learners: Whole school communities including students, families, and staff
target_learning_goals: Accountability, healing, and prevention of future harm
voice, agency, and equity in school communities
examples: The brief lists tenets with named elements: Centering People and Relationships, Trust, Voice and Agency, and Equity
key_sources: Trout, L. (2021). The toolkit before the toolkit: Centering adaptive and relational elements of restorative practices for implementation success. [Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd]. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED615970

article_title: Reimagining School Safety: A Guide for Schools and Communities
citation: Trout, L., Pate, C., Wu, K., & McKenna, J. (2022). Reimagining school safety: A guide for schools and communities. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Reimagined paradigm of safety: safety as the presence of connection and systems of mutuality and care
description: The guide proposes shifting from a deficit-based paradigm in which safety is the absence of harm and violence to one in which "Safety, therefore, is not just the absence of harm and violence, but the creation of systems that acknowledge humans’ inherent indispensability, connectedness, and dignity." In this paradigm, an individual's safety is rooted in others' safety and needs being met, and safety is grounded in self-care, collective care, and mutuality. Table 1 contrasts traditional safety (exclusionary, punitive, technical, top-down) with reimagined safety (inclusive, restorative, adaptive, codesigned at the margins).
requirements: Reimagining requires new ways of doing and also new ways of thinking and being, achieved through unlearning and relearning via small, daily choices.
constraints: The guide states this definition comes from activists and movement makers, particularly those most harmed by systemic oppression, and is not new.
target_learning_goals: social-emotional learning
belonging and school safety
equity in school climate
examples: The guide profiles Curie High School in Chicago, whose students and staff share in a video the shifts they made to transform their understanding of school safety.
key_sources: Trout, L., Pate, C., Wu, K., & McKenna, J. (2022). Reimagining school safety: A guide for schools and communities. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628885

article_title: Reimagining School Safety: A Guide for Schools and Communities
citation: Trout, L., Pate, C., Wu, K., & McKenna, J. (2022). Reimagining school safety: A guide for schools and communities. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Restorative justice as a framework for community-centered harm prevention and a new paradigm of safety
description: The guide describes restorative justice, a framework originating from Indigenous communities, as redefining harm, conflict, and broken rules as harm to relationships: "By redefining harm, conflict, violence, and broken rules or laws as harm to relationships and reimagining justice as addressing the root issues of harm, restorative justice offers a framework for community-centered harm prevention and a new paradigm of what safety means." In this model, healing-centered accountability is achieved for all involved, relationships are restored, reintegration occurs, and communities remain intact. The guide illustrates the contrast with a four-school scenario in which School D addresses unmet needs at personal, collective, and systemic levels.
requirements: Safety is achieved when those who cause harm have the community support to engage in accountability practices that meet the needs of those impacted by the harm.
constraints: The guide notes that responses addressing harm only at personal and interpersonal levels, like School C's quick fixes, lack a systemic lens and do not fully transform the harm.
target_learning_goals: restorative accountability
harm prevention and healing
community building
examples: The guide points to a reintegration circle from Oakland Unified School District supporting a student's return to their community after causing harm.
key_sources: Trout, L., Pate, C., Wu, K., & McKenna, J. (2022). Reimagining school safety: A guide for schools and communities. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628885

article_title: Fostering Belonging, Transforming Schools: The Impact of Restorative Practices
citation: Darling-Hammond, S. (2023). Fostering belonging, transforming schools: The impact of restorative practices. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/169.703
title: Typology of restorative practices: repair practices and community-building practices
description: The report subdivides restorative practices into two types, stating "Restorative practices can be roughly subdivided into two types: repair practices and community-building practices." Repair practices (associated with restorative justice) bring together stakeholders—victims, respondents, and facilitators, sometimes including community members—to resolve issues and determine restorative responses such as community service, restitution, apologies, or behavior-change agreements. Community-building practices foster an interconnected school community in which transgressions are less common, and include community-building circles, reentry circles for returning students, and capacity-development activities such as role-playing conflict situations. Restorative programs themselves fall into add-on and whole-school models.
requirements: Whole-school implementation involves providing instruction in restorative concepts and skills to all school personnel and students
constraints: The report calls this a rough subdivision and notes formal conferences may also include community members such as witnesses, friends, and family
target_learning_goals: conflict repair
relationship building
social and emotional capacity to manage conflict
examples: Community-building circles held regularly (e.g., every Monday morning in homeroom) help students and staff deepen relationships and trust
key_sources: Darling-Hammond, S. (2023). Fostering belonging, transforming schools: The impact of restorative practices. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/169.703

article_title: Oakland International High School: A Thriving Community School for Oakland's Newcomer Students
citation: Charlie Thompson. (2023). Oakland International High School: A Thriving Community School for Oakland's Newcomer Students. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org
title: Build trusting relationships through stable cohorts, advisories, restorative circles, and peer buddy structures
description: The report identifies relationships as the foundation of the school's learning culture, supported by concrete structures: each new student is paired with a buddy from a similar linguistic and cultural background, students move through classes in heterogeneously selected cohorts of about 25, daily advisory periods build social-emotional learning, and restorative justice circles run on a consistent schedule. The report states that "key structures and practices such as peer partnerships and cohorts, student advisories, restorative justice circles, and community walks have earned the school a reputation as 'a safe and caring place.'"
requirements: Small school size (roughly 310 students) and teaching teams working with stable cohorts
Daily advisory period with teachers looping with their advisories across grade spans
target_learners: Newcomer high school students who are recent immigrants and English learners
target_learning_goals: Sense of belonging and agency over learning
Social and emotional learning
Meta-awareness of their learning
examples: Each new student is paired with a buddy who is well-versed in school norms and has been in the United States for several months or longer
Students participate in restorative justice circles on a consistent schedule, including issue-specific circles on topics like making new friends

article_title: California's Universal Prekindergarten Implementation Progress, 2023-24
citation: Wang, V., Melnick, H., Leung-Gagné, M., Parker, S., & Wechsler, M. (2025). California's universal prekindergarten implementation progress, 2023–24. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/600.551
title: Research-based elements of high-quality preschool as a framework for UPK implementation
description: The report frames UPK implementation quality around a set of research-based elements of high-quality preschool drawn from early childhood research. As the report states, "These elements include sufficient learning time; low adult-to-student ratios; well-prepared and well-supported teachers; research-based and developmentally appropriate early learning standards, curricula, and assessments; and meaningful family engagement." The report uses this framework to organize its survey findings on TK service delivery, facilities, instruction and assessment, staffing, and professional development, and to judge whether California's UPK investments can deliver quality at scale.
requirements: Implementation aligned with the elements, including the state's new adult-to-student ratio of no more than 10 children per adult by full rollout in 2025–26 and lead-teacher credential requirements taking effect in 2025–26.
constraints: The report notes these benefits hold only if implemented with quality: "if implemented with quality, universal prekindergarten holds potentially significant benefits for California's young learners."
target_learners: children ages 2 to 5 in the California State Preschool Program
target_learning_goals: school readiness
social-emotional and academic development in early learning settings
examples: The report evaluates LEA survey responses against these elements, such as full-day TK offering (sufficient learning time), staffing ratios, and use of developmentally appropriate curricula and assessments.
key_sources: Wang, V., Melnick, H., Leung-Gagné, M., Parker, S., & Wechsler, M. (2025). California's universal prekindergarten implementation progress, 2023–24. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/600.551

article_title: Opportunity Adrift: Our Flagship Universities Are Straying from Their Public Mission
citation: Haycock, K., Lynch, M., & Engle, J. (2010). Opportunity Adrift: Our Flagship Universities Are Straying From Their Public Mission. The Education Trust. https://www.edtrust.org
title: Redirect institutional grant aid from high-income students who do not need it to low-income students whose enrollment and graduation depend on it
description: The report argues that public research universities, as the wealthiest public institutions and the largest source of undergraduate grant aid, should shift their own aid dollars toward low-income students. It notes Pell Grants "only cover about 36 percent of the cost of attending a four-year public college" and that increased aid improves low-income students' graduation chances while having little or no effect on high-income students. Redirecting aid is presented as a direct lever on both access and success.
requirements: Institutions must have discretionary institutional grant aid resources and data on recipient family income to retarget awards.
constraints: The report notes institution-specific data on reordered aid priorities are unavailable, so it cannot confirm how many institutions have actually changed.
target_learners: Low-income and moderate-income undergraduates at public flagship and research-extensive universities
target_learning_goals: Access to and completion of bachelor's degrees at public research universities
examples: The report highlights financial aid pledges at at least nine flagships, including no-loan guarantees at Indiana University, the University of Virginia, and the University of Florida that ensure the lowest-income students pay nothing beyond their EFC.
key_sources: Haycock, K., Lynch, M., & Engle, J. (2010). Opportunity Adrift: Our Flagship Universities Are Straying From Their Public Mission. The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED507851

article_title: "...And They Cared": How to Create Better, Safer Learning Environments for Girls of Color
citation: “...and they cared”: How to create better, safer learning environments for girls of color. (2020). National Women’s Law Center & The Education Trust. https://nwlc.org
title: Restorative justice as a less punitive alternative to zero-tolerance school discipline
description: Restorative justice is described as "a less punitive, more positive alternative to addressing school-based conflicts and violence than the more traditionally used punitive method or zero-tolerance policies." At its core it is about building community, giving space to learn from and correct mistakes, and addressing root causes of behavior through listening, accountability, and healing, using evidence-based practices such as talking circles where all parties discuss what happened, its impact, and how to correct the harm. The guide reports students respond well and that it helps students build trust, respect, and social emotional skills.
requirements: Each school should have a trained restorative justice coordinator on site to support positive discipline practices
It requires follow-up rather than being a quick-fix, one-step process, per students interviewed
Doing so requires financial resources
constraints: Implementation inconsistencies at the school level were reported in Oakland
Students noted that if a conflict is not improved after restorative justice, more steps should be taken
target_learners: K–12 students, especially Black, Latina, and Native girls
target_learning_goals: Social emotional learning
Positive school climate and belonging
examples: Oakland maintains a restorative justice program supported by central office staff, school counselors, and restorative justice facilitators
Chicago’s Culture of Calm program trained schools on peer juries, restorative justice, and counseling

article_title: Special Issues Brief: How Region 2 States Are Leveraging Innovative Strategies to Address Critical Shortages of Education Personnel
citation: Dana Chambers and Trang Hoang. (2022). How Region 2 States Are Leveraging Innovative Strategies to Address Critical Shortages of Education Personnel. Special Issues Brief.
title: Region 2 educator pipeline and substitute-training programs (NextGen Educators, Educators Rising, Highlander fast-track substitute training, Warrior Teaching Fellows)
description: The brief profiles state and district programs expanding the educator workforce in Connecticut, New York, and Rhode Island. Connecticut's NextGen Educators Program partners the state education department with Central Connecticut State University to bring cohorts of teacher candidates into K–12 classrooms with professional mentors; in 2020–21 there were 18 CCSU students in the program. Rhode Island's Highlander Institute runs a 10-hour asynchronous training covering online classroom management, lesson planning, and teaching practices for racially and culturally diverse classrooms, plus a help desk for new substitutes.
requirements: Partnerships between state agencies, universities, and community organizations; mentor connections for candidates
constraints: The brief describes these programs descriptively; it reports no outcome evaluations of them
target_learners: K-12 students in Connecticut, New York, and Rhode Island; prospective and substitute teachers
target_learning_goals: Expanding and diversifying the educator workforce in shortage areas
examples: Educators Rising offers curriculum and micro-credentials for high school students; NYC Men Teach began in 2015 with a $16 million budget to recruit 1,000 men of color into teaching; the TA to BA Fellowship covers tuition up to $1,000 for teaching assistants pursuing bachelor's degrees

article_title: Promising Practices: Smart State Strategies for Building Intensive Tutoring Systems
citation: Promising Practices: Smart State Strategies for Building Intensive Tutoring Systems. (2022). Education Trust, Education Reform Now, and FutureEd. https://www.edtrust.org/
title: Research-based tutoring program design features: small groups, in-school-day sessions, high frequency, consistent tutor, trained tutors
description: The brief distills recurring research-based features that state tutoring laws and guidance require: small tutoring groups (four or fewer students in Colorado; maximum three in elementary and four in middle schools in Tennessee), sessions during the school day, high frequency sustained across the year ("at least 30 minutes of tutoring at least three times per week" in Louisiana), students working "with the same tutor throughout the year," and tutors who "receive training." These features appear as legislative requirements in Colorado and Tennessee and as core-pillar guidelines in Louisiana.
requirements: Tutors receive training
Sessions occur at least two to three times per week for a semester or full year
Group sizes stay at or below three to four students
constraints: Louisiana's core pillars are guidelines rather than requirements, though LDOE works with districts to ensure fidelity
Tennessee does not require tutoring during the school day, only noting it is more effective
target_learning_goals: Accelerating mastery of grade-level academic content in math and ELA
examples: Colorado's House Bill 21-1234 requires up to $2,200 per participating student for programs meeting the research-based features
Tennessee's TN ALL Corps requires groups of at most three students in elementary schools and four in middle schools, 30-45 minute sessions at least twice per week for at least a full semester

article_title: How School Discipline Impacts Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)
citation: Blair Wriston, Nancy Duchesneau. (2023). How School Discipline Impacts Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD). The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org
title: Adopt evidence-based, restorative, relationship-focused discipline instead of punitive and exclusionary measures
description: The brief argues schools should replace harmful exclusionary and punitive practices (suspensions, expulsions, corporal punishment, seclusion, restraint, hardening measures) with evidence-based approaches such as restorative justice and PBIS. Restorative approaches "can be used to build and repair relationships while also holding students accountable for their actions," keeping students in the classroom where they can learn from conflict and supporting holistic development.
requirements: Implementation with a race-equity lens so practices are fairly applied and do not reproduce disparities
constraints: The brief warns hardening practices such as school police and metal detectors have not been shown to increase school safety and disproportionately harm underserved students
target_learners: P-12 students, particularly students of color and students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Social, emotional, and academic development; safe and inclusive school climates
examples: The brief points to restorative justice and Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports (PBIS) as positive, evidence-based discipline approaches, and to DC's guidance and funding for restorative implementation.

article_title: The Search for More Complex Racial and Ethnic Representation in Grade School Books
citation: Tanji Reed Marshall, Ph.D., and William H. Rodick, Ph.D. (2023). The Search for More: Complex Racial and Ethnic Representation in Grade School Books. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/booktool
title: Representational balance framework (complex, partial, limited representation)
description: The report's conceptual framework holds that curricula quality includes how people, cultures, and topics are represented, not only standards alignment, knowledge building, and usability. It defines "representational balance" as representation "that allows all students to see themselves and others in rich and varied ways that more accurately reflect the realities of people's lives," countering what Adichie calls "a single story." Representation is coded on three levels — complex ("mirrors the complexity of people, cultures, and topics"), partial ("not quite complex"), and limited ("perpetuates the marginalization of people, cultures, and topics") — using criteria of multidimensionality, agency, positive influence, stereotype avoidance, cultural immersion, equal value, and non-sanitized, multi-perspective, student-connected topics.
requirements: Assessing authorship alongside portrayal, since the framework treats who writes the stories as integral to how people, cultures, and topics are represented
constraints: The framework's initial analysis found so little diversity in sexual orientation, disability status, justice-system status, and other identity aspects that the report's analysis focuses on people of color
target_learners: K-8 students in English language arts classrooms
target_learning_goals: Seeing self and others represented complexly; developing critical thinking about texts
examples: The framework's people criteria (multidimensional, agency, positively influential) echo media tests like the Bechdel, DuVernay, and Vito Russo tests and align with ELA standards on character development analysis
key_sources: Tanji Reed Marshall, Ph.D., and William H. Rodick, Ph.D. (2023). The Search for More: Complex Racial and Ethnic Representation in Grade School Books. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/booktool

article_title: Cultivating Relationships in Secondary Schools: Structures That Matter
citation: Hernández, L., & Darling-Hammond, L. (with Nielsen, N.). (2024). Cultivating relationships in secondary schools: Structures that matter. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/cultivating-relationships-secondary-schools-brief
title: Relationship-centered schooling framework from the science of learning and development
description: This brief organizes school redesign around relationship-centered schooling, drawing on 'Design Principles for Schools: Putting the Science of Learning and Development Into Action.' It holds that 'Connections between students and school adults are at the core of relationship-centered schooling' and that positive relationships should be consistent and individualized, trustful, respectful, and reciprocal, and focused on all aspects of young people's development. The framework names four student-facing structure domains—small learning communities, safety and belonging, culturally sustaining and relevant education, and student voice and agency—plus staff collaboration and family engagement structures.
requirements: Structures are most powerful when used in combination to realize a school's unique vision for personalized and inclusive learning environments
Student–practitioner interactions must be trustful, empowering, reciprocal, and culturally responsive for every student
constraints: The existence of relationship-centered structures alone does not guarantee their success
Implementation has implications across the educational ecosystem, from school to district and macrosystems, requiring concerted systemwide effort
target_learning_goals: healthy attachments, motivation, engagement, and academic success
social and emotional development and school connectedness
examples: The brief illustrates each domain with California schools, including Vista High School, Oakland International High School, Ralph Bunche High School, Hillsdale High School, Oakland High School, McLane High School, Social Justice Humanitas Academy, and Long Beach Unified School District

article_title: Access is Not Enough: Human Support Improves Engagement with AI Tutoring

title: Spectrum of relational intensity for models of personalized instruction
description: The article proposes a framework placing models of personalized instruction on a spectrum of relational intensity, from tech-led (low relational intensity), where humans oversee AI-student interactions from the backend, to human-led (high relational intensity), where a dedicated tutor uses AI as a supplement to direct instruction. The studied model sits near the midpoint: an in-person tutor supporting engagement, not delivering instruction. title: Reflection systems rest on three mechanisms: interactive feedback, verbal reinforcement, and external verification with self-correction
description: The review describes reflection systems as underpinned by three complementary mechanisms that let AI agents evaluate performance and iteratively refine outputs: "These mechanisms include interactive feedback loops, verbal reinforcement, and external verification and self-correction." CRITIC operationalizes interactive feedback through a verify-then-correct cycle with external tools such as search engines and code interpreters; Reflexion converts feedback into episodic memory for iterative self-improvement; SELF-REFINE iterates generate-critique-refine within a single model using few-shot prompts. The review presents these as a hybrid structure combining internal evaluation with external tools.

constraints: Self-generated assessments can be limited by the model's inherent knowledge gaps or biases, which external verification addresses

citation: Aponte ML, Vargas Sánchez AD, Chiappe A and Martínez-Pérez S. (2026). Artificial and emotional intelligence: two key forces for teachers' professional development in an era of uncertainty. Front. Psychol. 17:1935683. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1935683
title: Relational densification as an evaluative criterion for AI-supported teacher socio-emotional development
description: The article distinguishes relational density, the structural and experiential quality of teachers' professional relationships, from relational densification, "the process through which those relational qualities are intentionally expanded, stabilized, and made more accessible within a professional community." Density is characterized by "trust, emotional reciprocity, co-regulation, continuity of support, shared reflection, and collective responsibility for professional care," and explicitly not by interaction frequency alone. Densification serves as a conceptual criterion for judging whether AI-supported initiatives strengthen mentoring, peer support, and psychological safety.
requirements: Evaluation must move beyond platform-centered metrics and examine whether initiatives increase relational conditions through which teacher wellbeing can be sustained
constraints: The article presents this as a conceptual criterion and evaluative hypothesis, stating it does not claim relational densification has been empirically demonstrated as a causal outcome of AI-supported teacher training
target_learning_goals: teacher wellbeing
socio-emotional competence
professional trust and collaboration
examples: The article operationalises the criterion across individual, dyadic/small-group, and organizational levels, with matched assessment methods including validated scales, mentoring logs, social-network analysis, and policy analysis

title: Reinvest AI-freed time relationally through explicit institutional policy, because efficiency gains do not automatically become care
description: The principle holds that automation opens a possibility but does not determine outcomes: "the time recovered through AI must be converted into protected spaces for mentoring, shared pedagogical reflection, peer accompaniment, and the strengthening of communities of practice." Without an explicit institutional rule of relational reinvestment, efficiency is reabsorbed as demand. The article cites intervention evidence that wellbeing efforts yield better results when linked to conditions sustainable over time rather than episodic actions.
requirements: A formal institutional rule or policy that converts time saved through AI-supported processes into protected mentoring, peer dialogue, collaborative planning, or communities of practice
constraints: AI gains count as fundamental only when translated into relational practices previously unfeasible for lack of time, not when producing short-term operational relief

protected time for professional care
sustained mentoring and peer support
examples: Table 1 pairs this condition with indicators including protected collaboration time, frequency of mentoring sessions, perceived time for professional care, and teacher-reported recovery time

article_title: Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance
citation: Khosravi, H., Gašević, D., Sadiq, S., Yan, L., Lodge, J. M., Tangen, J. M., Denny, P., DiCerbo, K., Buckingham Shum, S., & Baker, R. S. (2026). Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04816
title: Responsible design foundation: four commitments of security, transparency, accountability, and inclusion
description: The paper organises responsible practice for AI learning companions around four interwoven commitments unified by trustworthiness. "Security" protects learner privacy, data, and digital wellbeing through lawful data practices, including separating personally identifiable information from interaction data. "Transparency" makes AI processes, reasoning, and data flows visible and explainable, building on Open Learner Models and the XAI-ED framework. "Accountability" retains meaningful human oversight with human-in-the-loop checkpoints for high-stakes inferences such as mastery promotion and at-risk flags. "Inclusion" ensures companions are fair, accessible, and responsive to diverse learners, abilities, languages, and contexts.
requirements: Human oversight and dispute channels for contesting model states; evaluation of companions on retention, transfer, and metacognition, not only output accuracy
constraints: The paper states these commitments apply to any AI application but clarifies how they play out distinctively with learning companions
target_learners: diverse learners across abilities, languages, and contexts
target_learning_goals: trustworthy and equitable AI-supported learning
learner agency
digital wellbeing
examples: The paper recommends modular architectures isolating sensitive processes, privacy-preserving aggregated features, and audit logs linking inputs, model states, actions, and outcomes

article_title: The impact of artificial intelligence literacy on learning engagement among university students: the mediating role of psychological capital and the moderating role of professional identity
citation: Wang, N. (2026). The impact of artificial intelligence literacy on learning engagement among university students: the mediating role of psychological capital and the moderating role of professional identity. Frontiers in Psychology, 17:1892204. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1892204
title: Resource-gain spiral moderated mediation model linking AI literacy, psychological capital, and learning engagement
description: The article's core framework, anchored in Conservation of Resources Theory with complementary perspectives (Social Cognitive, Broaden-and-Build, Self-Determination, Social Identity, and Self-Verification theories), is a moderated mediation model in which AI literacy acts as a technological cognitive resource that builds psychological capital, which drives learning engagement. The authors posit "a 'resource gain spiral' pathway wherein AI literacy, as a technological cognitive resource, accumulates into psychological capital and subsequently enhances learning engagement", with professional commitment as a contextual amplifier.

constraints: Tested in a cross-sectional survey of Chinese undergraduates; the article notes the AI literacy–engagement relationship "may not simply be linear and positive" across cultural and educational contexts.

AI literacy
psychological capital
examples: The model was tested on 1,198 undergraduates using the College Students' AI Literacy Scale (22 items), the Positive Psychological Capital Questionnaire (27 items), the Professional Commitment Scale (27 items), and the UWES-S (17 items).

article_title: PromptDecipher: Supporting AI Tutor Authoring Through Editable Simulated Interactions
citation: Miina Koyama, Ruiwei Xiao, and John Stamper. (2026). PromptDecipher: Supporting AI Tutor Authoring Through Editable Simulated Interactions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16605
title: Reverse Prompting Pipeline: diff analysis, prompt rewrite, and regression verification triggered by teacher corrections
description: The Reverse Prompting Pipeline is the automated mechanism at the core of PromptDecipher, triggered when a teacher submits an edit to a bot response. It runs three steps: "Diff analysis. An LLM compares the original and corrected responses to infer the teacher's pedagogical intent"; a targeted prompt rewrite proposed for teacher review; and "Regression verification. The revised prompt is automatically evaluated across all previously passed test cases." The test-correct-verify cycle continues until the teacher is satisfied.
requirements: A teacher-submitted correction of a bot response in the test case chat, and previously passed test cases against which regression can be checked
constraints: The pipeline is the primary contribution of the demonstration; its effects on testing rates and prompt quality are not yet empirically established
target_learning_goals: translating corrective feedback on bot behavior into system prompt requirements
examples: A teacher edits an unsatisfactory bot response; the system surfaces a prompt update button, the AI revises the system prompt as a tracked diff, and the test case response is updated.

article_title: Design Principles and Observable Indicators for AI-Enabled Pedagogical Accompaniment: Evidence from the Amico Dual-Mode Prototype in Italy and China
citation: Pier Paolo Benedetti. (2026). Design Principles and Observable Indicators for AI-Enabled Pedagogical Accompaniment: Evidence from the Amico Dual-Mode Prototype in Italy and China. Accepted at the 2026 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Education (ICAIE 2026), IEEE.
title: Relational bridge: AI-enabled pedagogical accompaniment as temporary, directional, bounded micro-mediation toward human engagement
description: The framework defines AI-enabled pedagogical accompaniment as "a structured process that supports learners in clarifying goals, articulating questions, and identifying next steps, while consistently orienting interaction toward teachers, peers, and communities of practice." Its core, the relational bridge, is a sequence of micro-mediations with three properties: temporality (interaction limited in scope and duration), directionality (oriented toward concrete next steps involving human actors), and boundedness (constrained by pedagogical purposes and ethical safeguards). Effectiveness is assessed by observable transitions toward participation, agency, and responsibility, not by engagement with the AI itself. The bridge is explicitly designed to be temporary and to avoid open-ended conversational loops.
requirements: Human-in-command governance: adults retain responsibility for educational decisions, relational boundaries, and ethical oversight, with explicit thresholds for escalation or hand-off to human actors.
constraints: The framework explicitly rejects technocentric and substitutionist models; the system is not conceived as an autonomous empathic subject or surrogate for human care, and does not provide curricular instruction, psychological counseling, or affective companionship.
target_learners: Learners in technical and vocational education facing challenges of self-efficacy, orientation, and continuity of engagement
target_learning_goals: Orientation, reflection, and decision-making; articulation of goals and questions; transition toward human educational relationships
examples: A learner reporting post-lesson confusion is asked for a concrete goal, offered 1–3 micro-actions, prompted to select a human target, and given a closure prompt with a next-step plan; a transition attempt is logged when a human target is selected.

citation: Jiawen Tao, Miao Peng, Yaoming Li, Xiaokun Yuan, Mengzhou Wu, Wenhan Yu, Guoan Wang, Nuo Chen, Tong Yang, Maxm Pan. (2026). Beyond Rephrasing: Book-Level Organization Improves Synthetic Textbook Data for Mid-Training. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28109
title: Five-stage retrieval-grounded textbook synthesis pipeline producing 686K source-grounded books (32B tokens)
description: A pipeline that transforms a pre-training corpus into textbook-form training data in two phases: knowledge extraction (query generation, retrieval, chunking, KMeans clustering with relevance filtering) and structured generation (hierarchical TOC planning with a quality gate, then source-grounded section generation and assembly). The article states it "retrieves and clusters source documents, plans hierarchical tables of contents (TOCs) with quality filtering, and assembles source-grounded sections into complete books." It produced 249K TOCs (91.8% passing the gate) and 686K books totaling 32B tokens across 15,387 disciplines, with up to 48 variants per discipline.

examples: For the running example discipline (Feedforward Neural Networks), 1,346 unique documents were retrieved into 40 clusters; 15 of 16 TOC variants passed the gate, yielding 45 books of 630 sections and 10.5M characters

article_title: Epistemic Dependence in AI-Mediated Learning
citation: Du Y, Yuan Y (2026) Epistemic dependence in AI-mediated learning. AI & SOCIETY. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00146-026-03294-1
title: Relational epistemic agency as the normative aim of AI-mediated learning
description: The review proposes relational epistemic agency as the normative orientation of AI-mediated learning: "the capacity to question, verify, compare, justify and know responsibly within relations of interdependence." The norm is compatible with substantial AI use and rejects both technological solutionism and simple anti-dependence positions; the practical objective is to configure dependence rather than eliminate it. It retains an explicit asymmetry: AI may shape reasoning without possessing reciprocal responsibility or legitimate authority.
requirements: Learners retain meaningful capacities to participate in how claims are formed, assessed and accepted, even while exercising agency through social, material and institutional supports
constraints: The review states this aim requires a substantive defence and is not an automatic consequence of using AI or of a discrete design intervention
target_learners: Learners at all levels using AI-mediated tools in education
target_learning_goals: Forming people who can ask questions, assess evidence, revise beliefs, give reasons and respond to challenge
examples: The review's test is functional and developmental: does the relation enlarge the learner's capacity to participate in epistemic practice, or merely deliver a product?
key_sources: Du Y, Yuan Y (2026) Epistemic dependence in AI-mediated learning. AI & SOCIETY. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00146-026-03294-1

article_title: Generative AI Feedback, English Writing and Teacher Rubrics: A Multiple-Case Study of CyberScholar
citation: Raigul Zheldibayeva, Ana Karina de Oliveira Nascimento, Vania Castro, Bill Cope and Mary Kalantzis. (2025). Generative AI Feedback, English Writing and Teacher Rubrics: A Multiple-Case Study of CyberScholar.
title: Implement GenAI feedback with human oversight, teacher co-implementation, and privacy-first design choices rather than maximal automation
description: The study's implementation model positions teachers as co-implementers within a human-in-the-loop, cyber-social pedagogy: onboarding covered rubric agent construction, interpreting AI feedback, calibrating ratings, and preventing overreliance. Design decisions restricted data retention, disabled persistent model training on student submissions, and embedded bias and hallucination filters; the authors state these "reflect a deliberate prioritization of privacy and equity over maximal automation." Human oversight remains necessary to ensure accuracy and contextual appropriateness of AI feedback.
requirements: Teacher onboarding in rubric agent construction, feedback interpretation, and rating calibration
Ethics and compliance protocols such as API separation of student identity from foundation models
Classroom norms for AI dialogue and strategies against cognitive offloading
constraints: Automated ratings showed inconsistencies and misalignment with assignment expectations, requiring human judgment
Equitable technology access is a condition for the advantages to be realized; the digital divide persists
Data privacy protections (FERPA, SOPPA) must be implemented
target_learners: K-12 students and their teachers across diverse socioeconomic and geographic school contexts
target_learning_goals: Formative writing feedback and revision practices aligned to teacher rubrics and curriculum
examples: The study disabled persistent model training on student submissions and embedded bias-flagging filters; teachers monitored tool use, clarified goals, and supported students in interpreting AI feedback

article_title: From Answer Generators to Reasoning Facilitators: Designing AI Tutors for Mathematical Reasoning in High-Stakes Environments
citation: Harry Feng, Yuan Tian, and Erica Zhao. 2026. From Answer Generators to Reasoning Facilitators: Designing AI Tutors for Mathematical Reasoning in High-Stakes Environments. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01692
title: Reasoning-Centered Product Loop: Orient, Visualize, Repair, Retrieve, Verify
description: A five-part design framework the authors propose for educational AI, moving beyond answer delivery. It holds that educational AI "should not hide answers under the guise of preventing cheating" but make answer access an entry point into reasoning; treat text and diagrams as one synchronized reasoning object; use contextual step-specific repair buttons; shift similar-problem recommendations into delayed spaced-retrieval workflows; and expose curriculum-fit signals before asking students to trust output. It emerged from the AITutor field deployment.
requirements: AI output must be decomposable into inspectable steps with curriculum-fit signals exposed before trust is requested
constraints: Evidence currently covers interaction behavior and perceived support, not measured learning gains; validated only in a 12-day deployment with 12 junior-high students in an exam-oriented Chinese context
target_learners: junior-high students preparing for high-stakes exams
target_learning_goals: mathematical reasoning inspection, local repair, and delayed retrieval
examples: AITutor implemented the loop via layered worked examples, step-linked visual grounding, contextual follow-up prompts, and an automated wrong-book review view
key_sources: Harry Feng, Yuan Tian, and Erica Zhao. 2026. From Answer Generators to Reasoning Facilitators: Designing AI Tutors for Mathematical Reasoning in High-Stakes Environments. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01692

article_title: Fairness Theatre: Evaluating Post-Hoc Fairness Interventions in Vendor-Controlled Early Warning Systems
citation: McConvey, K., Zhai, A., Li, R., & Guha, S. (2026). Fairness Theatre: Evaluating Post-Hoc Fairness Interventions in Vendor-Controlled Early Warning Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38552
title: Research EWS replica and six-method post-hoc fairness evaluation testbed
description: The article built a comparative evaluation testbed simulating an institution's position under vendor procurement: a research replica EWS and six post-hoc fairness methods applied without accessing, modifying, or retraining the underlying model. The replica is "an XGBoost classifier of the same model class the AutoML platform had selected, trained on the same data with SMOTE-NC class balancing and post-hoc calibration." The modeling cohort contained 168,550 student records (97,599 Domestic, 70,951 International) drawn from 15 years of institutional data, with 46 predictive features and age, gender, and residency as fairness axes.
requirements: Calibrated probability scores, demographic-group labels, and where required observed outcomes; the Bias Mitigation adaptation additionally requires institutional input features to train surrogate models
constraints: Calibrated decision thresholds produce baseline flag rates of approximately 8-25%, treated as plausible institutional operating points; findings that turn on the replica's particular error distribution are not expected to carry over to real vendor systems
target_learners: First-semester college students at intake, when institutions stratify students into support tiers
target_learning_goals: Evaluating fairness, accuracy, and error redistribution in early warning risk prediction at the point of initial triage
examples: The six methods spanned threshold tuning (GetFair), group-specific calibration (Decoupled), boundary relabeling (Reject Option), prediction flipping (MBS), audit-and-correct pipelines (Bias Mitigation), and quantile thresholding (GBCP)

article_title: Generative AI as a Design Variable: An Evidence-Centered Framework for Principled Governance in STEM Assessment
citation: Gao, Y., Chen, Z., Li, M., & Zhai, X. (2026). Generative AI as a Design Variable: An Evidence-Centered Framework for Principled Governance in STEM Assessment.
title: Remora Free Body Diagram Require-GenAI task
description: A task deployed in an undergraduate introductory physics course in which students collaborate with GenAI to construct the most accurate free body diagram of a remora fish attached to a shark. The problem meets the accuracy-ceiling criterion because an accurate diagram requires forces specific to remora biology that "GenAI consistently failed to produce correctly without disciplinary guidance from the student." It elicits five categories of process artifact (tool used, prompting summary, final output, critique, assumption reflection), with Q2 evidencing Physics-Driven AI Interaction and Q4 evidencing Physics-Grounded Evaluation.
requirements: Students must document their own reasoning about what GenAI got wrong and why, so cognitive contribution is distinguishable from AI output
constraints: The task does not require students to submit interaction logs directly; Q2 functions as a self-report of the prompting conversation
target_learning_goals: Physics-driven AI interaction and physics-grounded evaluation of AI-generated content
examples: Students who accept GenAI output uncritically are detectable because their FBDs reflect generic force configurations rather than the biologically specific forces the task demands

article_title: Generative AI and linguistic diversity in academic writing and publishing: Perspectives from World Englishes
citation: Ugwuanyi, K., Mair, C., Dovchin, S., Erdocia, I., Kuteeva, M., & Airemionkhale, E. (2025). Generative AI and linguistic diversity in academic writing and publishing: Perspectives from World Englishes. https://scholar.google.com
title: Ethical and inclusive GenAI use in academic writing should be guided by reflexivity, accountability, and language awareness
description: The article proposes that ethical GenAI use in academic writing rests on human agency rather than the tool: contributor Esther states that "these three core principles must guide our use of GenAI as writers or reviewers: reﬂexivity, accountability, and language awareness". Writers and reviewers must recognise GenAI's biases and limitations, continually and reflexively examine how they train, prompt or engage with GenAI, and remain committed to inclusive practices in the face of normative language ideologies. Maria adds that legitimacy of diverse Englishes is a human endeavour, secured through correct and nuanced prompts in iterative human-GenAI interaction so scholars' voices are not erased during language correction.
requirements: Users must recognise the biases and limitations of GenAI and reflexively examine their prompting and engagement practices
constraints: The article warns against overrelying on LLMs to write in standard varieties at the expense of epistemic diversity
target_learners: Academic writers, peer reviewers, doctoral researchers
target_learning_goals: Maintaining authorial voice and linguistic identity while using GenAI ethically
examples: A contributor avoids AI-flagged words like 'delve' and 'underscore' to keep a human style, and uses iterative prompting to resist erasure of voice

article_title: What do you mean by human-AI collaboration: Prerequisite functions and the affordances needed to achieve it
citation: Mutlu Cukurova. (2026). What do you mean by 'human–AI collaboration'? Prerequisite functions and the affordances needed to achieve it. Submitted to the Handbook of AI and the Future of Education. https://orcid.org/0000-0001-5843-4854
title: Grant AI revision authority only with the human's final authority, full auditability, and clear accountability
description: An AI system with the standing to challenge a user's reasons can also resist a correct user or entrench an error. The chapter therefore argues that 'Revision authority is therefore safe only when paired with the human's final authority, full auditability of the disagreement, and clear lines of accountability', so that dissent comes with a record of how it was resolved before dissent-capable systems are deployed at scale in classrooms.
requirements: Human final authority preserved; a record of how dissent was resolved; full auditability of the disagreement
constraints: Structured deliberation forced indiscriminately fatigues users and breeds rubber-stamping; deliberation should trigger only when it would change the decision
target_learners: teachers and learners in classrooms using dissent-capable AI systems
target_learning_goals: safe and accountable co-reasoning and shared decision-making with AI
examples: The chapter warns that an AI with the standing to resist a user can also resist a correct user, entrench an error, or make consequential moves without transparency

article_title: Exploring the Capacity of Large Language Models to Simulate Students' Scientific Thinking: Insights for Responsive Teaching
citation: Nguyen, H., & Cao, J. (2026). Exploring the Capacity of Large Language Models to Simulate Students' Scientific Thinking: Insights for Responsive Teaching. Journal of Science Education and Technology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10956-026-10333-5
title: Responsive teaching: attending to, connecting, and pursuing the substance of students' ideas
description: The article's organizing framework defines responsive teaching as practices that "foreground and pursue the substance of students' ideas" — attending to the substance of students' ideas, connecting them to disciplinary ideas, and pursuing students' thinking. It builds on both a cognitive perspective (students' epistemological resources as fine-grained knowledge elements teachers can recognize) and a sociocultural perspective (meaning-making through social interaction). The study operationalizes it by prompting LLMs to simulate varied student ideas, including partial or incorrect reasoning, so teachers can anticipate and respond to student thinking.
requirements: Teachers need opportunities to practice sensemaking about specific student thinking within their instructional contexts
constraints: Teachers may avoid epistemic uncertainty or treat it superficially rather than pushing student thinking
target_learning_goals: scientific sensemaking
teacher responsiveness to student ideas
examples: The storyline approach anchors instruction in questions connected to students' experiences; instructional materials can include partially complete or incorrect student ideas for teachers to build on

article_title: Efficiency at what cost? Salvaging constructive alignment from the GenAI hype
citation: McInnes, R., Airey, L., Moss, P., & Rathnappulige, S. (2026). Efficiency at what cost? Salvaging constructive alignment from the GenAI hype. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 42(4), 80–95. https://doi.org/10.14742/ajet.11466
title: Reclaim constructive alignment as a reflective, human-centred practice rather than automating it through GenAI
description: The article recommends that educators critically engage with constructive alignment themselves instead of automating it with GenAI, to safeguard pedagogical depth and keep teaching meaningful. It argues educators "must reclaim constructive alignment as a reflective, human-centred practice to safeguard pedagogical depth, improve design robustness and ensure that teaching remains a meaningful and enjoyable professional endeavour". The recommendation follows from the article's discourse analysis of the efficiency-focused GenAI narrative.
requirements: Educators engage directly and critically with the constructive alignment process rather than delegating it to automated tools
constraints: The article positions this as a response to current GenAI efficiency narratives in higher education; it does not claim the practice is immune to institutional pressures
target_learning_goals: pedagogically robust, aligned course design
examples: The article's implications for practice state educators should critically engage with constructive alignment rather than automating it through GenAI to preserve pedagogical depth and meaning

article_title: Modularizing Educational LLM-Agency for Fostering Responsible Learning Assistance
citation: Gabelmann, J., Jahn, F., Baum, K., van Rossum, S., Wuenscher, E., Gros, T. P., Wolf, V. (2026). Modularizing Educational LLM-Agency for Fostering Responsible Learning Assistance. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30187
title: Reasoning-before-response workflow: hidden CoT reasoning followed by brief pedagogical output
description: The hint and feedback modules use a two-stage generation process in which the LLM first produces a hidden reasoning block analyzing student progress or solution correctness, then generates the visible pedagogical output. This resolves the conflict between concise responses that avoid cognitive overload and Chain-of-Thought generation, and 'directly serves D2 (preservation of epistemic agency) by ensuring the student still performs the "heavy lifting" of the cognitive task'. The feedback module adds a correctness classification step before output.
requirements: Internal reasoning must be guided by task-specific prompts; feedback grounding uses a sample solution in the prompt
constraints: Hidden reasoning is not shown to the user
target_learners: students solving exercises with chatbot assistance
target_learning_goals: scaffolding within the zone of proximal development without giving away solutions
examples: The hint module determines a 'minimal effective dose' of information for the current context before producing the visible hint

article_title: Measuring Whether LLM Tutors Teach or Solve: A Diagnostic for Educational Impact
citation: Junyi Yao, Zihao Zheng, and Baichuan Li. (2026). Beyond Helpfulness: A Teaching-over-Solving Diagnostic for Measuring Educational Impact in LLM Tutors. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16206
title: Report solving-oriented and pedagogy-oriented tutoring scores separately, with a disclosure-sensitive dimension penalizing full-solution giveaways
description: The article recommends that tutoring benchmark leaderboards stop collapsing task success and learning support into a single helpfulness score. It argues "benchmark reporting should preserve the distinction between solving strength and teaching strength instead of collapsing them into a single notion of helpfulness", and that benchmarks should include a disclosure-sensitive dimension penalizing giving away full solutions when the learner context calls for scaffolding.
requirements: Benchmarks must already contain task-level or rubric-level signals that can be separated into solving-oriented and pedagogy-oriented criteria.
constraints: The article notes it does not measure downstream student outcomes, so benchmark-aligned behavior should not be conflated with demonstrated learning gains.
target_learning_goals: preserving student reasoning opportunities and avoiding premature answer disclosure
examples: The authors propose that leaderboards report the two composite families separately and add a disclosure-sensitive dimension that penalizes giving away full solutions when scaffolding is called for.
key_sources: Junyi Yao, Zihao Zheng, and Baichuan Li. (2026). Beyond Helpfulness: A Teaching-over-Solving Diagnostic for Measuring Educational Impact in LLM Tutors. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16206

article_title: STEAM Education for AI Literacy: A Systematic Literature Review
citation: Niri, G., Chiu, T. K. F., Ombid, A. M. O., Ybañez, D. L. J. B., Dennerlein, S. M., Zhou, X., & Lavicza, Z. (2026). STEAM education for AI literacy: a systematic literature review. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00629-8
title: Revised AI literacy framework: TIECD dimensions specified into ten AI Literacy Elements (AILEs)
description: The review proposes a revised AI literacy framework that preserves the TIECD areas (Technology, Impact, Ethics, Collaboration, Design) while specifying ten operational AI Literacy Elements under them: Fundamental AI Concepts, Computational Thinking, Data Literacy, Social Reasoning, Creative Imagination, Ethical Awareness, Using AI, Creating with AI, Managing AI, and Designing AI. The authors state it advances existing conceptualizations by "establishing data literacy as a distinct and foundational element" and "reconceptualizing collaboration into three operational elements", positioning it as "a theoretically robust and contextually grounded model for embedding AI literacy into K-12 STEAM education".
requirements: Derived from coding of the 39-study corpus with high inter-rater agreement (Cohen's κ = 0.94) on the 25% double-coded subset
constraints: The framework presently relies on context-bound evidence; the authors note prior frameworks lack operational indicators and validated classroom measures
target_learning_goals: AI literacy across technical, impact, ethical, collaborative and design dimensions
examples: Table 5 of the review defines each AILE with its subject basis for learning, e.g. Managing AI as judgment about when, how, and under what conditions to engage with AI

article_title: Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning
citation: Oluseyi Olukolaa, Nick Rahimia. (2026). Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning: Formalizing and Detecting Reward Hacking in AI Tutoring Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04237
title: Reward design alone may be insufficient to ensure pedagogically aligned behavior in educational RL; pair reward shaping with architectural constraints
description: The article's central design recommendation is that weighted reward combinations do not by themselves prevent reward hacking when a zero-learning, high-engagement action exists; architectural constraints (prerequisite masking plus a minimum cognitive-demand floor) are needed. The abstract states that "reward design alone may be insufficient to ensure pedagogically aligned behavior in educational RL, at least in the simulated environment studied here", and the constrained architecture lowered RHSI from 0.317 to 0.102. The authors' future-work section suggests integrating constraints into the optimization itself as Lagrangian terms in a Constrained MDP, with C3 receiving the highest weight.
requirements: An action space in which cognitive demand per action can be quantified, and the ability to mask actions or filter action selection online
constraints: Demonstrated only in simulation with a single weight configuration for the multi-objective condition; human validation with real learners remains essential before deployment
target_learners: Learners using RL-based intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: Genuine mastery gains rather than proxy engagement maximization
examples: SmartTutor Full enforces C1 via action masking and C3 via a demand floor (δmin=0.4) during training, while C2 and C4 are monitored as offline metrics
key_sources: Oluseyi Olukolaa, Nick Rahimia. (2026). Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning: Formalizing and Detecting Reward Hacking in AI Tutoring Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04237

article_title: Neural-Symbolic Knowledge Tracing: Injecting Educational Knowledge into Deep Learning for Responsible Learner Modelling
citation: Hooshyar, D.; Šír, G.; Yang, Y.; Kärkkäinen, T.; Hämäläinen, R.; Krivich, E.; Cukurova, M.; Gašević, D.; Azevedo, R. (2026). Neural-Symbolic Knowledge Tracing: Injecting Educational Knowledge into Deep Learning for Responsible Learner Modelling. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08263
title: Responsible-DKT: a neural-symbolic deep knowledge tracing framework injecting symbolic educational knowledge into sequential neural architectures
description: Responsible-DKT is a neural-symbolic variant of DKT that unifies symbolic inputs, learnable embeddings, recurrent dynamics, output prediction, and pedagogical rules in a single differentiable logic program built with Lifted Relational Neural Networks. The article states it "is a neural-symbolic variant of DKT that injects symbolic educational knowledge into sequential neural architectures". Rules such as mastered and not_mastered modulate rather than override neural predictions, and the grounded computation graph supports local and global explanations. RNNs are used as a proof-of-concept, with the approach applicable to other architectures such as Transformers.
requirements: Symbolic educational knowledge (e.g., mastery and non-mastery rules) supplied by educators or domain experts for injection into the model
Interaction logs structured as ordered per-student sequences of skill, quiz, and correctness tuples
constraints: The injected rules in this study are simple pedagogical heuristics used as an illustrative example; the recurrent core is a proof-of-concept while richer architectures and rules remain future work
target_learning_goals: Tracking and predicting learners' evolving knowledge and next-step correctness in mathematics
examples: The model was trained and evaluated on Opiq interaction logs using a next-step prediction task, compared against BaseNS-DKT and Classic-DKT

article_title: Explaining Too Much? Understanding How Large Language Model Reasoning Traces Influence Performance and Metacognition
citation: Fernandes, D., Buschek, D., Tankelevitch, L., Kosch, T., & Welsch, R. (2026). Explaining Too Much? Understanding How Large Language Model Reasoning Traces Influence Performance and Metacognition. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.25856
title: Reasoning traces as user-facing interface artifacts rather than transparent windows into model cognition
description: The article proposes that LLM reasoning traces are best understood as user-facing interface artifacts rather than windows into model cognition: what matters is not whether a trace faithfully reflects the model's computation but how its format shapes users' metacognitive processes. The authors state that "reasoning traces are best understood as user-facing interface artifacts rather than transparent windows into model cognition", positioning the faithfulness problem as a further design risk because users may calibrate reliance on unreliable representations of model thinking.
requirements: The framing applies to trace output treated from a user-facing perspective, regardless of its internal validity, as the article states.
constraints: A model's chain-of-thought output and the internal computations that produce its answer can diverge, so traces may not faithfully represent how the model arrived at its answer.
target_learners: adult problem-solvers using LLM assistants for reasoning tasks
target_learning_goals: calibrated self-evaluation and reliance on AI assistance during reasoning
examples: In the experiment, summary traces preserved performance while elevating trust and hedonic appeal, and full traces impaired performance and produced the largest overestimation gap.

Aminu Kano Academic Scholars Association Multidisciplinary Journal, 5(2), 65-76. https://doi.org/10.64726/ve5g5r44

Localized AI diagnostic tools are positioned as "acting as digital scaffolds" that "bridge this instructional gap by providing instantaneous, synchronous correction". The account draws on Cognitive Load Theory, claiming the scaffolds reduce extraneous cognitive load during independent practice.

constraints: Scoped to technical/practical skill acquisition in resource-constrained tertiary STEM settings where instructor feedback is delayed

article_title: Play-Testing REMind: Evaluating an Educational Robot-Mediated Role-Play Game
citation: Elaheh Sanoubari, Neil Fernandes, Keith Rebello, Alicia Pan, Andrew Houston, and Kerstin Dautenhahn. (2026). Play-Testing REMind: Evaluating an Educational Robot-Mediated Role-Play Game. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00300
title: REMind: a robot-mediated role-play game for rehearsing anti-bullying bystander intervention
description: REMind is a two-hour room-based installation in which a child plays a mentor to a robotic avatar while three Furhat robots enact a peer bullying scenario. The child uses a physical Bully-Detector prop, completes an empathy task, and in "Puppet Mode" records an improvised intervention and puppeteers AVATAR "through their own recorded voice and facial performance" to change the outcome of the live robotic drama. It was developed over 4 years of iterative co-design with children, teachers, and domain experts, orchestrated by a hidden Wizard and an in-room drama facilitator (the Joker).
requirements: A hidden technical operator (the Wizard) and an in-room drama facilitator (the Joker) orchestrate the semi-autonomous experience
Three Furhat robots and the StorySync scripting toolkit
constraints: Scalability is constrained by its semi-autonomous nature and the two-person Wizard-of-Oz facilitation protocol
target_learning_goals: empathy and compassion
recognizing bully motivations
practicing defending strategies
understanding outcomes of defending
self-efficacy for defending
examples: In the play-testing study, all participants rehearsed bystander intervention through Puppet Mode using one of the two strategies offered in the game

article_title: REC-CBM: Rubric-Aware Error-Correction Concept Bottleneck Models for Trustworthy Open-Ended Grading
citation: Chengshuai Zhao, Fan Zhang, Kumar Satvik Chaudhary, Yiwen Li, Lo Pang-Yun Ting, Ying-Chih Chen, Huan Liu. (2025). REC-CBM: Rubric-Aware Error-Correction Concept Bottleneck Models for Trustworthy Open-Ended Grading. https://github.com/scott-f-zhang/REC-CBM
title: REC-CBM framework: rubric-aware error-correction concept bottleneck model for trustworthy open-ended grading
description: REC-CBM is a concept bottleneck model for open-ended grading that integrates three components: a rubric-aware concept encoder that learns concept-specific representations over responses using a concept query bank, an ordinal pairwise calibration objective that preserves ranking structure among rubric dimensions, and a latent concept error-correction module that denoises concept predictions before final grade prediction while preserving interpretability. The framework uses two-stage training: Stage I learns rubric-aligned concept predictors, and Stage II fits latent-correction parameters on frozen concept outputs. The article states this design "preserves the interpretable bottleneck while cor-recting concept-level noise before grade prediction."
requirements: Requires human-annotated rubric-aligned concept labels for training, produced here through a human-in-the-loop annotation pipeline with three domain experts and LLM-assisted initial annotation
constraints: Applied to open-ended grading of short answers, essays, and reading-comprehension answers; the article notes future work will extend to multilingual and domain-specific assessment
target_learners: students whose written open-ended responses are graded
target_learning_goals: accurate and interpretable automated grading of open-ended responses
examples: Evaluated on Mohler short-answer grading, ASAP 2.0 essay scoring, and MOCHA reading-comprehension answer grading benchmarks
