article_title: Teaching Prompt-Based Programming with LLMs: A 45-Minute Lesson with Guided Practice for End-User Programmers
citation: Keith Tran, Samiha Marwan, and Thomas Price. (2026). Teaching Prompt-Based Programming with LLMs: A 45-Minute Lesson with Guided Practice for End-User Programmers. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30547
title: Reusable structured prompt template built up across lesson sections
description: The lesson taught students a reusable template for constructing prompts, built up throughout the lesson sections, to help them remember to address each learning objective. The template prompts learners to "Write me a Python function that takes as input [describe the input, including its type] and it should output [describe the output, including its type], that [explain how the function transforms the input into the output]" plus an example input and expected output. It operationalizes the Gulf of Envisioning dimensions of describing the problem, phrasing prompts, and assessing output.
requirements: Instruction across the five learning objectives so students can fill each template slot (input, output, transformation, example)
constraints: Taught in the context of Promptly-style tasks requiring natural-language specification of computational intent rather than code writing
target_learning_goals: articulating inputs, outputs, and transformations to an LLM
reducing vague or underspecified prompts
examples: The template was built up throughout the lesson's five sections and used in guided Promptly practice

article_title: Representation Robustness under Executable Reasoning Constraints in Large Language Models for Mathematical Problem Solving
citation: Sagnik Nath, Edith Aurora Graf, Liang Zhang and Diego Zapata-Rivera. (2026). Representation Robustness under Executable Reasoning Constraints in Large Language Models for Mathematical Problem Solving. https://github.com/sagniknath91/HCI-2026-dataset/blob/main/datasheet.csv
title: Benchmark designers should use controlled families of representational variants rather than single-form problem instances
description: The article recommends that math benchmarks stop treating representationally equivalent formulations as interchangeable. Because performance varies substantially across representations of the same mathematical structure even under deterministic decoding, high benchmark scores may reflect "sensitivity to favored surface forms rather than stable representation-invariant ability". Controlled families of representational variants make it possible to distinguish robustness from overfitting to presentation style, and the article extends this to any domain admitting multiple surface realizations of the same structure.
requirements: Problems must admit multiple mathematically equivalent surface realizations (e.g., story, symbolic, word-equation, isomorphic paraphrase forms) so variants can be compared.
constraints: The article's evidence comes from middle-school through early high-school algebra problems solvable with one or two variable algebraic reasoning; it flags other domains only as facing similar potential risks.
target_learners: developers and evaluators of AI-assisted math problem solving systems
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of LLM math reasoning evaluation results
distinguishing representation-invariant reasoning from surface-form sensitivity
examples: The study instantiated each of 85 source story problems in story, symbolic-equation, word-equation, and isomorphic paraphrase variants and evaluated 5 LLMs across them under two interaction conditions.

title: ResidencyRL simulated clinical training environment with documentation API, LLM patient simulator, and structured autorater
description: ResidencyRL is an online multi-turn reinforcement learning training environment in which a clinical AI agent conducts complete simulated patient encounters. The environment exposes "an LLM-driven patient simulator and a structured API allowing the agent to document the encounter (e.g., diagnosis, management plan)", with rollouts scaling to 60 dialogue turns and 8 tool calls. target_learning_goals: Sequential clinical decision-making including history-taking, differential diagnosis, management planning, clinical documentation, and patient-centered communication
examples: The article shows a 22-turn training rollout in which the agent elicits a hidden Kratom tea consumption history by specifically asking about herbal supplements and correctly identifies Kratom-induced constipation as the primary diagnosis

title: Four-stage scenario generation pipeline with demographic sampling, quality verification, and adversarial extension packs
description: The scenario generation pipeline synthesizes and curates diverse clinical scenarios through four stages: demographic and behavioral attribute sampling from US population distributions including Big Five personality traits, condition-targeted LLM generation grounded in the DDXPlus evidence corpus, LLM-as-judge quality verification across five dimensions, and character-trigram TF-IDF deduplication. As the article states, "A generative proposer-judge pipeline synthesizes and curates diverse clinical scenarios based on targeted demographic and behavioral patient profiles." Two extension packs supplement the base scenarios: targeted history-taking scenarios across a four-domain taxonomy where critical information is withheld unless specifically prompted, and adversarial safety scenarios across a 9-category clinical safety taxonomy.
requirements: Requires scenario quality verification because scenario quality strictly upper-bounds downstream policy performance
Requires deduplication with cosine similarity threshold of 0.9 to prevent policy memorization of specific narratives
constraints: Sampling only common presentations may leave the model unprepared for unconventional case presentations where diagnostic error carries the highest clinical cost
Demographic homogeneity has the potential to induce representation bias

target_learning_goals: Robust diagnostic reasoning across diverse patient presentations, proactive information elicitation, and safety-critical clinical decision-making

title: Practice-based clinical mastery through progressively challenging simulated encounters
description: The article's organizing premise is that clinical competence, for AI as for physicians, is developed through practice rather than acquired through static knowledge testing alone. As the authors state, "ResidencyRL is built on a simple premise: clinical mastery, for AI as for physicians, is developed through practice." The framework draws a direct analogy to medical residency, where trainees convert academic knowledge into clinical expertise through years of supervised encounters with diverse feedback and progressively greater autonomy. It holds that a trainee who scores perfectly on examinations may still fail when presentations are atypical, and that the gap is a failure of clinical process rather than medical knowledge — a process that can be optimized through multi-turn RL in simulation.
requirements: Requires simulated environments with sufficient fidelity that competencies trained in simulation transfer to real clinical settings
Requires a curriculum spanning routine, targeted history-taking, and adversarial scenario types to develop distinct clinical competencies
constraints: Prospective validation with real-world workflows remains necessary to establish clinical utility
The competence ceiling of simulation-based training is bounded by environment fidelity
target_learners: Medical trainees (by analogy to residency education)
target_learning_goals: Sequential clinical reasoning, diagnostic accuracy, management quality, patient-centered communication, and safety-critical decision-making under uncertainty
examples: The article trains a Gemini 3.5 Flash agent across a curriculum of three environment types: routine telehealth consultations, targeted history-taking scenarios, and adversarial safety cases

article_title: Still Emerging: Understanding Generative AI Use in Higher Education
citation: Kahn P, Carrigan M, Wyman I, Liu R, Smith P, Andonegui AR, Murtagh L and Song F (2026) Still emerging: understanding Generative AI use in Higher Education. Front. Educ. 11:1885253. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1885253
title: Address GAI challenges through staff-student relationships and imagined affordances, not only AI literacy training
description: The article argues that framing the challenges of GAI in Higher Education as a technical problem of learning design or student AI literacy is insufficient. Because affordances are imagined relationally, staff must imagine both the tools and how students imagine them: "The affordances of GAI need to be imagined effectively by both students and staff if the technology is to serve educational purposes effectively." The authors recommend reconstructing the challenges in terms of teacher/student and peer relationships within which reflexivity is exercised.
requirements: Staff need sustained engagement and practical experimentation with GAI tools to appreciate educationally appropriate uses
constraints: The article cautions that experimentation relies on staff having the time and autonomy required, which an imperative to automate threatens to undercut
target_learning_goals: Educationally appropriate use of generative AI tools in academic study, teaching and assessment
examples: The study found staff possessed limited knowledge of student GAI use and that variation in staff use and expertise made it difficult for many staff to appreciate educationally appropriate uses or the extent to which students manifested them

article_title: Literacy demands placed on students in student–GenAI entanglements in higher education
citation: Sun, Z., Dohn, N. B., & Rehm, M. (2026). Literacy Demands Placed on Students in Student–GenAI Entanglements in Higher Education. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00697-7
title: Build explicit reflection into GenAI activities to develop meta-level literacy in recognizing and negotiating conflicting demands (reflection and negotiation)
description: The third design principle is reflection and negotiation, not just compliance. Because different entanglement types distribute epistemic work in structurally distinct ways and generate sometimes conflicting literacy demands across the three levels, the key competence students need is "not mastery of any single entanglement type, but the capacity to recognize the implicit expectations of a given context and negotiate tensions when those expectations conflict." Teachers can design for this by building explicit reflection into GenAI activities, asking students to articulate what the activity demanded, where they experienced tension or uncertainty, and how they navigated it.
requirements: Reflection must be built explicitly into GenAI activities, prompting students to articulate demands, tensions, and navigation strategies rather than only completing the task
constraints: Over time is required: the reflective practice develops competence to recognize literacy demands of novel entanglement types gradually
target_learning_goals: meta-level literacy: understanding what an activity requires, how epistemic responsibility is distributed, and how to act appropriately within the entanglement
examples: Asking students not only to complete a task with GenAI but to articulate what the activity demanded of them, where they experienced tension or uncertainty, and how they navigated it

article_title: Sycophantic AI makes human interaction feel more effortful and less satisfying over time
citation: Lujain Ibrahim, Franziska Sofia Hafner, Myra Cheng, Cinoo Lee, Rebecca Anselmetti, Robb Willer, Luc Rocher, Diyi Yang. (2026). Sycophantic AI makes human interaction feel more effortful and less satisfying over time. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07912
title: Relational account of AI sycophancy
description: The article's organizing framework: the central long-term risk of sycophantic AI lies not in distorted judgments from single conversations but in how repeated effortless affirmation reshapes users' close relationships. As the authors put it, "by providing effortless understanding, sycophantic AI can raise the bar against which human relationships are judged." Sycophantic AI supplies the emotional and esteem support people associate with close others, so human relationships that still require effort may come to feel insufficient, shifting patterns of social support at scale.
requirements: Repeated exposure over weeks, not single conversations, for the relational effects to emerge
constraints: Effects observed after three weeks; whether they intensify or plateau over months or years remains an open question
Sample reflects a particular cultural context; effects could differ in direction or magnitude in populations with different norms around social support
target_learners: Adult AI chatbot users seeking personal advice and support
target_learning_goals: Understanding how AI interaction styles shape users' expectations of and satisfaction with human relationships
examples: In the three-week longitudinal study, participants conversing with a sycophantic AI became nearly as likely to seek personal advice from it as from close friends and family

citation: Yanjia Li, Kelcy Kexin Han, Tianrui Hu, Yi-Fan Cao, Huamin Qu, Sicheng Song. (2026). SupplyNet: Supporting Visual Exploratory Learning in Supply Chain via Contextual Multi-Agent Simulation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24694
title: Reusable simulation architecture for dynamic relational learning environments
description: The article abstracts SupplyNet's pipeline into "a reusable simulation architecture for dynamic relational learning environments." A graph represents domain entities, dependencies, and time-varying states; agents and learners observe relevant subgraphs, take domain-specific actions, and trigger state transitions; a database stores temporal snapshots supporting replay, branching, and comparison. The reusable layer separates from a domain-specific layer so other subjects can reuse the architecture by replacing the domain schema, transition rules, agent heuristics, event types, and learning metrics.
requirements: Subjects must be modelable as dynamic relational systems involving multiple connected entities, local decisions or disturbances, delayed propagation of effects, and trade-offs that learners need to diagnose over time.
constraints: The architecture was designed and evaluated only in the supply chain management context; cross-subject instantiations are discussed as future work.
target_learners: university students in domains modelable as dynamic relational systems
target_learning_goals: diagnosing delayed propagation of effects and trade-offs in interconnected systems
examples: In SupplyNet the architecture is instantiated with business entities, logistics links, inventory-related states, ordering decisions, disruption events, and operational KPIs.

citation: Avijit Roy, Proma Roy. (2026). Structural Silence: When AI Infrastructure Fails Speakers of Underrepresented Languages — A Case Study in Bengali, the Digital Divide, and the Hidden Cost of English-Centric Design. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12278
title: Treat dataset construction for underrepresented languages as a primary research contribution, not supporting labor
description: The article argues dataset scarcity for underrepresented languages is a structural barrier shaped by funding and publication incentives, not a natural scarcity or individual researcher limitation. It states that "Recognizing dataset construction for underrepresented languages as a substantive research contribution, comparable to architectural innovation, is likely to be an important condition for changing that pattern." Researchers who treat such infrastructure as preliminary work reproduce the asymmetry that later appears in model performance.

constraints: The principle is argued from an analysis of institutional incentives, not tested empirically
target_learning_goals: Availability of native-language AI-assisted educational tools
examples: The article describes researchers building Bengali AI tools who must curate training examples, validate translations, develop benchmarks, and establish annotation protocols from scratch

citation: Wei J and Shang Y (2026). Beyond checking: verification quality, reliance calibration, and learning in generative AI-assisted higher education. Front. Psychol. 17:1965371. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1965371
title: Reliance calibration as an output-contingent classification of reliance decisions
description: The review defines reliance calibration as "an item-level, output-contingent classification of whether a reliance decision was appropriate given AI-output quality", distinguishing it from trust (a psychological attitude) and reliance (an observable decision). For mixed-quality outputs, calibration may be judged at claim level or on a graded appropriateness scale, because one response can contain accurate, incomplete, and misleading elements simultaneously. Accepting faulty content constitutes over-reliance; rejecting useful content constitutes under-reliance.
requirements: A reference standard for AI-output quality is required before a reliance decision can be classified as calibrated
constraints: A trust scale cannot substitute for an observed reliance decision
HCI reviews note heterogeneous definitions of appropriate reliance
target_learning_goals: appropriate reliance on AI assistance
examples: Zheng et al. combined AI competence/relevance, follow/not-follow behavior, and final correctness in 315 student-ChatGPT quiz conversations to distinguish appropriate and inappropriate reliance

article_title: The impact of career adapt-abilities on AI anxiety among English majors: a dual perspective analysis based on core self-evaluations at the person- and variable-centered
citation: Wang X (2026) The impact of career adapt-abilities on AI anxiety among English majors: a dual perspective analysis based on core self-evaluations at the person- and variable-centered. Front. Psychol. 17:1767791. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1767791
title: Integrated resource–internalization–anxiety pathway linking Career Construction Theory and Conservation of Resources Theory
description: The article proposes an integrative framework in which career adapt-abilities, as Career Construction Theory-defined psychosocial resources, reduce AI anxiety partly through core self-evaluations, the cognitive internalization mechanism emphasized in Conservation of Resources Theory. The article states that "adapt-abilities are not merely 'resources' in a general sense; they are theorized to generate mastery experiences and proactive coping, which are then consolidated into more positive core self-evaluations". Higher core self-evaluations then lower AI anxiety by weakening threat appraisal and enhancing perceived controllability. The framework predicts the protective effect is partially indirect and partially direct.
requirements: Career adapt-abilities must undergo cognitive appraisal and internalization into core self-evaluations to exert their protective function
constraints: Tested in a cross-sectional design among English majors facing AI-driven substitution pressures in language-related occupations
target_learners: English major undergraduates and graduate students in Chinese universities
target_learning_goals: Career adapt-abilities development
management of AI-related occupational anxiety
examples: The dual-analytic strategy tested the pathway via variable-centered mediation and person-centered latent profile analysis, with both strategies converging on the protective role of career adapt-abilities

article_title: Towards Synergistic Teacher-AI Interactions with Generative Artificial Intelligence
citation: Mutlu Cukurova, Wannapon Suraworachet, Qi Zhou, and Sahan Bulathwela. (2025). Towards Synergistic Teacher-AI Interactions with Generative Artificial Intelligence. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19580
title: Replacement, complementarity and augmentation as three levels of AI integration and their competence impacts
description: The chapter draws on Cukurova's three levels of AI integration along the automation-control spectrum. It states: "Replacement refers to a situation where AI systems independently operate teaching tasks without, or with minimal, teacher oversight (high AI automation with low teacher control)." Complementarity involves AI enhancing teacher capabilities with active teacher control, aiming to maintain or improve human competence, while augmentation seeks superior performance through interwoven interactions improving both agents. The chapter notes this conceptualisation does not clarify how interactions unfold at a granular level.
requirements: Understanding which integration level applies requires analysing the degree of AI automation versus teacher control in a given system
constraints: The framework does not clarify how interactions unfold at a granular level, offering limited guidance on how teacher-AI interactions should be productively designed
target_learning_goals: protecting and developing teacher competence under AI integration
examples: The chapter uses this spectrum to frame concerns that replacement can lead human competence to flatten or decline even when task performance improves

article_title: Understanding Student Effort Using Response-Time Propensities During Problem Solving
citation: Conrad Borchers, Lijin Zhang, Kexin Yang, Tomohiro Nagashima, and Benjamin W. Domingue. 2026. Understanding Student Effort Using Response-Time Propensities During Problem Solving. Proceedings of the Thirteenth ACM Conference on Learning @ Scale (L@S '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3774398.3811624
title: Response-time propensities: a difficulty-adjusted, trait-like measure of typical step-level pacing
description: Response-time propensities are a log-derived measure of students' typical step-to-step response timing in intelligent tutoring systems, estimated as student-level random intercepts from a hierarchical model of log-transformed step latencies with random effects for students and skills. The article defines them as "difficulty- and context-adjusted, trait-like differences in students' typical response timing during tutoring", where trait-like captures typical pacing while within-person speed can still vary across steps. They are intended as a process construct complementing correctness-based knowledge estimates, capturing how students distribute time across steps.
requirements: Step-level log data with timestamps, problem and step identifiers, knowledge components, and outcome codes, as logged by the tutoring systems
constraints: The article states response time remains an inherently ambiguous behavioral trace; longer delays may reflect classroom interruptions, off-task behavior, or reading time not distinguishable in log data alone
Results are bounded by step-based mathematics tutors in U.S. classrooms with short interaction cycles and limited text per step
target_learners: middle- and high-school mathematics students using step-based intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: effort regulation and persistence during multi-step algebra problem solving
examples: Student and skill random intercepts were estimated from log-transformed step-to-step response times across eight DataShop datasets collected between 2020 and 2023

Proceedings of the Thirteenth ACM Conference on Learning @ Scale (L@S '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3774398.3811624

article_title: With a Thermomix You Lose the Ability to Cook: A Kitchen Machine Analogy for Applications of Generative AI in Education
citation: Rummel, N., Nachtigall, V., & Panadero, E. (2026). “With a Thermomix You Lose the Ability to Cook”: A Kitchen Machine Analogy for Applications of Generative AI in Education.
title: Redesign assignments so learners critically engage with AI outputs rather than merely consume them
description: This principle holds that teachers should restructure tasks so that generative AI outputs become material for brainstorming, evaluation, and reflection rather than ready-made answers. In the article's terms, "the modification stage is evident when teachers redesign their assignments so that learners are not merely tasked with searching for information and synthesizing it, but are instead prompted to engage in new forms of interaction" such as critically evaluating AI-provided information and drawing their own conclusions. This positions AI as a catalyst for meaning-making and self-reflection.
requirements: Teachers must adapt assignments and learners need prior knowledge to engage productively, critically, and creatively with AI-generated material
constraints: The article notes reliance on AI for basic functions risks diminishing acquisition of foundational skills such as composing grammatically correct texts from scratch
target_learning_goals: critical thinking, creativity, and self-reflection with AI-generated material
examples: The article describes assignments prompting critique of AI outputs and use of ChatGPT for brainstorming, outlining, and evaluating information (Kim & Adlof, 2024)

article_title: Supporting self-regulated learning through generative AI feedback in online higher education: the importance of student perceptions of the source of feedback
citation: Yilmaz, M., Temur, H. B., Emmungil, L., Çelik, E., Gauthier, A., & Cukurova, M. (2026). Supporting self-regulated learning through generative AI feedback in online higher education: the importance of student perceptions of the source of feedback. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 23(16). https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00592-y
title: RefleX ED tutor-support tool presenting standardised SRL proxy scores
description: RefleX ED is a tool the authors developed to help tutors interpret behavioural data when drafting feedback. It "presents each student's standardised scores derived from observable indicators of SRLs behaviours" across the five SRL pillars (GS, TS, TM, HS, SE), with z-scores centred on zero so negative values signal a need for corrective feedback and positive values for reinforcement. It was used to generate the tutor-feedback condition in the study.
requirements: Requires a tutor with some familiarity with data interpretation to use effectively
constraints: Designed to lower, but not remove, the expertise barrier for interpreting behavioural data

article_title: The agency gap in AI-supported writing: how reactive and proactive agent designs shape multimodal reasoning
citation: Yueqiao Jin, Kaixun Yang, Roberto Martinez-Maldonado, Dragan Gašević and Lixiang Yan. (2025). The Agency Gap in AI-Supported Writing: How Reactive and Proactive Agent Designs Shape Multimodal Reasoning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04398
title: Reactive and proactive AI writing agents on a minimalist multimodal writing platform
description: The study developed two AI agents that manipulated conversational initiative while holding other features constant: both used the same interface, visual inputs, VizChat architecture, Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline, visualisation knowledge base, and multimodal GPT-4o model. The reactive agent generated only when the learner messaged; the proactive agent followed an expert-authored conversational state sequence, initiating orientation and ordered guiding questions per visual and giving confirmatory, clarifying, or corrective feedback grounded in visual evidence. The platform comprised a display area, a writing space, and a condition-specific chat or instructions component.
requirements: Requires the same underlying model, retrieval pipeline, and task materials across conditions so the contrast isolates who initiates and sequences support
constraints: The proactive sequence's triggering events, question order, target knowledge, and completion rules were fixed across participants; the prompt prohibited asking about non-displayed visuals and repeating questions
target_learners: medical and nursing students interpreting healthcare simulation visualisations
target_learning_goals: multimodal analytical writing from data visualisations
examples: In the proactive condition the sequence contained one question for the bar chart, two for the communication network, and three for the ward map, ending with a synthesis prompt

article_title: Adaptivity Makes Feedback Effective: Evidence From AI-Generated Feedback on Children's Plans
citation: Sukjaitham, S., Schaaf, M., Brod, G., & Breitwieser, J. (2026). Adaptivity Makes Feedback Effective: Evidence From AI-Generated Feedback on Children's Plans. Preprint. https://osf.io/4w6rz/overview?view_only=dd3ec8d2878243579a463ccd0d77d723
title: Response-contingent adaptivity as a core mechanism of feedback effectiveness
description: The article proposes that contingent adaptation of feedback to learners' momentary responses is a functionally relevant mechanism of feedback effectiveness, distinct from feedback quality, motivational tone, or structural clarity. In a preregistered experiment, feedback that addressed each child's specific plan produced larger plan-quality gains and higher perceived usefulness than structurally equivalent generic guidance. The authors conclude that "response-contingent adaptation constitutes a meaningful and functionally relevant dimension of instructional feedback", strengthening the interaction between feedback and the learner's evolving task performance rather than representing superficial customization.
requirements: A comparison condition matched on quality, structure, tone, and length is needed to isolate adaptivity as the active ingredient
constraints: Evidence comes from short-term effects in a highly structured setting with constrained tasks (children wrote only the if-component); generalization to complex, ill-defined tasks, other age groups, and less structured environments remains untested
target_learners: children aged 10-13 in fifth and sixth grade
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategy use, specifically planning with implementation intentions
examples: LLM feedback referenced the child's own plan (e.g., suggesting a concrete cue like finishing homework before starting), while generic guidance stated the same five quality criteria without referencing the response
key_sources: Sukjaitham, S., Schaaf, M., Brod, G., & Breitwieser, J. (2026). Adaptivity Makes Feedback Effective: Evidence From AI-Generated Feedback on Children's Plans. Preprint. https://osf.io/4w6rz/overview?view_only=dd3ec8d2878243579a463ccd0d77d723

article_title: Building AI Companions that Prioritize Learning over Performance
citation: Khosravi, H., Gašević, D., Sadiq, S., Yan, L., Lodge, J. M., Tangen, J. M., Denny, P., DiCerbo, K., Buckingham Shum, S., & Baker, R. S. (2026). Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04816
title: Responsible design foundation: security, transparency, accountability, and inclusion commitments
description: The responsible design foundation organises trustworthy practice around "four interwoven commitments: security, transparency, accountability, and inclusion". Security protects privacy, data, and digital wellbeing through lawful data practices and psychological safety; transparency makes AI processes visible and explainable, building on XAI-ED and Open Learner Models; accountability retains human oversight with human-in-the-loop checkpoints for high-stakes inferences and dispute channels; inclusion ensures companions are fair, accessible, and responsive to diverse learners, abilities, languages, and contexts.
requirements: High-stakes inferences such as mastery promotion, at-risk flags, and achievement predictions should incorporate human-in-the-loop checkpoints
constraints: The paper states accountability must be learning-aligned: companions should be evaluated on impact on retention, transfer, metacognition, and durable learning, not only output accuracy
target_learners: diverse learners, abilities, languages, and contexts
target_learning_goals: calibrated trust
learner agency
equitable access to AI-supported learning

article_title: LUDIA: A Design and Evidence Statement
citation: Stark, B., & Rostan, J. (2026). LUDIA: A design and evidence statement (Version 1.0). Ask LUDIA. https://askludia.com/en
title: Design AI planning tools to redirect attention from fixing the learner to reducing barriers in the design
description: The principle holds that the barrier lives in the design, not in the learner, and that an AI thought partner for inclusive design should embody this by default. LUDIA is described as "redirecting educators away from fixing the learner and towards reducing barriers in the design of instruction and learning environments", doing so in every exchange without being asked, and supporting educators in working through engagement, representation, and action and expression before a learner meets the barrier. The authors tie this to an asset-based mindset in which focusing on strengths and embracing learner variability creates space to identify and reduce barriers within the designer's circle of influence.
requirements: Every response must be grounded in the UDL framework and its Guidelines so the reasoning, not only the suggestion, is visible
constraints: The authors state this is a statement of intent, not a demonstrated effect; the model's tendency to validate user views is not removed by instruction
target_learners: Educators, instructional designers, and learning leaders
target_learning_goals: Anticipating who a design might exclude and reducing barriers before learners encounter them
examples: LUDIA supports educators in anticipating who a design might exclude, and why, at the moment a design decision is still open
key_sources: Stark, B., & Rostan, J. (2026). LUDIA: A design and evidence statement (Version 1.0). Ask LUDIA. https://askludia.com/en

article_title: Mapping the Distribution and Depth of Metacognitive Processes in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Evidence from Interaction Logs and Concurrent Think-Aloud Protocols
citation: Li Shijin & Liu Junjian. (2026). Mapping the Distribution and Depth of Metacognitive Processes in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Evidence from Interaction Logs and Concurrent Think-Aloud Protocols. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081365
title: Reciprocal monitoring–control architecture with planning as prospective control and regulation as adaptive control
description: The study organizes observable metacognitive processes through the reciprocal monitoring–control architecture, in which "monitoring provides information about the current state of cognition, whereas control selects, initiates, modifies, or terminates subsequent cognitive activity." Within it, planning is treated as prospective control and regulation as adaptive changes made after evaluation or feedback. The metacognitive agent is the learner, with GenAI treated as an external cognitive resource whose outputs become objects of monitoring and control; a prompt can externalize planning, a criterion judgment can externalize monitoring, and a targeted revision can externalize regulation.
requirements: Coding requires separating prospective organization (planning), evaluative checking without enacted change (monitoring), and observable modification after feedback or evaluation (regulation) as mutually exclusive primary labels
constraints: The study does not assess metacognitive knowledge, motivation, affect, monitoring accuracy, or learning outcomes; a fluent model response is not itself evidence of learner metacognition
target_learners: undergraduate students using generative AI for instructional-design tasks
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring and control during GenAI-assisted learning tasks
examples: In the 90-minute DeepSeek task, prompts specifying goals or constraints were coded as planning, judgments comparing model responses with task criteria as monitoring, and revisions after such judgments as regulation
key_sources: Li Shijin & Liu Junjian. (2026). Mapping the Distribution and Depth of Metacognitive Processes in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Evidence from Interaction Logs and Concurrent Think-Aloud Protocols. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081365

article_title: Mapping the Distribution and Depth of Metacognitive Processes in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Evidence from Interaction Logs and Concurrent Think-Aloud Protocols
citation: Li Shijin & Liu Junjian. (2026). Mapping the Distribution and Depth of Metacognitive Processes in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Evidence from Interaction Logs and Concurrent Think-Aloud Protocols. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081365
title: Design GenAI learning activities with reciprocal monitoring–control checkpoints that link criteria, judgments, and revisions
description: The article proposes, as a design hypothesis rather than an established recommendation, scaffolds that make the informational relation between monitoring and control explicit: "Such a scaffold could prompt learners to externalize a goal or evaluative criterion as prospective control, compare the current AI response or developing artifact with that criterion, select and justify an adaptation when a discrepancy is identified, and monitor the resulting state." In a ZPD-informed variant, prompt frequency and specificity could be adjusted or faded as learners demonstrate they can articulate and apply their own criteria.
requirements: Controlled studies comparing alternative scaffolds with independently assessed outcomes are needed before efficacy can be claimed
constraints: The authors state these features should be regarded as design propositions rather than evidence-based prescriptions, because the task explicitly encouraged planning and revision
target_learners: undergraduate learners working with generative AI on structured design tasks
target_learning_goals: coordinating monitoring with control when evaluating and revising AI-generated content
examples: The proposed cycle has learners state a criterion before generation, record a judgment after inspecting output, and connect any revision to that judgment, with new information returning the learner to any function

article_title: Community-Based AI Learning: Redistributing Artificial Intelligence's Epistemic Authority in Education
citation: Santiago Ojeda-Ramirez, Symone Gyles and Kylie Peppler. 2026. Community-Based AI Learning: Redistributing Artificial Intelligence's Epistemic Authority in Education. In Proceedings of 2026 Conference for Research on Equitable and Sustained Participation in Engineering, Computing, and Technology (RESPECT 2026). https://doi.org/10.1145/3796496.3811760
title: Redistribute epistemic authority by positioning AI as one voice among many in a community of inquiry
description: Community-based AI learning "refuses the configuration of AI as ultimate authority and, instead, positions learners as legitimate knowers of their communities." Authority becomes relational and conditional as learners evaluate when AI assistance is appropriate and when it should be resisted, supplemented, or rejected. In practice, AI outputs are evaluated through dialogue with people holding situated local knowledge, reorienting AI education from student-machine toward human-community epistemic relationships.
requirements: Learning spaces must include community members whose lived experience and local knowledge can shape what students accept or question in AI outputs
constraints: The redistribution does not dismiss AI; it reframes it as one interpretive input among others
target_learners: Students and educators in AI-integrated classrooms
target_learning_goals: Judging when AI assistance is appropriate, should be supplemented, or rejected
examples: Jadallah and Ballard are cited as finding that community members brought knowledge of specific watersheds, land histories, and local ecological conditions that professional scientists did not hold.
key_sources: Santiago Ojeda-Ramirez, Symone Gyles and Kylie Peppler. 2026. Community-Based AI Learning: Redistributing Artificial Intelligence's Epistemic Authority in Education. In Proceedings of 2026 Conference for Research on Equitable and Sustained Participation in Engineering, Computing, and Technology (RESPECT 2026). https://doi.org/10.1145/3796496.3811760

article_title: RAISE the Standard: A Framework for Transparent Reporting of Artificial Intelligence Studies in Education
citation: Allison, J. (2026). RAISE the Standard: A Framework for Transparent Reporting of Artificial Intelligence Studies in Education. Journal of Educational Computing Research, 64(1), 3-15. https://doi.org/10.1177/07356331251377430
title: Report AI system specification (model identity, version, configuration) as core methodological information
description: Because prompt outcomes and learner effects vary with model versions and settings, the article argues that reporting model identity, version, provider, access conditions, and key configuration choices is essential for interpreting results and enabling replication. It states: "Prompt outcomes and learner effects can change substantially with different model versions or settings, so transparent details regarding specifications is not optional but core methodological information." This grounds the AI System Specification domain of RAISE.
requirements: Manuscripts state which model was used, how the system was configured (e.g., prompts, fine-tuning parameters), and access conditions
target_learners: Researchers deploying AI tools in educational studies
target_learning_goals: Replicability and interpretability of AI intervention findings
examples: The editorial cites systematic reviews of prompt engineering in higher education stressing that model and setting details materially shape educational outputs
key_sources: Allison, J. (2026). RAISE the Standard: A Framework for Transparent Reporting of Artificial Intelligence Studies in Education. Journal of Educational Computing Research, 64(1), 3-15. https://doi.org/10.1177/07356331251377430

article_title: RAISE the Standard: A Framework for Transparent Reporting of Artificial Intelligence Studies in Education
citation: Allison, J. (2026). RAISE the Standard: A Framework for Transparent Reporting of Artificial Intelligence Studies in Education. Journal of Educational Computing Research, 64(1), 3-15. https://doi.org/10.1177/07356331251377430
title: Report the role and expertise of humans designing and overseeing AI tools
description: Outcomes depend on the human ecosystem around the AI: teacher facilitation, who designed prompts or systems, and the level of human oversight. The article grounds this in cited findings: "Knoth et al (2024) found that individuals with higher-quality prompt engineering skills predict the quality of LLM outputs, while Jacobsen and Weber (2025) conclude that educators must be skilled in prompt engineering and utilising AI tools to achieve optimal results." RAISE therefore calls for transparent reporting on both the role and expertise of those involved in designing and utilising AI tools.
requirements: Report who engineered prompts/systems and the pedagogical expertise involved
target_learners: Educators and researchers designing or facilitating AI-supported learning
target_learning_goals: Accurate attribution of effects to human facilitation versus AI system behaviour
examples: The Human Involvement domain (domain 6) of the checklist operationalises this reporting requirement

article_title: AI as a cognitive partner in learning: Emerging epistemic practices of reflective thought
citation: Dalsgaard, C., & Prilop, C. N. (2026). AI as a cognitive partner in learning: Emerging epistemic practices of reflective thought. Journal of Research on Technology in Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/15391523.2026.2695013
title: Framework for reflective thought: examination, construction, and empirical versus theoretical reflection as mediating processes
description: The article applies a framework for reflective thought (Dalsgaard, 2018, 2020), drawing on Dewey's inquiry and Schön's reflection-in-action, to analyze whether students' AI practices are epistemic. Reflective thought is goal-directed and performed through iterative processes of examination (goal-directed study of materials), construction (developing hypotheses, methods, solutions), and reflection. It operates with two kinds of reflection: "Empirical reflection is an evaluation of the result of an action (solution) in relation to the goal of the action", while theoretical reflection evaluates the solution in relation to concepts or theories. The framework is used to code interview data and to map how AI supports each process (Figures 1 and 3).
requirements: Tools define how goals can be achieved, so the framework presupposes identifying the mediating instruments in students' goal-directed activity
constraints: Developed from Dewey's and Davydov's distinctions; applied here to upper secondary students' schoolwork with generative AI chatbots
target_learning_goals: reflective thought and knowledge construction in subject-area schoolwork
examples: Students writing a political speech engage in empirical reflection by assessing whether it resembles an actual speech, and theoretical reflection by relating it to rhetorical devices such as logos and pathos
key_sources: Dalsgaard, C., & Prilop, C. N. (2026). AI as a cognitive partner in learning: Emerging epistemic practices of reflective thought. Journal of Research on Technology in Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/15391523.2026.2695013

article_title: A Framework for Evaluation of Large Language Models in Essay Assessment: Reliability, Alignment, and Causal Reasoning
citation: Tongxi Liu, Luyao Ye, Wei Yan. (2026). A framework for evaluation of large language models in essay assessment: Reliability, alignment, and causal reasoning. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100565
title: Validate LLM scoring systems for reliability before classroom deployment and adopt predefined reliability thresholds for high-stakes use
description: The article argues that just as human raters undergo calibration and moderation, LLMs should be empirically validated for reliability before classroom deployment. It recommends technical safeguards — "multi-run averaging, deterministic inference (via fixed random seeds or low-temperature decoding), and ensemble-based calibration" — as algorithmic counterparts to inter-rater moderation, and institutional adoption of predefined reliability thresholds (e.g., ICC ≥ 0.90) as operational standards for high-stakes assessments.
requirements: Empirical reliability validation of the model before deployment
Technical safeguards such as multi-run averaging or deterministic inference
Institutionally adopted reliability thresholds for high-stakes contexts
constraints: Grounded in the article's findings on long-essay scoring by non-native speakers in higher education; the article notes run-to-run variability, though statistically modest, may have substantive educational consequences
target_learners: Higher education students assessed with AI-assisted essay scoring
target_learning_goals: Fair, trustworthy, and reproducible automated writing assessment
examples: The article proposes ICC ≥ 0.90 as an operational standard for high-stakes AI scoring, mirroring the human benchmark established in its own data

article_title: Interleaved practice improves mathematics learning.
citation: Rohrer, D., Dedrick, R. F., & Stershic, S. (2015). Interleaved practice improves mathematics learning. Journal of Educational Psychology, 107(3), 900-908. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000001
title: Rearrange mathematics practice so a portion of each assignment mixes different kinds of problems (interleaved practice)
description: The article recommends rearranging, rather than rewriting, existing practice material: with interleaved practice, "a portion of each assignment includes a set of different kinds of problems presented in an intermixed order". This forces students to choose a strategy based on the problem itself and distributes problems of the same kind across assignments, producing spacing. The authors state creators of textbooks or software "need only rearrange practice problems before releasing the next edition, without altering the problems or lessons".
requirements: Assignments must include a small block of new-skill problems plus one problem on each of several previously learned skills
Teachers must present solutions and students correct errors; teacher buy-in benefits from understanding the logic of strategy choice
constraints: Benefits might have been smaller if test problems required greater transfer
A more intensive review might have benefited the blocked condition more
Generalization to a wider variety of material and more teachers and students remains unknown
target_learners: mathematics students across elementary, middle school, and college levels
target_learning_goals: strategy selection for mathematics problems
delayed retention of mathematics skills
examples: In the experiment, each assignment included four problems on the skill learned that day plus one problem on each of eight different skills learned previously; teachers reported they would use and recommend the intervention

article_title: Improving Students’ Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology
citation: Dunlosky, J., Rawson, K. A., Marsh, E. J., Nathan, M. J., & Willingham, D. T. (2013). Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4–58. https://doi.org/10.1177/1529100612453266
title: Replace rereading and highlighting with more effective techniques such as practice testing
description: The monograph recommends that students abandon the popular but inconsistently effective techniques of rereading and highlighting in favor of better-supported alternatives. It states that "Most students report rereading and highlighting, yet these techniques do not consistently boost students' performance, so other techniques should be used in their place (e.g., practice testing instead of rereading)." The recommendation follows directly from the low utility assessments of those techniques.
requirements: Students must be able to implement the replacement technique without assistance, per the monograph's selection criteria
target_learners: students from elementary grades through college regulating their own learning
target_learning_goals: improving retention and achievement across content domains
examples: The monograph explicitly names practice testing as the substitute for rereading

article_title: Annual Age-Grouping and Athlete Development
citation: Cobley, S., Baker, J., Wattie, N., McKenna, J. (2009). Annual Age-Grouping and Athlete Development. Sports Med 39, 235–256. https://doi.org/10.2165/00007256-200939030-00005
title: Relative age effects (RAEs) as participation and attainment constraints arising from annual age-grouping
description: The article defines RAEs as constraints on sport participation and long-term attainment that arise when athletes are organized into annual age-group cohorts. It states that RAEs occur "as a result of chronological age and associated physical (e.g. height) differences as well as selection practices in annual age-grouped cohorts." The framework links organizational strategy (annual age-grouping), physical maturation differences within cohorts, and selection practices as jointly producing the effect.
requirements: Annual age-grouped cohorts with selection practices that differentiate athletes within the cohort
constraints: The effect is framed for sport contexts organized by annual age-grouping
target_learning_goals: sport participation and long-term athlete attainment

article_title: Reflection and reflective practice in health professions education: a systematic review
citation: Mann, K., Gordon, J. & MacLeod, A. (2009). Reflection and reflective practice in health professions education: a systematic review. Adv in Health Sci Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-007-9090-2
title: Reflective practice as an integral component of professional learning that integrates theory and practice throughout courses of study
description: The review treats reflection and reflective practice as an educational process central to professional competence, in which students "act and to think professionally as an integral part of learning throughout their courses of study, integrating theory and practice from the outset". The review was designed to understand the key variables influencing this educational process, identify gaps in the evidence, and explore implications for educational practice and research. Its organizing premise is that reflective practice links professional action and thinking to learning across the whole course of study rather than to isolated exercises.
requirements: Educators embed reflection across courses of study rather than as isolated activities
constraints: The evidence base for the process is described as largely theoretical
target_learning_goals: professional competence
integration of theory and practice
examples: The review evaluated existing evidence about reflection and reflective practice and their utility in health professional education

article_title: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design
citation: Sweller, J., van Merrienboer, J.J.G. & Paas, F.G.W.C. (1998). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1022193728205
title: Design instruction to reduce working memory load and encourage schema construction
description: The article's central design principle is that instruction should be built on "the assumption that working memory load should be reduced and schema construction encouraged." Because working memory is limited while schema construction drives learning, presentation of information should be arranged to lower unnecessary load and support schema building. The article reports that a variety of novel instructional procedures were designed on this basis.
requirements: Instructional designers must know which activities impose working memory load and which support schema construction
target_learners: All learners of instructional materials designed under cognitive load theory
target_learning_goals: Optimizing intellectual performance through schema construction
examples: The article states that cognitive architecture structures "have been used to design a variety of novel instructional procedures" based on the load-reduction and schema-construction assumption
key_sources: Sweller, J., van Merrienboer, J.J.G. & Paas, F.G.W.C. (1998). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1022193728205

article_title: Are All Program Elements Created Equal? Relations Between Specific Social and Emotional Learning Components and Teacher–Student Classroom Interaction Quality
citation: Abry, T., Rimm-Kaufman, S.E. & Curby, T.W. (2017). Are All Program Elements Created Equal? Relations Between Specific Social and Emotional Learning Components and Teacher–Student Classroom Interaction Quality. Prevention Science, 18, 193–203. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-016-0743-3
title: Responsive Classroom core component indices: Morning Meeting, Rule Creation, Interactive Modeling, and Academic Choice
description: The Responsive Classroom approach is a school-based social and emotional learning program whose implementation was indexed through four core components. The article states that "Indices of teachers' implementation of Morning Meeting, Rule Creation, Interactive Modeling, and Academic Choice were derived from a combination of teacher-reported surveys and classroom observations." These component indices served as predictors of teacher–student classroom interaction quality among 143 treatment teachers in third, fourth, and fifth grade classrooms within a randomized controlled trial.
requirements: Implementation measured via a combination of teacher-reported surveys and classroom observations
target_learners: Elementary school students in third, fourth, and fifth grade
target_learning_goals: Social and emotional learning
Quality of teacher–student classroom interactions
examples: Ratings of teacher–student classroom interactions were aggregated across five observations conducted throughout the school year.
key_sources: Abry, T., Rimm-Kaufman, S.E. & Curby, T.W. (2017). Are All Program Elements Created Equal? Relations Between Specific Social and Emotional Learning Components and Teacher–Student Classroom Interaction Quality. Prevention Science, 18, 193–203. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-016-0743-3

article_title: Increased Course Structure Improves Performance in Introductory Biology
citation: Freeman Scott, Haak David, Wenderoth Mary Pat. (2011). Increased Course Structure Improves Performance in Introductory Biology. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.10-08-0105
title: Use pre-class reading quizzes on lower-order content to free class time for higher-order active learning
description: The article argues that reading quizzes focused on Levels 1 and 2 of Bloom's taxonomy shift the burden of learning basic vocabulary and concepts to the student, "free[ing] time in class for active learning exercises that challenge students to apply concepts, analyze data, propose experimental designs, or evaluate conflicting pieces of evidence." This answers the standard objection that active learning requires drastically reducing content coverage. Because Bloom's taxonomy is hierarchical, students cannot work at the application or analysis level without knowing the basic vocabulary and concepts, so the authors see reading quizzes as an essential component of successful highly structured course designs.
requirements: Reading quizzes must be paired with in-class activities that operate at higher Bloom's levels; without them, informal group activities or peer instruction with clickers are unlikely to be maximally effective
target_learners: Undergraduates in large introductory STEM gateway courses
target_learning_goals: Acquiring basic vocabulary and concepts independently, and developing application- and analysis-level skills in class
examples: Reading quizzes in the study consisted of 5–10 open-book, open-note multiple-choice questions delivered online, opening after class and closing the morning of the next class, summing to about 8% of total course points
key_sources: Freeman Scott, Haak David, Wenderoth Mary Pat. (2011). Increased Course Structure Improves Performance in Introductory Biology. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.10-08-0105

article_title: A new criterion for assessing discriminant validity in variance-based structural equation modeling
citation: Henseler, J., Ringle, C. M., & Sarstedt, M. (2015). A new criterion for assessing discriminant validity in variance-based structural equation modeling. J. of the Acad. Mark. Sci. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11747-014-0403-8
title: Use HTMT criteria rather than the Fornell-Larcker criterion or cross-loadings for discriminant validity assessment in variance-based SEM
description: The article recommends replacing the traditional Fornell-Larcker and cross-loadings checks with HTMT-based assessment: "we strongly recommend drawing on the HTMT criteria for discriminant validity assessment in variance-based SEM." The choice among HTMT.85, HTMT.90, and HTMT inference depends on the model set-up and how conservative the researcher wishes to be: HTMT.85 is the strictest standard, while HTMT.90 or HTMT inference suit settings where constructs are conceptually different but empirically hard to distinguish.
requirements: Access to item-level correlations or raw data to compute HTMT
A decision on the threshold or test variant appropriate to the constructs' conceptual similarity
constraints: HTMT.85 can point to problems where HTMT.90 and HTMT inference indicate validity is established; HTMT inference is unlikely to flag problems even at correlations close to 1.0 when loadings are homogeneous and high or the sample is large
target_learners: Researchers and practitioners applying variance-based SEM in marketing and other social sciences
target_learning_goals: Reliable evaluation of measurement models before interpreting structural relationships
examples: The authors suggest HTMT.90 or HTMT inference for technology acceptance models where intention to use and actual use are conceptually different but empirically difficult to distinguish, and HTMT.85 where the strictest standards are followed
key_sources: Henseler, J., Ringle, C. M., & Sarstedt, M. (2015). A new criterion for assessing discriminant validity in variance-based structural equation modeling. J. of the Acad. Mark. Sci. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11747-014-0403-8

article_title: INCIDENTAL L2 VOCABULARY ACQUISITION FROM AND WHILE READING
citation: Pellicer-Sánchez, Ana. (2016). Incidental L2 Vocabulary Acquisition From and While Reading: An Eye-Tracking Study. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 38(1), 97-130. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263115000224
title: Design extensive reading materials so that unknown vocabulary items recur about eight times for substantial incidental learning
description: The study's findings support building repeated encounters of unknown vocabulary into extensive reading materials. L2 readers needed about "three to four encounters" before reading times on unknown items dropped significantly, and by eight encounters previously unknown words were read like known words while form and meaning recognition reached high levels. Materials should therefore embed target items at least eight times within a limited time span.
requirements: Target items must recur multiple times within a single coherent text; the study embedded six nonwords, each repeated eight times, in a 2,300-word story with about 98% coverage of known vocabulary.
constraints: Gains were measured on an immediate posttest with advanced L2 readers; the delayed-test analysis included only 14 of the initial 23 participants, which the article notes makes generalizability less robust.
target_learning_goals: Incidental acquisition of word form and meaning from reading
examples: Participants read a 2,300-word story in which six nonwords and six control words each appeared eight times, with eye movements recorded and three vocabulary tests administered afterward.
key_sources: Pellicer-Sánchez, Ana. (2016). Incidental L2 Vocabulary Acquisition From and While Reading: An Eye-Tracking Study. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 38(1), 97-130. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263115000224

article_title: A Reconsideration of Cognitive Load Theory
citation: Schnotz, W., Kürschner, C. (2007). A Reconsideration of Cognitive Load Theory. Educational Psychology Review 19, 469–508. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9053-4
title: Reconsidered cognitive load theory distinguishing intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load and their conceptual problems
description: The article re-examines cognitive load theory by analyzing the conceptual distinctions between different kinds of cognitive load. It argues that "the theory allows different and contradicting possibilities to explain some empirical results", so that "various generalizations of empirical results become questionable". The theory is reconsidered from the perspective of Vygotski's zone of proximal development and from research on implicit learning.
requirements: The framework requires distinguishing task performance from learning as related but fundamentally different processes
constraints: The article states the conceptual distinctions between different kinds of cognitive load are not fully equivalent, making some generalizations questionable
target_learning_goals: knowledge and skill acquisition
key_sources: Schnotz, W., Kürschner, C. (2007). A Reconsideration of Cognitive Load Theory. Educational Psychology Review 19, 469–508. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9053-4

article_title: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design
citation: Sweller, J., van Merrienboer, J.J.G. & Paas, F.G.W.C. (1998). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1022193728205
title: Design instruction to reduce working memory load and encourage schema construction
description: The article states that cognitive load theory's cognitive architecture has been used to design novel instructional procedures "based on the assumption that working memory load should be reduced and schema construction encouraged." The principle directs designers to present information in ways that lower unnecessary working memory demands while supporting the building and automation of schemas in long-term memory.
requirements: An account of the learner's cognitive architecture, specifically limited working memory and schema-based long-term memory, from which the design guidelines are derived.
target_learners: learners generally, across domains addressed by cognitive load theory
target_learning_goals: schema construction and automation; optimized intellectual performance
examples: The article reports that these structures and functions of human cognitive architecture have been used to design a variety of novel instructional procedures.
key_sources: Sweller, J., van Merrienboer, J.J.G. & Paas, F.G.W.C. (1998). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1022193728205

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory and Complex Learning: Recent Developments and Future Directions
citation: van Merriënboer, J.J.G., Sweller, J. (2005). Cognitive Load Theory and Complex Learning: Recent Developments and Future Directions. Educ Psychol Rev 17, 147–177 (2005). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-005-3951-0
title: Use real-life tasks as the driving force for complex learning
description: The article endorses the current instructional-design view that whole, real-life tasks should organize complex learning rather than decontextualized part practice. It states that recent CLT developments relate to "the current view in instructional design that real-life tasks should be the driving force for complex learning." Because such tasks impose high intrinsic load, this principle must be paired with load-management methods such as scaffolding and fading.
requirements: New methods to manage the high intrinsic cognitive load of real-life tasks
constraints: Intrinsic cognitive load of real-life tasks is often high, so the principle cannot be applied without load management
target_learning_goals: Transferable performance of complex, real-life tasks
key_sources: van Merriënboer, J.J.G., Sweller, J. (2005). Cognitive Load Theory and Complex Learning: Recent Developments and Future Directions. Educ Psychol Rev 17, 147–177 (2005). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-005-3951-0

article_title: The effect of automated feedback on revision behavior and learning gains in formative assessment of scientific argument writing
citation: Pineda Corcho, Andrés Felipe. (2021). Modelo de evaluación formativa en cursos virtuales de Matemáticas y su aplicación en analítica de aprendizaje. Tesis de Doctorado en Ingeniería - Sistemas. https://repositorio.unal.edu.co/handle/unal/80892
title: Revisión sistemática de literatura sobre evaluación formativa y analíticas de aprendizaje en cursos virtuales
description: Como parte de la definición del modelo, la tesis realiza "una revisión sistemática de la literatura con el fin de identificar los últimos avances en cuanto a metodologías, herramientas, así como otros modelos aplicados en esta área". Esta revisión fundamenta el planteamiento del problema y las preguntas de investigación que guían el diseño e implementación del modelo de evaluación formativa integrado con analíticas de aprendizaje.
requirements: Partir de un marco conceptual que explore los conceptos base del trabajo
target_learners: investigadores y diseñadores de cursos virtuales
target_learning_goals: identificación de avances en metodologías y herramientas para evaluación formativa y analíticas de aprendizaje
key_sources: Pineda Corcho, Andrés Felipe. (2021). Modelo de evaluación formativa en cursos virtuales de Matemáticas y su aplicación en analítica de aprendizaje. Tesis de Doctorado en Ingeniería - Sistemas. https://repositorio.unal.edu.co/handle/unal/80892

article_title: Teacher Turnover and Teacher Shortages: An Organizational Analysis
citation: Ingersoll, R. M. (2001). Teacher Turnover and Teacher Shortages: An Organizational Analysis. American Educational Research Journal, 38(3), 499-534. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Teacher+Turnover+and+Teacher+Shortages+Ingersoll
title: Address organizational sources of low retention, not just recruitment, to solve school staffing problems
description: Because staffing problems stem primarily from excess demand created by departing teachers rather than insufficient supply, the article argues the solution lies in decreasing demand rather than increasing supply. As it concludes, "teacher recruitment programs alone will not solve the staffing problems of schools if they do not also address the organizational sources of low retention." Recruitment initiatives should therefore be paired with improvements to workplace conditions such as administrative support, student discipline, and faculty influence.
requirements: Policymakers must diagnose whether local staffing problems arise from turnover-driven excess demand rather than supply deficits before choosing interventions
constraints: The article's evidence base is the SASS/TFS surveys of the late 1980s through mid-1990s; self-reported departure reasons are retrospective attributions subject to bias
target_learners: Education policymakers, district administrators, and school leaders
target_learning_goals: Reducing school staffing problems and improving teacher retention
examples: The article contrasts the dominant supply-side policy response—troops-to-teachers, Teach for America, alternative licensing, and financial incentives—with its demand-side findings from the SASS/TFS analysis.
key_sources: Ingersoll, R. M. (2001). Teacher Turnover and Teacher Shortages: An Organizational Analysis. American Educational Research Journal, 38(3), 499-534. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Teacher+Turnover+and+Teacher+Shortages+Ingersoll

article_title: Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics
citation: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3
title: Record descriptions of behavior, not inferences, that are unambiguous and contextualized
description: The chapter holds that telemetry "should have the following properties: (a) is a description of behavior and not an inference about why behavior occurs, (b) is unambiguous," and (c) contains sufficient context to link the element to a specific player at a specific point. Logging an inference such as does not understand adding fractions may be inaccurate without validity evidence, restricts later analyses, and can subsume multiple events into uninterpretable aggregates; ambiguity should be avoided so single events remain distinguishable.
requirements: Validity evidence on any interpretation before logging it as an inference
A 1:1 correspondence between the data element and an event, e.g., uniquely identifying which of ten buttons was clicked
Two classes of context: student information (schooling, prior knowledge, demographics, motivation) and game experience information (game state variables, feedback)
constraints: Contextualization is bounded by what is feasible to encode about the conditions under which data were generated
target_learners: players of serious games whose logs are later analyzed by researchers
target_learning_goals: distinguishing actual gameplay behavior from interpretations of competency
examples: Adding two fraction objects incorrectly is logged descriptively as incorrect addition rather than inferentially as the player does not understand how to add fractions
key_sources: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3

article_title: Culture and Mathematics in School: Boundaries between "Cultural" and "Domain" Knowledge in the Mathematics Classroom and Beyond
citation: Na'ilah Suad Nasir, Victoria Hand and Edd V. Taylor. (2008). Culture and Mathematics in School: Boundaries between "Cultural" and "Domain" Knowledge in the Mathematics Classroom and Beyond. Review of Research in Education, Vol. 32. https://doi.org/10.3102/0091732X07308962
title: Reform mathematics classrooms share four design features: problematizing subject matter, distributed authority, student agency, and accountability to others' thinking
description: A line of research on mathematics classroom cultures identified key features of reform classrooms that foster productive, domain-based inquiry. The article enumerates them: "giving students the opportunity to problematize the subject matter in a way that is meaningful to them, distributing authority to them to develop and evaluate their mathematical methods, supporting students in exercising agency," and holding students accountable to each other's mathematical thinking and questioning. The pattern operates at lesson and classroom-community level, instantiated in studies by Boaler, Chazan, Engle & Conant, Hiebert et al., Lampert, and Yackel & Cobb.
requirements: Classroom norms and practices must be organized so students can problematize meaningful subject matter, exercise agency, and hold each other accountable
constraints: The review notes researchers have questioned how what counts as an argument or mathematical activity relates to participation forms students bring from home communities
target_learners: students in K-12 mathematics classrooms, particularly nondominant and marginalized students
target_learning_goals: productive domain-based mathematical inquiry
constructing and responding to mathematical arguments
examples: Lampert's fifth-grade classroom, where a sociomathematical norm emerged concerning how one engages in a mathematical argument
Railside detracked classrooms using Complex Instruction with groupworthy mathematical tasks
key_sources: Na'ilah Suad Nasir, Victoria Hand and Edd V. Taylor. (2008). Culture and Mathematics in School: Boundaries between "Cultural" and "Domain" Knowledge in the Mathematics Classroom and Beyond. Review of Research in Education, Vol. 32. https://doi.org/10.3102/0091732X07308962

article_title: Evidence-Based Strategies for Reading Instruction of Older Students with Learning Disabilities
citation: Roberts, G., Torgesen, J. K., Boardman, A., & Scammacca, N. (2008). Evidence-Based Strategies for Reading Instruction of Older Students with Learning Disabilities. Learning Disabilities Research & Practice, 23(2), 63–69. http://www.centeroninstruction.org/
title: Never substitute wide or repeated reading alone for explicit word study and comprehension strategy instruction
description: The article states plainly that for students with LD, reading practice by itself should not replace explicit instruction: "wide reading or repeated reading by itself should never substitute for systematic, explicit instruction in word study and comprehension strategy use." Fluency instruction may be most effective when combined with word-level and comprehension instruction, since improved fluency frees cognitive resources that strategy instruction helps students use.
requirements: Coordination of fluency practice with focused word-learning instruction tied to the passages used
constraints: Repeated reading gains generalize only to passages sharing many of the same words; effects of differing fluency approaches for older students need additional research
target_learners: Older students with learning disabilities who struggle with reading
target_learning_goals: Reading fluency
Word recognition
Reading comprehension
examples: The article recommends repeated reading of passages with instructional target words embedded in otherwise readable text, and teacher-supported wide reading of texts with a preponderance of known words
key_sources: Roberts, G., Torgesen, J. K., Boardman, A., & Scammacca, N. (2008). Evidence-Based Strategies for Reading Instruction of Older Students with Learning Disabilities. Learning Disabilities Research & Practice, 23(2), 63–69. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5826.2008.00264.x

article_title: Let me be your guide: physical guidance improves spatial learning for older adults with simulated low vision
citation: Barhorst-Cates Erica M., Rand Kristina M., Creem-Regehr Sarah H. (2017). Let Me be Your Guide: Physical Guidance Improves Spatial Learning for Older Adults with Simulated Low Vision. Experimental Brain Research. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00221-017-5063-8
title: Reduce mobility monitoring demands (e.g., via physical guidance) to support spatial learning during low-vision navigation
description: The principle holds that safety- and stability-related mobility monitoring consumes attentional resources that would otherwise support spatial learning of an environment, so physically supporting the learner's mobility frees resources for encoding. In the study, "the experimenter instructed the participant to hold onto the experimenter's arm throughout the path" in the guided condition while verbal route guidance was held constant. This improved pointing accuracy and the benefit grew with age.
requirements: The aid must reduce mobility demands without adding navigational guidance that divides attention; the article contrasts physical guidance with GPS-style aids that impair spatial learning
constraints: The cognitive-load (RT) and anxiety measures did not differ between conditions, so the mechanism is not confirmed
Tested only with simulated degraded acuity and contrast sensitivity in a real-world indoor building-scale environment; the article calls for testing in clinical low-vision populations
target_learners: adults navigating under degraded viewing conditions
target_learning_goals: survey knowledge / spatial memory of landmarks along a route
examples: Participants walked four unique real-world paths (109–121 m) wearing degraded-vision goggles, two guided and two unguided, with verbal instructions identical across conditions
key_sources: Barhorst-Cates Erica M., Rand Kristina M., Creem-Regehr Sarah H. (2017). Let Me be Your Guide: Physical Guidance Improves Spatial Learning for Older Adults with Simulated Low Vision. Experimental Brain Research. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00221-017-5063-8

article_title: The Adult Learner: Self-Determined, Self-Regulated, and Reflective
citation: Frank Kellenberg, Joel Schmidt, Christian Werner. (2017). The Adult Learner: Self-Determined, Self-Regulated, and Reflective. Signum Temporis 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1515/sigtem-2017-0001
title: Reflective learning as problem-initiated critical consideration aimed at implementing and evaluating solutions
