description: Reflective learning is defined as more than thinking: a process usually initiated in problem situations and aimed at solving the relevant problem through critical consideration with increased consciousness. Following Stangl, reflection must continue past finding a solution into implementing and critically evaluating concrete new behavior, so reflective learning must itself be learned. The article traces the concept from Dewey through Schön to Kolb's four-phase cyclic reflection model, the most frequently used in adult education.
requirements: Reflection must engage with implementation of the intended solution, so a concrete new behavior must be performed and then critically evaluated
constraints: The article states this type of learning is hardly taught in traditional forms of schooling, which do not encourage implementation of knowledge in concrete problem situations
target_learning_goals: problem-solving competence
professional skills and attitudes
examples: Kolb's four-phase model moves from concrete experience through deepened perception and reflection to a new and more differentiated understanding and a newly planned experience
key_sources: Frank Kellenberg, Joel Schmidt, Christian Werner. (2017). The Adult Learner: Self-Determined, Self-Regulated, and Reflective. Signum Temporis 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1515/sigtem-2017-0001

article_title: The Adult Learner: Self-Determined, Self-Regulated, and Reflective
citation: Frank Kellenberg, Joel Schmidt, Christian Werner. (2017). The Adult Learner: Self-Determined, Self-Regulated, and Reflective. Signum Temporis 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1515/sigtem-2017-0001
title: Reflection question tool: sample questions across self-determination, self-regulation and reflection from educator and learner perspectives
description: The reflection question tool is a checklist of sample questions organized by the three areas of self-determination, self-regulation and (self-)reflection, with self-regulation subdivided into plan, monitor and evaluate. It is divided into an Adult Educator Perspective section focusing on preparation of the learning task, and an Adult Learner Perspective section supporting the educator's own self-reflection. The authors state it is by no means comprehensive but provides ideas and direction for educators, trainers and teachers.
requirements: Should be used as orientation to design adult learning programs and reflect on the process, covering preparation, performance and reflection
constraints: The authors state it can be regarded as a basis for further developments through trial and examination in practice, i.e. it is not yet empirically validated
target_learning_goals: designing demand-oriented learning activities
educator self-reflection
examples: Table 1 lists questions such as what choice in terms of topics can be offered, whether strategies offered are effective for the task, and how well the approach worked
key_sources: Frank Kellenberg, Joel Schmidt, Christian Werner. (2017). The Adult Learner: Self-Determined, Self-Regulated, and Reflective. Signum Temporis 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1515/sigtem-2017-0001

article_title: The effects of prior knowledge and text structure on comprehension processes during reading of scientific texts
citation: Kendeou, P., & van den Broek, P. (2007). The effects of prior knowledge and text structure on comprehension processes during reading of scientific texts. Memory & Cognition, 35(7), 1567-1577. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03193591
title: Refutation texts support conceptual change by eliciting coactivation of prior knowledge and text information, enabling inconsistency detection
description: The article proposes a mechanism account of why refutation texts foster conceptual change: during online reading of refutation text, readers coactivate and integrate prior knowledge with text information, which allows them to detect the inconsistency between their knowledge and the text, triggering additional processing to establish coherence. The authors state that "refutation texts help readers engage in conceptual change learning by eliciting coactivation, thereby facilitating inconsistency detection and the establishment of coherence." The account is grounded in the convergent online findings of the two experiments.
requirements: The reader must hold prior knowledge (potentially misconceptions) related to the text topic so that coactivation and inconsistency detection can occur
The text must explicitly identify and refute the misconception rather than merely present correct information
constraints: Conceptual change processes elicited by refutation texts do not inevitably result in successful revision of incorrect ideas, as readers with misconceptions recalled less regardless of structure
The explanation-sentence reading time comparison should be interpreted with caution because explanations differed in content across texts
target_learners: readers of scientific texts with misconceptions about the text topic, such as undergraduates in introductory physics
target_learning_goals: conceptual change in science
comprehension of scientific texts
examples: In Experiment 1, readers with misconceptions generated conceptual change strategies such as experiencing cognitive conflict, responding to conflict, and contrasting information while reading refutation texts
In Experiment 2, readers with misconceptions spent more time reading Newton's law sentences than readers without misconceptions, but only in refutation texts
key_sources: Kendeou, P., & van den Broek, P. (2007). The effects of prior knowledge and text structure on comprehension processes during reading of scientific texts. Memory & Cognition, 35(7), 1567-1577. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03193491

article_title: Reporting and Interpreting Working Memory Performance in n-back Tasks
citation: Meule A (2017). Reporting and Interpreting Working Memory Performance in n-back Tasks. Front. Psychol. 8:352. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00352
title: Differentiate omission and commission errors and report signal-detection indices such as d' and C
description: The article recommends that researchers "not only report accuracy but also diﬀerentiate between omission and commission errors," since the two error types have different correlates. It further suggests reporting indices calculated from hits and false alarms, "such as discrimination index d′ and response bias C," as suggested by researchers using modified n-back versions.
requirements: Researchers must record hits, commission errors, and omission errors separately rather than a single accuracy figure.
constraints: Fine-grained analyses are framed as a way to clarify the n-back task's validity, which has been criticized for lacking clear associations with other working memory tasks.
target_learners: researchers assessing working memory with n-back tasks
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of working memory performance
examples: Kane et al. (2007) and Haatveit et al. (2010) used modified n-back versions with d' and C indices.
key_sources: Meule A (2017). Reporting and Interpreting Working Memory Performance in n-back Tasks. Front. Psychol. 8:352. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00352

article_title: Metacognition for strategy selection during arithmetic problem-solving in young and older adults
citation: Marie Geurten & Patrick Lemaire. (2017). Metacognition for Strategy Selection during Arithmetic Problem Solving in Young and Older Adults. https://www.google.com/search?q=Metacognition+for+Strategy+Selection+during+Arithmetic+Problem+Solving+in+Young+and+Older+Adults
title: Resource account of age invariance and decline in metacognition for strategy selection
description: The article proposes that the accuracy of older adults' metacognitive judgments depends on the cognitive resources a task requires: "Spared metacognitive skills with age would be found for less resource-consuming tasks, and age-related changes for more resource-consuming tasks." In this study, older adults matched young adults' retrospective accuracy under high demands (selection-execution) and exceeded it under low demands (selection-only, homogeneous problems), while their accuracy declined as demands increased. The account is offered to reconcile inconsistent aging findings across tasks.
requirements: Task demands must be measurable or manipulable so that metacognitive accuracy can be compared across less and more resource-consuming conditions
constraints: The authors state further investigations should corroborate the hypothesis, and suggest task-demand effects might be alleviated when crucial cues for accurate judgments are made more salient
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring of one's own strategy selection in arithmetic problem solving
effective regulation of subsequent strategy choices
examples: Older adults' RCJ accuracy was comparable to young adults' in the selection-execution task but higher in the selection-only task, particularly on homogeneous problems
key_sources: Marie Geurten & Patrick Lemaire. (2017). Metacognition for Strategy Selection during Arithmetic Problem Solving in Young and Older Adults. https://www.google.com/search?q=Metacognition+for+Strategy+Selection+during+Arithmetic+Problem+Solving+in+Young+and+Older+Adults

article_title: Self-Control Outdoes Fluid Reasoning in Explaining Vocational and Academic Performance—But Does It?
citation: Schmidt FTC, Lindner C, Etzel JM and Retelsdorf J (2020) Self-Control Outdoes Fluid Reasoning in Explaining Vocational and Academic Performance—But Does It? Front. Psychol. 11:757. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.00757
title: Resource-oriented response-conflict account of trait self-control
description: The article adopts a recent resource-oriented conceptualization of trait self-control in which highly self-controlled individuals succeed not by investing more effort but by handling response conflicts — competing behavioral tendencies between valued goals and short-term rewards — more effectively. The article states that "Individuals with higher self-control are more sensitive to detecting response conflicts, use more effortless strategies to deal with these conflicts" and downregulate them before they become obstacles. This account is used to predict that self-control matters more in high-stakes situations (grades) than low-stakes ones (research tests), where few response conflicts arise.
requirements: Achievement situations must involve response conflicts between valued long-term goals and more immediately rewarding alternatives for trait self-control to confer an advantage
constraints: The article notes it cannot explain whether response-conflict resolution is merely a preliminary step before higher-effort investment, which may actually explain the results
target_learning_goals: scholastic achievement as reflected in grades and standardized domain-specific test performance
examples: The study contrasted high-stakes major GPA with low-stakes curriculum-based mathematics and physics tests to test the account's differential predictions
key_sources: Schmidt FTC, Lindner C, Etzel JM and Retelsdorf J (2020) Self-Control Outdoes Fluid Reasoning in Explaining Vocational and Academic Performance—But Does It? Front. Psychol. 11:757. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.00757

article_title: The association between preschool children's social functioning and their emergent academic skills
citation: Arnold, D. H., Kupersmidt, J. B., Voegler-Lee, M. E., & Marshall, N. (2012). The Association between Preschool Children's Social Functioning and Their Emergent Academic Skills. Early Childhood Research Quarterly. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2011.12.009
title: Reciprocal model of social functioning and academic development with attention difficulties as a central early mechanism
description: The article describes a model of "reciprocal associations between social functioning and academic skills in which problems in either area can lead to difficulties in the other." In this model, attention difficulties limit children's ability to engage in learning activities and benefit from instruction; academic difficulties later breed frustration and aggression; and prosocial behavior serves as a protective factor by increasing teachers' investment and fostering persistence. The present cross-sectional study is offered as a step toward evaluating this model in low-SES preschoolers, not a full test of it.
requirements: Empirical evaluation differentiating aggression, attention difficulties, and prosocial skills, and controlling for their interrelations
constraints: The article states the study "does not provide a full test of the above model" and is cross-sectional, so reciprocal pathways are not tested
target_learners: Preschool children from low-SES, economically disadvantaged backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Emergent preliteracy, language, and mathematics development
examples: The study assessed 467 preschoolers with teacher-rated IOWA Conners and SSRS measures and independent Woodcock-Johnson and PPVT-III academic tests, analyzed with HLM
key_sources: Arnold, D. H., Kupersmidt, J. B., Voegler-Lee, M. E., & Marshall, N. (2012). The Association between Preschool Children's Social Functioning and Their Emergent Academic Skills. Early Childhood Research Quarterly. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2011.12.009

article_title: The Effects of Acute Exercise on Mood, Cognition, Neurophysiology, and Neurochemical Pathways: A Review
citation: Basso Julia C., Suzuki Wendy A. (2017). The Effects of Acute Exercise on Mood, Cognition, Neurophysiology, and Neurochemical Pathways: A Review. Brain Plasticity. https://doi.org/10.3233/BPL-160040
title: Reticular-activating hypofrontality theory of acute exercise
description: Dietrich's reticular-activating hypofrontality theory explains brain resource allocation during exercise. As the review states, "during exercise, the brain's finite supply of energy and resources is shifted from areas involved in cognitive processing like the prefrontal cortex towards areas that are important for motor movement and coordination", causing prefrontal hypoperfusion during exercise, followed by a rebound surge of oxygenated blood that enhances prefrontal function. The review presents fNIRS findings on prefrontal activation after exercise in the context of evaluating this theory.
requirements: Requires measurement of prefrontal and motor-region activity during and after exercise, e.g., via fNIRS or fMRI, to evaluate the hypoperfusion and rebound sequence
constraints: The review notes the theory concerns the period during and immediately following exercise; the fNIRS studies it discusses measured only up to 15 minutes after exercise cessation
target_learning_goals: executive function and inhibitory control
mood regulation
examples: The review evaluates the theory using fNIRS studies showing increased left dorsolateral prefrontal activation during Stroop performance after a 10-minute moderate-intensity exercise bout
key_sources: Basso Julia C., Suzuki Wendy A. (2017). The Effects of Acute Exercise on Mood, Cognition, Neurophysiology, and Neurochemical Pathways: A Review. Brain Plasticity. https://doi.org/10.3233/BPL-160040

article_title: Multi-method brain imaging reveals impaired representations of number as well as altered connectivity in adults with dyscalculia
citation: Bulthé Jessica, Prinsen Jellina, Vanderauwera Jolijn, Duyck Stefanie, Daniels Nicky, Gillebert Céline R., Mantini Dante, Op de Beeck Hans P., De Smedt Bert. (2019). Multi-method brain imaging reveals impaired representations of number as well as altered connectivity in adults with dyscalculia. Neuroimage, 190, 289-302. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2018.06.012
title: Representation-impairment versus disrupted-access hypotheses of neurodevelopmental learning disorders
description: The article organizes its investigation around two hypotheses about the etiology of neurodevelopmental learning disorders such as dyscalculia: impaired cognitive representations versus disrupted connectivity and impaired access to intact representations. It notes these "hypotheses are not mutually exclusive" and applies a multi-method brain imaging approach combining univariate and multivariate fMRI with functional and structural connectivity to test both in one sample. The study concludes both hold: representations are impaired and access is altered.
requirements: Multi-method imaging combining representation-quality measures (MVPA decoding) with connectivity measures in the same sample and task
constraints: Tested in adults with dyscalculia performing a number comparison task; the authors note dyscalculia is heterogeneous and its neural correlates cannot be reduced to one or a few brain areas
target_learners: adults with dyscalculia (specific learning disorder with impairment in mathematics)
target_learning_goals: numerical magnitude processing and calculation-related number representations
examples: 24 adults with dyscalculia and 24 pairwise-matched controls performed symbolic and non-symbolic number comparison in the scanner while univariate, MVPA, and connectivity data were collected
key_sources: Bulthé Jessica, Prinsen Jellina, Vanderauwera Jolijn, Duyck Stefanie, Daniels Nicky, Gillebert Céline R., Mantini Dante, Op de Beeck Hans P., De Smedt Bert. (2019). Multi-method brain imaging reveals impaired representations of number as well as altered connectivity in adults with dyscalculia. Neuroimage, 190, 289-302. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2018.06.012

article_title: Influence of aging on visual perception and visual motor integration in Korean adults
citation: Kim E, Park Y-K, Byun Y-H, Park M-S, Kim H. (2014). Influence of aging on visual perception and visual motor integration in Korean adults. Journal of Exercise Rehabilitation 10(4):245-250. https://doi.org/10.12965/jer.140147
title: Regularly check visual perception and visual-motor integration from an individual's 50s as a critical period for detecting cognitive decline
description: The article recommends that visual perception (VP) and visual-motor integration (VMI) be assessed periodically starting in a person's 50s, because scores on both the K-DTVP-2 and VMI-3R were significantly decreased by then relative to the 20s. It states "it can be suggested that VP and VMI should be regularly checked from an individual's 50s, which is a critical period for detecting cognitive decline by aging." Both instruments could be used for determining the level of cognitive deficit by aging.
requirements: Trained examiners; the article reports all examiners completed educational training and pretests verified inter-examiner reliability before the survey.
constraints: The article notes it could not yet be determined which measurement is the most reliable and sensitive to detect cognitive decline by aging.
target_learning_goals: Detecting age-related cognitive decline through visual perception and visual-motor integration screening
examples: The cross-sectional survey measured 283 adults aged 20-79 across six 10-yr age groups in Daegu and Gyeongbuk, Korea, from April to August 2011.
key_sources: Kim E, Park Y-K, Byun Y-H, Park M-S, Kim H. (2014). Influence of aging on visual perception and visual motor integration in Korean adults. Journal of Exercise Rehabilitation 10(4):245-250. https://doi.org/10.12965/jer.140147

article_title: Development of abstract mathematical reasoning: the case of algebra
citation: Susac A, Bubic A, Vrbanc A and Planinic M (2014) Development of abstract mathematical reasoning: the case of algebra. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 8:679. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2014.00679
title: Teachers should repeatedly encourage formal reasoning rather than assuming equation-rearrangement skill transfers after one exposure
description: The article's concluding recommendation is that mastery of equation rearrangement cannot be presumed from a single exposure, because the concrete-to-abstract transition unfolds over years. As the authors state, "teachers should use every opportunity to encourage students to use formal reasoning – both pattern recognition and effective application of mathematical rules and known procedures." This applies across mathematics and science contexts such as physics problem solving.
requirements: Instruction must recur across grades and subjects, since all participants had been taught rearrangement at least one year prior yet still struggled with all-symbol equations.
constraints: The supporting evidence covers simple three-term equations with multiplication/division only; even 16–17-year-olds struggled with the slightly more complex C equations.
target_learners: Students aged 13–17 in lower-secondary and early-secondary mathematics and science courses
target_learning_goals: Abstract algebraic reasoning
equation rearrangement
transfer of equation-solving skill across contexts
examples: In the study, even students taught rearrangement a year earlier were only 82% accurate on all-symbol equations, and half of participants reported concrete strategies such as inserting numbers.
key_sources: Susac A, Bubic A, Vrbanc A and Planinic M (2014) Development of abstract mathematical reasoning: the case of algebra. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 8:679. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2014.00679

article_title: Math Anxiety in Second and Third Graders and Its Relation to Mathematics Achievement
citation: Wu SS, Barth M, Amin H, Malcarne V and Menon V (2012) Math anxiety in second and third graders and its relation to mathematics achievement. Front. Psychology 3:162. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2012.00162
title: Remediate math anxiety early, attending to both its numerical and its situational and social aspects
description: The article argues that because math anxiety's detrimental effects on math achievement can be detected in the earliest stages of formal math learning, educators and researchers should remediate math anxiety and its deleterious effects in young children. The authors conclude that remediation may require attention to both the domain-specific numerical information processing aspect and the domain-general situational and social aspect of math anxiety, since both subscales were independently related to achievement.
requirements: Assessment with an age-appropriate measure such as the SEMA to identify math anxiety during the earliest stages of math skill development
constraints: The article states additional research is necessary to clarify the behavioral and neural mechanisms by which math anxiety influences math learning in second and third grades
target_learners: second and third graders (7- to 9-year-old children)
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement in early elementary school
examples: The study found both the Numerical Processing Anxiety and Situational and Performance Anxiety subscales significantly correlated with the WIAT-II Math Composite score
key_sources: Wu SS, Barth M, Amin H, Malcarne V and Menon V (2012) Math anxiety in second and third graders and its relation to mathematics achievement. Front. Psychology 3:162. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2012.00162

article_title: Appropriation of a representational tool in a second-language classroom
citation: Wen, Y., Looi, C.-K., & Chen, W. (2015). Appropriation of a representational tool in a second-language classroom. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 10(1), 77–108. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9208-0
title: Representational tool for collaborative L2 writing in a networked classroom
description: A technology-mediated representational tool used by students in small groups during collaborative second-language writing activities. The study investigates "the appropriation of a representational tool by students in small groups" and finds the tool carries "beneficial affordances... that supplement face-to-face communication for second language learning". It functions as one medium among several in a networked classroom where face-to-face and online interactions intertwine.
requirements: Integration into small-group collaborative writing activity
A networked classroom environment combining face-to-face and online interaction
target_learning_goals: second-language writing
collaborative learning
examples: Students in small groups used the tool alongside face-to-face communication during collaborative L2 writing activities in the case study
key_sources: Wen, Y., Looi, C.-K., & Chen, W. (2015). Appropriation of a representational tool in a second-language classroom. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 10(1), 77–108. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9208-0

article_title: The new information literate: Open collaboration and information production in schools
citation: Andrea Forte. (2015). The new information literate: Open collaboration and information production in schools. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. 10:35–51. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9210-6
title: Four dimensions of responsibility for contributing to new knowledge
description: The article unpacks the responsibility students experience when contributing to knowledge building along two axes: shared versus individual, and local versus global. Shared responsibility means advancing a group's knowledge, as in knowledge-building classrooms and some Wikipedia articles; global context means viewing contributions as a social good potentially used by unknown others. In these studies, "the classroom wiki activities did not engender a shared sense of responsibility in the local context of the classroom, it did engender a sense of individual responsibility at a more global level."
requirements: Public information production tasks that place students in the role of supporting others' information needs
constraints: In these studies the shared/local quadrant was not realized; realizing full potential requires guidance and opportunities to support and challenge one another in justifying and critiquing claims
target_learners: High school students contributing to public online information resources
target_learning_goals: Taking responsibility for the quality of shared information; collective cognitive responsibility
examples: Students wrote disease pages and science articles on a public wiki read by unknown others, reporting responsibility for accuracy even if nobody used the resource
key_sources: Andrea Forte. (2015). The new information literate: Open collaboration and information production in schools. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. 10:35–51. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9210-6

article_title: ReaderBench: Automated evaluation of collaboration based on cohesion and dialogism
citation: Mihai Dascalu, Stefan Trausan-Matu, Danielle S. Mcnamara, Philippe Dessus. (2015). ReaderBench – Automated Evaluation of Collaboration based on Cohesion and Dialogism. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9226-y
title: ReaderBench environment for automated evaluation of collaboration from cohesion and dialogism
description: ReaderBench is the system the article introduces as implementing automated evaluation of collaboration based on cohesion and dialogism. Motivated by the growing use of CSCL, it addresses "the need for automated tools capable of supporting tutors in the time-consuming process of analyzing conversations", housing the two proposed collaboration-assessment models.
requirements: Requires the cohesion-based and dialogical analysis models to be operational so tutors are supported in analyzing conversations.
target_learning_goals: Automated support for tutors analyzing CSCL conversations
key_sources: Mihai Dascalu, Stefan Trausan-Matu, Danielle S. Mcnamara, Philippe Dessus. (2015). ReaderBench – Automated Evaluation of Collaboration based on Cohesion and Dialogism. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9226-y

article_title: Reflective assessment in knowledge building by students with low academic achievement
citation: Yang, Y., van Aalst, J., Chan, C.K.K., & Tian, W. (2016). Reflective assessment in knowledge building by students with low academic achievement. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9239-1
title: Reflective assessment as collaborative, embedded metacognitive assessment for knowledge building
description: Reflective assessment is a framework in which students reflect on criteria or learning goals, generate their own feedback, and improve ongoing learning. The article states it "does not merely evaluate what students have done and point to the next predetermined step, but involves student directing their efforts to improve their ongoing learning." It is collaborative: "not everyone in the community needs to be highly metacognitive for the process to be effective." Students scaffold one another's metacognitive development through social modeling. The study deployed it with KCA to support knowledge building in low-achieving students.
requirements: Requires tools that collect data automatically and present them in a ready-for-use format
Requires prompt sheets or structured supports to help students make sense of assessment data
constraints: Was studied in one class with an exceptionally experienced teacher; generalizability is uncertain
Only two of four KCA questions were used due to available instructional time
target_learning_goals: collaborative inquiry
metacognitive regulation
knowledge building
collective responsibility for community knowledge
examples: Students used KCA prompt sheets to record multiple sets of KCA results, interpret data, and plan actions in a Grade 11 visual-arts course
key_sources: Yang, Y., van Aalst, J., Chan, C.K.K., & Tian, W. (2016). Reflective assessment in knowledge building by students with low academic achievement. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9239-1

article_title: Multiple forms of regulation and coordination across levels in educational settings
citation: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law, Gerry Stahl, Carolyn P. Rosé. (2018). Multiple forms of regulation and coordination across levels in educational settings. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9274-1
title: Study regulation at the interpersonal level, focusing on the interdependency between individual action and social context
description: The editorial reports that Su et al. advocate studying regulation "using the inter-personal level as the starting point and focusing on the interdependency between individual action and social context", rather than conceptualizing regulation mainly as self-regulation with the individual as unit of analysis. Analysis across self-regulation, co-regulation, and social regulation levels is recommended for CSCL research.
requirements: Analysis on self-regulation, co-regulation, and social regulation levels, as in the Su et al. study's aim.
target_learners: collaborative learners in small groups, e.g., second-language students
target_learning_goals: social and content regulation during collaborative learning
examples: Su et al.'s 16-week wiki-supported ESL literature-circle study analyzed chat logs with coding for social intentionality, regulation processes, and emotions.
key_sources: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law, Gerry Stahl, Carolyn P. Rosé. (2018). Multiple forms of regulation and coordination across levels in educational settings. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9274-1

article_title: Capturing the participation and social dimensions of computer-supported collaborative learning through social network analysis: which method and measures matter?
citation: Mohammed Saqr, et al. (2020). Capturing the participation and social dimensions of computer-supported collaborative learning through social network analysis: which method and measures matter? International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 15:227–248. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09322-6
title: Report SNA methodological choices in detail so learning-analytics research can be compared and replicated
description: The article recommends that researchers reporting on social network analysis in learning analytics document their operationalization choices, because measurement robustness underpins reproducibility. It states that "the results emphasize the need for researchers who report on SNA to present in detail their methodological choices so that research is better able to be compared, replicated, and ultimately generalized." The article enumerates nine reportable items, from tie definition and weighting through software versions to community-finding parameters.
requirements: Reports must state tie definition, direction, network mode, weight scheme, node and edge counts, aggregation method and duration, software and versions, visualization software, and community-finding method and parameters
constraints: The guidance is based on evidence from problem-based learning courses in medical higher education
target_learners: learning analytics researchers and educators analyzing CSCL forum data
target_learning_goals: reproducible and valid measurement of participation and social dimensions of collaborative learning
examples: The study itself compared multigraph, simplified and weighted configurations and reported tie definitions, weighting, normalization and software (Igraph in R version 3.52)
key_sources: Mohammed Saqr, et al. (2020). Capturing the participation and social dimensions of computer-supported collaborative learning through social network analysis: which method and measures matter? International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 15:227–248. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09322-6

article_title: Supporting perspective taking across chasms of thinking: Do real-time analytics hold the key?
citation: Carolyn Rosé · Sanna Järvelä. (2022). Supporting perspective taking across chasms of thinking: Do real-time analytics hold the key?. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09378-6
title: Use real-time analytics as automated assessment in action that prompts growth through group awareness
description: The editorial argues the issue's final two articles show how new analytic methods and digital trace data "can be fashioned into tools to prompt learners and teachers in the practice of CSCL", positioning real-time analytics as automated assessment in action displayed through awareness tools to prompt growth. Real-time sensing enables awareness, offering learners a position of agency.
requirements: Technical analytics work enabling awareness through real-time sensing of collaborative processes
constraints: The two supporting articles focus on K-12 education, per the editorial
target_learning_goals: prompting growth
regulating engagement
collaborative learning
examples: iTalk-iSee makes talk processes visible to students; Wikiglass is used by both teachers and students
key_sources: Lb0

article_title: Fostering regulatory processes using computational scaffolding
citation: Leonardo Silva, António Mendes, Anabela Gomes, Gabriel Fortes. (2023). Fostering regulation of learning processes among programming students using computational scaffolding. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2023) 18:67–100. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09388-y
title: RESPE: a CSCL platform embedding individual and social regulatory scaffolds for programming learning
description: RESPE is a CSCL environment for introductory programming whose scaffolds foster SRL and social regulation across "cognition, metacognition, behavior, and motivation". Scaffolds include a learning journal, software planner, SRL tips, an intelligent agent, error visualization and analysis, learning dashboard, debug, course progress, exercise solution, and social features such as a collaborative software planner, ranking, dialogue support agent, forum, and help request. Source code is released under CC BY-NC 4.0 at https:// github. com/ lsoar esesi lva/ 32bits, and scaffolds are presented in mandatory or manually activated formats.
requirements: An online introductory programming course with individual and collaborative exercises hosted on the platform; access to the programming editor is gated on answering the software planner questions
constraints: The professor (first author) knew which group his students belonged to, while participants were blind to condition
target_learners: novice programmers with little or no programming background in online university courses
target_learning_goals: learning of programming (variables, conditionals, loops, functions in Python) with regulatory skill support for planning, monitoring, and self-evaluation
examples: In the trial, 70 individual and 8 collaborative exercises were delivered on the platform; students with regulatory support achieved higher grades, and only the social-regulation group excelled at collaborative activities.
key_sources: Leonardo Silva, António Mendes, Anabela Gomes, Gabriel Fortes. (2023). Fostering regulation of learning processes among programming students using computational scaffolding. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2023) 18:67–100. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09388-y

article_title: Talk to the machine: Unleashing the potential of AI to scale dialogic education and reduce polarization
citation: Yifat Ben-David Kolikant, Omri Hadar, Asaf Salman. (2025). Talk to the machine: Unleashing the potential of AI to scale dialogic education and reduce polarization. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09461-8
title: Responsiveness: the extent and ways one's response takes into account and builds on previous posts, both logically and emotionally
description: The authors introduce responsiveness as a construct for analyzing discussion contributions, defining it as "the extent and ways one's response takes into account and builds on previous posts, both logically and emotionally". They position it against transactivity, which they describe as celebrating the cognitive-epistemic dimension; responsiveness was coined "to allow sensitivity to the social-emotional dimension as well". High responsiveness addresses the essence of the post both logically and emotionally; low responsiveness vaguely refers to the main point or addresses a social-emotional aspect without connection to the core content.
requirements: Analysis of posts in sequence, examining how each builds on previous posts logically and emotionally.
constraints: Applied in this article to analysis of chatbot-generated and human posts in ten discussions on contentious topics.
target_learners: Participants in dialogic discussions on contentious topics
target_learning_goals: Analyzing and supporting constructive discussion that attends to both epistemic and socio-emotional dimensions
examples: The authors coded each LlamaLo post for whether it addressed the essence of the post both logically and emotionally (high) or vaguely referred to the main point (low).
key_sources: Yifat Ben-David Kolikant, Omri Hadar, Asaf Salman. (2025). Talk to the machine: Unleashing the potential of AI to scale dialogic education and reduce polarization. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09461-8

article_title: From individual annotations to shared attention: How re-annotation supports collaborative knowledge building in CSCL
citation: Yiqiu Zhou and Jina Kang. (2026). From individual annotations to shared attention: How re-annotation supports collaborative knowledge building in CSCL. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09486-7
title: Re-annotation as a construct distinguishing reciprocal annotation uptake from annotation initiation
description: The article introduces re-annotation as an analytical lens on social annotation: an annotation behavior in which a learner annotates the same referent a peer just did, signaling shared attention. It distinguishes two behavior types: "Initiating annotation denotes a learner's first act of marking or highlighting a digital object", while "Re-annotation refers to a subsequent annotation made on the same referent by another learner within a short temporal window." The concept reframes annotation as a call-and-response cycle between individual contributions and collective meaning-making.
requirements: A time threshold (120 s, informed by prior conversational-episode analysis) must be set to operationalize re-annotation as deliberate, timely engagement rather than coincidence.
constraints: Operationalized for visual highlights on constellations in a simulation where only one constellation can be highlighted per device at a time; line drawing was excluded due to infrequent use.
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge construction
shared attention and mutual awareness in group problem-solving
examples: During Task 1 (hemisphere identification), an initial annotation of Ursa Major externalized one student's hypothesis, and a peer's subsequent re-annotation reinforced it as a shared point of reference.
key_sources: Yiqiu Zhou and Jina Kang. (2026). From individual annotations to shared attention: How re-annotation supports collaborative knowledge building in CSCL. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09486-7

article_title: Putting self-regulated learning and teaching into practice: insights from two science teachers and their students
citation: Avivit Arvatz, Boaz Hadas, Rotem Waitzman, Yehudit Judy Dori (2025). Putting self-regulated learning and teaching into practice: insights from two science teachers and their students. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09719-6
title: Four-level rubric for teachers' reflective prompts adapted from Van Manen's reflective levels
description: The study adapts Van Manen's (1977) cumulative levels of reflection into a four-level rubric for classifying teachers' reflective prompts in learning modules. "Level 1 involves basic descriptive reflections" guiding students to content knowledge; "Van-Manen's practical reflection level was split in two, where Level 2 prompts reflection using limited SRL terminology" and Level 3 encourages concrete problem-solving commentary; "The highest level, Level 4, prompts critical reflections and fosters SRL." It enabled tracking teachers' SRL&T growth across a year of module design, with a parallel rubric for student reflective responses.
requirements: Prompts must be analysed independently of student responses for unbiased evaluation
Inter-rater reliability established: κ = 0.801, p < 0.001 on 15 reflective items
constraints: Rubric was developed and applied in a specific study context of two science teachers' online modules
target_learners: Science teachers in professional development programs
target_learning_goals: Teachers' assessment knowledge and SRL&T capability development
examples: Analysis of 44 reflective prompts using the rubric, with examples like Adam's low-level recall prompt and Ben's high-level insight prompt
key_sources: Avivit Arvatz, Boaz Hadas, Rotem Waitzman, Yehudit Judy Dori (2025). Putting self-regulated learning and teaching into practice: insights from two science teachers and their students. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09719-6

article_title: Do medium and Context Matter when learning from multiple complementary Digital texts and videos?
citation: Lucia Mason, Christian Tarchi, Angelica Ronconi, Lucia Manzione, Natalia Latini, Ivar Bråten. (2022). Do medium and Context Matter when learning from multiple complementary Digital texts and videos? Instructional Science (2022) 50:653–679. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09591-8
title: RESOLV context model: readers construct a mental model of the reading context that shapes task engagement
description: The reading as problem solving (RESOLV) model holds that readers first build a subjective mental representation of the context in which reading occurs, from cues they perceive as important, and then build a task model of the end goal and means. The article uses RESOLV to motivate its authoritativeness manipulation: "readers initially construct a mental model of the context in which reading takes place", including the requester and the digital venue. The study tested whether a professor-on-Moodle versus friend-on-Facebook context was represented in learners' context models and moderated engagement, integration, and calibration.
requirements: Context cues (requester, platform) must be perceived as relevant by readers and represented in their context model for authoritativeness to influence processing
constraints: The article notes it remained possible that authoritativeness might not be represented in participants' context models, and prior research indicates students often disregard source characteristics
target_learners: university students learning from online informational sources
target_learning_goals: integrated understanding of complex issues across multiple complementary sources
examples: Participants in the more authoritative condition read that a professor recommended two texts/videos posted on Moodle after a classroom discussion; those in the less authoritative condition read that a friend tagged them in two Facebook posts after an out-of-school discussion
key_sources: Lucia Mason, Christian Tarchi, Angelica Ronconi, Lucia Manzione, Natalia Latini, Ivar Bråten. (2022). Do medium and Context Matter when learning from multiple complementary Digital texts and videos? Instructional Science (2022) 50:653–679. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09591-8

article_title: How are Lao teachers’ goals for teaching associated with their instructional practices?
citation: Anongsack Mahavong, József Balázs Fejes. (2026). How are Lao teachers' goals for teaching associated with their instructional practices? Instructional Science, 54, 6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09756-1
title: Foster teachers' relational goals alongside mastery goals to support favorable instructional practices
description: The article concludes that relational goals — teachers' aspiration to foster close and supportive student relationships — play a central role in shaping effective instructional practices, including recognition, grouping, and mutual respect. It states that "the results underscore the central role of relational goals in shaping effective instructional practices." Because relational and mastery goals were linked to distinct practices in the Lao sample, supporting both goal orientations may address complementary socioemotional and task-focused aspects of teaching.
requirements: Teachers with endorsement of relational goals alongside mastery goals; teacher self-report assessment of goals and practices
constraints: Findings are cross-sectional, so causal inferences cannot be drawn; the sample was a convenience sample from a single Lao province; fostering goals has not been tested interventionally in this study
target_learning_goals: classroom motivational climate, teacher–student and student–student relationships, mastery-oriented instruction
examples: In the Lao SEM models, relational goals predicted mastery-oriented instruction and the grouping, recognition, and mutual respect practices.
key_sources: Anongsack Mahavong, József Balázs Fejes. (2026). How are Lao teachers' goals for teaching associated with their instructional practices? Instructional Science, 54, 6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09756-1

article_title: The modality effect reverses in a virtual reality learning environment and influences cognitive load
citation: Patrick Albus, Tina Seufert. (2023). The modality effect reverses in a virtual reality learning environment and influences cognitive load. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09611-7
title: Boundary-condition account of the reverse modality effect in immersive VR
description: The article explains the reversed modality effect in VRLE via boundary conditions known from classical multimedia research: the modality effect "can be reversed if, for example, when longer or more complex texts are presented or when the learning environment is self-paced". Stable visual text permits re-reading and self-regulated reading strategies, whereas transient auditory text depends on presentation speed; in VR, immersion, constant visual change, and seductive details further strain the visual channel and distract attention. The account integrates CTML, CLT, and the Colavita visual dominance effect as candidate explanations.
requirements: Applies to immersive VR learning environments with additional verbal information alongside rich visual content
constraints: The Colavita effect has primarily been studied in audio-visual discrimination tasks, not learning environments
Whether learners look around during narration is unknown without eye-tracking data
target_learners: adult students learning science content in immersive VR
target_learning_goals: recall, comprehension and transfer of science material presented in VR
examples: The study shortened texts to about 40 words on average and integrated visual text dynamically into the VRLE to remove prior boundary conditions, yet the effect still reversed
key_sources: Patrick Albus, Tina Seufert. (2023). The modality effect reverses in a virtual reality learning environment and influences cognitive load. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09611-7

article_title: How to assist the students while learning from text? Effects of inserting adjunct questions on text processing
citation: Alba Rubio, Eduardo Vidal-Abarca, Marian Serrano-Mendizábal. (2022). How to assist the students while learning from text? Effects of inserting adjunct questions on text processing. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09592-7
title: Read&Learn web-based system for recording reading and question-answering processes
description: Read&Learn is a computer web-based system used to present texts and adjunct questions and to record students' online reading actions (Vidal-Abarca et al., 2018). Text segments and questions are masked and "To read a masked segment, students had to click on it", which lets the system register which segments are consulted, when, and for how long, classifying rereading as relevant or non-relevant per question. In this study it delivered both the inserted-question single-screen condition and the post-reading two-screen condition.
requirements: Masked segments that students unmask by clicking, enabling registration of reading actions
Segment-level classification of text as relevant or non-relevant for each question
constraints: The article notes unmasking may make scanning the text slightly more difficult, and recommends comparing question-timing effects in a more natural environment with unmasked texts
target_learners: college students reading expository science texts
target_learning_goals: measuring and supporting reading strategy use and question-answering during text study
examples: Used to record time reading the text and questions for the first time, rereading of relevant and non-relevant information, and number of segments consulted while searching
key_sources: Alba Rubio, Eduardo Vidal-Abarca, Marian Serrano-Mendizábal. (2022). How to assist the students while learning from text? Effects of inserting adjunct questions on text processing. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09592-7

article_title: Gaming the system mediates the relationship between gender and learning outcomes in a digital learning game
citation: Baker, R. S., Richey, J. E., Zhang, J., Karumbaiah, S., Andres-Bray, J. M., Nguyen, H. A., Andres, J. M. A. L., & McLaren, B. M. (2025). Gaming the system mediates the relationship between gender and learning outcomes in a digital learning game. Instructional Science, 53, 203–238. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09679-3
title: Design digital learning games to reduce gaming-the-system behavior for male students, particularly in self-explanation activities
description: The article recommends that future design iterations of the game target disengagement behaviors among male students. As the authors state, "future design iterations of the game could focus on reducing gaming behaviors for male students, which might improve learning outcomes for female students as well." Because lower gaming mediated better learning, reducing gaming for the group that games more is a lever for improving outcomes for all students. Understanding gender-based differences in game behaviors can inform game design that promotes better learning outcomes for all students.
requirements: Detectors or behavioral measures of gaming the system must be available to identify where and for whom disengagement occurs
constraints: Simply making it more difficult to game the system leads students to find new ways to game the system, per prior work the article cites
target_learners: late elementary and middle school students
target_learning_goals: decimal number concepts and operations
behavioral engagement in digital learning games
examples: Across three Decimal Point studies, male students gamed the system significantly more than female students in the self-explanation step in the game condition, and this difference mediated gender differences in delayed posttest learning.
key_sources: Baker, R. S., Richey, J. E., Zhang, J., Karumbaiah, S., Andres-Bray, J. M., Nguyen, H. A., Andres, J. M. A. L., & McLaren, B. M. (2025). Gaming the system mediates the relationship between gender and learning outcomes in a digital learning game. Instructional Science, 53, 203–238. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09679-3

article_title: SimLab: an intervention to promote expansive learning and organisational change in team-based emergency care simulation
citation: O'Hare, S., Kajamaa, A., Conn, R., & Gormley, G. (2025). SimLab: an intervention to promote expansive learning and organisational change in team-based emergency care simulation. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09734-7
title: Reflection wall and reflection diaries as flexible between-session tools for documenting disturbances and aha moments
description: To support the longitudinal learning process without adding scheduled sessions, SimLab introduced flexible tools: a reflection wall and reflection diaries in which "SimLab participants and their colleagues documented both disturbances and 'aha moments' in their daily work". The vertical writing surfaces carried the activity system as a reference, allowing temporal analysis of the emerging model across sessions, and served as second stimuli supporting double stimulation during facilitated discussions.
requirements: Requires writing surfaces displaying the activity system model and placement accessible to participants and colleagues between sessions
constraints: Used within a four-month SimLab programme at one general practice
target_learners: interprofessional general practice team members and their colleagues
target_learning_goals: documenting workplace disturbances and insights
collaborative modelling of new emergency care practices
examples: Reflection wall notes were among the artefacts complementing the 157 minutes of audio-recorded discussion in the analysis
key_sources: O'Hare, S., Kajamaa, A., Conn, R., & Gormley, G. (2025). SimLab: an intervention to promote expansive learning and organisational change in team-based emergency care simulation. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09734-7

article_title: Demonstration-based training (DBT) in the design of a video tutorial for software training
citation: Hans van der Meij, Jan van der Meij. (2016). Demonstration-based training (DBT) in the design of a video tutorial for software training. Instr Sci 44:527–542. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9394-9
title: Follow each task demonstration with a short review recap to support retention of the procedure
description: A review is "a short recap of the main steps in a procedure" presented after a demonstration, reiterating task completion in abbreviated form to support retention. Because it comes after the demonstration, "its presence does not affect the design of the demonstration." In the reported experiment the review tutorial surpassed the demonstration-only control on practice, immediate and delayed post-tests and on post-training task relevance.
requirements: Reviews follow the demonstration automatically (in the study, after a 2-s pause) and summarize task completion in condensed format lasting between 13 and 26 seconds
constraints: The review increased presentation time by about 20 percent, so benefits may partly reflect longer exposure; the authors state this merits further research
target_learners: novice software users in primary and secondary schools
target_learning_goals: retention of software procedures; procedural knowledge development
examples: In the study, each task review followed automatically after the demonstration for that task, beginning after the 2-s pause at the end of the demonstration, introduced with the statement 'You are now done, but remember …'
key_sources: Hans van der Meij, Jan van der Meij. (2016). Demonstration-based training (DBT) in the design of a video tutorial for software training. Instr Sci 44:527–542. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9394-9

article_title: Facilitation strategies responding to emotional displays in PD discourse: navigating relational and learning goals
citation: Dana Vedder-Weiss, Rotem Tractenberg-Maslaton, Karin Sarfati-Shaulov. (2025). Facilitation strategies responding to emotional displays in PD discourse: navigating relational and learning goals. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09737-4
title: Two-continuum framework mapping facilitation responses to emotion displays onto recognizing (relational) and exploring (learning) goals
description: The article proposes a conceptual framework in which facilitator responses to teacher emotional displays are mapped onto two continuums: recognizing the emotion, which serves relational goals (emotional support, solidarity, trust), and exploring the emotion, which serves learning goals (examining underlying beliefs, implications, and response possibilities). The authors state they "identified seven facilitation strategies (summarized in Table 3) and mapped them onto two continuums (see Fig. 2): (1) recognizing the emotion (relational goal); (2) exploring the emotion (learning goal)." The framework offers a repertoire rather than a normative ranking of strategies.
requirements: A PD group discussing problems of practice in which teachers display emotions that facilitators respond to
constraints: The authors note the location of strategies on the map is far from precise, as they do not have analytic tools to measure the extent of recognition and exploration
target_learners: PD facilitators of teacher collaborative learning groups
target_learning_goals: Navigating tensions between relational and learning goals when responding to teacher emotional displays
examples: The article maps seven strategies onto the two continuums, dividing them roughly into those that close the space to discuss emotions and those that open it
key_sources: Dana Vedder-Weiss, Rotem Tractenberg-Maslaton, Karin Sarfati-Shaulov. (2025). Facilitation strategies responding to emotional displays in PD discourse: navigating relational and learning goals. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09737-4

article_title: Effects of representational guidance during computer-supported collaborative learning
citation: Jeroen Janssen, Gijsbert Erkens, Paul A. Kirschner, Gellof Kanselaar. (2008). Effects of representational guidance during computer-supported collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9078-1
title: Representational guidance: different external representations express, make salient, and stimulate different information and cognitive processes
description: Representational guidance is the account that different external representations (ERs) afford different reasoning and learning because of what they can express and emphasize. The article states that "different ERs are capable of expressing different information (e.g., cause and effect relationships versus temporal relationships), make different information salient" and stimulate different cognitive processes. It uses this account to explain why the Graphical and Textual Debate-tools, which offer different guidance, produced different outcomes, and notes effects depend on circumstances such as the kind of task.
requirements: The representational format must be matched to the task and to the information it should make salient for the reasoning intended.
constraints: The article notes the effects of representational guidance "can differ depending on the speciﬁc circumstances (e.g., the kind of task to be performed)", so a given guidance may help one task and hurt another.
target_learning_goals: argumentative reasoning and historical reasoning
constructing argumentative representations of a debate
examples: The study operationalized representational guidance as the difference between the GD-tool (distinguishing arguments, supports, refutations, visualizing support strength and progress) and the TD-tool (listwise, text-based).
key_sources: Jeroen Janssen, Gijsbert Erkens, Paul A. Kirschner, Gellof Kanselaar. (2008). Effects of representational guidance during computer-supported collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9078-1

article_title: Effects of representational guidance during computer-supported collaborative learning
citation: Jeroen Janssen, Gijsbert Erkens, Paul A. Kirschner, Gellof Kanselaar. (2008). Effects of representational guidance during computer-supported collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9078-1
title: Take representational guidance into account during instructional design because it affects group and individual performance
description: When designing CSCL or other activities in which learners co-construct external representations, the choice of representational format is a design variable with measurable consequences, not a neutral medium. The article concludes that "representational guidance has an impact on group and individual performance and should therefore be taken into account during instructional design." Designers should therefore deliberately select the representation (e.g., graphical versus textual argumentation formats) in light of the desired reasoning and products.
requirements: Designers must have access to or be able to create alternative representational formats so the guidance offered can be matched to task demands.
constraints: The article notes a given kind of guidance may be positive for one kind of task and negative for another, so the choice must be evaluated per task.
target_learners: secondary education students working in small groups
target_learning_goals: argumentation quality
representation construction
individual knowledge acquisition
examples: In the study, switching only the representational format of the Debate-tool while holding task, sources, and CSCL environment constant produced differences in representation quality, essay quality, and post-test performance.
key_sources: Jeroen Janssen, Gijsbert Erkens, Paul A. Kirschner, Gellof Kanselaar. (2008). Effects of representational guidance during computer-supported collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9078-1

article_title: Successfully carrying out complex learning-tasks through guiding teams’ qualitative and quantitative reasoning
citation: B. Slof, G. Erkens, P. A. Kirschner, J. Janssen, J. G. M. Jaspers. (2012). Successfully carrying out complex learning-tasks through guiding teams' qualitative and quantitative reasoning. Instr Sci 40:623–643. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9185-2
title: Representational scripting: sequencing part-tasks and matching each tool's ontology to part-task demands
description: Representational scripting integrates collaboration scripts with representational tools so that the problem-solving process is sequenced into part-tasks whose demands are made explicit, and each tool's representational guidance is congruent with those demands. According to the article, a script is "a set of instructions regarding to how the group members should interact, how they should collaborate and how they should solve the problem". A tool's ontology (its objects, relations and combination rules) makes certain concepts and interrelationships salient: less expressive, first-order ontologies support qualitative causal inference-making, while more expressive, second-order ontologies support quantitative inference-making. In the study, a causal tool was matched to the problem–solution phase and a simulation tool to the solution–evaluation phase.
requirements: A learning-task analysis to determine the sequence and demands of the part-tasks so that part-task congruent tools can be developed
constraints: The article states the design principles do not automatically apply to other domains, learning tasks and settings; effects depend on the characteristics of the learning task and the involved knowledge domains
target_learners: secondary-school students (novices) working on complex learning tasks in teams
target_learning_goals: acquiring a well-developed qualitative and quantitative understanding of a domain and applying it to solve complex problems
examples: In the study, teams carried out a business-economics advisory task in the VCRI CSCL environment, using a causal representational tool in the problem–solution phase and a simulation tool in the solution–evaluation phase
key_sources: B. Slof, G. Erkens, P. A. Kirschner, J. Janssen, J. G. M. Jaspers. (2012). Successfully carrying out complex learning-tasks through guiding teams' qualitative and quantitative reasoning. Instr Sci 40:623–643. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9185-2

article_title: Supporting reflection to improve learning from self-generated concept maps
citation: Elise H. Eshuis, Judith ter Vrugte, Ton de Jong. (2022). Supporting reflection to improve learning from self-generated concept maps. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09299-7
title: Reflection as the joint operation of cognitive and metacognitive processing driving knowledge integration from concept maps
description: The article frames learning from concept maps as knowledge integration requiring both cognitive processing (organizing and elaborating knowledge) and metacognitive processing (monitoring and regulating one's cognitive activities). Following Davis, it treats these as unified in "reflection": "reflection can focus on goals or on one's own thinking (metacognition), or on content itself (sense-making)". Identifying weaknesses in one's knowledge is positioned as the gateway process that makes the other knowledge-integration processes likely. The study's supports (example, prompts, discussion) are designed to trigger and sustain this reflection.
requirements: Students must engage in comparing and contrasting their own knowledge against a frame of reference, such as an example concept map
constraints: Students scarcely spontaneously engage in the required (meta)cognitive processes, and often employ them suboptimally
target_learning_goals: domain knowledge integration in electricity and electric power transmission
examples: The study operationalized reflection support as a combined concept map with highlighted differences, reflection prompts, and a teacher-guided classroom discussion.
key_sources: Elise H. Eshuis, Judith ter Vrugte, Ton de Jong. (2022). Supporting reflection to improve learning from self-generated concept maps. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09299-7

article_title: Task-related and social regulation during online collaborative learning
citation: Janssen, J., Erkens, G., Kirschner, P. A., & Kanselaar, G. (2010). Task-related and social regulation during online collaborative learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-010-9061-5
title: Groups collaborating online should devote effort to regulating the collaboration itself, since social regulation supports group performance
description: The article concludes that regulating the collective activity—discussing collaboration strategies, monitoring the group process, and evaluating how the group collaborated—supports group performance, whereas regulation efforts concentrated only on the task showed no such effect. The authors state that "when groups devoted more energy to regulating the collaboration, they performed better" and that "a minimum amount of regulation of social activities is a prerequisite for successful group performance." This principle directs CSCL designers and teachers to prompt and support socially shared regulation, not merely task planning.
requirements: Group members must be interdependent on a shared group product so that coordinating the collaboration matters
constraints: The supporting evidence is correlational, from secondary students on history inquiry tasks; the authors note no causal inferences could be made, and social activities (non-regulative socializing) negatively predicted performance
target_learners: Secondary education students working in small groups in CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: Effective coordination of collaborative group processes during inquiry tasks, leading to better group products
examples: In the study, regulation of social activities included planning the collaboration (3.30% of messages), monitoring the group process (5.45%), and evaluating the group process (less than 1%)
key_sources: Janssen, J., Erkens, G., Kirschner, P. A., & Kanselaar, G. (2010). Task-related and social regulation during online collaborative learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-010-9061-5

article_title: Team regulation, regulation of social activities or co-regulation: Different labels for effective regulation of learning in CSCL
citation: Nadira Saab. (2012). Team regulation, regulation of social activities or co-regulation: Different labels for effective regulation of learning in CSCL. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9085-5
title: Taxonomy of regulation labels in CSCL: task regulation, team regulation, regulation of social activities, and co-regulation
description: The article distinguishes the labels different researchers use for forms of regulation during CSCL. Saab et al. distinguish task regulation (orientation, monitoring, and evaluation of the task) from team regulation (planning of activities and monitoring of the team process). Janssen et al. distinguish regulation of task-related activities from regulation of social activities, differentiating "activities that are performed in the content space of the collaborative learning process and activities with a social-relational function." Lajoie and Lu use co-regulation, "a form of collaboration that is needed to acquire shared understanding," involving multiple group members building shared mental models. The article argues these labels describe effective regulation of learning in CSCL.
requirements: A coding scheme or analytic distinction between task-focused and socially focused regulative activities
constraints: The labels are used inconsistently across research groups; the article's purpose is to relate them rather than standardize them
target_learning_goals: regulation of task performance and of collaboration during CSCL
examples: Grounding, or establishing shared understanding, is given as an example of a social activity; asking questions as an example of a task-related activity
key_sources: Nadira Saab. (2012). Team regulation, regulation of social activities or co-regulation: Different labels for effective regulation of learning in CSCL. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9085-5

article_title: Far Transfer of Metacognitive Regulation: From Cognitive Learning Strategy Use to Mental Effort Regulation
citation: Wirth, J., Weber-Reuter, X.-L., Schuster, C., Fleischer, J., Leutner, D., & Stebner, F. (2025). Far Transfer of Metacognitive Regulation: From Cognitive Learning Strategy Use to Mental Effort Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09983-x
title: Distinction between required mental effort (mental load) and invested mental effort as the basis for effort regulation
description: Following Paas and van Merriënboer (1994), the article distinguishes mental load, renamed "required mental effort," imposed by the task and learner characteristics, from mental effort, renamed "invested mental effort," the mental capacity learners actually invest. Required effort "is passively experienced by learners" and is hardly modifiable within a task, whereas invested effort "results from the active allocation of germane resources in learning" and is a strategic decision, making investing mental effort a learning strategy. The article incorporates Grund et al.'s (2024) decomposition into effort-by-complexity, effort-by-need frustration, and effort-by-allocation, and argues there is no direct link between required and invested effort, citing Arslan-Ari's (2013) opposite-pattern finding.
requirements: Regulation requires learners to evaluate whether invested effort corresponds to required effort, using cues, since neither can be directly evaluated at the object level
constraints: Required mental effort is determined by relatively stable task and learner characteristics and cannot be lowered within a task except by adapting learning goals
target_learning_goals: strategic allocation of mental effort to learning tasks
key_sources: Wirth, J., Weber-Reuter, X.-L., Schuster, C., Fleischer, J., Leutner, D., & Stebner, F. (2025). Far Transfer of Metacognitive Regulation: From Cognitive Learning Strategy Use to Mental Effort Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09983-x

article_title: Editor’s Note
citation: Dan Robinson. (2011). Editor's Note. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9167-6
title: Reserve prescriptive recommendations for scholarly outlets that synthesize efficacy studies, not empirical research articles
description: This principle holds that empirical research articles should report only what the study found — causal, correlational, or descriptive conclusions — while prescriptive recommendations for practice belong in outlets that "synthesize the efficacy studies for a particular intervention." The editorial argues this separation protects the field from building recommendations on "anecdotes, observations, and self-report data."
requirements: A synthesis of efficacy studies for the particular intervention must exist or be conducted before prescriptions are issued
constraints: The editorial states prescriptive statements are rarely appropriate in empirical research articles
target_learners: educational researchers, authors, reviewers, and editors
target_learning_goals: standards for causal claims and evidence-based prescriptive recommendations in educational research
examples: The journal EDPR's 'Research into Practice' article category, defined as articles "written for practitioners that summarize research on educationally relevant topics and prescribe implications for practice," is cited as the intended outlet for such prescriptions
key_sources: Dan Robinson. (2011). Editor's Note. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9167-6

article_title: Bridging Reasoning in Mathematics and Science: a Document Analysis of Applying and Reasoning in the TIMSS Assessment Framework and the Case for Utilization of Resources
citation: Kyong Mi Choi, Jin Mun, Brian Hand. (2026). Bridging Reasoning in Mathematics and Science: a Document Analysis of Applying and Reasoning in the TIMSS Assessment Framework and the Case for Utilization of Resources. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10115-2
title: Design instruction that strengthens reasoning through discipline-specific procedural engagement
description: The article proposes that instruction can strengthen reasoning by engaging students in discipline-specific procedural tasks—the applying domain—rather than treating reasoning as a decontextualized general skill. The authors state their insight "offers a conceptual foundation for designing instruction that strengthens reasoning through discipline-specific procedural engagement." Because procedural knowledge is conceptualized as a mobilizable resource, rich applying experiences are positioned as the foundation learners draw on when reasoning within and across mathematics and science.
requirements: Procedural tasks should be recognized and related across disciplines so that applying experiences can support reasoning in both mathematics and science
constraints: The proposal is an exploratory hypothesis grounded in the semantic structure of TIMSS framework documents and does not directly examine learner-level performance or instructional effects
target_learning_goals: Domain-specific reasoning in mathematics and science
examples: The authors analyzed the applying and reasoning components of the TIMSS assessment frameworks across four cycles to build the conceptual foundation for this instructional approach
key_sources: Kyong Mi Choi, Jin Mun, Brian Hand. (2026). Bridging Reasoning in Mathematics and Science: a Document Analysis of Applying and Reasoning in the TIMSS Assessment Framework and the Case for Utilization of Resources. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10115-2

article_title: Reply to Sana et al.’s (2022) Commentary on Rest-from-Deliberate-Learning as a Mechanism for the Spacing Effect
citation: Ouhao Chen, Fred Paas, John Sweller. (2022). Reply to Sana et al.'s (2022) Commentary on Rest-from-Deliberate-Learning as a Mechanism for the Spacing Effect. Educational Psychology Review, 34, 1851–1858. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09678-1
title: Rest-from-deliberate-learning framework: working memory resources deplete with cognitive effort and replenish with rest, explaining part of the spacing effect
description: The framework assumes that "working memory resources diminish with cognitive effort and replenish with rest", providing an explanation of the spacing effect that is distinct from the interleaving effect. It was proposed to resolve mixed results of spacing and interleaving rather than as a theory of everything. The authors state its scope covers learning tasks, not simple processing tasks unrelated to learning.
requirements: Rest must involve no intentional learning, since without intentional learning there is no reason to assume a working memory load
constraints: Cannot account for lag effects (spacing effects found when shorter and longer intervals between repetitions are compared)
Does not apply to processing tasks unrelated to learning, such as digit shadowing tasks that did not require any learning
Whether rest and its effect on working memory are important for the spacing effect must ultimately be determined empirically
target_learning_goals: retention of learned material under spaced versus massed practice
