examples: Chen et al. (2018) is cited as the only published study the authors know that specifically tested the hypothesis, providing evidence for it
key_sources: Ouhao Chen, Fred Paas, John Sweller. (2022). Reply to Sana et al.'s (2022) Commentary on Rest-from-Deliberate-Learning as a Mechanism for the Spacing Effect. Educational Psychology Review, 34, 1851–1858. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09678-1

article_title: Building Bridges Between Self-Regulation and Cognitive Load—an Invitation for a Broad and Differentiated Attempt
citation: Tina Seufert. (2020). Building Bridges Between Self-Regulation and Cognitive Load—an Invitation for a Broad and Differentiated Attempt. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 1151–1162. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09574-6
title: Self-regulation as a function of resources and imposed cognitive load: an inverted-u relationship with task difficulty
description: The review proposes that the relation between self-regulation and cognitive load depends on learners' resources—cognitive, motivational, and affective—drawing on the INVO-model of individual prerequisites for successful learning (Hasselhorn & Gold, 2006). Task difficulty comprises affordances of accomplishing the task on both object and meta levels. Two forces moderate a reverse u-shaped relationship between task difficulty and required self-regulation: available resources decrease with increasing difficulty, and imposed load increases with it. As the review states, "Only with medium task difficulty, resources and load are balanced to allow for effective self- regulation: learners have sufficient resources to deal with the task, and regulation can help to use these resources more effectively."
requirements: Learners must have sufficient cognitive, motivational, and affective resources (prior knowledge, strategy skills, interest, willingness) relative to task difficulty
constraints: At very low difficulty learners have no need to regulate; at very high difficulty resources are insufficient and imposed load too high, so regulation fails
target_learners: Learners across task-difficulty levels whose available resources vary
target_learning_goals: Effective self-regulation of learning under varying cognitive load
examples: Fig. 1 depicts self-regulation as low at easy and difficult tasks and highest at medium task difficulty
key_sources: Tina Seufert. (2020). Building Bridges Between Self-Regulation and Cognitive Load—an Invitation for a Broad and Differentiated Attempt. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 1151–1162. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09574-6

article_title: Still No Convincing Evidence for a Causal Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Reply to Núñez-Regueiro et al., 2025
citation: Kimmo Sorjonen, Bo Melin, Gustav Nilsonne. (2025). Still No Convincing Evidence for a Causal Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Reply to Núñez-Regueiro et al., 2025. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10083-7
title: Reciprocal effects model (REM) of academic self-concept and achievement, including its extended RI-CCLPM-C operationalization
description: The REM consists of two claims: achievement affects self-concept (skill-development) and self-concept affects achievement (self-enhancement). Marsh et al. concluded both occur at different rates, with the achievement effect more or less instantaneous and the self-concept effect slower; this temporal dynamic is captured statistically by the constrained random-intercept contemporaneous and cross-lagged panel model (RI-CCLPM-C), which Núñez-Regueiro et al. call the "extended REM". This commentary challenges the empirical support for the self-enhancement component.
requirements: Longitudinal data on self-concept and achievement across multiple waves
A specified timescale structure matching the RI-CCLPM-C, which the authors argue was endorsed after evaluating only a limited set of models
constraints: The authors argue support for the REM appears sensitive to specific modeling choices, so the hypothesis should probably not be seen as corroborated
target_learning_goals: understanding the relationship between academic self-concept and achievement over time
examples: Marsh et al. (2024) fitted the RI-CCLPM-C to longitudinal data and concluded both skill-development and self-enhancement effects occur at different rates
key_sources: Kimmo Sorjonen, Bo Melin, Gustav Nilsonne. (2025). Still No Convincing Evidence for a Causal Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Reply to Núñez-Regueiro et al., 2025. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10083-7

article_title: Directional Ordering of Self-Concept, School Grades, and Standardized Tests Over Five Years: New Tripartite Models Juxtaposing Within- and Between-Person Perspectives
citation: Herbert W. Marsh, Reinhard Pekrun, & Oliver Lüdtke. (2022). Directional Ordering of Self-Concept, School Grades, and Standardized Tests Over Five Years: New Tripartite Models Juxtaposing Within- and Between-Person Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09662-9
title: Reciprocal Effects Model (REM) of academic self-concept and achievement
description: The REM is a causal theoretical model holding that academic self-concept and achievement each cause the other over time, integrating the earlier skill-development model (achievement → self-concept) and self-enhancement model (self-concept → achievement). The article states the hypothesis "is clearly causal" and that "the REM generated a substantial research literature that treats these reciprocal effects as causal." It is tested with longitudinal cross-lagged panel data and underpins the study's a priori hypotheses.
requirements: At least two, preferably three or more, waves of longitudinal data measuring both self-concept and achievement
Structural equation modeling to test directional ordering
constraints: The article prefers the term directionality to causality, noting interpretation is compromised by potential unmeasured covariates
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept in mathematics
mathematics achievement
examples: The study tests REM hypotheses with tripartite RI-CLPMs and CLPMs on five waves of PALMA data

article_title: Embodied Learning Environments for Graphing Motion: a Systematic Literature Review
citation: Carolien Duijzer, Marja Van den Heuvel-Panhuizen, Michiel Veldhuis, Michiel Doorman, & Paul Leseman. (2019). Embodied Learning Environments for Graphing Motion: a Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09471-7
title: Design embodied graphing environments with real-world elements so students can link personal experiences and physical actions to formal mathematics or physics concepts
description: Among the mediating factors the review uncovered, real-world context is the most frequently mentioned (15 articles). The review reports that "through a learning environment containing real-world elements, links can be made between students ' personal experiences, physical actions, and formal mathematics or physics concepts". Real-world contexts also draw on students' prior knowledge and experiences and present the environment as a natural venue for scientific exploration, for example microcomputer-based laboratories providing genuine scientific experiences.
requirements: Learning environment elements must be recognizable from or connected to students' real-world experiences, such as authentic graphs or real objects in motion
constraints: Some reviewed environments use simplified worlds; Solomon et al. use the term micro world for a learning environment less complex than the real world
target_learners: Primary through higher education students in mathematics and physics
target_learning_goals: Connecting bodily and real-world motion experiences to formal graphing concepts such as distance–time and velocity–time relations
examples: Mitnik et al. let students study the motion of a real robot in an explorative, immersive environment; Holbert and Wilensky used authentic player-created graphs resembling typical velocity–time graphs
key_sources: Carolien Duijzer, Marja Van den Heuvel-Panhuizen, Michiel Veldhuis, Michiel Doorman, & Paul Leseman. (2019). Embodied Learning Environments for Graphing Motion: a Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09471-7

article_title: The Teacher’s Invisible Hand: A Meta-Analysis of the Relevance of Teacher–Student Relationship Quality for Peer Relationships and the Contribution of Student Behavior
citation: Endedijk, H. M., Breeman, L. D., van Lissa, C. J., Hendrickx, M. M. H. G., den Boer, L., & Mainhard, T. (2022). The Teacher's Invisible Hand: A Meta-Analysis of the Relevance of Teacher–Student Relationship Quality for Peer Relationships and the Contribution of Student Behavior. Review of Educational Research, 92(3), 370–412. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211051428
title: Prevent or reduce negative aspects of teacher–student relationships, especially for students with behavioral problems, to support classroom peer relationships
description: The meta-analysis supports a practice principle for teachers: because negative aspects of the teacher–student relationship are especially predictive of peer relationships and partially carry the effect of student behavior onto peer relationships, teachers should prioritize avoiding or reducing conflict and negativity in dyadic relationships. As the article concludes, "For teachers, preventing or reducing negative aspects in their relationships with students who have behavioral problems can positively affect classroom peer relationships."
requirements: Teachers who interact daily with the same students, particularly in preschool and primary settings where one teacher teaches most subjects
constraints: The evidence base is correlational and longitudinal rather than experimental at the level of teacher practice; experimental studies manipulated teacher feedback only in vignette designs
target_learners: students with behavioral problems in preschool, primary, and secondary education
target_learning_goals: healthy peer relationships and classroom social integration
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 1,475 effect sizes and found negative teacher–student relationship aspects particularly predictive of peer relationships, supporting the recommendation to prioritize reducing relational negativity
key_sources: Endedijk, H. M., Breeman, L. D., van Lissa, C. J., Hendrickx, M. M. H. G., den Boer, L., & Mainhard, T. (2022). The Teacher's Invisible Hand: A Meta-Analysis of the Relevance of Teacher–Student Relationship Quality for Peer Relationships and the Contribution of Student Behavior. Review of Educational Research, 92(3), 370–412. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211051428

article_title: Gaining Insight Into Human Nature: A Review of Literature Classroom Intervention Studies
citation: Schrijvers, M., Janssen, T., Fialho, O., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2019). Gaining insight into human nature: A review of literature classroom intervention studies. Review of Educational Research, 89(1), 3-45. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654318812914
title: Design literature activities in which students activate, annotate, and reflect on personal life and reading experiences in writing
description: The review derives instructional design principles from the interventions that showed full or partial empirical support. One principle concerns writing activities in which students are "activating, annotating, and reflecting on personal life and reading experiences". The principle links literature lessons to adolescents’ own experiences so that reading becomes a resource for self-examination and understanding others.
requirements: Writing activities must connect to students’ personal life and reading experiences, as the supported interventions did
target_learning_goals: insight into human nature
insight into oneself
understanding of others
examples: The review derived this principle from its subsequent analysis of interventions with full or partial empirical support

article_title: What If We Look at the Body? An Embodied Perspective of Collaborative Learning
citation: Juliene Madureira Ferreira. (2021). What If We Look at the Body? An Embodied Perspective of Collaborative Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09607-8
title: Taxonomy of regulatory frameworks in collaborative learning: from self-regulation to socially shared regulation
description: The review organizes CL research around regulatory systems of learning at individual and group levels. Zimmerman's sociocognitive model conceptualized self-regulated learning (SRL) around essential elements such as time control, goal setting, self-reflection, and self-efficacy. The sociocultural model frames coregulation as 'a transitional process; an ability that starts with the regulations imposed by the teacher and then evolves to the SRL.' The constructionist model addresses socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL), the joint metacognitive regulation among group members, and the situative model adds context and nonverbal behaviors. The article stresses these are 'distinct ways of theorizing and investigating learning process,' not a gradual evolution.
requirements: Each model requires its own analytical unit: individual metacognition for SRL, teacher–learner mediation for coregulation, group dialogue for SSRL, and situated context for the situative model.
constraints: The article notes nonverbal behaviors are still analyzed as a separate aspect of the storyline of events even under the situative approach.
target_learners: students across educational stages working in groups
target_learning_goals: regulation of learning in collaborative tasks
metacognitive and socio-emotional aspects of collaboration
examples: The review traces how SRL research decentralized the teacher's role, how coregulation studies linked socioemotional interactions to self-regulation, and how SSRL research revealed joint metacognition patterns in group dialog.
key_sources: Juliene Madureira Ferreira. (2021). What If We Look at the Body? An Embodied Perspective of Collaborative Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09607-8

article_title: Re-Experiencing vs. Self-Explaining: Comparing Generative Learning Activities in VR
citation: Valdemar Stenberdt, Ban Mouid Shiwalia, Guido Makransky. (2025). Re-Experiencing vs. Self-Explaining: Comparing Generative Learning Activities in VR. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10096-2
title: Re-experiencing: a generative learning activity in which learners watch a 3D VR replay of their own past performance to engage visualizing and enacting modes
description: Re-experiencing is a newly conceptualized generative learning activity in which a learner is recorded performing a task and then rewatchs the recording in immersive VR, shifting "from being the one carrying out a task to being a reflective observer". Building on the generative sense-making framework, it is designed to engage the visualizing mode (the replay provides visual material as an instructional scaffold) and the enacting mode (learners can move freely, watch from any angle, and mimic the replay), while reducing the extraneous load of recalling past actions. The replay pauses at mistakes and displays temporally aligned feedback on a wrist info screen.
requirements: An immersive VR implementation that records the learner's performance and replays it in 3D with free movement and a first-person embodied perspective
Corrective feedback that can be temporally aligned with mistakes in the replay
constraints: The article notes re-experiencing is not restricted to immersive VR lessons, but the study's implementation builds on technological features of the VR medium
Expected benefits rest on the affordances of agency, presence, and embodiment as theorized, not directly manipulated
target_learners: high school students learning laboratory procedures
target_learning_goals: procedural and motor skills such as pipetting
reflection on and improvement of one's own performance
examples: In the study, students assigned re-experiencing watched a replay of their first pipetting task in VR, with the corrective feedback visible on a clipboard and mistake-specific feedback shown on a wrist info screen as the replay paused at each mistake.
key_sources: Valdemar Stenberdt, Ban Mouid Shiwalia, Guido Makransky. (2025). Re-Experiencing vs. Self-Explaining: Comparing Generative Learning Activities in VR. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10096-2

article_title: Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement’s Directional Ordering
citation: Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., & Núñez-Regueiro, F. (2024). Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement's Directional Ordering. Educational Psychology Review, 36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09887-w
title: Reciprocal effects model (REM) of academic self-concept and achievement
description: The REM is the article's substantive explanatory framework, integrating the earlier skill-development model (prior achievement leads to subsequent self-concept) and self-enhancement model (prior self-concept leads to subsequent achievement) into one bidirectional account. Marsh "argued for a reciprocal model of effects whereby better ASCs lead to better achievement, and better achievement leads to better ASCs." Support for the skill-development path is described as well-established, so the critical issue is the self-enhancement path. The framework underpins the article's a priori hypotheses and its claim that interventions should concurrently enhance self-concept and achievement.
requirements: Longitudinal panel data with multiple waves of both constructs, and statistical models whose assumptions are made explicit
constraints: Causal interpretations from longitudinal correlational models remain susceptible to third-variable confounding, as the article notes citing Wu et al.'s caution
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept and mathematics achievement development
examples: The article cites meta-analyses (Huang 2011; Valentine et al. 2004; Wu et al. 2021) as extensive support for REM predictions, nearly all based on traditional lag1-only CLPMs
key_sources: Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., & Núñez-Regueiro, F. (2024). Cracking Chicken-Egg Conundrums: Juxtaposing Contemporaneous and Lagged Reciprocal Effects Models of Academic Self-Concept and Achievement's Directional Ordering. Educational Psychology Review, 36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09887-w

article_title: Commentary on the Special Issue
citation: Gary D. Phye. (2012). Commentary on the Special Issue. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-012-9211-1
title: Involve teachers and building administrators in partnerships when implementing learning principles in schools
description: Commenting on the Agarwal, Bain, and Chamberlain article, the author argues that successful classroom implementation of basic learning principles depends on collaboration: "The involvement of both teachers and building administration is a critical factor in the successful implementation of the principles discussed herein." Partnerships build mutual appreciation, promote implementation, and give researchers insight into classroom complexity. His stated concern is that only a small number of students were impacted over a 5-year period, raising dissemination and scaling questions.
requirements: A collaborative partnership between researchers and educational personnel
constraints: The author notes the small number of students impacted over a 5-year period and questions how such positive efforts can be disseminated on a broad scale
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention and classroom application of learning principles
examples: The commentary describes the Agarwal et al. article as a positive story about facilitating educational reform through researcher-educator collaboration
key_sources: Gary D. Phye. (2012). Commentary on the Special Issue. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-012-9211-1

article_title: Educating the Developing Mind: Towards an Overarching Paradigm
citation: Demetriou, A., Spanoudis, G., & Mouyi, A. (2011). Educating the Developing Mind: Towards an Overarching Paradigm. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9178-3
title: Developmental milestones of representation: dual representation, logical necessity, and conditional representations
description: The review organizes representational development into milestones. Around ages 3-4 children differentiate representations from the objects they represent, which DeLoache called dual representation and which opens the way for intentional symbol use. Around ages 7-8 children grasp that representations constrain each other, the beginning of logical necessity. In early adolescence, conditional representations let thinkers view systems of representations from the point of view of each other, making thought suppositional and foresighted.
requirements: Gradual emergence of language bringing representations as such into focus for reflection
constraints: Milestone ages are modal characterizations of development, not strict boundaries
target_learning_goals: symbol use, systematic classification, hypothetical and proportional reasoning
key_sources: Demetriou, A., Spanoudis, G., & Mouyi, A. (2011). Educating the Developing Mind: Towards an Overarching Paradigm. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9178-3

article_title: An Interactive Layers Model of Self-Regulated Learning and Cognitive Load
citation: Joachim Wirth, Ferdinand Stebner, Melanie Trypke, Corinna Schuster, & Detlev Leutner. (2020). An Interactive Layers Model of Self-Regulated Learning and Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09568-4
title: Resonant states as a mechanism of unconscious self-regulation in sensory memory
description: Adapting Grossberg's Adaptive Resonance Theory, the authors propose that when sensory information matches expectations retrieved from long-term memory, bottom-up and top-down processes amplify each other, creating a resonant state in sensory memory. Resonant states can stay unconscious, allowing information to interact with long-term memory and contribute to learning without being transferred to working memory, without achieving consciousness, and without inducing cognitive load. Strong mismatched information instead transfers to working memory and induces cognitive load.
requirements: Resonance requires a match between bottom-up sensory information and top-down long-term memory information, such as schemes or expectations
constraints: Resonance is proposed as necessary but not sufficient for consciousness; resonant states that stay in sensory memory remain unconscious
target_learning_goals: implicit and incidental learning
automatic strategy use
unconscious metacognitive regulation
examples: The authors illustrate the mechanism with driving a car: steering remains unconscious as long as the road is straight, but a construction area with unexpected traffic signs transfers information to working memory and induces cognitive load
key_sources: Joachim Wirth, Ferdinand Stebner, Melanie Trypke, Corinna Schuster, & Detlev Leutner. (2020). An Interactive Layers Model of Self-Regulated Learning and Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09568-4

article_title: Does Retrieval Demand Moderate the Effectiveness of Covert Retrieval Practice? Comparing Covert and Overt Retrieval Practice for Learning Key Terms and Definitions
citation: Michelle L. Rivers, Paige E. Northern, Sarah K. Tauber. (2025). Does Retrieval Demand Moderate the Effectiveness of Covert Retrieval Practice? Comparing Covert and Overt Retrieval Practice for Learning Key Terms and Definitions. Educational Psychology Review (2025) 37:61. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10040-4
title: Retrieval dynamics hypothesis
description: The retrieval dynamics hypothesis explains when overt and covert retrieval practice differ in effectiveness. It posits that retrieving a single unit of information is relatively automatic and easy, whereas retrieving multiple interconnected units (e.g., definitions) is more demanding and, when done covertly, may terminate prematurely or be non-exhaustive. The article states that "retrieving multiple interconnected units of information (e.g., definitions, especially for novice learners) imposes higher retrieval demands, making overt retrieval more effective because it promotes exhaustive recall and self-monitoring during the process." The two experiments tested and found partial support for its predictions.
requirements: Material whose retrieval demand can be characterized along a low-to-high continuum (the article operationalizes demand as the type of to-be-retrieved material)
constraints: The article found only partial support: the overt advantage did not significantly differ by number of idea units, and the authors call the idea-unit operationalization of retrieval demand overly simplistic.
target_learners: undergraduate students learning declarative concepts (key terms and definitions)
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of key terms and definitions of declarative concepts
key_sources: Michelle L. Rivers, Paige E. Northern, Sarah K. Tauber. (2025). Does Retrieval Demand Moderate the Effectiveness of Covert Retrieval Practice? Comparing Covert and Overt Retrieval Practice for Learning Key Terms and Definitions. Educational Psychology Review (2025) 37:61. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10040-4

article_title: The Yet Underestimated Importance of Communicating Findings from Educational Trials to Teachers, Schools, School Authorities, or Policy Makers (Comment on Brady et al. (2023))
citation: Zitzmann, S., Machts, N., Hübner, N., Schauber, S., Möller, J., & Lindner, C. (2023). The Yet Underestimated Importance of Communicating Findings from Educational Trials to Teachers, Schools, School Authorities, or Policy Makers (Comment on Brady et al. (2023)). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09776-8
title: Report responder rates in addition to effect sizes so stakeholders can understand the consequences of implementing a treatment
description: Adapting a practice from clinical research, the article recommends that alongside an effect size measure, findings from a responder analysis be communicated: the relative frequencies of students whose outcomes improved substantially. Because responder rates "emerge from individual students’ percentages change and are thus an intuitive way of summarizing findings, stakeholders can better infer their practical significance." This applies to learning research and other outcomes such as stress reduction.
requirements: Percentage change computed for each student as (post − pre) / pre · 100%, classification into categories of change based on reasonable cutoffs, and counting students per category to yield responder rates
constraints: The efficacy of communicating responder rates needs to be tested empirically before conclusive recommendations can be formulated
target_learners: teachers, schools, school authorities, policy makers
target_learning_goals: stakeholder understanding of practical significance of treatment effects on student outcomes
examples: The article presents a hypothetical trial's responder rates as an easy-to-interpret bar chart (Fig. 1) with cutoffs of 0% and 50%
key_sources: Zitzmann, S., Machts, N., Hübner, N., Schauber, S., Möller, J., & Lindner, C. (2023). The Yet Underestimated Importance of Communicating Findings from Educational Trials to Teachers, Schools, School Authorities, or Policy Makers (Comment on Brady et al. (2023)). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09776-8

article_title: The Yet Underestimated Importance of Communicating Findings from Educational Trials to Teachers, Schools, School Authorities, or Policy Makers (Comment on Brady et al. (2023))
citation: Zitzmann, S., Machts, N., Hübner, N., Schauber, S., Möller, J., & Lindner, C. (2023). The Yet Underestimated Importance of Communicating Findings from Educational Trials to Teachers, Schools, School Authorities, or Policy Makers (Comment on Brady et al. (2023)). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09776-8
title: Choose responder-analysis cutoffs from theory or empirical research rather than arbitrarily
description: The article acknowledges the criticism that cutoffs for classifying students' percentage change into categories may seem arbitrary, and answers it: "the cutoffs may come from theory; for example, from expert considerations of what should at least be learned during a course/period of time. Or, they may come from empirical research." When theory is vague and findings rare, illustrative cutoffs may provide a starting point but not a definite definition.
requirements: Cutoffs grounded in theory (e.g., expert considerations of minimum expected learning) or in previous empirical research on expected learning gains
constraints: Classifying students is problematic when percentage change is assessed with low reliability; the article points to Zitzmann et al. (2023) for a way to deal with this problem
target_learning_goals: accurate classification of individual students' learning gains for stakeholder communication
examples: The authors used cutoffs of 0% and 50% in their Fig. 1 example, explicitly labeled as illustrative and not very valid
key_sources: Zitzmann, S., Machts, N., Hübner, N., Schauber, S., Möller, J., & Lindner, C. (2023). The Yet Underestimated Importance of Communicating Findings from Educational Trials to Teachers, Schools, School Authorities, or Policy Makers (Comment on Brady et al. (2023)). article_title: Opting Out as an Untapped Resource in Instructional Design: Review and Implications
citation: Yael Sidi · Rakefet Ackerman. (2024). Opting Out as an Untapped Resource in Instructional Design: Review and Implications. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09879-w
title: Region of Proximal Learning framework for strategic opting out
description: The Region of Proximal Learning framework explains learners' self-regulated choices about which task components to engage. Learners "continue to work on each task item as long as they metacognitively sense progress while thinking", and disengage from tasks exceeding their self-perceived trajectory. The review extends this framework to opting out, proposing that effective strategic opting out rests on "a fine-tuned balance between the perceived challenge level of each task item and the motivation to overcome it", so motivated students can be taught when and what to quit.
requirements: Learners must metacognitively sense progress while thinking to sustain engagement on task items
constraints: Tasks perceived as overly simplistic fail to stimulate cognitive advancement, while excessively challenging tasks may exceed current cognitive capacity
target_learners: students in learning and assessment contexts, from primary school to higher education
target_learning_goals: strategic effort regulation and self-regulated learning task choice
examples: The review interprets output-bound accuracy findings through this framework: by adjusting confidence thresholds to motivation and opting out of uncertain responses, learners engage tasks at the right challenge level
key_sources: Yael Sidi · Rakefet Ackerman. (2024). Opting Out as an Untapped Resource in Instructional Design: Review and Implications. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09879-w

article_title: Does Embodiment in Virtual Reality Boost Learning Transfer? Testing an Immersion-Interactivity Framework
citation: Klingenberg, S., Bosse, R., Mayer, R. E., & Makransky, G. (2024). Does Embodiment in Virtual Reality Boost Learning Transfer? Testing an Immersion-Interactivity Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09956-0
title: Real-life transfer test with behavior-anchored rating scale rated from head-mounted camera video
description: The main outcome measure was a real-life transfer test in which each student individually performed a serial dilution with concrete laboratory assets identical to the virtual ones. It "measured a total of 22 items, which were grouped into three overall domains: laboratory safety, dexterity, and accuracy of serial dilution," developed with a psychometrics expert and a subject matter expert. Each participant wore a head-mounted action camera, and "the real-life transfer test video of each participant was rated by two independent raters, using a behaviour-anchored rating scale." Interrater reliability (linear weighted Kappa) was 0.877 for safety, 0.575 for dexterity, and 0.361 for accuracy.
requirements: Two independent raters trained on the behavior-anchored rating scale, and head-mounted cameras recording first-person video of each performance
constraints: Interrater reliability for accuracy of serial dilution was rated poor (Kappa = 0.361) and for dexterity fair (0.575) by the article's own standards
target_learners: high school students who completed the virtual pipetting lesson
target_learning_goals: transfer of a learned technical procedure from a virtual environment to real-world performance
examples: Dexterity items such as 'put on a pipette tip correctly' were scored 0-4, and disagreements between raters were resolved by using the mean score
key_sources: Klingenberg, S., Bosse, R., Mayer, R. E., & Makransky, G. (2024). Does Embodiment in Virtual Reality Boost Learning Transfer? Testing an Immersion-Interactivity Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09956-0

article_title: Transforming Self-regulated Learning – Multimodal Insights and Future Directions
citation: Tina Seufert. (2026). Transforming Self-regulated Learning – Multimodal Insights and Future Directions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10119-6
title: Resource-based model of SRL: regulation as a function of the balance between learner resources, task demands, and instructional context
description: Drawing on cognitive load theory and Seufert's (2018) model integrating cognitive load with self-regulated learning, the paper proposes that SRL should be understood as a function of the dynamic balance between learners' resources, task demands, and instructional context. It states that "regulation is most likely to occur when learners operate within a zone of optimal challenge—where the task is demanding enough to require regulation, but not so complex as to exceed their cognitive capacity." This adds an explanatory dimension to CAMM: regulation is shaped by the interplay between task demands and available learner resources.
requirements: Cognitive and motivational resources must be available and not entirely consumed by external demands or task-related load for planning, monitoring, or regulation to take place.
constraints: Under high cognitive load or in complex tasks, even well-developed regulatory skills may fail to unfold.
target_learners: Learners in multimodal and classroom learning environments, particularly those facing high task complexity
target_learning_goals: Enabling self-regulated learning by matching task demands to learners' cognitive and motivational resources
examples: The paper cites Kubsch et al.'s finding that prior knowledge becomes relevant later in the regulation process as support for treating learner characteristics as temporally sensitive rather than stable moderators.
key_sources: Tina Seufert. (2026). Transforming Self-regulated Learning – Multimodal Insights and Future Directions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10119-6

article_title: Classroom Management Scripts: a Theoretical Model Contrasting Expert and Novice Teachers’ Knowledge and Awareness of Classroom Events
citation: Charlotte E. Wolff, Halszka Jarodzka, Henny P.A. Boshuizen. (2020). Classroom Management Scripts: a Theoretical Model Contrasting Expert and Novice Teachers' Knowledge and Awareness of Classroom Events. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09542-0
title: Frame classroom management as a learning concern rather than a behavioral concern in teacher education
description: The article argues that because experts center student learning in interpreting events while novices emphasize behavior, teacher education should reframe classroom management around learning. It recommends "making new teachers aware that enabling conditions can be rather subtle, and reframing classroom management as a learning concern rather than a behavioral concern" as an area programs could explore more thoroughly, and reinforcing teachers' agency to counter the tendency to blame students.
requirements: Teacher education programs must address enabling conditions and teacher agency explicitly with beginner teachers
target_learning_goals: classroom management expertise
interpretation of classroom events
examples: The article suggests reinforcing the agency and influence of teachers on classroom situations may aid novices in overcoming the tendency to finger students as the cause of problems
key_sources: Charlotte E. Wolff, Halszka Jarodzka, Henny P.A. Boshuizen. (2020). Classroom Management Scripts: a Theoretical Model Contrasting Expert and Novice Teachers' Knowledge and Awareness of Classroom Events. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09542-0

article_title: A Systematic Review of Peer Assessment Design Elements
citation: Alqassab, M., Strijbos, J.-W., Panadero, E., Fernández Ruiz, J., Warrens, M., & To, J. (2023). A Systematic Review of Peer Assessment Design Elements. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09723-7
title: Refined definition of peer assessment as a learning phenomenon in social constellations, organized by a four-category coding scheme
description: The review defines peer assessment as "a learning phenomenon where individuals or social constellations (e.g., pair, group, team, community)—within a physical and/or virtual environment—exchange, react to, interact and/or act upon information about individual performance and/or individual contributions" with the purpose of accomplishing shared and individual learning goals. It extends Topping's (1998) definition to cover social constellations and virtual environments, and frames instructional scaffolds provided by agents (teacher, peer, self, technology) as fadable supports. The definition underpins a coding scheme of 27 design elements grouped into four categories: context (what designers cannot manipulate), instructional design (what designers can manipulate), outcomes, and moderators/mediators.
requirements: Peer assessment must be clearly distinguished from other peer-assisted learning activities such as peer tutoring, peer modelling, peer monitoring, and peer coaching
constraints: The coding scheme was built on Gielen et al.'s (2011) refinement of Topping's (1998) typology, with variables refined from contemporary reviews
target_learning_goals: domain-specific knowledge or skills
social skills
examples: The coding scheme includes 22 instructional design elements such as purpose, object, privacy, contact, matching, training, and revision
key_sources: Alqassab, M., Strijbos, J.-W., Panadero, E., Fernández Ruiz, J., Warrens, M., & To, J. (2023). A Systematic Review of Peer Assessment Design Elements. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09723-7

article_title: Let Learners Monitor the Learning Content and Their Learning Behavior! A Meta-analysis on the Effectiveness of Tools to Foster Monitoring
citation: Dignath, C., van Ewijk, R., Perels, F., & Fabriz, S. (2023). Let Learners Monitor the Learning Content and Their Learning Behavior! A Meta-analysis on the Effectiveness of Tools to Foster Monitoring. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09718-4
title: Reactivity and reminder effects as the mode of action of monitoring tools
description: The article explains monitoring tools' operation through two mechanisms. The reactivity effect holds that directing attention to one's learning already changes behavior: "This shift of attention focus alone is already assumed to elicit behavior change, also called the reactivity effect (Zimmerman, 2002)." The reminder effect holds that tool questions act as cues that prompt strategy use in the moment of learning. Tools thus engage learners in monitoring and control processes within the SRL cycle, drawing on Winne and Hadwin's COPES model in which monitoring compares products against standards.
requirements: Tools must include questions or prompts that focus the learner's attention on their understanding or learning behavior during the learning process.
constraints: The reactivity account is presented as an assumption from prior theory rather than a mechanism tested within this meta-analysis.
target_learners: students from primary school through higher education and adult learners
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning skills, metacognitive monitoring of comprehension and learning behavior
examples: Learning journals with self-recording prompts such as registering one's actions during task performance; prompts for monitoring understanding such as asking which main points have not yet been understood.
key_sources: Dignath, C., van Ewijk, R., Perels, F., & Fabriz, S. (2023). Let Learners Monitor the Learning Content and Their Learning Behavior! A Meta-analysis on the Effectiveness of Tools to Foster Monitoring. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09718-4

article_title: Personal Reflections on Science Communication and Sharing Retrieval Practice Research with Teachers
citation: Pooja K. Agarwal. (2024). Personal reflections on science communication and sharing retrieval practice research with teachers. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09839-w
title: retrievalpractice.org website, downloadable practice guides, and email newsletter for teachers
description: A suite of free science-communication resources developed by the author from 2012 onward: a 10-page practice guide on retrieval practice refined through teacher focus groups and classroom observation, six additional practice guides on interleaving, transfer, spaced retrieval, metacognition, early childhood, and interpreting meta-analyses, the retrievalpractice.org website (created 2014), and a Mailchimp email newsletter begun around 2016. All materials are "freely available for download under Creative Commons Licensing," with translations in Spanish, Portuguese, Dutch, and Mandarin.
requirements: Brief PDFs formatted for printing and easy to forward via email; iterative feedback from K–12 teachers and administrators shaped the guides
constraints: The author reports creating original weekly content required vast time, energy, and unpaid labor, plus unanticipated platform expenses; the newsletter was paused during COVID and later reduced to monthly
target_learning_goals: Understanding and implementing retrieval practice, spacing, interleaving, and metacognitive strategies in classrooms
examples: The first 10-page guide included accessible research descriptions, practical tips, FAQs, and an implementation checklist, and omitted graphs except a pie chart showing reduced test anxiety
key_sources: Pooja K. Agarwal. (2024). Personal reflections on science communication and sharing retrieval practice research with teachers. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09839-w

article_title: Turning Roadblocks into Speed Bumps: A Call for Implementation Reform in Science Communication About Retrieval Practice
citation: Sumeracki, M. A., Nebel, C. L., Kaminske, A. N., and Kuepper-Tetzel, C. E. (2024). Turning roadblocks into speed bumps: a call for implementation reform in science communication about retrieval practice. Educational Psychology Review, 36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09854-5
title: Educator workshops on retrieval practice as the authors' science-communication vehicle
description: The authors report that their efforts to increase science communication with educators "have included workshops", through which they engage educators in conversation about implementing retrieval practice. These workshops are the setting in which the three recurring concerns about workload, scope of usefulness, and test anxiety surfaced, and in which the authors attempted to address them by discussing nuances of the retrieval practice literature. The article describes the workshops as the experiential basis for its commentary.
requirements: Face-to-face or interactive conversation with educators so that concerns can surface and be discussed
constraints: The article reports no formal evaluation of the workshops' effects on educator implementation
target_learners: Educators (teachers and instructors) learning about retrieval practice
target_learning_goals: Understanding and implementing retrieval practice effectively in teaching
examples: The authors describe describing ways they have attempted to leverage existing literature to address educator concerns during workshop conversations
key_sources: Sumeracki, M. A., Nebel, C. L., Kaminske, A. N., and Kuepper-Tetzel, C. E. (2024). Turning roadblocks into speed bumps: a call for implementation reform in science communication about retrieval practice. Educational Psychology Review, 36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09854-5

article_title: Happy Together? On the Relationship Between Research on Retrieval Practice and Generative Learning Using the Case of Follow-Up Learning Tasks
citation: Julian Roelle, Tino Endres, Roman Abel, Niklas Obergassel, Matthias Nückles, Alexander Renkl. (2023). Happy Together? On the Relationship Between Research on Retrieval Practice and Generative Learning Using the Case of Follow-Up Learning Tasks. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09810-9
title: Retrieval practice as consolidation of mental representations in memory
description: The review characterizes retrieval practice (test-enhanced learning) as learning tasks requiring learners to retrieve studied information from memory, whose main theoretical function is consolidation. It states that retrieval practice is assumed to consolidate the respective retrieved knowledge in memory and hence enable learners to maintain their knowledge or performance originating from that knowledge over long periods of time. The review uses this function as one of two complementary functions organizing follow-up learning task design.
requirements: Tasks must require learners to retrieve the studied information from memory, e.g., via closed-book format
constraints: Benefits are largest when the format of the posttest questions matches the answer formats of the follow-up learning task, per the review
target_learners: learners studying factual and conceptual content after initial instruction
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of studied content
key_sources: Julian Roelle, Tino Endres, Roman Abel, Niklas Obergassel, Matthias Nückles, Alexander Renkl. (2023). Happy Together? On the Relationship Between Research on Retrieval Practice and Generative Learning Using the Case of Follow-Up Learning Tasks. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09810-9

article_title: Moving Beyond Fulfillment: Wisdom Years Stories of Passion, Perseverance, and Productivity
citation: Kiewra, K.A., Walsh, J. & Labenz, C. (2023). Moving Beyond Fulfillment: Wisdom Years Stories of Passion, Perseverance, and Productivity. Educ Psychol Rev 35, 20. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09747-z
title: Retire to something rather than simply retiring
description: The article's first conclusion advises readers: "Do not retire, but if you do, retire to something." The principle holds that continued productivity in the wisdom years comes from avoiding an aimless retirement and instead redirecting one's energies toward a purposeful pursuit, as illustrated by the interviewed participants who shun retirement and remain productive.
requirements: A purposeful pursuit or goal to retire toward, rather than retirement as an end in itself.
constraints: Grounded in the experiences of seven exceptionally productive interviewees; the article does not test this advice experimentally.
target_learning_goals: maintaining purpose and productivity after career transitions
examples: The article's conclusion lists "Do not retire, but if you do, retire to something" as its first advice-laden conclusion.
key_sources: Kiewra, K.A., Walsh, J. & Labenz, C. (2023). Moving Beyond Fulfillment: Wisdom Years Stories of Passion, Perseverance, and Productivity. Educ Psychol Rev 35, 20. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09747-z

article_title: Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead
citation: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2
title: Reward-learning framework of knowledge acquisition and motivation transformations
description: The reward-learning framework of knowledge acquisition (Murayama, 2022) explains how individuals initiate and sustain learning: individuals engage in learning "because gaining knowledge is intrinsically rewarding and often linked to positive emotional experiences". Awareness of a knowledge gap triggers curiosity and expectation of the rewarding value of new information, and acquired knowledge reinforces future learning via an internal loop, while an external loop sustains long-term interest through generating new questions, increasing valuation, and enhancing capability. The article extends the framework with extrinsic rewards (Bardach & Murayama, 2025) as an entry point for unmotivated learners, whereby extrinsic-reward motivation can transform into intrinsic-reward motivation—referred to as motivation transformations—and links the framework to TESSERA-based personality development.
requirements: Extrinsic rewards act as an entry point that sets in motion the positive feedback loop of internally rewarding learning processes
constraints: The article argues extrinsic factors do not contradict intrinsic ones and can go hand in hand, countering views that extrinsic rewards undermine intrinsic motivation
target_learning_goals: initiation and sustained engagement in learning, curiosity, interest, and long-term trait development
examples: Students who initially learn to satisfy parents' or teachers' expectations experience rewarding engagement and knowledge acquisition, kick-starting the intrinsically rewarding learning process
key_sources: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2

article_title: Is a Preference for Realism Really Naive After All? A Cognitive Model of Learning with Realistic Visualizations
citation: Skulmowski, A., Nebel, S., Remmele, M., & Rey, G. D. (2022). Is a Preference for Realism Really Naive After All? A Cognitive Model of Learning with Realistic Visualizations. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09638-1
title: Specify the geometry, shading, and rendering design choices of learning materials to create reproducible realism comparisons
description: The article recommends that research papers provide standardized information about learning materials so that a particular level of realism can be recreated with the same or other learning contents. A well-defined degree of realism is achieved when 'researchers and practitioners have enough information concerning the learning materials available to recreate that particular level of realism'. Authors should report software packages, plug-ins, unusual settings, and design choices such as whether the same 3D model underlies realistic and schematic versions and whether texture maps were used.
requirements: Reports should include the name of the software package(s) used, whether special plug-ins or unusual settings were utilized, and design choices made during production of the learning materials
constraints: The article notes most papers already include excerpts of the learning materials but that categorization of existing research is often impossible due to missing information
target_learning_goals: comparable, replicable research on realism in learning materials
examples: The article proposes assessing visualizations concerning their geometry, shading, and rendering, and categorizing previous studies along these dimensions in Table 2
key_sources: Skulmowski, A., Nebel, S., Remmele, M., & Rey, G. D. (2022). Is a Preference for Realism Really Naive After All? A Cognitive Model of Learning with Realistic Visualizations. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09638-1

article_title: How Are Curiosity and Interest Different? Naïve Bayes Classification of People’s Beliefs
citation: Donnellan, E., Aslan, S., Fastrich, G. M., & Murayama, K. (2021). How Are Curiosity and Interest Different? Naïve Bayes Classification of People's Beliefs. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09622-9
title: Reward-learning framework: curiosity and interest as folk psychological concepts constructed from knowledge-acquisition experiences
description: The reward-learning framework of knowledge acquisition holds that curiosity and interest are labels people assign to their own experiences of information seeking. Under this account, "curiosity and interest are commonsense (also termed naïve or folk) psychological concepts, intuitively and subjectively constructed by people to describe feelings resulting from underlying psychological processes to which they lack true introspective access". Because no agreed expert definitions exist, the framework proposes that the non-expert consensus view can serve as the reference definition for future empirical work, complementing top-down theoretical approaches.
requirements: Requires treating definitional consensus as a starting point for, not evidence of, distinct underlying psychological processes
constraints: The article states we cannot currently make hard distinctions at the level of specific psychological or neural processes
target_learners: adult online participants defining curiosity and interest
target_learning_goals: conceptual clarity on the distinction between curiosity and interest in knowledge acquisition
examples: Study 1 elicited free-text definitions (minimum 80 words each) from online participants and trained a Naïve Bayes classifier on them
key_sources: Donnellan, E., Aslan, S., Fastrich, G. M., & Murayama, K. (2021). How Are Curiosity and Interest Different? Naïve Bayes Classification of People's Beliefs. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09622-9

article_title: Process Account of Curiosity and Interest: A Reward-Learning Perspective
citation: Kou Murayama, Lily FitzGibbon & Michiko Sakaki. (2019). Process Account of Curiosity and Interest: A Reward-Learning Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09499-9
title: Reward-learning framework of autonomous knowledge acquisition
description: The article presents a framework in which knowledge acquisition itself serves as a reward: recognizing a knowledge gap motivates information-seeking, acquisition generates a rewarding experience, and that experience "strengthens the further information-seeking behavior by increasing the expected reward value of new information." An expanded knowledge base also generates new questions, forming a positive feedback loop that enables sustainable learning. The framework is built on reinforcement-learning models but incorporates knowledge-specific features such as new knowledge creating room for further gaps.
requirements: The framework centers on reward learning as the key to understanding sustainable knowledge acquisition, so a rewarding experience upon knowledge acquisition is required for the loop to form
constraints: The authors acknowledge that the framework is still preliminary
target_learning_goals: sustained autonomous knowledge acquisition
information-seeking behavior
examples: The article illustrates the loop with a student learning to solve quadratic equations, whose understanding may prompt wondering whether cubic equations can be solved similarly
key_sources: Kou Murayama, Lily FitzGibbon & Michiko Sakaki. (2019). Process Account of Curiosity and Interest: A Reward-Learning Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09499-9

article_title: Looking Beyond the Hype: Understanding the Effects of AI on Learning
citation: Bauer, E., Greiff, S., Graesser, A. C., Scheiter, K., & Sailer, M. (2025). Looking Beyond the Hype: Understanding the Effects of AI on Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10020-8
title: Mitigate AI over-reliance by keeping learners actively engaged in reflective processes before or during AI output generation
description: This principle holds that risks of learners uncritically accepting AI outputs can be reduced by structuring reflective human input around AI use. The article states that "the risks of over-reliance on potentially suboptimal outputs can be mitigated if professionals are actively engaged in reflective processes before or during the generation of AI outputs", citing cognitive forcing functions that elicit initial judgments before AI outputs appear. It recommends designing AI-enhanced learning opportunities that prioritize cognitive engagement.
requirements: Learners or professionals must be prompted to make initial judgments or engage in reflection before or while AI outputs are generated
constraints: The article notes effective prevention strategies in educational contexts are yet to be explored; the supporting evidence comes from workplace learning contexts
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
self-regulated learning
maintaining domain-specific and transversal skills
examples: The article describes cognitive forcing functions that initiate human inputs, such as initial judgments, before AI outputs are generated, and notes explanations accompanying AI outputs can help users critically assess information
key_sources: Bauer, E., Greiff, S., Graesser, A. C., Scheiter, K., & Sailer, M. (2025). Looking Beyond the Hype: Understanding the Effects of AI on Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10020-8

article_title: Preregistration and registered reports
citation: Preregistration and Registered Reports. (2021). https://osf.io/ya594
title: Registered reports: a two-phase publication format with in-principle acceptance before results are known
description: Registered reports are a journal publication format, developed by the journal Cortex for neuroscience, that integrates preregistration with peer review in two phases. Authors submit a Phase I manuscript with introduction, background, and method including pre-specified analytic plans; if reviewers and editors find merit, "the article is then granted “in-principle” acceptance", meaning publication is agreed regardless of the direction or magnitude of findings, provided the study is conducted as agreed with documented modifications. The article edited an AERA Open special topic publishing some of the first registered reports in educational psychology.
requirements: Peer review must occur at least before data analysis, and ideally before data collection begins, so reviewers evaluate design without knowing results
constraints: Field studies requiring negotiation with local stakeholders may be incompatible with rigid preregistration timelines; articles can still be rejected after in-principle acceptance for implementation flaws
target_learning_goals: increasing transparency and replicability of educational research
reducing publication bias against null findings
examples: The AERA Open special topic (2018-2020) published registered reports on student-teacher relationships, researcher trustworthiness perceptions, text framings for college matriculation, and gifted education identification policies; three of seven articles had graduate student lead authors
key_sources: Preregistration and Registered Reports. (2021). https://osf.io/ya594

article_title: A critical analysis of the current motivation theories in educational psychology: Why the same theories continue to dominate
citation: Murayama, K., & von Keyserlingk, L. (2025). A critical analysis of the current motivation theories in educational psychology: Why the same theories continue to dominate.
title: Reward-learning framework of knowledge acquisition: long-term intellectual engagement as a positive feedback process
description: Murayama and colleagues' reward-learning framework extends reward learning models and "explains long-term voluntary engagement as a causal positive feedback process that surrounds the rewarding value of information, knowledge structure, and information-seeking behavior". Learning is motivated by meta-cognitive awareness of uncertainty; acquired knowledge produces a rewarding feeling, elicits new questions, increases the value of topic knowledge, and increases the ability to understand new information, sustaining engagement without external rewards. The framework explains engagement without using constructs like interest, curiosity, or intrinsic motivation, treating them as emergent properties.
requirements: The framework still relies on some theoretical constructs (value or perceived competence) and does not explain how value is represented and calculated in the mind
constraints: The authors avoided calling it a theory because it remains underspecified; it is a first step toward a more elaborative theory
target_learners: learners engaging in voluntary intellectual activities
target_learning_goals: sustaining long-term voluntary engagement and information-seeking in a domain
examples: The article illustrates the framework with a person persisting in learning statistics: acquired knowledge reveals knowledge gaps, raising the expected rewarding value of further information
key_sources: Murayama, K., & von Keyserlingk, L. (2025). A critical analysis of the current motivation theories in educational psychology: Why the same theories continue to dominate. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2025.2473894

article_title: Math anxiety and math achievement in primary school children: Longitudinal relationship and predictors
citation: Szczygieł M.; Szűcs D.; Toffalini E. (2024). Math anxiety and math achievement in primary school children: Longitudinal relationship and predictors. LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION. https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101906
title: Reciprocal Theory of the math anxiety–math achievement relationship
description: The Reciprocal Theory holds that math anxiety and math achievement influence each other over time, rather than one direction alone. The article tested it against the Deficit Theory (achievement predicts anxiety) and the Debilitating Anxiety Theory (anxiety predicts achievement), reporting that "MATH at T1 predicted MA at T2 and MA at T1 predicted MATH at T2 (supporting the Reciprocal Theory)" in 337 Polish primary school children.
requirements: Longitudinal data with math anxiety and math achievement measured at multiple time points to test cross-lag prediction in both directions
constraints: Evidence comes from primary school children in Poland across first and second grade; the article does not print effect sizes in the available text
target_learners: Primary school children (first and second grade)
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement and math anxiety development
examples: The study analyzed longitudinal data at three time points: T0 (beginning of first grade), T1 (end of first grade), and T2 (end of second grade).
key_sources: Szczygieł M.; Szűcs D.; Toffalini E. (2024). Math anxiety and math achievement in primary school children: Longitudinal relationship and predictors. LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION. https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101906

article_title: Strategies for regulating achievement emotions: Conceptualization and relations with university students’ emotions, well-being, and health
citation: Stockinger, K., Dresel, M., Marsh, H. W., & Pekrun, R. (2025). Strategies for regulating achievement emotions: Conceptualization and relations with university students' emotions, well-being, and health. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102089
title: Support students in reappraising control and value appraisals to increase enjoyment and decrease anxiety and boredom
description: Grounded in control-value theory, the article argues that reappraisal of achievement-related appraisals is a key lever for regulating achievement emotions: "Boostingperceivedcontrolshouldhelpincreaseenjoymentand decrease anxiety or boredom resulting from overchallenge". Across the three studies, reappraisal and competence development showed the most pronounced links with target emotions and were implied to be especially adaptive strategies for educators to foster.
requirements: Instruction should target students' perceived control and value appraisals, the proximal antecedents of achievement emotions in control-value theory
constraints: Evidence is largely correlational; the article states cross-sectional relations may reflect different causal feedback loops, so causal direction is unresolved
target_learning_goals: regulating enjoyment, anxiety, and boredom in academic settings
examples: The RAEQ includes reappraisal items targeting perceived value of learning materials and perceived competence and control over learning, such as reminding oneself there are more important things in life when nervous during studying
key_sources: Stockinger, K., Dresel, M., Marsh, H. W., & Pekrun, R. (2025). Strategies for regulating achievement emotions: Conceptualization and relations with university students' emotions, well-being, and health. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102089

article_title: Boosting debiasing: Impact of repeated training on reasoning
citation: Nina Franiatte, Esther Boissin, Alexandra Delmas, Wim De Neys. (2024). Boosting Debiasing: Impact of Repeated Training on Reasoning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101845
title: Repeat debiasing training sessions to further boost sound intuiting beyond a single-shot intervention
description: A repeated debias training approach schedules multiple short explanation-based training sessions on classic reasoning tasks rather than a single session. The article's Studies 1 and 2 show the first session lets most trained reasoners answer correctly already at the intuitive stage, and repetition adds further gains: the second session lifted final accuracy by a further 11.2 points, and the authors present the results "as a proof-of-principle for a repeated debias training approach."
requirements: Training uses brief plain-English explanations that state both the correct response and the typical biased response, with no performance feedback and no formal algebraic equations
constraints: The second-session gain was much smaller than the first (approximately 11.6 vs 43.1 points) with only marginal Block x Group interactions
Session 2 Block x Group interactions reached only marginal significance (p = .05 final, p = .06 initial)
Task order within the battery may matter: the training effect trended weaker for the last task, possibly due to fatigue
target_learners: adult reasoners recruited via Prolific Academic
initially biased reasoners on classic heuristics-and-biases tasks
target_learning_goals: avoiding biased intuitive responses on conflict reasoning problems
applying probabilistic and logical principles such as the conjunction rule and base-rate use
examples: Participants received a first one-hour training session with pre-intervention, intervention, and post-intervention blocks on three tasks, a second session two days later with modified problem contents, and a third session two months later in Study 2
key_sources: Nina Franiatte, Esther Boissin, Alexandra Delmas, Wim De Neys. (2024). Boosting Debiasing: Impact of Repeated Training on Reasoning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101845

article_title: Contrasting orthographically similar words facilitates adult second language vocabulary learning
citation: Baxter, P.A.; Bekkering, H.; Dijkstra, A.F.J.; Droop, W.; Hurk, M.M. van den; Léoné, F.T.M. (2022). Contrasting orthographically similar words facilitates adult second language vocabulary learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101582
title: Representational specification account of similarity and contrasting in L2 vocabulary learning
description: The article proposes that new L2 word representations are initially underspecified and that similarity between items sharpens them: "representations sharpen over time, allowing learners to make increased distinctions between words as vocabulary grows." Contrasting tasks draw attention to distinctive lexical information, enabling more specific form and form-meaning representations. The account yields three hypotheses: contrasting as a general desirable difficulty, direction-dependent effects, and benefits only for underspecified (new L2) dimensions.
requirements: Learners must encounter similar items whose representations are not yet fully specified, so that attention to distinctive information drives sharpening
constraints: Form and meaning similarity mainly cause errors while representations are still underspecified; once stabilized, similarity should no longer confuse learners
target_learning_goals: L2 vocabulary acquisition and form-meaning linking
examples: Experiment 1 contrasted orthographically or semantically similar L2 words via sorted versus shuffled multiple-choice triplets with identical word lists across conditions
key_sources: Baxter, P.A.; Bekkering, H.; Dijkstra, A.F.J.; Droop, W.; Hurk, M.M. van den; Léoné, F.T.M. (2022). Contrasting orthographically similar words facilitates adult second language vocabulary learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101582

article_title: Category change in the absence of cognitive conflict.
citation: Ramsburg, J. T., & Ohlsson, S. (2015). Category Change in the Absence of Cognitive Conflict. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Category+Change+in+the+Absence+of+Cognitive+Conflict%22
title: Resubsumption Theory of non-monotonic conceptual change without cognitive conflict
description: Resubsumption Theory explains how non-monotonic cognitive change can occur without cognitive conflict. Its core idea is that "An object, event, or phenomenon subsumed under some concept, schema, or (informal) theory X can be understood differently by being assimilated to, or subsumed under, an alternative concept, schema, or (informal) theory Y." Because knowledge structures created in one domain can apply to other domains, two structures may be activated in parallel and compete for control of action; competition is resolved by accumulated evidence of higher cognitive utility, not by logical falsification or dissatisfaction with the prior conception.
requirements: Multiple knowledge structures that can each apply to the same domain must be available for parallel activation and response competition
constraints: The theory only claims knowledge representations are abstract, not bound to their domain of origin, and is agnostic about other aspects of knowledge; its processes are not logic-like and conflicts are competitions among knowledge structures rather than logical contradictions
target_learners: Learners with entrenched prior conceptions undergoing conceptual change, e.g., science students
target_learning_goals: Non-monotonic conceptual change: replacing an initial conception with a contradictory alternative conception
examples: The article's re-categorization experiments operationalize the theory: participants master an initial category (black nuclei determine oxygen resistance), the definition silently changes to bent ribosomes, and learners shift without falsifying feedback
key_sources: Ramsburg, J. T., & Ohlsson, S. (2015). Category Change in the Absence of Cognitive Conflict. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Category+Change+in+the+Absence+of+Cognitive+Conflict%22

article_title: Teacher behavior and peer liking and disliking: The teacher as a social referent for peer status.
citation: Hendrickx, M. M. H. G., Mainhard, M. T., Oudman, V. S., Boor-Klip, H. J., & Brekelmans, J. M. G. (2017). Teacher Behavior and Peer Liking and Disliking: The Teacher as a Social Referent for Peer Status. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(4), 546-558. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000157
title: Teachers should refrain from openly negative behavior toward students, particularly those at risk of peer rejection
description: Because negative teacher behavior toward a student was transmitted to peers' disliking of that student via peers' perceptions of the teacher's disliking, the article draws a practical implication for classroom practice: teachers should avoid openly negative behavior directed at individual students. As the abstract puts it, "it may be important for teachers to refrain from openly negative behavior toward students, particularly those at risk of peer rejection." This targets the disliking pathway, the one the study supported.
requirements: Teachers must be aware that their behavior toward individual students is observed by the peer group and interpreted as a signal of the teacher's liking or disliking.
constraints: The recommendation is hedged by the authors ("may be important") and rests on evidence concerning negative behavior and peer disliking only.
target_learners: Elementary school students, particularly those at risk of peer rejection
target_learning_goals: Preventing peer rejection and supporting positive peer relationships
examples: The study found negative teacher behavior predicted peers' disliking of a student six months later via perceived teacher disliking.
key_sources: Hendrickx, M. M. H. G., Mainhard, M. T., Oudman, V. S., Boor-Klip, H. J., & Brekelmans, J. M. G. (2017). title: Revised two-column word order for the Terman vocabulary test with young children
description: A reordered two-column word list for the Terman (Stanford Revision) vocabulary test, arranged from tabulated credit totals for kindergarten and Grade I children. The author states the new order "makes the two lists more nearly equal in difficulty, so that the use of one alone is somewhat more accurate," and that mimeographed sheets may easily be made up in this order or in a similar order derived from the data.

article_title: The education and control of the emotions.
citation: Henry, T. S. (1916). The Education and Control of the Emotions. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/
title: Control emotion by reclassifying the stimulus through judgment, changing the attitude taken toward it
description: Following Pillsbury, the article holds that real control of emotion is effected at the source by classifying, and thus controlling, the situation which calls the emotion forth. 'Sensations and stimuli which are capable of being classified in different ways arouse different emotions upon the basis of that classification' — the same remark may be an insult from a stranger or a jest from a friend. Thorndike frames this as learning to judge the situation objectively by the facts, not subjectively by the feelings.
requirements: The stimulus must fall outside the class of fundamental instincts most closely linked with their stimuli, since the attitude is only to a considerable extent under one's control
constraints: The article notes this control is available only to some degree, and that the attitude is chiefly controllable for stimuli outside fundamental instinct-linked classes
target_learning_goals: inhibition of undesirable emotional reactions such as anger through objective judgment of the situation
examples: The article describes a teacher relieving an over-emotional state in a child by counseling and reasoning, where explanation of the situation may change the object of the feeling and draw it into harmless or useful channels; and directing the attention elsewhere until the occasion for the emotion is past.
key_sources: Henry, T. S. (1916). The Education and Control of the Emotions. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/

article_title: The education and control of the emotions.
citation: Henry, T. S. (1916). The Education and Control of the Emotions. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/
title: Redirect emotions toward proper objects and sublimate primitive feelings by attaching them to other objects and processes
description: For emotions good or bad only according to their objects, such as ambition, pride and anger, control involves proper direction; the article argues it matters to be able to hate aright. Closely allied is sublimation, defined by Colvin and Bagley as 'the method which attempts to lift a strong feeling bodily out of the instinct to which it naturally belongs and to fasten it firmly to another object and to an entirely different process'. Effective control thus lies in forming attitudes, ideals and sentiments attached to the original emotion as a core.
requirements: Appropriate ideas must be attached to the original emotion as a core to form attitudes, ideals and sentiments
constraints: The Freudians use the term sublimation exclusively for the sexual instincts, though the article extends it by a similar interpretation to other emotions
target_learning_goals: directing emotions such as ambition, pride and anger toward proper objects
sublimating primitive instincts into socially valuable sentiments
examples: Colvin and Bagley's illustrations: the Salvation Army enlisting a military organization with suggestions of physical combat in the service of peaceable ideals, and the Boy Scout movement attaching feelings connected with primitive instincts to objects insuring only symbolic responses.
