article_title: Reading comprehension on handheld devices versus on paper: A narrative review and meta-analysis of the medium effect and its moderators.
citation: Salmerón, L., Altamura, L., Delgado, P., Karagiorgi, A., & Vargas, C. (2023). Reading comprehension on handheld devices vs. on paper: A narrative review and meta-analysis of the medium effect and its moderators. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://dx.doi.org/10.1037/edu0000830
title: Reading for Understanding framework organizing screen inferiority moderators into reader, text, activity, and socio-cultural context
description: The article uses the Reading for Understanding framework (Snow et al., 2002) as its organizing taxonomy for potential moderators of the screen inferiority effect on handheld devices. The framework conceives comprehension as extracting and constructing knowledge, where "Comprehension occurs as the interaction of three main elements: reader (individual abilities, knowledge and attitudes), text (any form of print or digital text), and activity (purpose, processes, and consequences of reading), that take place within a particular socio-cultural context." The review maps moderator evidence onto these four elements and codes study variables accordingly for meta-regression.
requirements: Applied to reading-medium research, requires coding of study characteristics into reader, text, activity, and socio-cultural context variables for moderator analysis
constraints: The authors note most previous research has focused on the text and activity levels, and to a lesser extent the reader and socio-cultural context
target_learners: autonomous readers across educational stages, from primary school to undergraduates
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension of print and digital texts
examples: The review's coding scheme classified educational stage, text genre and length, navigation mode, device type, time limit, question type, session modality, and publication year as moderators within the four framework elements.
key_sources: Salmerón, L., Altamura, L., Delgado, P., Karagiorgi, A., & Vargas, C. (2023). Reading comprehension on handheld devices vs. on paper: A narrative review and meta-analysis of the medium effect and its moderators. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://dx.doi.org/10.1037/edu0000830

article_title: A book on physical growth by a French writer.
citation: No author line. (1920). New Publications. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/
title: Take repeated physical measurements at regular intervals so educators can know the child intimately and individualize education
description: Godin's book argues that the only worthwhile physical measurements are those admitting comparison with previous states of development of the same individual, and that such comparisons are valid only when measurements are repeated at regular intervals. The review quotes him: repeated measurements are necessary "in order to enable the teacher and educator to know the child intimately and profoundly," making possible a degree of individualization of education unknown in the past. Measures are taken semi-annually to preserve variations in growth rhythm.
requirements: Measurements must be repeated at regular intervals, semi-annually in Godin's scheme, for comparisons with previous states of the same individual to be valid.
constraints: The reviewer notes the book includes no actual data, which makes the volume seriously unsatisfactory.
target_learners: school-age children from birth to puberty
target_learning_goals: individualization of education based on each child's physical development
examples: Godin's book includes many charts and diagrams illustrating segmental development from birth to puberty, with measures taken semi-annually.

article_title: The Teaching of Natural Science.
citation: J. C. B. (1915). Editorial. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Volume VI, Number 10. Warwick & York. https://archive.org
title: Reorganize science teaching from bottom to top to develop students' keenest interest in broader knowledge of scientific discoveries.
description: The editorial's central design recommendation: science teaching at every level should be reorganized so that instruction develops, in the author's words, "the keenest possible interest in the student for a broader knowledge of scientific discoveries in the world about him." It is offered as a corrective to the formal disciplinary and specialization-dominated approaches criticized throughout the editorial. No implementation details or supporting data are provided.
requirements: Science instruction must shift away from insistence on consecration to scientific method and from technical and mathematical treatment that obscures the cultural and general aspects of science.
constraints: The recommendation is stated as an editorial opinion for general education, not a tested intervention; the article offers no evidence of its effectiveness.
target_learning_goals: developing interest in scientific discoveries
cultivating a scientific temper of thought
examples: The editorial contrasts its recommendation with current practice: elementary observational study of nature decried as unscientific, high school physics overemphasizing experimentation and mathematics, and college courses eliminating the general student body.

article_title: An outline for institutional education and treatment of young offenders.
citation: William Healy and Augusta F. Bronner. (1916). An Outline for Institutional Education and Treatment of Young Offenders. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Reward-based discipline outperforms punishment in institutions for young offenders
description: The authors recommend highly individualized discipline built on rewards rather than penalties, holding that "stimulus to doing better is more apt to result from the promise of rewards than the administering of penalties." Delinquents should have goals to work toward as the reward of good behavior, and with constructive treatment discipline problems largely tend to disappear.
requirements: Punishments must be highly individualized according to the personalities involved
constraints: The authors state that coercion and punishment by inflicting pain are the lowest levels of control
target_learning_goals: improved behavior and character building
examples: The outline advises goals toward which the delinquent works as the reward of good behavior, and warns against deceit, pedantry, and demonstrations of irrationality as methods

article_title: What is reading ability?
citation: Wyman, J. B., & Wendle, M. (1921). What is Reading Ability? The Journal of Educational Psychology, 518-531. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=%22What+is+Reading+Ability%22
title: A reliability coefficient alone cannot establish what function a test measures; other objective information about a test is necessary
description: The article argues that a reliability coefficient only measures agreement between forms of a test and "do their reliability coefficients or their norms guarantee that they are good tests of reading ability?" It therefore validates tests against external criteria — teachers' estimates and expert-weighted test combinations — before saying what they measure. The studies demonstrate this method on reading and English tests.
requirements: An external criterion of the ability in question must be obtained, such as teacher estimates or a weighted combination of expert-judged tests, against which each test is correlated
constraints: Teachers' estimates are themselves fallible; the article reports their reliability as only 0.84 in the grade VIII study and an estimated 0.45 for high school teachers' grades
target_learning_goals: silent reading ability
English ability
examples: Two criteria were built: the averaged independent rankings of two teachers, and a combination of all tests weighted by averaged judgments of two professors and three graduate students

The report states he "emphasized particularly the necessity of restandardizing tests for use in Canada which are imported from the United States." This principle applies to any educational setting adopting tests normed on a different population.

article_title: Identifying reciprocities in school motivation research: A review of issues and solutions associated with cross-lagged effects models.
citation: Fernando Núñez-Regueiro, Jacques Juhel, Pascal Bressoux, Cécile Nurra. (2021). Identifying Reciprocities in School Motivation Research: A Review of Issues and Solutions Associated With Cross-Lagged Effects Models. Journal of Educational Psychology, 114 (5), pp.945-965. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000700
title: Reciprocal-effects theory of motivation: development as a function of reciprocal effects between beliefs about the self and school achievement
description: The article uses as its case study "the pervading theory that motivation develops as a function of reciprocal effects between beliefs about the self (e.g., academic self-concept) and school achievement". This theory posits bidirectional, cross-occasion influences: self-beliefs such as academic self-concept affect subsequent achievement, and achievement in turn affects subsequent self-beliefs. Much of the supporting evidence for such school motivation theories comes from cross-lagged modeling of longitudinal data, which is precisely the method the review critiques.

constraints: Evidence for the theory relies on modeling methods whose reliability depends on the convergence assumption the review questions

school achievement

article_title: The reading comprehension and vocabulary knowledge of children with poor reading comprehension despite adequate decoding: Evidence from a regression-based matching approach.
citation: Spencer, M., Wagner, R. K., & Petscher, Y. (2019). The Reading Comprehension and Vocabulary Knowledge of Children with Poor Reading Comprehension despite Adequate Decoding: Evidence from a Regression-Based Matching Approach. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000274
title: Regression-based matching technique for testing delay versus deficit hypotheses
description: A statistical technique described by Stanovich and Siegel (1994) that tests whether a skill is developmentally delayed or deficient by predicting the skill from achievement level and then adding a group contrast. The article states it "does not introduce the possibility of regression artifacts, allows the entire sample to be retained for analysis, and allows for a wide range of achievement levels to be included within a single continuous framework." Here it predicted PPVT vocabulary from SAT-10 comprehension, then entered an SCD/typical-reader grouping variable.

constraints: The present study notes it is unable to partial out the possible artifact of regression to the mean when children are selected on poor performance on a single measure

examples: Applied to five cohorts of second graders from the Florida PMRN database with four-level multilevel models (students nested in classrooms, schools, districts).

article_title: Reading for university or for myself? Effects of context and beliefs about science on college students’ document selection.
citation: Cornelia Schoor, Jean-François Rouet, and M. Anne Britt (2024). Reading for University or for Myself? Effects of Context and Beliefs about Science on College Students' Document Selection. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116 (3), pp.317-345. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000849
title: RESOLV theory of reading as problem solving with context and task models
description: RESOLV (REading as problem SOLVing) posits that most reading serves a specific purpose, so readers decide what to read and how. According to the article, "these decisions are based on a context model and a task model": readers build a context model by feature extraction of external elements (task, requester, audience, supports and obstacles) and internal aspects (knowledge, values, beliefs, skills), and an activated task schema yields a task model that "will drive reading decisions such as what to read, how to read, and when to stop". The study uses RESOLV to predict that the same task question produces different selection decisions depending on the external context scenario.
requirements: Readers must have acquired task schemata from many exposures to certain types of tasks within a situation or context
target_learners: college and university students reading about science
target_learning_goals: adaptive selection of appropriate reading strategies and sources for a given task and context
examples: In both experiments, a university seminar scenario versus a personal podcast scenario was used to activate different task schemata for the identical task question.

article_title: Test anxiety, emotion regulation, and achievement: Lagged and contemporaneous reciprocal relations.
citation: Putwain, D. W., Nicholson, L. J., & Pekrun, R. (2025). Test anxiety, emotion regulation, and achievement: Lagged and contemporaneous reciprocal relations. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://repository.essex.ac.uk/40904/
title: Reciprocal effects model of anxiety and achievement (within control-value theory)
description: The reciprocal effects model (REM), proposed by Pekrun and later part of control-value theory, integrates the interference and deficit accounts of the anxiety-achievement correlation. In this model, anxiety lowers achievement through cognitive-motivational processes including impaired working memory functions and avoidance motivation, while poor achievement provides negative competence feedback that lowers control appraisals, a proximal antecedent of anxiety. Over successive iterations, "test anxiety and achievement would relate in reciprocal vicious cycles". The present study's five-wave findings provide direct support for the model for test anxiety specifically.
requirements: Longitudinal data with repeated measures of both anxiety and achievement allowing autoregressive controls
constraints: The model proposes that anxiety often, although not always, lowers achievement
target_learners: upper-secondary students preparing for high-stakes exit exams
target_learning_goals: reducing anxiety-related underachievement in exam performance
examples: The study tested the REM with five waves of data and found the predicted negative reciprocal relations between test anxiety and achievement

article_title: The moderating role of popular peers’ achievement goals in 5th- and 6th-graders’ achievement-related friendships: A social network analysis.
citation: Laninga-Wijnen, L., Ryan, A., Harakeh, Z., Shin, H., & Vollebergh, W. A. M. (2018). Popularity norms are measured as "the within-classroom correlation between popularity and behaviors or attitudes" (also called norm salience). Because adolescents are "highly attuned to the behaviors and attitudes of popular peers, as these behaviors and attitudes are reputationally salient," the goals popular students endorse become positively valued classroom standards. target_learning_goals: Academic achievement in math and science
examples: The study operationalized popularity norms as within-classroom correlations between peer-nominated popularity and mastery or performance goals, splitting 46 classrooms into low, moderate, and high norm types by quartiles.

article_title: The mitigating effect of repeated memory reactivations on forgetting
citation: MacLeod, S., Reynolds, M. G. & Lehmann, H. (2018). The mitigating effect of repeated memory reactivations on forgetting. npj Science of Learning 3:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0025-x
title: Reconsolidation account of memory strengthening through reactivation
description: The article interprets its findings within reconsolidation theory: each time a memory is reactivated it "undergoes a new bout of consolidation", with cellular/synaptic plastic changes contributing to memory maintenance. The authors propose that repeated descriptive and component reactivations strengthened 28-day image memories via these reconsolidation bouts, while 1-h benefits likely reflected short-term synaptic facilitation supporting working memory. They also relate the findings to Distributed Reinstatement Theory, in which repeated reactivations extend the neural network supporting a memory beyond the hippocampus.

constraints: The 1-h improvement cannot be attributed to protein-synthesis-dependent reconsolidation because the interval was too short
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of studied visual material (episodic memory)
examples: Participants received three equally spaced reactivations during retention intervals of 1 h, 9 days, or 28 days, then completed an in-lab free-recall test

citation: Zhang, R., Zhang, L., Hao, X.-M., Dreher, J.-C., & Qu, C. (2026). Learning to adaptively cooperate through social interactions during childhood and adolescence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00423-9
title: Developmental reinforcement-learning framework of reward-based versus belief-based social learning in the Chicken game
description: The article builds a hierarchical Bayesian reinforcement-learning framework contrasting a reward-based model that updates action values from experienced payoffs via Rescorla-Wagner prediction errors, a belief-based model that tracks the opponent's probability of choosing Swerve, and a second-order belief model additionally tracking opponents' second-order beliefs. Each family had sub-models with one or two learning rates and a preference parameter θ. The framework was applied to a child-friendly Chicken game against pre-programmed high-competitive and low-competitive opponents across five age groups, with "lower values indicate better out-of-sample prediction accuracy" for LOOIC model comparison.
requirements: Repeated interaction with opponents whose behavioral tendencies can be manipulated, plus trial-by-trial choice data suitable for hierarchical Bayesian fitting
constraints: The second-order belief model did not fit the current data well in children
The authors note findings are based on a specific strategic interaction paradigm and may depend on the structure of the task and payoff matrix
target_learning_goals: adaptive social decision-making in social dilemmas
learning opponents' behavioral tendencies
examples: Study 1 used a simplified payoff matrix without negative losses for preschoolers, while Study 2 used a full matrix with losses for ages 6-17
key_sources: Zhang, R., Zhang, L., Hao, X.-M., Dreher, J.-C., & Qu, C. (2026). Learning to adaptively cooperate through social interactions during childhood and adolescence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00423-9

article_title: Timing of reward cues alters the interaction between reward and interest on memory over time
citation: Zhongyu Hu & Jiongjiong Yang. (2025). Timing of reward cues alters the interaction between reward and interest on memory over time. npj Science of Learning 10:82. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00374-7
title: Reward-cue timing framework: controlling quality of rewards determines encoding priority and selective consolidation of reward- versus interest-associated information
description: The article proposes that manipulating the timing of reward cues "influences the controlling quality of extrinsic reward, alters the relative priority of reward and intrinsic motivation, and in turn modulates the allocation of encoding resources". Pre-clip cues make reward a controlling factor that enhances salience of rewarded stimuli, while post-clip cues preserve intrinsic motivation so high-interest stimuli guide encoding. Both patterns then depend on selective, sleep-associated consolidation, consistent with the dopaminergic memory consolidation hypothesis and the adaptive memory consolidation framework.
requirements: Reward cues must be temporally separated from encoding (before vs. after stimuli) to manipulate controlling quality
constraints: The interactive effects emerged only at the 1-day delay, not at immediate testing
Findings were obtained with film clips and intentional memory instructions; the authors note future studies could use other material types, such as trivia questions, to replicate
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of learned material
examples: Experiment 1 cued rewards before film clips and found memory enhancement for low-interest clips at 1 day; Experiment 2 cued rewards after clips and found enhancement for high-interest clips at 1 day
key_sources: Zhongyu Hu & Jiongjiong Yang. (2025). Timing of reward cues alters the interaction between reward and interest on memory over time. npj Science of Learning 10:82. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00374-7

article_title: Integrating educational knowledge: reactivation of prior knowledge during educational learning enhances memory integration
citation: Marlieke Tina Renée van Kesteren, Lydia Krabbendam and Martijn Meeter (2018). Integrating educational knowledge: reactivation of prior knowledge during educational learning enhances memory integration. npj Science of Learning 3:11. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0027-8
title: Design curricula so new learning follows reactivation of previously learned, congruent information
description: The article argues that education should actively reactivate prior knowledge while new information is studied, because reactivation during encoding strengthens the association of new material with existing knowledge networks. It stresses "the necessity for a curriculum where knowledge is slowly expanded and previously learned information is often revisited to allow strong knowledge networks to form". Reactivation helps even when new information does not match prior knowledge.
requirements: Learners must possess relevant prior knowledge (pre-experimental B–C links) that can be reactivated during new learning, as in the article's curriculum-based stimuli
constraints: The reactivation component was, by the authors' own admission, "an extreme simpli ﬁcation of reactivation in classroom learning"; effects were shown with word-picture-description stimuli, not full lessons
target_learners: first-year university students (psychology and family studies)
target_learning_goals: retention and integration of new curricular subject matter with existing knowledge
examples: Participants were instructed to reactivate the associated B-picture by generating a mental image during AC-encoding and rated their subjective reactivation strength as strong, a bit, or none
key_sources: Marlieke Tina Renée van Kesteren, Lydia Krabbendam and Martijn Meeter (2018). Integrating educational knowledge: reactivation of prior knowledge during educational learning enhances memory integration. npj Science of Learning 3:11. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0027-8

article_title: Brief memory reactivations induce learning in the numeric domain
citation: Gilad Schrift, Dror Dotan and Nitzan Censor. (2022). Brief memory reactivations induce learning in the numeric domain. npj Science of Learning 7:18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00136-9
title: Memory reactivation-reconsolidation framework as an account of reactivation-induced numeric learning
description: The article frames brief reactivations within the reconsolidation framework: as stabilized memories are reactivated, either by retrieval or by a reminder cue, they revert to a labile state and can be modified by incoming inputs during offline re-stabilization. The authors state that "the reactivation process facilitates learning associated with declarative human memory, and exists also in a mathematical context", and speculate that neural reactivations within the fronto-parietal numerical cognition network may support consolidation of hippocampus-dependent memories. The neural mechanisms remain to be determined.
requirements: Encoded, consolidated memories that can be reactivated by a brief reminder cue
constraints: The neural mechanisms underlying this form of reactivation-induced learning remain to be determined, per the article
target_learning_goals: Rote memorization and fluent retrieval of arithmetic facts
examples: Reactivations consisted of five seconds of visual-auditory presentation of each fact in random order, for a total of 40 seconds per session
key_sources: Gilad Schrift, Dror Dotan and Nitzan Censor. (2022). Brief memory reactivations induce learning in the numeric domain. npj Science of Learning 7:18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00136-9

article_title: Relational thinking and relational reasoning: harnessing the power of patterning
citation: Patricia A Alexander. (2016). Relational thinking and relational reasoning: harnessing the power of patterning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.4
title: Relational thinking versus relational reasoning: intuitive versus intentional pattern processing
description: The article distinguishes two coupled processes for discerning meaningful patterns in informational streams. Relational thinking is the spontaneous, in-the-moment coupling of percepts and concepts, while relational reasoning is the purposeful harnessing of pattern recognition for higher-order learning and performance. As the article puts it, relational thinking is "more fleeting, external, and rather effortless and unconscious in nature", whereas relational reasoning "has a more enduring, representational quality and which demands effort and intentionality". The two are compared on locus, temporal frame, and cognitive demands.
requirements: Both processes operate in concert to allow the coupling of percepts and concepts
constraints: The boundaries between the intuitive and intentional systems may not be categorically distinct, per the article
target_learners: learners across the lifespan, from infancy through adulthood
target_learning_goals: perceiving meaningful patterns in informational streams
higher-order cognitive processing
examples: Table 1 juxtaposes the two forms on locus (in mundi versus in mente), temporal frame, general nature, and cognitive demands
key_sources: Patricia A Alexander. (2016). Relational thinking and relational reasoning: harnessing the power of patterning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.4

article_title: Achievement motivation modulates Pavlovian aversive conditioning to goal-relevant stimuli
citation: Yoann Stussi, Aude Ferrero, Gilles Pourtois and David Sander. (2019). Achievement motivation modulates Pavlovian aversive conditioning to goal-relevant stimuli. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0043-3
title: Relevance detection model of preferential emotional learning
description: The relevance detection model derives from appraisal theories of emotion and holds that preferential emotional learning is driven not by a threat-specific mechanism but by rapid detection of whether a stimulus is relevant to the organism's concerns—its goals, needs, motives, or values. The article frames it as asserting that "Stimuli that are detected as relevant to the organism’s concerns beneﬁt from preferential emotional learning, regardless of their valence and evolutionary status per se." The findings—facilitated conditioning to goal-relevant stimuli in high achievers—are presented as supporting this model over preparedness and fear module theories.
requirements: Requires a stimulus appraised as relevant to the organism's current concerns, which vary across individuals and contexts
constraints: In this study the goal-relevance was temporary and task-bound, and the resulting learning bias was modest and transient, with no differential resistance to extinction
target_learning_goals: preferential aversive (emotional) learning to concern-relevant stimuli
examples: Participants with high achievement motivation more readily acquired a conditioned response to neutral geometric figures that had been goal-relevant in a spatial cueing task, despite the figures holding no inherent threat value or evolutionary significance
key_sources: Yoann Stussi, Aude Ferrero, Gilles Pourtois and David Sander. (2019). Achievement motivation modulates Pavlovian aversive conditioning to goal-relevant stimuli. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0043-3

article_title: A better alignment between chronotype and school timing is associated with lower grade retention in adolescents
citation: Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, Andrea P. Goldin, Mariano Sigman and María Juliana Leone. (2023). A better alignment between chronotype and school timing is associated with lower grade retention in adolescents. npj Science of Learning 8:21. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00171-0
title: Rethink grade retention as an educational practice, since its incidence depends on the alignment of chronotype with school timing
description: The article argues that grade retention, a controversial practice already associated with dropout, lower performance and deepened inequalities, is not applied equally fairly across chronotypes. The authors state that "grade retention is not equally fair when students ' chronotype is considered", because late chronotypes in morning timings face higher retention odds, and conclude this "strongly supports the idea of rethinking grade retention as an educative practice".
requirements: Schools considering retention decisions would need information on students' chronotype (e.g. MCTQ-based MSFsc) to evaluate the fairness of the practice
constraints: The article emphasises the need for translational studies and more local evidence before implementing educational public policies
target_learners: Adolescents in secondary school, particularly morning-attending students with later chronotypes
target_learning_goals: Timely progression through secondary school (avoiding grade retention)
examples: The study measured which 1st-year students (2015) did not timely reach 5th year (2019) and linked retention odds to chronotype, school timing and grades
key_sources: Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, Andrea P. Goldin, Mariano Sigman and María Juliana Leone. (2023). A better alignment between chronotype and school timing is associated with lower grade retention in adolescents. npj Science of Learning 8:21. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00171-0

article_title: Combining perspectives in multidisciplinary research on inequality in education
citation: Louise Elffers, Eddie Denessen and Monique Volman. (2024). Combining perspectives in multidisciplinary research on inequality in education. npj Science of Learning 9:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00215-z
title: Reflect on education's dual role as both producer and reducer of inequality
description: Educational interventions may remedy or aggravate inequality, sometimes both at once. The article identifies "reflection on the potential role of education as both a producer and reducer of inequality" as a third principle, noting that "Remediation and aggravation of inequality may even happen as the result of the same educational intervention." Researchers studying interventions for disadvantaged students should not assume they contribute to equality.
requirements: When studying interventions for disadvantaged or underperforming students, researchers must take into account potential negative treatment effects as well, rather than assuming interventions contribute to equality
constraints: The article notes it is difficult to determine to what extent a treatment such as tracking helped or hampered development, especially if control groups cannot be put in place
target_learning_goals: Evaluating educational interventions for their counterfactual impact and unintended effects on inequality
examples: The article cites literature such as the work of Van de Werfhorst and Mijs and Marks as informing reflections on the potential counterfactual impact or unintended effects of interventions
key_sources: Louise Elffers, Eddie Denessen and Monique Volman. (2024). Combining perspectives in multidisciplinary research on inequality in education. npj Science of Learning 9:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00215-z

article_title: Reading experience reveals shared and idiosyncratic neural patterns during text comprehension
citation: Song, M., Li, L., He, D. & Cai, Q. (2025). Reading experience reveals shared and idiosyncratic neural patterns during text comprehension. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00390-7
title: Design reading interventions that account for both the quantity and the diversity of learners' reading materials
description: The article proposes that its neurocognitive link between cumulative reading experience and real-time comprehension has implications for education. The authors recommend "designing reading interventions that take into account the quantity and diversity of reading materials", and suggest that "customizing reading experiences to align with individual exposure levels may enhance cognitive engagement, improve comprehension efficiency, and foster critical thinking and empathy development." The principle treats reading experience as an experiential index shaping how shared or individualized readers' neural processing of texts will be.
requirements: Assessment of learners' print exposure quantity and topical distribution, e.g. with an instrument like the tART
constraints: The supporting evidence is correlational; factors such as IQ, socioeconomic status, personal interests and cognitive traits may have modulated the association, limiting causal interpretation
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension efficiency, critical thinking, and empathy development
examples: The study profiled 39 college students' reading across nine topics with the tART and linked topic distributions to precuneus/DMN activity during narrative reading
key_sources: Song, M., Li, L., He, D. & Cai, Q. (2025). Reading experience reveals shared and idiosyncratic neural patterns during text comprehension. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00390-7

article_title: The dynamics of state math anxiety vary by paradigm and timing during arithmetic
citation: Yao, X., Huber, J.F., Li, Z., Findik, Y., Nuerk, H.-C. & Artemenko, C. (2026). The dynamics of state math anxiety vary by paradigm and timing during arithmetic. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00398-z
title: Reciprocal theory of math anxiety and performance
description: The article presents a reciprocal theory integrating cognitive disruption, reduced competency, and interpretation accounts of math anxiety. Rather than treating these as mutually exclusive, it states that "a bidirectional relationship between math anxiety and math performance" exists, so that anxiety and performance influence each other and create a vicious cycle. The study's data are interpreted against this backdrop: trait math anxiety shapes state anxiety responses and performance, while lower performance may in turn feed higher state and eventually trait anxiety.
requirements: The theory presupposes that both trait and state math anxiety are assessed to capture the bidirectional relation between anxiety and performance over time.
constraints: The article states the assumption that lower performance induces higher state math anxiety over time requires further investigation, as state math anxiety was not assessed at the trial level in the current study.
target_learning_goals: arithmetic performance
managing math anxiety during mathematics learning
examples: The study tested trait and state math anxiety simultaneously while participants performed arithmetic, and interpreted the replicated anxiety-complexity effect via the disruption account's working-memory mechanism.
key_sources: Yao, X., Huber, J.F., Li, Z., Findik, Y., Nuerk, H.-C. & Artemenko, C. (2026). The dynamics of state math anxiety vary by paradigm and timing during arithmetic. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00398-z

article_title: Comparing feedback learning and arousal responses in Down, Fragile X, and Williams syndromes
citation: Hallman, A. E. Z., Willfors, C., Frick, M. A., Nordgren, A. & Kleberg, J. L. (2026). Comparing feedback learning, pupil dilation, and gaze allocation in intellectual disability. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00438-2
title: Simplified reward contingency reversal task with eye tracking for feedback learning in intellectual disability
description: This is a simplified deterministic reinforcement learning paradigm combined with eye tracking, designed to be feasible for individuals with intellectual disability in the mild to moderate range. Each trial presented "a pair of pictures, and participants were required to choose one of the options", with win feedback indicated by a thumbs up and a sound and loss feedback by a thumbs down and a matched sound. "After four consecutive correct responses (wins), the reward contingency reversed without warning, resulting in a loss", and the task included five achievable blocks with a maximum of 25 trials. The authors state the paradigm "support[s] the use of this paradigm in ID populations and provide[s] a robust foundation for examining syndrome-specific differences in physiological feedback processing."
requirements: Instructions were given both in written and oral form and "adjusted based on the participant's receptive language skills", with two practice trials before the task.
constraints: The task was intentionally simplified; the authors note the lack of observable adaptation difficulties likely reflects this simplicity rather than the absence of cognitive flexibility difficulties, and recommend more complex paradigms for future work.
target_learners: Individuals with intellectual disability in the mild to moderate severity range, including Down, Fragile X, and Williams syndromes, aged 6 to 60 years
target_learning_goals: Reinforcement learning: associating choices with rewards and losses from deterministic feedback
examples: Participants completed up to 25 two-alternative trials while a Tobii eye tracker recorded pupil dilation and gaze; those with a proportion of optimal choices below 0.6 were excluded.
key_sources: Hallman, A. E. Z., Willfors, C., Frick, M. A., Nordgren, A. & Kleberg, J. L. (2026). Comparing feedback learning, pupil dilation, and gaze allocation in intellectual disability. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00438-2

article_title: Children’s neurodevelopment of reading is affected by China’s language input system in the information era
citation: Zhou, W., Kwok, V. P. Y., Su, M., Luo, J., & Tan, L. H. (2020). Children's neurodevelopment of reading is affected by China's language input system in the information era. npj Science of Learning, 5:3. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0062-0
title: Restrict pinyin input use and promote orthography-based input methods including handwriting to preserve visuo-orthographic encoding of Chinese characters
description: The authors recommend that, to protect intermediate Chinese readers' character learning, frequent use of the pronunciation-based pinyin input method should be limited and orthography-based input such as handwriting should be encouraged. They write: "To preserve visuo-orthographic encoding of Chinese characters, we would recommend to restrict the use of pinyin input, and promote orthography-based input methods including handwriting." The recommendation rests on the study's associations between pinyin typing and weaker reading-network activation, connectivity, gray matter, and character reading fluency.
requirements: Learners must be intermediate Chinese readers (around ages 9-11) who have moved past initial pinyin-supported decoding, since the authors hold that beginning readers rely on pinyin to bridge spoken and written language.
constraints: The supporting evidence is cross-sectional, showing associations between pinyin typing frequency and brain/behavioral measures rather than experimentally established causal effects.
target_learners: Chinese elementary school children in grades 4-6 (intermediate readers, ages 9-11)
target_learning_goals: Chinese character recognition and reading fluency
visuo-orthographic analysis of Chinese characters
examples: The study grouped 45 children by daily pinyin typing time (more or less than 15 min per day) and found more frequent typists showed weaker cortical activations, weaker functional connections, less gray matter in the left middle frontal region, and lower character reading fluency.
key_sources: Zhou, W., Kwok, V. P. Y., Su, M., Luo, J., & Tan, L. H. (2020). Children's neurodevelopment of reading is affected by China's language input system in the information era. npj Science of Learning, 5:3. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0062-0

article_title: Brain activity links performance in science reasoning with conceptual approach
citation: Bartley, J. E., Riedel, M. C., Salo, T., Boeving, E. R., Bottenhorn, K. L., Bravo, E. I., Odean, R., Nazareth, A., Laird, R. W., Sutherland, M. T., Pruden, S. M., Brewe, E. & Laird, A. R. (2019). Brain activity links performance in science reasoning with conceptual approach. npj Science of Learning 4:20. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0059-8
title: Resource framework: physics cognition as dual knowledge-structure and control-structure processes along an axis of knowledge compilation
description: The article adopts a resource framework in which physics cognition relies on dual "knowledge structure" and "control structure" processes: students apply executive functions to select or inhibit associational patterns grounding their physical reasoning. Knowledge structures are "flexible, contextually primed collections of linked knowledge elements called 'resources'" activated to scaffold reasoning. Differences among students are described along an axis of compilation or memory chunking: students without precompiled structures must assemble associations during reasoning, whereas experts access well-developed associational patterns. The authors use this framework to interpret their neuroimaging findings, mapping CEN/DAN activity to control structures and DMN involvement to associational mappings in semantic or episodic memory.
requirements: Students must learn to activate stable associations between physical laws to support long deductive chains during problem solving
constraints: The authors acknowledge results may be specific to the FCI questions used, and that additional brain dynamics may be relevant for different kinds of physics problem solving
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of Newtonian mechanics
physics problem-solving proficiency
examples: Groups A and B were interpreted as applying predominantly Newtonian (compiled) thinking, while Group C utilized multiple modules characterized by simple, vague, or confused ideas that differed across problems
key_sources: Bartley, J. E., Riedel, M. C., Salo, T., Boeving, E. R., Bottenhorn, K. L., Bravo, E. I., Odean, R., Nazareth, A., Laird, R. W., Sutherland, M. T., Pruden, S. M., Brewe, E. & Laird, A. R. (2019). Brain activity links performance in science reasoning with conceptual approach. npj Science of Learning 4:20. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0059-8

article_title: Dissipation of reactive inhibition is sufficient to explain post-rest improvements in motor sequence learning
citation: Mohan W. Gupta and Timothy C. Rickard. (2022). Dissipation of reactive inhibition is sufficient to explain post-rest improvements in motor sequence learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00140-z
title: Reactive inhibition accrual-and-dissipation model of motor sequence learning
description: The model assumes that "learning is concurrent with performance", that reactive inhibition (RI) builds during continuous performance and slows RT, and that RI dissipates during breaks. It predicts the largest post-rest improvement when long trials are paired with short breaks, without invoking any offline facilitating consolidation. The article argues this account is sufficient to explain post-rest improvements after a 300 s rest and that facilitating consolidation "does not appear to be necessary".
requirements: Within-trial and across-break RI dynamics must be measured or controlled when inferring offline gains from post-rest improvements
constraints: The study was not designed to estimate RI accrual and dissipation rates; the article notes more research is needed on the exact relative rate and whether it is constant across on-task durations
target_learners: adults learning motor sequences with the non-dominant hand
target_learning_goals: motor sequence skill learning
examples: Four groups trained 360 s on a finger-tapping task with trial lengths of 10 s or 30 s and breaks of 10 s or 30 s, then rested 300 s before a 60 s test
key_sources: Mohan W. Gupta and Timothy C. Rickard. (2022). Dissipation of reactive inhibition is sufficient to explain post-rest improvements in motor sequence learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00140-z

article_title: Reducing Workload in Short Answer Grading Using Machine Learning
citation: Rebecka Weegar · Peter Idestam-Almquist. (2024). Reducing Workload in Short Answer Grading Using Machine Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00322-1
title: Review all automated grading output to ensure fair and correct grading, particularly in high-stakes exams
description: The article argues that even a very accurate automated grader cannot fully replace manual grading, because disagreement with a human grade may be spurious and graders can be sensitive to manipulation. It therefore evaluates a setup in which "the output of the classifier was manually reviewed and corrected when needed", measuring workload including this full review. This makes fairness for students a design requirement rather than an optional check.
requirements: A workflow must budget time for reviewing every automatically scored answer, not only suspected errors
constraints: Even with a very accurate classifier, fully replacing manual grading is not yet possible in high-stakes exams
target_learners: higher education students in large introductory courses
target_learning_goals: correct and fair assessment of short-answer exam responses
examples: In the evaluated exam grading, all classifier output was reviewed in clusters using a spreadsheet program, and the overall workload reduction of 64-74% was achieved with this complete review in place
key_sources: Rebecka Weegar · Peter Idestam-Almquist. (2024). Reducing Workload in Short Answer Grading Using Machine Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00322-1

article_title: Reciprocal Tutoring: Design with Cognitive Load Sharing
citation: Chih-Yueh Chou & Tak-Wai Chan. (2015). Reciprocal Tutoring: Design with Cognitive Load Sharing. International Artificial Intelligence in Education Society. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0083-7
title: Reciprocal tutoring as peer tutoring with alternating tutor and tutee roles
description: Reciprocal tutoring is defined as a form of cooperative learning in which a task is partitioned into tutoring and tuteeing sub-tasks distributed among agents, with dyads taking turns in the two roles. The authors define it: BReciprocal tutoring is a form of cooperative learning by adopting the 'divide and conquer 'strategy. A learning task is partitioned into sub-tasks of tutoring and 'tuteeing'where tuteeing is learning by working on the solution while being tutored.^ They phrase the scenario as the tutor's tutor tutors the tutor who tutors the tutee, making it a type of peer tutoring that enables peer students to tutor other students.
requirements: A protocol is required to assist agents in playing their roles to complete their sub-tasks and to collaborate in completing the entire learning task
constraints: The scope is designing protocols and computer supports for reciprocal tutoring, such as sub-task partition, roles of agents, virtual agents, and computer scaffolding tools
target_learners: Peer students acting as tutors and tutees
target_learning_goals: Learning-by-tutoring and learning-by-being-tutored
examples: Figure 6 illustrates a scenario where a student tutors a tutee while the system plays the role of the tutor's tutor
key_sources: Chih-Yueh Chou & Tak-Wai Chan. (2015). Reciprocal Tutoring: Design with Cognitive Load Sharing. International Artificial Intelligence in Education Society. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0083-7

article_title: The Evolution of Research on Digital Education
citation: Pierre Dillenbourg. (2016). The Evolution of Research on Digital Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0106-z
title: Reflect table: an interactive furniture display supporting participation balance
description: The Reflect table is furniture-based ambient output designed to help teams balance participation: "LEDS embedded in the table in front of team members display the amount of speech produced by each of them." It illustrates 'modest computing', in which displayed information is not the focus of attention, resolution is low, and no interpretation is proposed. It supports self-awareness that triggers reflection and self-regulation at the team level.
requirements: A physical team workspace in which the table's low-resolution display can be seen peripherally rather than attended directly
constraints: It displays simply a level of noise without any intelligence, which the author notes can hardly be considered aligned with the goals of AIED
target_learning_goals: balanced participation and team-level self-regulation in collaborative learning
examples: Used as the example of self-awareness ('group mirrors') contrasted with Lantern's awareness of others
key_sources: Pierre Dillenbourg. (2016). The Evolution of Research on Digital Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0106-z

article_title: Enhancing Procedural Writing Through Personalized Example Retrieval: A Case Study on Cooking Recipes
citation: Mejia-Domenzain, P., Frej, J., Neshaei, S. P., Mouchel, L., Nazaretsky, T., Wambsganss, T., Bosselut, A., & Käser, T. (2025). Enhancing Procedural Writing Through Personalized Example Retrieval: A Case Study on Cooking Recipes. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00405-1
title: RELEX: an adaptive learning system for personalized example-based procedural writing feedback
description: RELEX (REcipe Learning through EXamples) is a learning system for procedural writing that provides each learner with a tailored example recipe, personalized in-text highlighting, explanatory suggestions, and a reflection space. Its stated purpose is to "facilitate procedural writing by providing students with tailored examples, accompanied by relevant annotations and reflective prompts". It targets structure, clarity, and specificity, retrieves examples from over 180,000 rated recipes, and was evaluated in a 2x2 controlled study with 200 participants.
requirements: A database of rated recipes (RELEXset) and a fine-tuned quality predictor (RELEXset-Predictor) to select higher-quality examples in real time
constraints: Instantiated in the cooking-recipe domain, chosen for familiarity and relevance to culinary students and chef apprentices
target_learners: Chef apprentices and culinary students; recruited study participants aged 18-30 with at least an undergraduate degree
target_learning_goals: Procedural writing quality: structure, clarity, and specificity of recipes
examples: A learner requesting feedback on a chicken recipe is shown the similar, higher-quality "Louisiana Chicken" recipe with missing structural elements highlighted and reflection questions posed
key_sources: Mejia-Domenzain, P., Frej, J., Neshaei, S. P., Mouchel, L., Nazaretsky, T., Wambsganss, T., Bosselut, A., & Käser, T. (2025). Enhancing Procedural Writing Through Personalized Example Retrieval: A Case Study on Cooking Recipes. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00405-1

article_title: Enhancing Procedural Writing Through Personalized Example Retrieval: A Case Study on Cooking Recipes
citation: Mejia-Domenzain, P., Frej, J., Neshaei, S. P., Mouchel, L., Nazaretsky, T., Wambsganss, T., Bosselut, A., & Käser, T. (2025). Enhancing Procedural Writing Through Personalized Example Retrieval: A Case Study on Cooking Recipes. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00405-1
title: Five-function personalized example feedback pattern: on-demand analysis, similar better example, colored highlighting, dismissible suggestions, reflection space
description: RELEX operationalizes personalized example-based feedback through five interface functionalities: F1 an Analyze button requesting feedback and new examples on demand; F2 a better, similar recipe retrieved per learner; F3 colored highlighting of missing structure, clarity, and specificity aspects; F4 short, deletable explanation tips on highlighted elements; and F5 a Reflection Space prompting self-explanation and comparison. "The five design functionalities of RELEX (see Table 1) are based on design requirements derived from user interviews as well as from literature."
requirements: Each functionality must trace to at least one user requirement (U1-U5 from ten user interviews) or literature requirement (L1-L5 from example-based learning design principles)
constraints: Explanations should be short and minimalist and should not tell learners things they already know, per the cited design principles
target_learners: Learners writing procedural texts, including culinary students and study participants aged 18-30
target_learning_goals: Improving structure, clarity, and specificity of procedural texts through active example processing
examples: F3 highlights missing elements such as "List each ingredient separately" in the example recipe with separate colors; F5 poses the questions "What aspects of this example recipe do you find interesting, useful, convincing, and which not?" and "What deficiencies does your recipe have compared to the example recipe on the right?"

article_title: Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education
citation: Julien Broisin, Rémi Venant & Philippe Vidal. (2017). Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 27:154–180. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0079-3
title: Scaffolding capacities required for an educational-oriented remote laboratory
description: The article defines a set of pedagogical capabilities that remote laboratory environments must provide to effectively support practical learning: a common view of the experiment, shared control over remote experiments, synchronous communication tools, social/artifact awareness tools, learning analytics for tutoring, and a user-friendly authoring tool. The authors motivate this with the claim that "the scaffolding around the lab may be at least as important as the lab itself" and with a survey where students pointed to help and support and engagement. They use the framework to evaluate six existing remote lab projects, concluding they "do not focus on pedagogical concerns".
requirements: The remote lab environment should give learning actors access to a common view of the experiments and shared control, plus synchronous communication, awareness, learning analytics and authoring capacities
constraints: Existing projects studied (iLab, LiLa, LabShare, WebLab-Deusto, Lab2Go, Go-Lab) partially or fully lack most of these capacities, and none takes experiment instructional design into account
target_learners: distant learners in STEM higher education
target_learning_goals: inquiry skills and practical disciplinary skills through remote laboratory work

article_title: Three Algorithms for Grouping Students: A Bridge Between Personalized Tutoring System Data and Classroom Pedagogy
citation: Lechuga, C. G., & Doroudi, S. (2023). Three Algorithms for Grouping Students: A Bridge Between Personalized Tutoring System Data and Classroom Pedagogy. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00309-y
title: Reciprocal pairing method: greedy pairing of students with complementary knowledge for reciprocal peer tutoring
description: A pairing method supporting Reciprocal Peer Tutoring in ALEKS classes without modules. It simultaneously forms pairs where "Complementary knowledge refers to when each student in the pair possesses some knowledge that the other does not," and identifies the content each pair should focus on, aiming for exchanges in the tutee's zone of proximal development. Pairing uses a greedy rank-based approach because "such an optimal solution for a typical class size of 15–25 is extremely expensive computationally and perhaps impossible."
requirements: An ALEKS class without pre-determined modules, so individual strengths can be drawn from the entire curriculum
Student-model knowledge states over hundreds of skills to identify complementary knowledge
constraints: Uses a greedy approach rather than an optimal pairing configuration due to computational expense; the article notes such a greedy approach could be run many times to yield better solutions
target_learners: K-12 students in ALEKS classes without modules
target_learning_goals: Reciprocal peer tutoring in which students interchange tutor and tutee roles on content each is ready to learn
examples: The article positions the method as the first study interested in forming reciprocal pairs with complementary knowledge, avoiding student-developed questions and one-sided tutoring exchanges.

description: This document is the retraction notice printed ahead of an article in Int J Artif Intell Educ whose title asserted that "Worked Examples are more Efficient for Learning than High-Assistance Instructional Software". It focuses on "three indicators—gaze synchronization, language conformance, and emotional matching through facial expression" to establish an index of synchronization during PCA-mediated collaborative learning. citation: Ijaz Ul Haq, Manoli Pifarré, Estibaliz Fraca. (2024). Novelty Evaluation using Sentence Embedding Models in Open-ended Cocreative Problem-solving. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00392-3
title: Use reliable pre-trained sentence embedding models to provide real-time novelty feedback that helps teachers and students regulate collaborative ideation
description: The article argues that automatic novelty scores from reliable sentence embedding models can be translated into actionable, real-time feedback for teachers and student groups during cocreation. "The provision of real-time novelty feedback addresses a crucial pedagogical concern in promoting creativity", and feedback "acts as a mediator, facilitating communication among students about their problem resolution". Scores can be sorted into low, medium, and high novelty categories, each receiving specific guidance to enhance communication and orchestrate cocreation processes.

constraints: Grounded in one case study of 25 secondary students in a single PBL science project

target_learning_goals: Creative idea generation and collaborative ideation during open-ended problem-solving
examples: Translating novelty scores from a pool of ideas co-generated by student groups into tailored guidance across high, medium, and low novelty categories

article_title: Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops
citation: VanLehn, K. (2015). Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0056-x
title: Regulative loop framework: systems that repeatedly compare performance to a gold standard and act to close the gap
description: The article proposes that tutoring and CSCL systems be seen as instances of a single negative-feedback, goal-seeking loop. In it, students apply knowledge to a task, producing a performance that is "a comparison of the performance against some gold standard and an adjustment to the students' knowledge that brings their performance closer to the gold standard." Computer systems can take over varying amounts of this loop, yielding self-regulation, mirroring, formative assessment or coaching. The framework unifies ITS and regulative CSCL systems.
requirements: A task on which students produce an observable performance, a gold standard to compare it against, and a mechanism for adjustment
constraints: The class probably includes most ITS but only some CSCL systems, namely those taking a regulative rather than a structural approach
target_learners: individual students and small groups in ITS and CSCL settings
target_learning_goals: domain skills, self-regulation, collaboration, motivation, depending on the knowledge type addressed
examples: Fig. 1 depicts the regulative loop based on the one in Soller et al. 2005, with terminology changed by the present author
key_sources: VanLehn, K. (2015). Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0056-x

article_title: Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops
citation: VanLehn, K. (2015). Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0056-x
title: Four-way classification of regulative activity: self-regulation, mirroring, formative assessment, coaching
description: The article classifies regulative approaches by how much of the loop the system executes. If students execute the whole loop themselves, the activity is self-regulation; if the system monitors performance and presents it back, mirroring; if it also compares to a gold standard and reports the comparison, formative assessment; if it additionally generates advice or modifies the task or context, coaching. Coaching is "just what an intelligent tutoring system typically does."
requirements: A regulative loop with a monitorable student performance and a gold standard
constraints: Although Soller et al. intended the classification for collaborative learning, the article argues it applies equally to single-student activities
target_learning_goals: improving performance toward a gold standard across cognitive, meta-cognitive, collaborative and motivational knowledge
examples: Mirroring characterizes reflective debriefing and open learner modeling, where the system presents a display of the student's performance, often as a timeline
key_sources: VanLehn, K. (2015). Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0056-x

article_title: Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops
citation: VanLehn, K. (2015). Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0056-x
title: Four dimensions for classifying regulative loop systems: knowledge type, recipient, change process, granularity
description: Beyond the main classification, the article augments it with four independent dimensions, summarized in Table 1: "Type of knowledge: Cognitive, meta-cognitive, collaborative skill, motivations; Recipient: Student, teacher, activity structure (interventions only); Type of change process: Reminding, persuasion, teaching, remediation; Granularity: Step, task, module." Knowledge type distinguishes cognitive knowledge, meta-cognitive knowledge addressed by meta-tutors, collaboration skill, and motivations. Recipient covers whether information goes to the student directly, to a teacher, or restructures the activity.
requirements: A regulative loop system to which the dimensions are applied
constraints: The type of change process in students' minds is unobservable; designers often have such a process in mind when designing advice
target_learners: students in ITS and CSCL environments, individually or in groups
target_learning_goals: classifying and designing regulative support across cognitive, meta-cognitive, collaborative and motivational goals
examples: MTDashboard monitors students and small groups and presents information to the teacher on a handheld dashboard, who may choose which groups to visit
key_sources: VanLehn, K. (2015). Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0056-x

article_title: Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops
citation: VanLehn, K. (2015). Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0056-x
title: Granularity of regulative loops: step, task, and module grain sizes
description: The fourth dimension is the grain size at which performance and knowledge are analyzed. "A step is the smallest user interface action for which it makes sense to call it correct or incorrect." A task is the smallest unit of user activity that is logically and informationally independent of preceding and following units; a complete physics problem solution is a task, but a single equation is not. A module, chapter or unit is a larger grain size of learning activities addressing the same topic.
requirements: User activity that can be segmented into units at the chosen grain size
constraints: Entering the first character of an equation is too small to be a step; entering a single equation is not a task because it depends on variable definitions and other equations
target_learners: students working on step-based tasks in tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: correcting performance at the appropriate grain of analysis
examples: In physics, typing in an equation is a step; a complete solution of a physics problem is a task
key_sources: VanLehn, K. (2015). Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0056-x

article_title: Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops
citation: VanLehn, K. (2015). Regulative Loops, Step Loops and Task Loops. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0056-x
title: Regulative loop systems: a class spanning ITS and regulative CSCL systems
description: The article proposes the name "regulative loop systems" for instructional systems conforming to Fig. 1. This class "probably includes most ITS but only some CSCL systems, namely those that take a regulative approach instead of a structural one." Structural work explores novel tasks whose structure elicits improved learning, while regulative work augments existing tasks with regulatory mechanisms interacting with students as activity occurs. A CSCL script system becomes regulative if it also checks whether students followed the scripts and mirrors, assesses or intervenes.
requirements: Monitoring of student performance against a gold standard with mirroring, assessment or intervention
constraints: Excludes purely structural CSCL systems that do not monitor whether students followed scripts
target_learners: students in ITS and regulative CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: bringing student performance closer to a gold standard during learning activities
examples: A CSCL system that asks students to follow scripts would be structural, yet becomes a regulative loop system if it determines whether students followed the scripts

description: Because experiments showed that starting with a student model already consistent with the learner's actual learning styles produced fewer learning problems and greater average performance, the article argues that "the reuse of student models in new courses is essential." It proposes that emerging patterns could enable sharing student models between different platforms, including learning styles characteristics, so that different adaptive educational systems collaboratively and continuously evolve the student model over time.

article_title: An editorial on replication studies and scaling up efforts
citation: J. Michael Spector, Tristan E. Johnson, Patricia A. Young. (2015). An editorial on replication studies and scaling up efforts. Education Tech Research Dev 63:1–4. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-014-9364-3
title: Typologies of replication studies (Lykken's three types; Schmidt's direct vs. conceptual)
description: The editorial presents two classifications of replication studies. Lykken (1968) identified three types: literal, operational, and constructive replications. Schmidt (2009) re-categorized them into direct and conceptual replications, "with direct replications being the preferred path by many as they preserve the original instrumentation and approach." ETR&D accepts both direct and conceptual replications.
requirements: Replication studies require access to the original study's instruments and procedures, which the editorial says researchers often withhold
constraints: Literal replication is described as nearly impossible to conduct and may suffer the same experimental biases as the original
target_learning_goals: improving the scientific rigor and generalizability of educational technology research
examples: ETR&D issued a call for papers reporting replication studies following the 2014 National Technology Leadership Summit

article_title: An editorial on replication studies and scaling up efforts
citation: J. Michael Spector, Tristan E. Johnson, Patricia A. Young. (2015). An editorial on replication studies and scaling up efforts. Education Tech Research Dev 63:1–4. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-014-9364-3
title: Replication studies should be conducted to make educational technology research more scientific and ground large-scale implementation
description: The editorial argues that replications add confidence in findings, enable generalization beyond the original setting, and can identify biases in the original study. ETR&D "urges researchers to conduct such studies so as to make educational technology research more scientific and provide a firm and convincing foundation for large-scale implementations and impact studies."
requirements: Researchers need willingness to conduct replications and access to original instruments and procedures
constraints: Direct replications are preferred by many because they preserve original instrumentation, but the journal accepts conceptual replications too

enabling generalization of educational technology findings
examples: ETR&D welcomes meta-analytic studies that analyze and synthesize experimental findings across related studies

article_title: Improving K-12 Teachers’ Acceptance of Open Educational Resources by Open Educational Practices: A Mixed Methods Inquiry
citation: Hengtao Tang, Yu-Ju Lin, & Yingxiao Qian. (2021). Improving K-12 Teachers' Acceptance of Open Educational Resources by Open Educational Practices: A Mixed Methods Inquiry. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10046-z
title: Renewable assignments as an open educational practice intervention for teacher OER acceptance
description: Renewable assignments are an OEP in which learners adapt OER and produce and distribute self-generated OER beyond the classroom, engaging in "practices of manipulating OER while completing non-disposable course projects." In this study the intervention had four phases — learning about effective assessment, planning an OER-based assessment, developing and implementing it, and revising and publishing with open licenses — each ending with a formative assessment. Participants searched, adapted/created, implemented, and published OER-based assessments to benefit future students and educators.

Sufficient time for participants to search and adapt OER

article_title: Developing educational materials about risks on social network sites: a design based research approach
citation: Vanderhoven, E., Schellens, T., Vanderlinde, R., & Valcke, M. (2015). Developing educational materials about risks on social network sites: A design-based research approach. Ghent University. https://biblio.ugent.be
title: Design-based research as a four-step iterative methodology for developing educational materials
description: The article operationalises Reeves' (2006) design-based research model, in which "a design-based approach involves four sequential steps: (1) analysis of practical problems, (2) development of solutions based on existing knowledge, (3) evaluation research of the solutions in practice, and (4) reflection on the produced design principles", with iterative cycles of testing and refinement. The authors applied all four steps with researchers collaborating with practitioners throughout, and argue the full-process demonstration contributes to the design-based research literature.
requirements: Close cooperation between researchers and practitioners, such as educational publishers, developers, teachers and headmasters
Flexibility in methods across iterations to meet newly revealed needs
constraints: The authors note design-based research is very time consuming (three consecutive years for eight studies) and it is difficult to know when the design is good enough to finalize

media literacy regarding online risks
examples: The study's eight studies were mapped onto the four steps: three exploratory studies, five intervention iterations, and a final reflection producing four design principles

article_title: Instructional design students’ design judgment development
citation: Muruvvet Demiral-Uzan, Elizabeth Boling. (2024). Instructional design students’ design judgment development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10361-1
title: Reflection-in-action as the lens for explaining design judgment development
description: Drawing on Schön (1983), the article treats reflection-in-action—reflection made while designing—as the mechanism through which design judgment develops. The article states that reflections "can be made while designing (reflection- in-action), and that these are key to development of design judgment." In the analysis, each coded judgment was re-coded for whether reflection was employed, using indicators such as whether consequences of choices were considered, moves were tried out, and inquiry was involved, linking reflective practice to judgment development over the semester.
requirements: Indicators for coding reflection: consideration of consequences of choices, trying out design moves, and inquiry in the design situation
Data must allow reconstruction of students' thinking at moments of judgment, e.g., interviews prompted by design documents
constraints: Because experienced students may have reflected previously, it can be difficult to capture whether a judgment was made with reflection, as reported for Husain
target_learners: master's-level instructional design students in introductory ID courses
target_learning_goals: developing design judgment through reflective design practice
examples: Segments where students deeply considered and questioned what they had done and why were coded as design judgment made with reflection; statements without these indicators were coded as lacking reflection

title: Reuse programmed instructional-design scenarios to reduce development time and assure quality
description: Because designing technology-enhanced learning environments is costly and time-consuming — the article cites estimates "of the number of hours required to produce 1 h of instruction have ranged from 100 (Tannenbaum 2001) to 300 (Merrill & ID2 Research Group 1998)" — reuse of the instructional design supports time efficiency and quality assurance. SCY implements this by providing re-usable scenarios already programmed in the learning environment, so "no programming is required from the instructional designer," while an authoring system lets designers set parameters such as scaffolding level or create new scenarios. The approach balances ready-made structures with adaptability, echoing Murray's point that customization, extensibility, and scriptability characterize proficient authoring systems.
