article_title: Educators enacting online learning support roles in remote educational experiences
citation: Wardrip, P.S. (2021). Educators enacting online learning support roles in remote educational experiences. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 213–216. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09883-1
title: Treat remote learning as broader than online learning, since some remote instruction is not device-mediated
description: The article recommends that educators and researchers distinguish remote learning from online learning when adapting instructional practice. In the Notes, the author explains: "I will use the term remote learning to acknowledge that some school districts and learning organizations, either by choice or circumstance, have offered other forms of learning not mediated by a computational device." Design guidance for remote learning should therefore cover non-device-mediated formats such as worksheet packets as well as online formats.
requirements: Definitions of remote instruction should explicitly account for formats not mediated by computational devices
constraints: The distinction is drawn in the specific context of the COVID-19 pandemic shift to remote schooling
target_learners: School students receiving remote instruction, including those reached via packets and other non-device formats
target_learning_goals: Designing and evaluating instructional practice across the full range of remote learning formats
examples: The author cites examples of non-device-mediated remote learning such as "a packet of worksheets" offered by districts "either by choice or circumstance"
key_sources: Wardrip, P.S. (2021). Educators enacting online learning support roles in remote educational experiences. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 213–216. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09883-1

article_title: Taking educational games seriously: using the RETAIN model to design endogenous fantasy into standalone educational games
citation: Gunter, G.A., Kenny, R.F. & Vick, E.H. (2008). Taking educational games seriously: using the RETAIN model to design endogenous fantasy into standalone educational games. Education Tech Research Dev, 56, 511–537. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-007-9073-2
title: RETAIN design and evaluation model for educational games
description: RETAIN is a design and evaluation model for educational games developed by the authors to judge how well academic content is integrated with game play. Per the abstract, it was developed "to aide in the evaluation of how well academic content is endogenously immersed and embedded within the game's fantasy and story context". It also addresses transfer of knowledge and repeated use of content so it becomes automatic. The article positions it as the new design paradigm for standalone educational games.
requirements: Academic content must be endogenously immersed and embedded within the game's fantasy and story context for the model's evaluation to apply
target_learning_goals: academic skills and knowledge acquisition
transfer of knowledge
automatic availability of learned content
examples: The article discusses RETAIN as a model for designing endogenous fantasy into standalone educational games
key_sources: Gunter, G.A., Kenny, R.F. & Vick, E.H. (2008). Taking educational games seriously: using the RETAIN model to design endogenous fantasy into standalone educational games. Education Tech Research Dev, 56, 511–537. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-007-9073-2

article_title: Taking educational games seriously: using the RETAIN model to design endogenous fantasy into standalone educational games
citation: Gunter, G.A., Kenny, R.F. & Vick, E.H. (2008). Taking educational games seriously: using the RETAIN model to design endogenous fantasy into standalone educational games. Education Tech Research Dev, 56, 511–537. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-007-9073-2
title: Design educational games so repetitive usage makes academic content available for automatic use and supports transfer
description: The article holds that educational game design should encourage repeated engagement with academic content until it can be used automatically, and should promote transfer of knowledge. The abstract says the RETAIN model addresses games that "promoters transfer of knowledge, and encourages repetitive usage to that content becomes available for use in an automatic way". Repetition within the game's fantasy context is thus treated as a mechanism for fluent, transferable learning.
requirements: Game mechanics that encourage repetitive usage of the embedded academic content
target_learning_goals: transfer of knowledge
automaticity of academic content use
examples: RETAIN is described as evaluating whether a game encourages repetitive usage so content becomes available for automatic use
key_sources: Gunter, G.A., Kenny, R.F. & Vick, E.H. (2008). Taking educational games seriously: using the RETAIN model to design endogenous fantasy into standalone educational games. Education Tech Research Dev, 56, 511–537. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-007-9073-2

article_title: Negotiating social justice issues in research and practice in the field of learning, design, and technology: a multiple case study
citation: Walters, K., & Kopcha, T. J. (2025). Negotiating social justice issues in research and practice in the field of learning, design, and technology: a multiple case study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10542-6
title: A process model of centering social justice: centering, identifying tensions, and interpersonal design practices
description: The article proposes a visual process (Fig. 3) in which centering social justice sits at the middle of a balance among designer perspective, others' needs and perspectives, and project goals; tensions emerge as wavy lines from perceived imbalance; and interpersonal design practices respond to restore balance. The authors state "the how emerged as a process that included centering social justice, identifying tensions, and attending to both through interpersonal design practices," offering it as a representation other designers can use.
requirements: Designers must develop awareness of current and historical power dynamics and how they impact a project and team relationships as work evolves
constraints: The process is situated: it was derived from four cases and the authors argue design practices should not be de-contextualized across contexts
target_learning_goals: Negotiating social justice issues responsively within instructional projects
examples: Figure 3 displays the assertions as a triangle with centering social justice in the middle, dotted circle for ongoing attention, and wavy lines for tensions.
key_sources: Walters, K., & Kopcha, T. J. (2025). Negotiating social justice issues in research and practice in the field of learning, design, and technology: a multiple case study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10542-6

article_title: Negotiating social justice issues in research and practice in the field of learning, design, and technology: a multiple case study
citation: Walters, K., & Kopcha, T. J. (2025). Negotiating social justice issues in research and practice in the field of learning, design, and technology: a multiple case study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10542-6
title: Designers centering social justice should adopt a reflexive, responsive approach rather than model-centric design
description: The article recommends that designers go beyond models and adopt a reflexive approach, "an ongoing practice in which they question themselves and their position within a design project so that the process is more equitable for all involved." Because the thinking behind practices mattered more than any specific practice, designers should develop awareness of power dynamics and situate themselves and others within socio-cultural contexts, possibly by focusing on the 'why' behind their design practices.
requirements: Opportunities for introspection in which designers evaluate their own perspectives and reflect on how those perspectives facilitate or impede project work
constraints: This responsive approach is uncommon in the LDT literature, which more often treats design practices as transferable across contexts
target_learners: Learning designers, LDT scholars, and designers preparing to work with marginalized communities
target_learning_goals: Equitable design processes that attend to positionality, power, and context
examples: Participants such as Case 3 reflected on their position of authority ("As a white woman, I don't feel like I should be the defining voice on what moves forward in the project") and amplified marginalized perspectives instead.
key_sources: Walters, K., & Kopcha, T. J. (2025). Negotiating social justice issues in research and practice in the field of learning, design, and technology: a multiple case study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10542-6

article_title: The research we have is not the research we need
citation: Thomas C. Reeves, Lin Lin. (2020). The research we have is not the research we need. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09811-3
title: Educational technology research should be reoriented toward making a difference in the lives of learners
description: The article closes its analysis with a values-oriented recommendation: research on emerging learning technologies should be judged by whether it makes a difference for learners. The authors write that readers should be “always striving to make a difference in the lives of learners around the world,” framing learner impact as the ultimate aim of the research program the special issue represents.
requirements: Research efforts should be framed around serious problems related to teaching, learning, and performance rather than technologies alone
target_learning_goals: improving teaching, learning, and performance outcomes
examples: The concluding commentary of the special issue on systematic review research on emerging learning environments and technologies delivers this recommendation to its readers.
key_sources: Thomas C. Reeves, Lin Lin. (2020). The research we have is not the research we need. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09811-3

article_title: What makes for readable writing and reading success
citation: Audio-Visual Communication Review, digest items abstracted by E. G. Sherburne, Jr. and Edmund Faison. (1955). Audio-Visual Communication Review. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=audio-visual+communication+review
title: Two-ladder classification of readability: easy-difficult and interesting-dull parameters
description: The University of Illinois readability survey organizes readability measurement around two principal parameters. The easy-difficult ladder covers vocabulary difficulty, word length, sentence length and complexity, and parts-of-speech difficulty; the interesting-dull ladder covers references to people, verb-adjective ratios, image-bearing and human-interest words, and early-learned words and localisms. The survey reports that "Readability measures, for the most part, classify writing on two principal parameters", making this the organizing framework of the reviewed literature.
requirements: Applying the framework requires measuring stylistic elements such as vocabulary difficulty, sentence length and complexity, and human-interest word counts as listed in the survey
constraints: The survey notes the formulas deal with stylistic qualities of prose rather than with its meaning
target_learners: adult readers of printed instructional material
target_learning_goals: comprehension of written text
engagement with written material
examples: The survey lists the easy-difficult elements as vocabulary difficulty, length of words, length and complexity of sentence, and difficulty related to parts of speech
key_sources: Audio-Visual Communication Review, digest items abstracted by E. G. Sherburne, Jr. and Edmund Faison. (1955). Audio-Visual Communication Review. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=audio-visual+communication+review

article_title: Design and effects of representational scripting on group performance
citation: B. Slof, G. Erkens, P. A. Kirschner, J. G. M. Jaspers. (2010). Design and effects of representational scripting on group performance. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9148-3
title: Representational scripting: sequencing phase-related part-tasks with ontologically congruent external representations
description: Representational scripting integrates scripting and representational tools so that the phase-related part-tasks of a problem-solving process are made explicit and sequenced, evoking specific problem representations. The article defines a script as "a set of instructions regarding to how the group members should interact, how they should collaborate and how they should solve the problem". It structures complex tasks into problem orientation, problem solution and solution evaluation phases, each matched to a zero-, first- or second-order external representation whose expressiveness and processability supply the required representational guidance.
requirements: The representational guidance of a specific ER must be congruent (matched) with the part-task demands and activities of a specific problem phase
Students must be made aware of the different problem phases and their required problem representations
constraints: An ER is seldom effective for all part-task demands and activities
The effect of the design does not automatically apply to all complex learning-tasks
target_learners: non-expert secondary education students carrying out complex learning-tasks collaboratively
target_learning_goals: carrying out complex learning-tasks
creating qualitative and quantitative problem representations
examples: In the study, the complex business-economics task was divided into three phases and groups in the match condition received a conceptual ER, then a causal ER, then a simulation ER, each matched to its phase
key_sources: B. Slof, G. Erkens, P. A. Kirschner, J. G. M. Jaspers. (2010). Design and effects of representational scripting on group performance. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9148-3

article_title: Automated assessment system for programming courses: a case study for teaching data structures and algorithms
citation: Andre L. C. Barczak, Anuradha Mathrani, Binglan Han, Napoleon H. Reyes. (2023). Automated assessment system for programming courses: a case study for teaching data structures and algorithms. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10277-2
title: Allow repeated code resubmission with automated feedback to encourage practice and build coding competencies
description: The article recommends an assessment design in which students may resubmit code repeatedly and receive automated feedback, so that practice drives competency building. As the authors state, "the strategy of allowing students to resubmit codes multiple times and provide them with automated feedback encourages them to practice and build their coding competencies". In the DSA course this was implemented by the automarker, which marked each submission against test cases and gave clues for debugging before the deadline.
requirements: An automated assessment tool that evaluates submissions against test cases and returns feedback clues
Assignments with a deadline within which resubmissions are permitted
constraints: The article notes students may otherwise rely on numerous trial-and-error submissions rather than leverage the tool for critical thinking
target_learners: undergraduate computer science students in practice-oriented programming courses
target_learning_goals: building programming and coding competencies through sustained practice
examples: Students were given endless opportunities to resubmit their codes multiple times until the assignment deadline, with the automarker displaying marks and clues after each attempt
key_sources: Andre L. C. Barczak, Anuradha Mathrani, Binglan Han, Napoleon H. Reyes. (2023). Automated assessment system for programming courses: a case study for teaching data structures and algorithms. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10277-2

article_title: An experimental comparison of conclusion-drawing by the communicator and by the audience
citation: Hovland, Carl I., and Mandell, Wallace. (1952). An Experimental Comparison of Conclusion-Drawing by the Communicator and by the Audience. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 47, 581-88. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Resistance-to-acceptance account of post-communication opinion change
description: The abstract's general conclusion offers a mechanism account of delayed opinion change: content is learned equally from trustworthy and untrustworthy sources, but an "initial resistance to the acceptance of the material presented by an untrustworthy source" suppresses immediate agreement. If this resistance diminishes with time while the content is forgotten more slowly, agreement with the untrustworthy source increases after the communication. The abstract presents this as an explanatory assumption for the observed data rather than a separately tested model.
requirements: Applies to communications where the content itself provides the basis for the opinion, so that content is retained longer than the resistance to accepting it
constraints: Presented by the abstractor as an explanatory assumption accounting for the post-communication opinion changes, not as a directly tested prediction
target_learning_goals: opinion change and retention of communicated factual content
examples: The abstracted four-week follow-up showing equal retention but increased agreement with the untrustworthy source
key_sources: Hovland, Carl I., and Mandell, Wallace. (1952). An Experimental Comparison of Conclusion-Drawing by the Communicator and by the Audience. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 47, 581-88. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02716997

article_title: Bridging strategy gaps in programming: the role of visual scaffolding for learners with low cognitive ability
citation: Huang, S. C.-F., Chen, Z.-H., Lin, Y.-T., & Yeh, M. K. (2026). Bridging strategy gaps in programming: the role of visual scaffolding for learners with low cognitive ability. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10684-1
title: Real-time visual scaffolding programming system with color-coded blocks and synchronized visual output
description: Two custom-built programming systems were developed using the Unity engine and Google Blockly, with an interface divided into task description, programming tool, and top-down and bottom-up tracking windows. The experimental system adds real-time visual scaffolding: "the results of the programming blocks were displayed in real time on the left side of the interface, within both top-down and bottom-up tracking windows." Each code block was color-coded to match arrows and lines in the visual output, serving as signaling cues that guide attention and reduce the need to mentally simulate program execution.
requirements: Learners solve block-based programming tasks (loops, conditions, functions) in the system so the tracking windows and real-time output can guide strategy use
constraints: The intervention period in the study was relatively short, and learner performance may depend on their familiarity with the system
target_learners: Adult novice programmers with at least six months of programming learning experience, including low-EF learners
target_learning_goals: Programming strategy use (top-down versus bottom-up) and problem-solving during block-based programming tasks
examples: Participants solved three tasks—loops, conditions, and functions—moving a target through checkpoints with as few blocks as possible, with the experimental group seeing color-coded real-time program output
key_sources: Huang, S. C.-F., Chen, Z.-H., Lin, Y.-T., & Yeh, M. K. (2026). Bridging strategy gaps in programming: the role of visual scaffolding for learners with low cognitive ability. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10684-1

article_title: Supporting online learners’ regulation skills with the help of learning analytics and generative artificial intelligence
citation: Mutluhan Yilmaz, Andrea Gauthier, Mutlu Cukurova. (2026). Supporting online learners' regulation skills with the help of learning analytics and generative artificial intelligence. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10595-1
title: RefleXED tutor-support tool for LA-driven feedback provision
description: RefleXED is a practical tool developed in this study to support tutor-generated feedback. It "displays each student’s standardised SRLs proxy scores, cluster information based on the result of RQ1, and comprehensive insights into the SRLs pillars used in the study", while automatically retrieving the student's first name from the database. Tutors see only IDs, cluster membership and proxy scores, with tooltips explaining each proxy's behavioural variables and calculations, helping them craft tailored feedback regardless of familiarity with statistical terms. It was used by the control-condition tutor in the quasi-experiment.
requirements: Requires LMS log data processed into standardised SRLs proxy scores and cluster labels per student
constraints: Tutors access only student ID, cluster, and standardised proxy scores, without visibility of student names
target_learners: higher education students in online courses
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning skills (goal setting, task strategies, time management, help-seeking, self-evaluation)
examples: The study's single tutor used RefleXED's feedback creation interface to compose personalised messages for the control group across two intervention weeks
key_sources: Mutluhan Yilmaz, Andrea Gauthier, Mutlu Cukurova. (2026). Supporting online learners' regulation skills with the help of learning analytics and generative artificial intelligence. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10595-1

article_title: A bibliography of production, utilization, and research on instructional films
citation: RESEARCH ABSTRACTS: FILMS. (1953). Research abstracts, p. 819. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Instructional+Film+Research+Program
title: Ash and Jaspen study of optimum physical viewing conditions for a rear-projection daylight screen
description: A 1953 technical report (SDC 269-7-37, Special Devices Center under contract with the Instructional Film Research Program at Pennsylvania State College) by Ash and Jaspen studying the effects on learning of viewing angle, distance from the screen, and room illumination as these apply to the rear-projection, cabinet type, 16mm movie projector. The abstract prints only the purpose and identifies the three variables studied; no results are given in the abstract.
requirements: Applies to use of the rear-projection, cabinet type, 16mm movie projector with a daylight screen
constraints: The abstract reports purpose and variables only; no findings are printed in the supplied text
target_learners: viewers of instructional films in classroom projection settings
target_learning_goals: learning from 16mm instructional films under varying physical viewing conditions
examples: The three manipulated or studied conditions named are viewing angle, distance from the screen, and room illumination
key_sources: RESEARCH ABSTRACTS: FILMS. (1953). Research abstracts, p. 819. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Instructional+Film+Research+Program

article_title: The learner centric ecology of resources: A framework for using technology to scaffold learning
citation: Rosemary Luckin. (2008). The Learner Centric Ecology of Resources: A Framework for using Technology to Scaffold Learning. Computers & Education 50, 449-462. https://www.veselproject.net
title: Design technology-mediated learning for reciprocal teacher-learner relationships around different expertise
description: Because learners may know more about technologies that could act as learning tools than the experts who know the subject matter, the article argues that "It should be a collaborative relationship where the more able partner is both the teacher and the learner, but with respect to different expertise". New educational theories are needed to encompass situations where the balance between learner and teacher or mentor control is constantly changing. The article links this to Bruner's notion of learning by transaction and the inadequacy of translating obuchenie simply as instruction.
requirements: Teachers and experts need to know enough about learning technologies to scaffold learning, while learners need to know how to use these tools to learn subject matter
constraints: The article presents this as an observation suggesting the need for further exploration, not a tested finding
target_learners: learners and teachers/experts in technology-mediated settings
target_learning_goals: subject or skill learning supported through mutually beneficial collaboration
examples: The cited e-Science work by Underwood, Smith, Luckin & Fitzpatrick on enabling educational e-Science communities to grow and build contexts to share and exploit resources
key_sources: Rosemary Luckin. (2008). The Learner Centric Ecology of Resources: A Framework for using Technology to Scaffold Learning. Computers & Education 50, 449-462. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2007.09.018

article_title: Show and ‘tool’: How lecture recording transforms staff and student perspectives on lectures in higher education
citation: MacKay, J. R. D. (2018). Show and ‘Tool’: How lecture recording transforms staff and student perspectives on lectures in higher education. University of Edinburgh.
title: Recording a lecture transforms the act occurring in the teaching space, affecting proximate and ultimate concerns differently for staff and students
description: The constructivist grounded theory generated in this study holds that 'the act of recording a space was considered transformative, creating a digital artefact'. The analysis separated concerns into proximate issues occurring within the lecture space (lectures as tool versus stage show) and ultimate issues outside it (canonicity versus safety net). The theory is that 'recording a lecture transforms the act occurring within that teaching space into something else', disrupting both concern types differently for each group. Recordings act as digital objects that may commodify the teaching act.
requirements: Findings derive from constructivist grounded theory analysis with participant checking via mixed engagement committees; replication requires qualitative data from staff and students in the implementing institution
constraints: The author states the findings 'may not be entirely generalisable' and 'can only be applied in the context of this specific institute', and the student sample was first-year undergraduates only
target_learning_goals: understanding how lecture recording changes the lecture space and its use for learning
examples: The study analysed 13 staff interviews and 159 student free-text survey responses during a 2018 institute-wide lecture recording rollout at a Russell Group university
key_sources: MacKay, J. R. D. (2018). Show and ‘Tool’: How lecture recording transforms staff and student perspectives on lectures in higher education. University of Edinburgh. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.05.019

article_title: Improving children's written grammar and style: revising and editing with HARRY
citation: C.E. Holdich, P.W.H. Chung and R.G. Holdich. (2004). Improving children's written grammar and style: revising and editing with HARRY. Computers & Education, Vol 42, pp1-23. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/2.5/
title: Revision-support systems for children must explain how to make improvements, not just identify weaknesses
description: Drawing on earlier systems, the article argues that flagging weaknesses is insufficient for young writers: "The main limitation of both CATCH and StoryStation was that although the systems encouraged revision and identified weaknesses, neither system made it clear to children how to make improvements." HARRY therefore pairs detection of weaknesses with conversational prompts suggesting concrete improvement techniques, implementing teaching activities such as synonym substitution and sentence combining. This principle shapes the design of editing feedback in children's writing tools.
requirements: Prompts must be explicit about how to make effective changes and highlight significant features whose correction yields improvements
constraints: The article's supporting evidence for this principle comes from reported failures of two prior systems (CATCH largely unsuccessful; StoryStation pupils confused by mixed positive/negative feedback)
target_learners: Children and young adolescent writers learning to revise and edit
target_learning_goals: Effective revision strategies such as debating word choice and varying sentence constructions
examples: CATCH's prompts, such as 'the highlighted words may not be necessary. Do you want to make changes?', did not produce improvements; HARRY instead suggests e.g. replacement synonyms for the word [nice]
key_sources: C.E. Holdich, P.W.H. Chung and R.G. Holdich. (2004). Improving children's written grammar and style: revising and editing with HARRY. Computers & Education, Vol 42, pp1-23. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/2.5/

article_title: Re-thinking physics teaching with web-based learning
citation: Chandra, Vinesh & Watters, James J. (2012). Re-thinking physics teaching with web-based learning. Computers and Education, 58(1), 631-640. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.09.010
title: Reflexive pedagogies: dialogue, task options, feedback loops, and mixed knowledge processes in blended delivery
description: Getsmart's learning activities were "driven by reflexive pedagogies" comprising four design characteristics: "a) activities which encouraged dialogue and group collaboration; b) a range of task options which catered for learner diversity; c) a feedback loop to facilitate learning, and d) activities which represented a mix of knowledge acquisition processes." The discussion maps these onto cognitive apprenticeship methods such as coaching, scaffolding, and articulation through online chat.
requirements: Web-based lessons, tests, online chats, and interactive activities must be linked to the four reflexive design characteristics
target_learning_goals: physics concept understanding and complex reasoning
examples: Online chats encouraged dialogue and group collaboration; web pages and real-world links catered for learner diversity
key_sources: Chandra, Vinesh & Watters, James J. (2012). Re-thinking physics teaching with web-based learning. Computers and Education, 58(1), 631-640. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.09.010

article_title: Multivariate characterization of university students using the ICT for learning
citation: Vega-Hernández, M.-C., Patino-Alonso, M.-C., & Galindo-Villardón, M.-P. (2018). Multivariate characterization of university students using the ICT for learning. Computers & Education, 121, 124–130. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.004
title: REATIC questionnaire measuring learning styles and ICT use in university students
description: The REATIC questionnaire (De Moya Martínez et al., 2011) is a 60-item instrument rated on a Likert scale from 1 (Nothing) to 4 (Much), used here to "measure the relationship between learning styles and ICT in university student education". Its items fall into four blocks: knowledge about ICT, use of ICT, consideration of ICT, and use of ICT according to learning style, the last grouped into active, reflective, theoretical and pragmatic styles following Alonso, Gallego and Honey.
requirements: Respondents rate 60 items on a Likert scale of 1 (Nothing) to 4 (Much)
constraints: Validated with Spanish university students at the University of Salamanca
target_learning_goals: ICT use for learning
learning styles
examples: Used with 2117 University of Salamanca students in the 2013–2014 academic year
key_sources: Vega-Hernández, M.-C., Patino-Alonso, M.-C., & Galindo-Villardón, M.-P. (2018). Multivariate characterization of university students using the ICT for learning. Computers & Education, 121, 124–130. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.004

article_title: Augmentative and Alternative Communication Intervention Targets for School-Aged Participants with ASD and ID: A Single-Case Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Ganz, J. B., Pustejovsky, J. E., Reichle, J., Vannest, K. J., Foster, M., Fuller, M. C., Pierson, L. M., Wattanawongwan, S., Bernal, A. J., Chen, M., Haas, A. N., Skov, R., Smith, S. D., & Yllades, V. (2022). Augmentative and Alternative Communication Intervention Targets for School-Aged Participants with ASD and ID: a Single-Case Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Review Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40489-022-00326-6
title: Report standardized participant characteristics and prior communication modes so AAC interventions can be individualized
description: The article recommends that single-case researchers provide richer baseline descriptions of participants so future AAC interventions can be matched to learner profiles. It argues that "more detailed participant descriptions" could identify skills mediating intervention success and enable customization of modes and functions. Without such reporting, moderators of outcome cannot be determined.
requirements: Studies must describe standardized diagnostic, cognitive, and social-communication assessment information, joint attention and imitation mastery, and prior communication mode use.
constraints: The article notes most standardized and normed assessments lack standards for modification for individuals who use AAC.
target_learners: school-aged learners with ASD and/or ID and complex communication needs
target_learning_goals: social-communication skills via AAC
examples: The meta-analysis found pre-intervention comprehension skills and word use were seldom reported, preventing determination of which participant characteristics predict better outcomes with particular modes.
key_sources: Ganz, J. B., Pustejovsky, J. E., Reichle, J., Vannest, K. J., Foster, M., Fuller, M. C., Pierson, L. M., Wattanawongwan, S., Bernal, A. J., Chen, M., Haas, A. N., Skov, R., Smith, S. D., & Yllades, V. (2022). Augmentative and Alternative Communication Intervention Targets for School-Aged Participants with ASD and ID: a Single-Case Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Review Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40489-022-00326-6

article_title: Training Individuals to Implement Discrete Trials with Fidelity: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Joelle Fingerhut and Mariola Moeyaert. (2022). Training Individuals to Implement Discrete Trials with Fidelity: A Meta-Analysis. Focus on Autism and Other Developmental Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/10883576221081076
title: Use complete behavioral skills training to teach discrete trial implementation
description: The article concludes that because BST is statistically significantly effective for raising DTT implementation fidelity, "behavior skills training is recommended for discrete trial training implementation instruction." BST combines feedback, instruction, modeling, and rehearsal, and the meta-analysis shows complete BST outperforms trainings using only some components. The recommendation applies across implementers, since 69% of participants had no prior DTT experience.
requirements: Training should include all four BST components (feedback, instruction, modeling, rehearsal) delivered together and/or sequentially
constraints: More research is needed to determine BST effectiveness for teaching DTT in home environments and to parents, who were only 13% of participants
target_learning_goals: implementing discrete trial training with fidelity
examples: The meta-analysis of 46 SCED studies found BST-trained participants implemented DTT with 96.06% fidelity on average, above the 90% mastery threshold used in prior studies

article_title: The Effects of Problem Posing on Student Mathematical Learning: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Roslinda Rosli, Mary Margaret Capraro & Robert M. Capraro. (2014). The Effects of Problem Posing on Student Mathematical Learning: A Meta-Analysis. International Education Studies, 7(13). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/ies.v7n13p227
title: Review student performance in the four learning outcome areas before adopting a problem-posing program
description: The article recommends that school leaders ground adoption decisions in baseline performance across the four coded outcome areas: knowledge-based, ability-based, skill-based, and attitude-beliefs. By reviewing how students perform in each area, leaders can customize the program to student needs and set reasonable expectations. The article states leaders "should consider the four learning outcomes" before deciding on a problem-posing program.
requirements: Baseline information on student performance in knowledge, problem solving skill, problem posing ability, and attitude areas
constraints: Effect estimates rest largely on quasi-experimental designs; a one-group design tends to inflate effect sizes
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
problem solving skills
problem posing ability
attitudes toward mathematics
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 14 datasets from 13 studies (approximately 1,316 participants) and reported mean effect sizes ranging from .76 to 1.31 across the four outcome areas.

article_title: Exploring the use of low-cost simulation in nursing education: a scoping review.
citation: Frangi Duccio, Bardacci Yari, Magi Camilla Elena, El Aoufy Khadija, Longobucco Yari, Iovino Paolo, Amato Carla, Balestri Chiara, Forciniti Carolina, Rasero Laura, Iozzo Pasquale, Lucchini Alberto, Bambi Stefano. (2025). Exploring the use of low-cost simulation in nursing education: a scoping review. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2025-099968
title: Report detailed cost data when evaluating low-cost simulation interventions, as inconsistent cost reporting prevents validation of cost claims
description: The review identifies inconsistent cost reporting as a central barrier to evaluating low-cost simulation: only 38% of included studies reported cost-related factors, and the authors state that "the lack of objective cost data limits the ability to validate this categorisation across contexts". The principle calls on researchers and educators to report cost items — materials, simulators, sessions, maintenance, instructor fees and consumables — when implementing or studying low-cost simulation.
requirements: Cost reporting should cover not only initial material and equipment expenses but also ongoing costs for maintenance, instructor fees, consumable materials and repeated sessions
constraints: The review notes the literature lacks a standard cost benchmark, complicating direct comparisons between studies
target_learning_goals: Cost-effective simulation-based clinical skills training
examples: The review found only 15 of 39 studies reported cost-related factors, with materials and simulator costs most frequently itemised

article_title: Assessment and evaluation of prescribing competences: A systematic review and recommendations.
citation: McLachlan JC, Auta A, Ajiboye A. (2025). Assessment and evaluation of prescribing competences: A systematic review and recommendations. British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bcp.16033
title: Commission research on the predictive validity of prescribing competence assessments
description: The review recommends that national authorities and regulators commission research exploring how well current prescribing assessments predict later workplace performance, "with particular regard to patient safety", and that institutions consider measuring predictive validity of their own assessments. It further recommends creating national datasets analogous to the UK Medical Education Database to empower such analyses.
requirements: Outcome measures such as subsequent sanctions, Fitness to Practise issues, or retrospective chart review by trained pharmacists
constraints: Retrospective chart review is acknowledged as expensive and time-consuming, though no lower-cost methods with the same validity have been published
target_learning_goals: Prescribing competence
examples: The review cites studies using peer ratings, prescribing indicators from claims data, supervisor ratings, and disciplinary proceedings as outcome measures

article_title: Assessment and evaluation of prescribing competences: A systematic review and recommendations.
citation: McLachlan JC, Auta A, Ajiboye A. (2025). Assessment and evaluation of prescribing competences: A systematic review and recommendations. British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bcp.16033
title: Routinely collect demographic data in prescribing competence assessments to enable subgroup analysis
description: The review recommends that candidates in prescribing competence assessments be invited on a voluntary basis to provide demographic data including protected characteristics, so that subgroup analysis of differential attainment can be performed. This responds to the finding that national data sources show significant, unexplained group differences while the published literature reports no demographic analysis.
requirements: Voluntary provision of demographic data including age, sex, disability and ethnicity
constraints: The causes of differential performance are described as complex and outside the scope of the review
target_learning_goals: Prescribing competence
examples: The UK Prescribing Skills Assessment, NHS National Pharmacist Recruitment Programme and GPhC Registration Assessment publish demographic performance data

Understanding simulation-based learning for health professions students from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds: a scoping review. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-024-10384-6
title: Incorporate reflective debriefing and guided reflection into SBL for CALD students
description: The review finds reflection was "valued by students from CALD backgrounds as a crucial component of SBL activities, offering opportunities to identify their strengths and weaknesses". article_title: Enhancing sustainability competencies: A systematic review of educational interventions for dietitians and nutrition professionals.
citation: Lörzing R, Bartelmeß T. (2025). Enhancing sustainability competencies: A systematic review of educational interventions for dietitians and nutrition professionals. Nutrition & Dietetics. https://doi.org/10.1111/1747-0080.70046
title: Redman and Wiek's unified framework of eight key competencies for advancing sustainability transformations as an analytic lens for dietetics education
description: The review uses the unified framework of competencies for advancing sustainability transformations by Redman and Wiek, which "identifies eight key competencies—systems‐thinking, futures‐thinking, values‐thinking, strategies‐thinking, inter‐ and intra‐personal competencies, implementation competence and integration competence—complemented by disciplinary, general and professional competencies." It serves as the basis for assessing how and which sustainability competency areas the educational interventions address (research question 1), with interventions mapped from learning outcomes, objectives, structure and content.
requirements: Interventions must be describable in enough detail to map learning outcomes, objectives, structure and content to the framework's competencies
constraints: The review notes the Redman and Wiek and Lozano et al. frameworks are not directly comparable due to differing definitions of sustainability competencies, so no definite conclusion links pedagogical approaches to these competencies
target_learners: Dietitians and nutrition professionals, including students in nutrition-related programs
target_learning_goals: Sustainability competencies for supporting food system transformation

citation: Zhang YuKun, Wang YuWei, Jiang ManYu, Sun XiHui, Tang LiYoong. (2026). Effectiveness of non-technical skills training for healthcare professionals in emergency departments: a systematic review. Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13049-026-01574-9
title: Reinforce NTS training in the workflow by pairing core simulation with in-situ drills, cognitive aids, and visual prompts.
description: The review's second actionable principle is to "reinforce in the workflow", noting that "programmes that pair core simulation with in-situ drills, cognitive aids, and visual prompts demonstrate better transfer to clinical behaviour, particularly in trauma and cardiac arrest pathways". This reflects the review's finding of an evolution from isolated courses toward system-embedded learning, with reinforcement strategies maintaining training effects.

In-situ drills, cognitive aids, or visual prompts integrated into clinical workflow
target_learners: Healthcare professionals working in emergency departments
target_learning_goals: Transfer of trained teamwork and communication behaviours to clinical practice
examples: Included studies employed supplementary strategies including in-situ refreshers, educational newsletters, and visual reminders.

article_title: Effectiveness of multiple teaching methods in standardized training of internal medicine residents in China: a network meta-analysis.
citation: Guan Cheng Ye, Chun Ping Liu, Wei Li, Hua Chao Zhu, Liu Lv, Zhen Hong Zhu, Yong Hong Wang, Jie Hu, Xiao Jia Zheng, Jing Ying Fang, Yu Cao Ma, Ming Xuan Liu, Yi Wen Wang, Ying Kai Gao, Zi Yu Zhang, Lu Ming Zhao, Cun Xiang Xie, Min Yee Lim, Hai Long Wang. (2025). Effectiveness of multiple teaching methods in standardized training of internal medicine residents in China: a network meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07020-1
title: Replace passive lecture-based learning with active, problem-oriented methods in resident standardized training
description: The article argues that LBL leaves students "only learning passively" and lacking independent thinking, and concludes that "the standardized training and education of resident physicians in China urgently need to change the teaching mode and awaken students' awareness of self-directed learning". It recommends actively altering teaching techniques to enhance mastery of clinical knowledge and skills, supported by NMA evidence that PBL-based methods outperform LBL across outcomes.
requirements: Requires teachers to take a guiding and supportive role, with students independently thinking through problems via group discussion or literature review
constraints: The article notes the shift is challenging for students facing heavy learning tasks and graduation pressure, accustomed to passive learning since youth
target_learners: internal medicine residents in standardized training in China
target_learning_goals: theoretical performance
clinical thinking
self-directed learning
examples: The NMA compared 13 interventions across 74 studies and found new methods significantly outperformed LBL on theoretical, practical, medical record, and satisfaction outcomes

article_title: Findings Favor Haptics Feedback in Virtual Simulation Surgical Education: An Updated Systematic and Scoping Review.
citation: Sayed Azher, Aralia Mills, Jinzhi He, Taliah Hyjazie, Junko Tokuno, Andrea Quaiattini, and Jason M. Harley. (2024). Findings Favor Haptics Feedback in Virtual Simulation Surgical Education: An Updated Systematic and Scoping Review. Surgical Innovation. https://doi.org/10.1177/15533506241238263
title: Taxonomy of replicated haptic interactions in surgical virtual simulations
description: The review organizes the haptic characteristics implemented across included studies into replicated interaction types: sense of collision or touch, drilling sensations, force changes from interacting with different tissue types, and haptic guidance along predefined paths. It reports that "sense of collision or touch (n = 12) ... drilling (n = 7) ... and force changes due to interactions with different tissue types (eg, skin, adipose tissue, vessels, n = 4) ... were the replicated haptic interactions", while 24 studies did not elaborate on the haptic characteristics provided. Delivery was most commonly via haptic arms (n = 23) or laparoscopic simulators (n = 10), often reinforced with visual and auditory cues for realism.
requirements: Haptic hardware such as haptic arms (eg, Phantom Omni) or laparoscopic simulator instrument handles/trocars to deliver force feedback
constraints: The review notes heterogeneity across surgical domains: dentistry and orthopedics emphasize drilling sensations with limited empirical support for their realism, while laparoscopic simulations lack replication of nuanced tactile properties of soft tissues and solid organs
target_learning_goals: surgical task performance
tissue handling
drilling skills
instrument manipulation
examples: The review describes the Phantom Omni arm, a mobile arm with six degrees of freedom that participants manipulate to feel haptic feedback generated via a control box

article_title: Impact and Assessment of Research Integrity Teaching: A Systematic Literature Review.
citation: Crean Daniel, Gordijn Bert, Kearns Alan J. (2024). Impact and Assessment of Research Integrity Teaching: A Systematic Literature Review. Science and Engineering Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11948-024-00493-1
title: Rest's four-stage ethical decision-making process as the organizing framework for evaluating RI teaching claims
description: The review organizes its analysis around Rest's (1986) distinction of four stages of the ethical decision-making process. As the article states, "Rest (1986) distinguishes four stages of the ethical decision-making process, i.e. awareness, reasoning, motivation, and action", and these stages "are often mentioned as aims / goals of RI teaching". The review built a rubric guided by these stages to classify whether each of 86 eligible sources claimed RI teaching improves or does not improve each stage, and whether claims carried primary or secondary evidence.
requirements: Sources must make claims about how RI teaching affects one or more of the four stages for the rubric to classify them
constraints: The review excluded the impact of mentors, role-models, advisors, or supervisors, focusing only on formal RI teaching
target_learners: researchers at undergraduate, postgraduate, and principal investigator levels
target_learning_goals: research integrity ethical awareness, reasoning, motivation, and action
examples: The rubric in Fig. 2 classified each eligible source's claims by stage, treating 'behaviour' as the term primarily used for action

article_title: Towards best practice in developing motor skills: a systematic review on spacing in VR simulator-based psychomotor training for surgical novices.
citation: Fahl Jan Torge, Duvivier Robbert, Reinke Laurens, Pierie Jean-Pierre E. N., Schönrock-Adema Johanna. (2023). Towards best practice in developing motor skills: a systematic review on spacing in VR simulator-based psychomotor training for surgical novices. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04046-1
title: Retrieval-and-reconsolidation account of the spacing effect in psychomotor skill learning
description: The review assembles mechanistic explanations for why spaced training works: each session begins with active retrieval of the skill memory, and "each retrieval results in more profound (re)consolidation into the memory", allowing new movements to be integrated into existing memory. It adds complementary accounts: adaptive consolidation signalling regular future use, rest and sleep providing muted sensory input that reduces retrograde interference, and reduced reactive inhibition. The review stresses these are theoretical explanations and the reality may involve multiple mechanisms at once.
requirements: Spacing must distribute practice of the same material over repeated encounters separated by interstudy intervals, so that active retrieval occurs at the start of each session
constraints: The review states these are just theoretical explanations and alleged mechanisms; the reality might be more complex and involve multiple mechanisms at the same time
target_learning_goals: acquisition and retention of surgical psychomotor skills
examples: The review uses this account to interpret why spaced groups showed steeper learning curves and why sleep-containing intervals between sessions support consolidation

article_title: Technology-enhanced simulation-based learning in orthodontic education: A scoping review.
citation: SIPIYARUK Kawin, KAEWSIRIRAT Prachworrakit, SANTIWONG Peerapong. (2023). Technology-enhanced simulation-based learning in orthodontic education: A scoping review. Dental Press Journal of Orthodontics. https://doi.org/10.1590/2177-6709.28.3.e2321354.oar
title: Use technology-enhanced simulations for repetitive practice with immediate feedback to support self-directed learning and patient safety
description: The review argues technology-enhanced simulations should be designed so learners can repeat tasks with immediate feedback: they "allow users to perform required tasks repetitively until the expected outcomes are achieved", and with immediate feedback they support self-directed learning, reducing the need for one-to-one instructor support. The authors explain task repetition through the 'role of failure', in which students rethink or reperform tasks based on feedback from failure, and note simulators let learners improve skills in a safe environment, reducing treatment risk and enhancing patient safety.
requirements: Immediate feedback within the simulation to support self-directed learning
Unlimited training sessions, which the review notes come despite high setup costs and trained staff requirements
constraints: The review presents this as an argument from cited literature rather than a tested result of this review
target_learners: dental undergraduates preparing for clinical practice
target_learning_goals: psychomotor clinical skills
orthodontic knowledge and skills
patient safety
examples: The review cites the haptic simulation allowing users to perform the required steps of orthodontic bracket placement on a virtual patient, and the scenario-based software providing questions with immediate feedback

citation: Howie Erin K., Perryman Kristi L., Moretta Joseph, Cameron Laura. (2023). Educational outcomes of recess in elementary school children: A mixed-methods systematic review. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0294340
title: Recess as a unique developmental opportunity beyond physical activity
description: The review frames recess as more than a physical activity bout: it combines physiological activity with being outdoors, social interaction, and creative free play, each with proposed developmental benefits. It notes recess "includes social interaction, where children have opportunities to develop social skills, practice conflict resolution, and problem-solving skills". This framework motivates examining recess effects on educational outcomes beyond what exercise alone explains.
requirements: Recess defined as a regular unstructured break in the school day, typically outdoors
constraints: The review excluded interventions where recess was manipulated into structured activity, so the framework applies to unstructured recess

problem solving
creativity
attention
examples: The review cites Piaget's classification of play stages and outdoor-walk studies as background for the framework

citation: Howie Erin K., Perryman Kristi L., Moretta Joseph, Cameron Laura. (2023). Educational outcomes of recess in elementary school children: A mixed-methods systematic review. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0294340
title: Daily recess duration may beneficially exceed the CDC-recommended 20 minutes when split into shorter periods

academic achievement
classroom behavior

article_title: Review Ecosystems to access Educational XR Experiences: a Scoping Review

title: A review ecosystem is the environment that hosts and maintains experiential reviews of interactive experiences
description: The article defines a review ecosystem as "the environment that hosts and maintains these reviews" of interactive applications such as games and eduXR experiences. article_title: Teaching with AI: A Systematic Review of Chatbots, Generative Tools, and Tutoring Systems in Programming Education
citation: Said Elnaffar, Farzad Rashidi, Abedallah Zaid Abualkishik. (2026). Teaching with AI: A Systematic Review of Chatbots, Generative Tools, and Tutoring Systems in Programming Education. International Journal of Learning, Teaching and Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.26803/ijlter.25.1.1
title: Framework for effective and responsible integration of AI tools in programming education
description: The review proposes a concise five-element framework for the effective and responsible integration of AI tools in programming education. It recommends utilizing AI to provide hints and guidance rather than full solutions, teaching learners to write clear prompts and evaluate AI output, adapting prompts to students' language and local practices, combining AI use with assessments and honor codes to prevent misuse, and maintaining instructor oversight to explain AI outputs and correct misunderstandings. The framework aims to elevate AI "from mere coding assistant to a tool that supports learning, thinking, and ethical use in programming courses".
requirements: Instructor active involvement to explain AI outputs, correct misunderstandings, and guide the learning process
Learners taught prompt skills including writing clear prompts, identifying errors in AI output, and evaluating results carefully
Assessments, simple detection tools, and honor codes combined with AI use to prevent misuse
constraints: The framework is proposed by the review based on its synthesis of 58 studies rather than empirically validated as a whole in this article
target_learning_goals: independent problem-solving and critical thinking
ethical and effective use of AI tools
programming skill development
examples: The review recommends step-by-step problem solving using AI for hints and guidance rather than full solutions, enabling students to think critically
