article_title: How well do health professionals interpret diagnostic information? A systematic review.
citation: Whiting Penny F, Davenport Clare, Jameson Catherine, Burke Margaret, Sterne Jonathan A C, Hyde Chris, Ben-Shlomo Yoav. (2015). How well do health professionals interpret diagnostic information? A systematic review. BMJ Open. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4521525/
title: Report diagnostic test accuracy using natural frequencies rather than probabilities to support health professionals' probabilistic reasoning
description: The review concludes that presenting test accuracy information as natural frequencies — joint frequencies of two events, such as the number of women who test positive and have breast cancer — rather than as conditional probabilities improves health professionals' post-test probability estimation and speed of calculations. The authors state that presenting probabilities as frequencies may improve understanding of test accuracy information and note this approach has been embraced by the Cochrane Collaboration and GRADE.
requirements: The diagnostic scenario must provide prevalence, sensitivity and specificity information that can be converted into natural frequency counts
constraints: Evidence for improved estimation comes from five studies including three RCTs; the review notes further research is needed on how presentation format influences disease management decisions
target_learners: health professionals including doctors, nurses, midwives and physiotherapists
target_learning_goals: interpreting diagnostic test accuracy information
estimating post-test probability of disease
examples: Five studies including three RCTs found more accurate post-test probability estimation with natural frequencies than probabilities
Two studies found professionals spent an average of 25% more time assessing probability-format scenarios
key_sources: Whiting Penny F, Davenport Clare, Jameson Catherine, Burke Margaret, Sterne Jonathan A C, Hyde Chris, Ben-Shlomo Yoav. (2015). How well do health professionals interpret diagnostic information? A systematic review. BMJ Open. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4521525/

article_title: A real-world approach to Evidence-Based Medicine in general practice: a competency framework derived from a systematic review and Delphi process.
citation: Galbraith Kevin, Ward Alison, Heneghan Carl. (2017). A real-world approach to Evidence-Based Medicine in general practice: a competency framework derived from a systematic review and Delphi process. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5415750/
title: Real-world EBM competency framework for general practice: mindfulness, pragmatism, and knowledge of the patient
description: The article proposes a three-competency framework for Evidence-Based Medicine in general practice, derived from a systematic review and Delphi consensus. It states: "A simple competency framework was constructed, that acknowledges the constraints of real-world general practice: (1) mindfulness - in one's approach towards EBM itself, and to the influences on decision-making; (2) pragmatism - in one's approach to finding and evaluating evidence; and (3) knowledge of the patient - as the most useful resource in effective communication of evidence." Mindfulness means open awareness of biases and influences on decisions; pragmatism means using trusted pre-appraised evidence sources rather than systematic searching; knowledge of the patient means using the therapeutic relationship to judge when and how to communicate evidence. The framework is intended for GP training, continuing professional development, and routine care.
requirements: Further validation of the framework as an educational resource and as a strategy for actual practice, as the authors state
constraints: Deliberately excludes search and critical-appraisal skills as core competencies, based on the review's finding that these lacked credibility for routine general practice work
target_learning_goals: Applying evidence-based medicine in routine general practice
Communicating evidence to patients
Reflecting on decision-making influences
examples: A clinical scenario in which a GP considers prescribing a sleeping tablet, pauses to check her reasoning (mindfulness), consults the TRIP database for a pre-appraised synopsis (pragmatism), and tailors the recommendation to the patient's preferences (knowledge of the patient)
key_sources: Galbraith Kevin, Ward Alison, Heneghan Carl. (2017). A real-world approach to Evidence-Based Medicine in general practice: a competency framework derived from a systematic review and Delphi process. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5415750/

article_title: Comparing a Program Implemented under the Constraints of an RCT and in the Wild
citation: Newman, D., Lazarev, V., & Zacamy, J. (2016). Comparing a Program Implemented Under the Constraints of an RCT and in the Wild. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Explanations of rigorous evaluation designs should explicitly acknowledge the constraints the design imposes, or the value of the evidence may be lost in translation
description: Because the constraints and processes an RCT imposes may be salient to practitioners and evaluation stakeholders, the article argues they should be recognized when explaining rigorous designs. It states that failing to do so risks the value of the resulting evidence being lost in translation. The article illustrates the principle by identifying which program-related characteristics differ between its RCT and wild-implementation contexts and by proposing quasi-experimental estimation of the program's likely impact outside the trial.
requirements: Systematic evidence comparing RCT and non-experimental implementation contexts, such as matched surveys of teachers and principals in both contexts
constraints: Where the RCT uses a researcher-administered outcome measure, direct outcome comparison with wild sites is not possible and only characteristic-level contrasts are feasible
target_learners: high school teachers implementing literacy programs
target_learning_goals: improved academic literacy through discipline-specific instruction
examples: The authors compared teacher and principal survey responses across RCT treatment and Scale-up schools and used the contrasts to approximate potential impacts of the RCT's ecological invalidity.
key_sources: Newman, D., Lazarev, V., & Zacamy, J. (2016). Comparing a Program Implemented Under the Constraints of an RCT and in the Wild. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567633

article_title: 'Literacy Octopus' Dissemination Trial: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Lord, P., Rabiasz, A., and Styles, B. (2017). 'Literacy Octopus' Dissemination Trial: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN84508118
title: Theory of Change spectrum from passive dissemination to active supported research engagement
description: Appendix D sets out a Theory of Change positioning dissemination approaches on a spectrum from limited support (passive dissemination to a large number of schools, cheapest, least effect) through light support with an individual/classroom focus, to more active school-wide support with a smaller number of schools (more expensive, greatest effect). The trial tested the passive end: "The Theory of Change for the Literacy Octopus Dissemination Trial posits the question whether inexpensive ‘push’ dissemination approaches will have an effect." The null result answers that this end of the spectrum alone does not improve attainment.
requirements: Testing the spectrum's active end requires the companion Evidence-based Literacy Support trial, which added proactive provider support
constraints: The spectrum's ordering of effect by support level is a hypothesis; this trial only tested the passive end and found no effect
target_learners: Primary schools and their headteachers in England
target_learning_goals: School-wide use of research evidence to improve literacy outcomes
examples: The trial sent inexpensive materials to 10,000 schools to test the cheapest, largest-reach end of the spectrum
key_sources: Lord, P., Rabiasz, A., and Styles, B. (2017). 'Literacy Octopus' Dissemination Trial: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN84508118

article_title: Estimating Individual Treatment Effect from Educational Studies with Residual Counterfactual Networks
citation: Siyuan Zhao and Neil Heffernan. (2016). Estimating Individual Treatment Effect from Educational Studies with Residual Counterfactual Networks. Proceedings of the 10th International Conference on Educational Data Mining. https://educationaldatamining.org/
title: Residual Counterfactual Networks (RCN)
description: RCN is an end-to-end neural model for estimating individual treatment effects under the Rubin-Neyman causal model. It "first learns a balancing representation of deep features" by minimizing an Integral Probability Metric (MMD or Wasserstein distance) between control and treated distributions, then "learns a residual mapping" on that representation so the estimated treatment effect depends on the balanced features. It extends Balancing Neural Networks and Counterfactual Regression by adding a residual block for the treated population only.
requirements: Requires the no-hidden-confounding (strong ignorability) assumption, whose validity the article states must be determined by domain knowledge
Requires a binary intervention setting with both control and treated samples present
constraints: IPMs can only measure the distance between two distributions, so extension to multiple treatments would need pairwise IPMs, which the article says would be computationally time-consuming
target_learning_goals: estimating which intervention (e.g., video vs. text hint) benefits an individual student
examples: Applied to an ASSISTments skill-builder experiment predicting assignment completion, and to the IHDP semi-simulated dataset
key_sources: Siyuan Zhao and Neil Heffernan. (2016). Estimating Individual Treatment Effect from Educational Studies with Residual Counterfactual Networks. Proceedings of the 10th International Conference on Educational Data Mining. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED596589

article_title: The Impact of Reading Success Academy on High School Reading Achievement
citation: Burlison, K., & Chave, J. (2014). The Impact of Reading Success Academy on High School Reading Achievement. Journal for Leadership and Instruction. https://www.scopeonline.us
title: Reading Success Academy small-group reading intervention
description: The Reading Success Academy was an academic skills intervention program using research-based instructional practices for low-achieving students in small-group instructional sessions. Its core instructional components "consisted of a focus lesson, mini-lesson, and an instructional passage," delivered through pre-, during, and post-reading strategies. In this study it was implemented for ninth-graders pulled from social studies classes three times a week over an eight-week period in 2011-2012, integrating the social studies curriculum with reading strategies tailored to individual student reading data.
requirements: Small-group instructional sessions implemented during the school day, with students pulled from social studies classes three times a week
constraints: In this implementation it was limited to ninth-grade students who had become nonproficient readers based on eighth-grade and ninth-grade FCAT scores, over an eight-week period
target_learning_goals: reading proficiency on standardized assessments
reading comprehension and higher order processing
examples: Implemented at a comprehensive high school in the southeast during the 2011-2012 school year to prepare students for the 2012 reading FCAT
key_sources: Burlison, K., & Chave, J. (2014). The Impact of Reading Success Academy on High School Reading Achievement. Journal for Leadership and Instruction. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1081400

article_title: Errors of Students Learning with React Strategy in Solving the Problems of Mathematical Representation Ability
citation: Sari, D.P., Darhim, & Rosjanuardi, R. (2018). Errors of students learning with REACT strategy in solving the problems of mathematical representation ability. Journal on Mathematics Education, 9(1), 121-128. https://jme.ejournal.uns.ac.id
title: REACT strategy: a constructivism-based contextual teaching strategy of Relating, Experiencing, Applying, Cooperating, and Transferring
description: REACT is a learning strategy based on constructivism that the article describes, citing CORD (2012), as "based on the teaching contextual learning strategy which is structured to encourage the involvement of students in the classroom". REACT is an acronym of Relating, Experiencing, Applying, Cooperating, and Transferring. In this study teachers used it across 10 meetings in an experimental class, with students working on worksheets and asking the teacher or peers when facing difficulty.
requirements: Structured contextual learning activities that encourage student involvement in the classroom, including hands-on (experiencing) activity per CORD (1999)
constraints: In this study it was implemented in eighth-grade geometry (cube, cuboid, pyramid) over 10 meetings with a posttest but no pretest
target_learning_goals: mathematical representation ability (visual, verbal, and symbolic)
examples: The experimental class learned cube and pyramid surface-area and volume material with REACT strategy for 10 meetings, then took a 60-minute posttest on mathematical representation ability
key_sources: Sari, D.P., Darhim, & Rosjanuardi, R. (2018). Errors of students learning with REACT strategy in solving the problems of mathematical representation ability. Journal on Mathematics Education, 9(1), 121-128. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1173659

article_title: Explanatory Modeling in Science through Text-Based Investigation: Testing the Efficacy of the Project READI Intervention Approach
citation: Susan R. Goldman, Cynthia Greenleaf, Mariya Yukhymenko-Lescroart, Willard Brown, Mon-Lin Monica Ko, Julia M. Emig, MariAnne George, Patricia Wallace, Dylan Blaum, & M. Anne Britt. (2019). Explanatory Modeling in Science Through Text-Based Investigation: Testing the Efficacy of the Project READI Intervention Approach. American Educational Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831219831041
title: Project READI framework: reading for understanding as evidence-based argumentation from multiple sources within disciplinary practices
description: Project READI conceptualizes reading for understanding as engaging adolescents in evidence-based argumentation (EBA), in which "claims are asserted and supported by evidence that has principled connections to the claim," with the nature of claims, evidence, and principles differing across disciplines. It joins a comprehension perspective (constructing mental representations through close reading, analysis, and synthesis) with a disciplinary literacies perspective, so that disciplinary reasoning practices are integrated with the literacy practices that support them. Multiple sources include verbal and visual, static and dynamic forms.
requirements: Instruction must be developmentally appropriate and situated in authentic disciplinary practices
Tasks must supply multiple sources of information across media and representational modes
constraints: What counts as valid argument depends on each discipline's epistemology and discourse norms, so the framework must be re-specified per discipline
target_learners: adolescents in middle and high school
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
evidence-based argumentation
disciplinary literacy
examples: The science instantiation specified learning goals of close reading, synthesis across multiple text sources, constructing explanatory models, justifying and critiquing explanations, and demonstrating science epistemology through inquiry dispositions
key_sources: Susan R. Goldman, Cynthia Greenleaf, Mariya Yukhymenko-Lescroart, Willard Brown, Mon-Lin Monica Ko, Julia M. Emig, MariAnne George, Patricia Wallace, Dylan Blaum, & M. Anne Britt. (2019). Explanatory Modeling in Science Through Text-Based Investigation: Testing the Efficacy of the Project READI Intervention Approach. American Educational Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831219831041

article_title: Explanatory Modeling in Science through Text-Based Investigation: Testing the Efficacy of the Project READI Intervention Approach
citation: Susan R. Goldman, Cynthia Greenleaf, Mariya Yukhymenko-Lescroart, Willard Brown, Mon-Lin Monica Ko, Julia M. Emig, MariAnne George, Patricia Wallace, Dylan Blaum, & M. Anne Britt. (2019). Explanatory Modeling in Science Through Text-Based Investigation: Testing the Efficacy of the Project READI Intervention Approach. American Educational Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831219831041
title: Five core constructs of disciplinary knowledge for argumentation from multiple texts
description: The Project READI disciplinary teams agreed on "five categories of knowledge about a discipline, which we labeled core constructs": epistemology; inquiry practices and reasoning strategies; overarching concepts, themes, principles, and frameworks; forms of information representation/types of texts; and discourse and language structures. Each discipline specifies these constructs in its own epistemic terms; Table 1 gives the science specification, pairing each general definition with what it means for text-based investigation in science. The taxonomy defines what students need to know about a discipline to support comprehension and production of argumentation.
requirements: Specification must be worked out per discipline, since claims, evidence, and warrants differ across disciplines
constraints: The general definitions are shared, but the science instantiation (e.g., models as approximations subject to revision) does not transfer to other disciplines without respecification
target_learners: adolescent science, history, and literature students
target_learning_goals: disciplinary knowledge for argumentation
epistemological understanding
evidence evaluation
examples: In science, epistemology was specified as knowledge expressed as models and theories that are approximations with limitations, based on sound empirical data, socially constructed, parsimonious, and subject to revision
key_sources: Susan R. Goldman, Cynthia Greenleaf, Mariya Yukhymenko-Lescroart, Willard Brown, Mon-Lin Monica Ko, Julia M. Emig, MariAnne George, Patricia Wallace, Dylan Blaum, & M. Anne Britt. (2019). Explanatory Modeling in Science Through Text-Based Investigation: Testing the Efficacy of the Project READI Intervention Approach. American Educational Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831219831041

article_title: Explanatory Modeling in Science through Text-Based Investigation: Testing the Efficacy of the Project READI Intervention Approach
citation: Susan R. Goldman, Cynthia Greenleaf, Mariya Yukhymenko-Lescroart, Willard Brown, Mon-Lin Monica Ko, Julia M. Emig, MariAnne George, Patricia Wallace, Dylan Blaum, & M. Anne Britt. (2019). Explanatory Modeling in Science Through Text-Based Investigation: Testing the Efficacy of the Project READI Intervention Approach. American Educational Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831219831041
title: Four-phase learning progression for onboarding novice science readers into text-based explanatory modeling
description: The Strand 2 design work produced "a four-phase learning progression" staging the introduction and progressive deepening of learning goals. Phase 1 establishes classroom routines supporting reading, reasoning, and talking about biology; Phase 2 moves students from generic strategies to those tailored to biological principles and models; Phase 3 instantiates the routines in inquiry constructing explanatory models motivated by driving questions or conundra intended to induce puzzlement; Phase 4 deepens modeling by constructing, justifying, and critiquing alternative models with more independent work. Practices are introduced through modeling and explicit instruction, then scaffolded with templates providing language stems, following a cycle of individual, small-group, and whole-class discussion.
requirements: Iterative instructional cycle: modeled practices followed by scaffolded student use with feedback
Sequenced text sets reflecting a range of complexity and representational forms
constraints: Weeks per phase were approximations expected to vary across teachers and classrooms
target_learning_goals: close reading of science texts
synthesis across sources
constructing, justifying, and critiquing explanatory models
examples: In the efficacy study the progression was instantiated across a 20-22 week semester with a Reading Models module, a Homeostasis module (~4-5 weeks), and an MRSA module (~5-6 weeks)
key_sources: Susan R. Goldman, Cynthia Greenleaf, Mariya Yukhymenko-Lescroart, Willard Brown, Mon-Lin Monica Ko, Julia M. Emig, MariAnne George, Patricia Wallace, Dylan Blaum, & M. Anne Britt. (2019). Explanatory Modeling in Science Through Text-Based Investigation: Testing the Efficacy of the Project READI Intervention Approach. American Educational Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831219831041

article_title: Explanatory Modeling in Science through Text-Based Investigation: Testing the Efficacy of the Project READI Intervention Approach
citation: Susan R. Goldman, Cynthia Greenleaf, Mariya Yukhymenko-Lescroart, Willard Brown, Mon-Lin Monica Ko, Julia M. Emig, MariAnne George, Patricia Wallace, Dylan Blaum, & M. Anne Britt. (2019). Explanatory Modeling in Science Through Text-Based Investigation: Testing the Efficacy of the Project READI Intervention Approach. American Educational Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831219831041
title: Project READI science instructional modules with student notebooks, text sets, and scaffold templates
description: The intervention materials were curricular modules assembled from the Strands 2 and 4 design work, provided to intervention teachers to ensure consistency across classrooms. "These were assembled into student notebooks and text sets ('readers')." The notebooks included descriptions of activities, instructions, and templates of worksheets that scaffolded reading, reasoning, and modeling activities; the design assumed teacher facilitation and mediation, supported by annotated teacher guides carrying guidance and tips from teachers involved in the iterative design process. Complete modules were made available at www.projectreadi.org.
requirements: Teacher facilitation and mediation of students' notebook use, guided by annotated teacher versions
constraints: Materials were provided rather than teacher-created to produce consistency across intervention teachers in an RCT
target_learning_goals: text-based inquiry
explanatory modeling of biological phenomena
examples: Modules covered the Reading Models module, the Homeostasis module (~4-5 weeks) including feedback mechanisms and diabetes as a case of homeostasis disruption, and the MRSA module (~5-6 weeks) on evolution and antibiotic resistance
key_sources: Susan R. Goldman, Cynthia Greenleaf, Mariya Yukhymenko-Lescroart, Willard Brown, Mon-Lin Monica Ko, Julia M. Emig, MariAnne George, Patricia Wallace, Dylan Blaum, & M. Anne Britt. article_title: Developing Content-Area Academic Literacy: A Randomized Control Trial of the Reading Apprenticeship Improving Secondary Education (RAISE) Project
citation: Fancsali, C., Abe, Y., & Pyatigorsky, M. (2016). Developing Content-Area Literacy: The Reading Apprenticeship Improving Secondary Education (RAISE) project: A Randomized Controlled Trial. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Reading Apprenticeship framework: four interacting dimensions of classroom learning culture centered on a metacognitive conversation
description: Reading Apprenticeship is an instructional framework that helps teachers support discipline-specific literacy by attending to "four interacting dimensions of classroom learning culture: Social, Personal, Cognitive, and Knowledge-Building." At its center is an ongoing metacognitive conversation carried on internally through metacognitive reading and reasoning routines and externally through talk about reading relationships, classroom resources, and the knowledge needed to make sense of complex texts. RAISE operationalized it through intensive teacher professional development.
requirements: Teachers receive professional development and ongoing on-site support to implement the framework's practices
target_learners: high school students in ELA, biology, and U.S. history classes
target_learning_goals: discipline-specific literacy and reading comprehension of complex academic texts
examples: RAISE delivered 65 hours of face-to-face professional development over 12 months plus teacher-leader on-site support across 42 high schools
key_sources: Fancsali, C., Abe, Y., & Pyatigorsky, M. (2016). Developing Content-Area Literacy: The Reading Apprenticeship Improving Secondary Education (RAISE) project: A Randomized Controlled Trial. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED566986

article_title: Project Based Learning: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Menzies, V., Hewitt, C., Kokotsaki, D., Collyer, C. and Wiggins, A. (2016). Project Based Learning: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/public/files/Projects/EEF_Project_Protocol_ProjectBasedLearning.pdf
title: REAL Projects structure: essential question, academic content, drafts with critique, student-created product, exhibition and authentic audience
description: The Learning through REAL Projects intervention defines a reusable project pattern in which teachers from different subjects design projects driven by a real-world question and culminating in a publicly exhibited output. Each project had to include "an essential question—driving the whole project; significant academic content built in; multiple drafts of work and critique on work provided by peers, teachers and others", a student-created final project, public exhibition, and an authentic audience. Projects may still include traditional teaching where it supports the project product.
requirements: Projects planned in conjunction with the English department and at least one other discipline
Timetabled for at least 20% of the Year 7 timetable (40-50% recommended) with at least one extended project of six full days
Pupils taught in blocks lasting at least half a day
A member of the school leadership team on the leading team
constraints: The authentic audience was often an issue and public exhibition was sometimes challenging for schools to facilitate
Not all schools maintained mixed-ability classes throughout the year
target_learners: Year 7 pupils in mixed-ability classes in English secondary schools
target_learning_goals: literacy and high-quality written work
21st Century Skills such as team working, communication and research skills
engagement with school and learning
examples: All schools began by adapting the Innovation Unit's A to Z book project, in which pupils researched a topic, wrote and redrafted text and images, got the book published and launched it at a student-led book launch.
key_sources: Menzies, V., Hewitt, C., Kokotsaki, D., Collyer, C. and Wiggins, A. (2016). Project Based Learning: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/public/files/Projects/EEF_Project_Protocol_ProjectBasedLearning.pdf

article_title: Design and Validation of a Questionnaire to Measure Research Skills: Experience with Engineering Students
citation: Cobos Alvarado, F., Peñaherrera León, M., & Ortiz Colon, A. M. (2016). DESIGN AND VALIDATION OF A QUESTIONNAIRE TO MEASURE RESEARCH SKILLS: EXPERIENCE WITH ENGINEERING STUDENTS. Journal of Technology and Science Education. http://dx.doi.org/10.3926/jotse.227
title: Use research-based learning so students develop research skills from the undergraduate level onward
description: The article advocates incorporating research-based learning (RBL) from students' first academic years rather than leaving research training to postgraduate study, so that research becomes a pillar of education rather than a requirement. It lists advantages attributed to Chávez (2013), Rojas and Méndez (2013) and Morales, Rincón and Romero (2004), including that RBL "Promotes students during their years of study are able to develop the skills necessary to investigate (critical thinking, analysis, synthesis, leadership, creativity, entrepreneurship, problem solving, etc.)". The AHABI questionnaire is offered as a tool to evaluate such programs.
requirements: Linking academic programs with the institution's research areas and research groups; teacher capacity to direct the research process
constraints: Advantages are attributed to cited authors rather than tested in this article's own data
target_learners: undergraduate university students, especially in engineering
target_learning_goals: critical thinking, analysis, synthesis, leadership, creativity, entrepreneurship, problem solving, research skills
examples: The study's experimental group was exposed to the RBL method while the control group remained free from its influence, in a quasi-experimental design with pre-existing groups

article_title: The Effect of Authentic Problem-Based Vocabulary Tasks on Vocabulary Learning of EFL Learners
citation: Fateme Shir Mohammadi. (2017). The Effect of Authentic Problem-Based Vocabulary Tasks on Vocabulary Learning of EFL Learners. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 5(3). https://www.ijels.aiac.org.au
title: Researcher-made 30-item multiple-choice vocabulary posttest with item analysis
description: The study's outcome measure was a researcher-designed posttest of the 30 vocabulary items taught in the course, consisting of "30 multiple-choice items". Item analysis was run to measure ratios of item discrimination (ID) and Item Facility (IF), and reliability was measured using Cronbach Alpha (α=.85). Items were selected beforehand using Wesche and Paribakht's vocabulary knowledge scale, which tested 95 items to identify words learners did not know prior to the study.
requirements: Items must be drawn from the vocabulary actually taught in the treatment
constraints: The same 30 items were used to design the post-test, so the measure covers only the taught item set
target_learning_goals: vocabulary recall
vocabulary retention
examples: The Nelson vocabulary proficiency test, a thirty-item test for intermediate learners, was used as the homogeneity test to form the groups

article_title: Causal Mediation in Educational Intervention Studies
citation: Greg Roberts, Nancy Scammacca, and Garrett J. Roberts. (2018). Causal Mediation in Educational Intervention Studies. Behavioral Disorders, 43(4), 457–465. https://doi.org/10.1177/0198742917749560
title: Measure the mediator with strong reliability, ideally with multiple measures or latent variables
description: The article recommends minimizing measurement error in the mediator because low reliability biases key paths: "the effect of the mediator on the outcome (Path b) is under-estimated and the effect of treatment on the outcome (Path c′) is over-estimated, assuming ab is positive." It suggests using measures with well-documented reliability, collecting data with more than one measure to cross-reference rankings, and building latent variables in structural equation models to model measurement error explicitly.
requirements: Measures with strong reliability are required, particularly for measuring the mediator
constraints: Self-report measures of internal processes are subject to response bias and may not be sufficiently valid, particularly with young children
target_learners: students in school-based intervention studies, including young children
target_learning_goals: accurate estimation of mediated treatment effects on behavioral and achievement outcomes
examples: The article notes self-monitoring measures often rely on self-report with high or unknown measurement error, making it difficult to measure self-monitoring of 6- and 7-year-olds with the reliability necessary to estimate its mediating effect
key_sources: Greg Roberts, Nancy Scammacca, and Garrett J. Roberts. (2018). Causal Mediation in Educational Intervention Studies. Behavioral Disorders, 43(4), 457–465. https://doi.org/10.1177/0198742917749560

article_title: The Effectiveness of Computers on Vocabulary Learning among Preschool Children: A Semiotic Approach
citation: Basoz, T. & Can, T., D. (2016). The effectiveness of computers on vocabulary learning among preschool children: A semiotic approach. Cypriot Journal of Educational Science, 11(1), 02-08. http://sproc.org/ojs/index.php/cjes/
title: Researcher-developed 20-item picture vocabulary test for preschool EFL learners
description: The study's outcome measure was a vocabulary test developed by the researcher, which "included the pictures of 20 target vocabulary" words such as cat, dog, chicken, sheep, lemon, and to dance. It was administered as a pre-test before the four-week experiment and readministered as an identical post-test in the fifth week to measure vocabulary gain in both the CAVI and TVI groups.
requirements: Administered identically as pre-test and post-test to both groups to allow gain comparison
constraints: Developed by the researcher for this single study rather than a standardised instrument
target_learners: preschool children (5-year-olds) learning English as a foreign language
target_learning_goals: receptive knowledge of 20 target English vocabulary words
examples: Pre-test means were .31 (CAVI) and .36 (TVI); post-test means rose to 13.31 and 14.78 respectively.

article_title: Teacher Viewpoints of Instructional Design Principles for Visuals in a Middle School Math Curriculum
citation: Clinton, V. & Cooper, J.L. (2015, April). Teacher Viewpoints of Instructional Design Principles for Visuals in a Middle School Math Curriculum. Paper presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Educational Research Association Annual Meeting, Chicago, IL.
title: Retain representational visuals that provide critical support for understanding a lesson's context, because coherence and multimedia principles conflict for them
description: Because removing representational visuals is supported by the coherence principle but not the multimedia principle, the article treats their removal as theoretically uncertain, noting representational visuals may help English Language Learners with reading comprehension. The authors therefore kept "representational visuals that provided critical support for understanding the context of a lesson." Teacher survey responses supported this caution, showing mixed views on such visuals.
requirements: Decisions about removing representational visuals require judging whether the visual provides critical support for understanding the lesson context
constraints: The article states the use of visuals for aesthetic purposes only could increase interest, although this has not been shown to benefit learning
target_learners: middle school mathematics students, including English Language Learners
target_learning_goals: understanding the context of story problems and lesson contexts in mathematics
examples: Figure A7 shows a representational visual included in the revised curriculum to assist with vocabulary from the lesson context, retained in both original and revised versions
key_sources: Clinton, V. & Cooper, J.L. (2015, April). Teacher Viewpoints of Instructional Design Principles for Visuals in a Middle School Math Curriculum. Paper presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Educational Research Association Annual Meeting, Chicago, IL. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED574965

article_title: The Effect of Self-Assessment on EFL Learners' Self-Efficacy
citation: Sasan Baleghizadeh and Atieh Masoun. (2013). The Effect of Self-Assessment on EFL Learners' Self-Efficacy. TESL Canada Journal/Revue TESL du Canada, Volume 31, Issue 1. https://teslcanadajournal.ca
title: Integrate comprehensive, regular, formative self-assessment into language teaching to build learner self-efficacy
description: Because the study found that a biweekly, ungraded, formative self-assessment component significantly raised EFL learners' self-efficacy, the authors recommend that "language teachers are strongly recommended to include comprehensive self-assessment in their teaching practice". They suggest applying self-assessment after each unit of work as a scaffolding tool to focus learners' attention on a target issue, and pairing self-assessment techniques with appropriate instructional feedback.
requirements: Self-assessment should be formative rather than summative, presenting regular feedback rather than grades
Teachers should provide positive feedback for successful performance and discuss exemplars
constraints: Evidence comes from one quasi-experimental study with adult intermediate female learners in a single Iranian institute; the authors note self-assessment might be related to an individual's cultural background
target_learners: EFL learners in language institute classrooms
target_learning_goals: self-efficacy for language learning
examples: In the study, experimental-group students self-assessed for about 30-35 minutes at the end of each unit on a biweekly basis three times over a seven-week course, were told they would not receive any score, and the teacher presented successful student performances as exemplars
key_sources: Sasan Baleghizadeh and Atieh Masoun. (2013). The Effect of Self-Assessment on EFL Learners' Self-Efficacy. TESL Canada Journal/Revue TESL du Canada, Volume 31, Issue 1. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1033761

article_title: Dynamic Assessment, Potential Giftedness and Mathematics Achievement in Elementary School
citation: Nicoleta Laura Popa, Ramona Loredana Păuc. (2015). Dynamic Assessment, Potential Giftedness and Mathematics Achievement in Elementary School. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 8, Number 2. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN-2065-1430
title: Adapted Romanian teacher and parent forms of Renzulli's Scales for rating behavioral characteristics of superior students
description: Potential giftedness was estimated with two adapted forms (for teachers and parents) of Renzulli's Scales of Behavioral Characteristics of Superior Students, in the Romanian adaptation by C. Cretu (1999). The teacher form has 51 items and the parent form 46 items on six-point Likert scales covering "learning, mathematics and sciences, creativity, leadership and motivation"; internal consistency ranged from .66 to .94 (teacher form) and .87 to .92 (parent form).
requirements: Both teacher and parent forms completed per child, with the mean of the two average scores used in analyses
constraints: The scales collected teachers' and parents' perceptions of ability levels rather than a clear distinction between gifted and non-gifted students
target_learning_goals: identifying potential giftedness to interpret responses to dynamic assessment
examples: Scores on the mathematics and science scales correlated positively with math pretest scores (r= .40 for the parent form; r= .42 for the teacher form), which the article reports as indicating good levels of convergent validity

The evaluation matched up to eight students per school into pairs by pretest text reading level and English language learner status, randomly assigning one member of each pair to treatment.

article_title: The Effectiveness of Teaching Number Relationships in Preschool
citation: Jung, M., Hartman, P., Smith, T., & Wallace, S. (2013). The Effectiveness of Teaching Number Relationships in Preschool. International Journal of Instruction, 6(1). https://www.e-iji.net
title: Short daily small-group number relationships activities using rekenrek, software, and ten-frame
description: The intervention pattern consisted of three activities introduced in teacher training sessions: "Three ac tivities (rekenrek, Building Block software, ten-frame) were introduced at the training sessions." Teachers delivered them Monday to Thursday for 5 to 10 minutes during the first circle period, with rekenrek twice weekly and the other activities once weekly. Each activity was designed to strengthen children's understanding of number relationships, with quantities starting at 3 to 5 and extending up to 8.

parts-whole relationships
more-and-less relationships

article_title: The Effect of Reciprocal-Teaching Strategy on Learning Outcomes and Attitudes of Qassim-University Students in "Islamic Culture"
citation: Al-Harby, J. S. S. (2016). The Effect of Reciprocal-Teaching Strategy on Learning Outcomes and Attitudes of Qassim-University Students in "Islamic Culture". Journal of Education and Practice, 7(6). https://www.iiste.org
title: Reciprocal teaching as a four-strategy dialogue-based instructional framework
description: The article presents reciprocal teaching as an instructional activity grounded in Vygotsky's account of social interaction in classroom dialogue, developed by Palincsar and Brown. It is "a strategy that is based on the dialogue exchanged between the teacher and the students, among students and their peers", in which text is divided into sections and taught through four stages: "summarizing, posing questions, clarifying and predicting", conducted in small cooperative groups led by the teacher, who intervenes only when necessary. The study operationalised this framework in a teacher's guide for the experimental group.
requirements: A teacher trained in the four strategies, including an initial training session in summarizing conducted by the teacher
constraints: The article applies the framework to text-based course content divided into sections

target_learning_goals: comprehension of course content
dialogic and social skills
question formation and prediction skills
examples: The researcher prepared a teacher's guide encompassing three lectures based on the strategy for the experimental group.

article_title: The Impact of Electronic Mind Maps on Students' Reading Comprehension
citation: Mohammad Mahmoud Talal Mohaidat. (2018). The Impact of Electronic Mind Maps on Students' Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 11(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n4p32
title: Researcher-built 30-item reading comprehension test covering three comprehension levels
description: The study's measurement instrument is a multiple-choice reading achievement test constructed from the taught texts and the grade 9 Teacher Guide. Items were written "in accordance with the three reading comprehension levels (reading lines, reading between lines, reading behind the lines)". After jury validation and piloting, five items were dropped, leaving 30 items (10, 11 and 9 across the three levels), scored 0-30. Test-retest reliability over two months was r = 0.89.

difficulty coefficients 0.33-0.77 and discrimination coefficients 0.33-0.80 judged acceptable

article_title: The Effects of Reciprocal Teaching on Reading Comprehension of Iranian EFL Learners
citation: Leila Ashegh Navaie. (2018). The Effects of Reciprocal Teaching on Reading Comprehension of Iranian EFL Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 9(4). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.9n.4p.26
title: Reciprocal Teaching Procedure: scaffolded dialogue around four comprehension-fostering and comprehension-monitoring strategies
description: The Reciprocal Teaching Procedure (RTP), designed by Palincsar and Brown (1984), is an explicit instructional strategy in which teacher and students take turns leading a dialogue about a text while applying four strategies: "generating one's own questions, summarizing parts of the text, clarifying word meanings and confusing text passages, and predicting what might come next in the text". Instruction is scaffolded: the teacher first models the strategies explicitly, then gradually fades involvement as students take turns as dialogue leaders, shifting responsibility to learners. The article applies RTP as the treatment for improving EFL reading comprehension.
requirements: An instructor who explicitly models the four strategies in early stages before students lead the dialogue
Students who take turns acting as discussion leaders as the teacher fades involvement
target_learners: students in schools, universities, or private language institutes
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
comprehension-fostering and comprehension-monitoring strategies
examples: In the study, the teacher read a text section aloud, modeled questioning, summarizing, clarifying, and predicting, then transferred the discussion-leader role to students over 15 sessions.

citation: Bogale, Y. N. (2018). Conceptualizing Reading to Learn: Strategy Instruction and EFL Students' Reading Comprehension. International Journal of Curriculum and Instruction 10(2), 93–117. http://ijci.wcci-international.org
title: Researcher-developed 30-item EFL reading comprehension pre/post tests
description: Because standardized tests for Ethiopian university EFL students were unavailable, the researcher developed reading tests of two passages with multiple-choice questions, 30 items asking participants to employ "their specific knowledge of meta-cognitive reading strategies when reading a text". After item analysis (items with difficulty 20%–80% accepted), 52 of the initial 60 items were analyzed; reliability was alpha=.72 (pretest) and alpha=.73 (posttest, n=55), and pre/post difficulty means (.6010 and .6130) were judged comparable.
requirements: Items must pass difficulty analysis (20%–80% accepted) and reliability above 0.7
constraints: Designed specifically for the Ethiopian EFL university context; True/False items were excluded from analysis
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
metacognitive reading strategy knowledge
examples: Questions were mapped to four strategies: determining main ideas, guessing meanings, drawing inferences, and previewing

article_title: Scaffolding Fidelity and Adaptation in Educational Program Implementation: Experimental Evidence from a Literacy Intervention
citation: David M. Quinn, James S. Kim. (2017). Scaffolding Fidelity and Adaptation in Educational Program Implementation: Experimental Evidence From a Literacy Intervention. American Educational Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831217717692
title: READS for Summer Learning: Core and Adaptive versions
description: READS for Summer Learning is a summer literacy intervention for elementary students designed to narrow income-based reading skill gaps, combining school- and home-based components. Core READS delivers eight matched summer books with trifolds guiding a reading routine, six scripted end-of-year lessons, a family literacy event, and summer nudges. Adaptive READS adds collaborative grade-level working meetings, online modules on the program's research-based principles, and school-developed adaptation plans, with teachers permitted to adjust book lists, family outreach, lessons, and nudges within core program principles.
requirements: Teachers must teach at least six READS lessons preparing students to use the reading routine independently
Each school must host at least one family event where parents learn about READS
Students must receive matched books over the summer
constraints: In the study, eligibility was limited to schools that were 75% or more free or reduced-price lunch
target_learners: elementary school students in high-poverty schools

summer independent reading engagement
examples: Common adaptations included locally developed plans to improve parent outreach and increase attendance at the family literacy event, and changes to students' summer book lists

article_title: L2 Reading Fluency Progression Using Timed Reading and Repeated Oral Reading
citation: Shimono, T. R. (2018). L2 reading fluency progression using timed reading and repeated oral reading. Reading in a Foreign Language, 30(1). http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl
title: Reading fluency as automatic word recognition enabling rapid, effortless comprehension
description: The article frames reading fluency as rooted in automatic word recognition, requiring well-specified phonological, orthographic, and semantic word knowledge retrieved while consuming few cognitive resources. It describes this process as "ballistic," meaning rapid and unstoppable, so that with a sufficiently automatized L2 mental lexicon readers comprehend accurately at a suitable rate with perceived effortlessness. The study operationalizes fluency as reading rate in standard words per minute plus sufficient comprehension, using a 70% multiple-choice benchmark.
requirements: Measurement requires standardized rate (standard words per minute) and a comprehension criterion; the article uses Nation's 70% benchmark
constraints: The article notes rate gains sometimes do not transfer to other texts unless there is large vocabulary overlap, and repetitive rereading can harm motivation
target_learning_goals: L2 silent reading fluency
reading rate
reading comprehension
examples: The study used Reading Power passages written mostly at the first 1,000 word-frequency level, matched to participants' Vocabulary Size Test results

title: Teach vocabulary with multiple exposures, interaction, multi-sensory input, personal associations, and explicit systematic instruction

The author argues ASL signing meets all of these criteria, since signs are highly iconic, motoric, and motivating, allowing hearing students to see, say, and sign words.

sight word fluency

citation: Quinn, D. M., & Kim, J. S. (2016). Predictors and Moderators of Teacher Learning and Changes in Practice: Evidence from a Randomized Trial of a Teacher-Adapted Literacy Program. SREE Spring 2016 Conference abstract.

Adaptive READS replaces top-down management with grade-level team adaptation based on school-specific data.

article_title: REACH: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Luke Sibieta. (2016). REACH: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/
title: REACH: a targeted one-to-one reading support programme for Years 7–8 delivered by trained teaching assistants, in two variants (RI and LC).
description: REACH is a targeted reading support programme designed to improve reading accuracy and comprehension in pupils with reading difficulties in Years 7 and 8, based on research by the Centre for Reading and Language at York and delivered by specially trained teaching assistants. The report states "In both versions, pupils received three one to one 35 minute sessions each week for 20 weeks." REACH RI consists of reading books at an appropriate level with running records, phoneme awareness instruction, letter-sound instruction, and phonological linkage training; REACH LC adds metacognitive strategies, comprehension and inference work, written narrative, and multiple-context vocabulary training. target_learning_goals: reading accuracy
reading comprehension
phoneme awareness
vocabulary
examples: In the trial, each school provided one to three TAs who delivered one-to-one 35-minute sessions three times per week for 20 weeks, with pupils withdrawn from lessons other than English.

citation: Liliarti, N., & Kuswanto, H. (2018). Improving the Competence of Diagrammatic and Argumentative Representation in Physics through Android-based Mobile Learning Application. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 106-122. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.1138a

description: The developers synthesized a matrix serving as a guideline for the learning media, organized by the indicators of diagrammatic and argumentative representation (giving factual content, building an argument of a physical phenomenon, making a diagram before calculation, giving a diagram and building an argumentation) crossed with materials on Newton's law, Archimedes' law, and convection. article_title: Impact of Leadership Style of Teacher on the Performance of Students: An Application of Hersey and Blanchard Situational Model
citation: Shaukat Ali Raza and Asma Sikandar. (2018). Impact of Leadership Style of Teacher on the Performance of Students: An Application of Hersey and Blanchard Situational Model. Bulletin of Education and Research, 40(3), 73-94. https://journals.pu.edu.pk
title: Readiness-matched teaching style pattern: directive behaviors for low readiness, empowering behaviors for high readiness
description: This pattern operationalizes the situational model as concrete teacher behaviors per readiness level, adapted from Halima (2006). At R1 the teacher "Defines what, were, when, how and by whom to be done" with one-way communication and close supervision; at R2 decisions are explained and two-way communication encouraged; at R3 the teacher listens, encourages participation and builds confidence; at R4 the teacher delegates tasks and decision making and decreases control on students' activities.

constraints: The article notes it is very difficult for an individual teacher to organize content in line with the four teaching styles
target_learners: grade-8 students spanning low to high readiness levels
target_learning_goals: improved achievement in subject-matter content (General Science)
examples: The experimental group was taught by following the four styles suggested by the Hersey and Blanchard model according to the four readiness-level categories
