article_title: Structured Read-Aloud in Middle School: The Potential Impact on Reading Achievement
citation: Jennifer Kohart Marchessault, Karen H. Larwin. (2013). Structured Read-Aloud In Middle School: The Potential Impact On Reading Achievement. Contemporary Issues In Education Research, Volume 6, Number 2. http://www.cluteinstitute.com/
title: Use read-aloud in middle school to leverage students' higher listening capacity and expand exposure to texts above their instructional level
description: The article argues read-aloud should not be dismissed as an elementary technique. Because "many students have a higher listening capacity level than reading level," reading aloud lets middle school students access materials above their instructional level through listening, so that comprehension becomes the end result when the only task is listening. It also positions the teacher as a model of positive reading behaviors and a bridge for scaffolding connections between text and real life.
requirements: Students should be active participants in the text, with questioning techniques used to ensure attention and correct comprehension answers
constraints: The potential weakness of read-aloud can be seen as being too teacher-directed or lacking the release of responsibility to the students to take ownership of the learning
While one cannot say that read-aloud is the best technique for daily instruction, simply dismissing read-aloud as an elementary technique is being short-sighted
target_learners: struggling readers whose reading ability does not match expected texts
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
vocabulary development
engagement and motivation to read independently
examples: The study added read-alouds to the traditional middle school curriculum in two sixth-grade classrooms and measured DORA gains relative to control classrooms
key_sources: Jennifer Kohart Marchessault, Karen H. Larwin. (2013). Structured Read-Aloud In Middle School: The Potential Impact On Reading Achievement. Contemporary Issues In Education Research, Volume 6, Number 2. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1073207

article_title: Reform-Based-Instructional Method and Learning Styles on Students' Achievement and Retention in Mathematics: Administrative Implications
citation: M. N. Modebelu & C. C. Ogbonna. (2014). Reform-Based-Instructional Method and Learning Styles on Students' Achievement and Retention in Mathematics: Administrative Implications. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies 2(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.2n.2p.48
title: Reform-based instructional method for mathematics (discussion, manipulatives, varied strategies, reviewed exercises)
description: The experimental treatment was a reform-based instructional method combining whole-class discussion with varied instructional strategies adapted to students' learning styles. Its printed features include that "Discussion method was employed to encourage every student to talk mathematics", manipulatives were provided for demonstration of concepts and student interaction, supervised short written review exercises ended each lesson, and the Collin Rose learning style questionnaire identified auditory, visual and tactile learners. The traditional comparison condition used lesson notes along the traditional expository method with teacher-led explanation and take-home assignments with no immediate feedback.
requirements: Research assistants who were the regular mathematics classroom teachers delivered both conditions
The Collin Rose learning style questionnaire was administered to identify students' learning styles
constraints: Studied with year-one NCE students in two Anambra State Colleges of Education on the coordinate geometry content of equations of straight lines and of circles
target_learners: Year-one National Certificate in Education (NCE) mathematics students in Colleges of Education
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement in coordinate geometry (equations of straight lines and circles)
Retention of mathematics knowledge
examples: The experimental group of 61 students was taught with the reform-based method while the control group of 58 was taught with the traditional expository method
key_sources: M. N. Modebelu & C. C. Ogbonna. (2014). Reform-Based-Instructional Method and Learning Styles on Students' Achievement and Retention in Mathematics: Administrative Implications. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies 2(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.2n.2p.48

article_title: ReflectED: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Gary Motteram, Sophina Choudry, Afroditi Kalambouka, Graeme Hutcheson and Amanda Barton. (2016). ReflectED: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/public/files/Projects/EEF_Project_Protocol_ReflectED.pdf
title: ReflectED programme: 28 weekly half-hour metacognition lessons with Evernote-recorded reflections
description: ReflectED is a primary-school metacognition programme developed by Rosendale Primary School. "ReflectED consists of 28, weekly, half-hour lessons, which teach pupils strategies they can use to monitor and manage their own learning." Pupils record audio, photographed and written reflections on Evernote, code them with tags and a colour system (green for success, blue for mastery, yellow for struggling, red for stuck), and review records over time; teachers can search tagged notes to identify pupil needs. Delivery was supported by Rosendale mentors, London Connected Learning Centre online support, an initial day of training and three half-day hub meetings.
requirements: Schools need tablet or laptop computers able to run Evernote and an effective wireless network, as the intervention relies on technology use
Participating teachers attend two and a half days of training over the year
constraints: The evaluated intervention lasted one academic year, but ReflectED is designed as a continuous approach across primary school rather than a one-off intervention
Some teachers reported finding it hard to fit in all lessons and struggled to use the database of reflections to inform teaching
target_learning_goals: Metacognition and learning-to-learn skills: setting and monitoring goals, assessing progress, identifying strengths and challenges
examples: Rosendale trained teachers from 30 schools in five English areas to deliver ReflectED over the academic year 2014/15, with lesson plan packs, a website, digital resources and weekly reminders and tips
key_sources: Gary Motteram, Sophina Choudry, Afroditi Kalambouka, Graeme Hutcheson and Amanda Barton. (2016). ReflectED: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/public/files/Projects/EEF_Project_Protocol_ReflectED.pdf

article_title: The Evaluation of Effectiveness of Reciprocal Teaching Strategies on Comprehension of Expository Texts
citation: Gulhiz Pilten. (2016). The Evaluation of Effectiveness of Reciprocal Teaching Strategies on Comprehension of Expository Texts. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i10.1791
title: Reciprocal teaching implementation sequence with prompt cards and rotating leader roles
description: The article operationalises reciprocal teaching as a nine-step weekly cycle over 8 expository texts: explicit teaching of the four stages with a written prompt worksheet, teacher modelling by reading aloud and thinking aloud at the start of each week, gradual transfer of responsibility, small groups of 4-5 members, and rotating leader and participant roles. The leader manages discussion using prompt cards asking questions such as "What is the main idea of the text?" while participants fill in their own prompt cards, and the teacher circulates, gives feedback and takes the participant role in each group.
requirements: Teacher modelling repeated at the beginning of every week; written prompt worksheets and prompt cards; small groups of 4-5 members
constraints: The teacher reported initial student difficulty understanding the strategy, which repeated modelling reduced
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension of expository texts through predicting, clarifying, questioning and summarizing
examples: Implemented for 11 weeks with 8 expository texts in a Turkish fourth-grade classroom
key_sources: Gulhiz Pilten. (2016). The Evaluation of Effectiveness of Reciprocal Teaching Strategies on Comprehension of Expository Texts. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i10.1791

article_title: Effectiveness of an Intervention Program in Fostering Academic Resilience of Students at Risk of Failure at Secondary School Level
citation: Muhammad Irfan Arif and Munawar S. Mirza. (2017). Effectiveness of an Intervention Program in Fostering Academic Resilience of Students at Risk of Failure at Secondary School Level. Bulletin of Education and Research, 39(1), 251-264. https://ber.journals.pu.edu.pk
title: Resilience Assessment Scale (RAS)
description: The Resilience Assessment Scale is a 40-item, 5-point Likert instrument developed by the researchers by adapting items from the Resiliency Attitudes and Skills Profile (Hurtes, 2001) and the Connor-Davidson resilience scale (2003). It measures "the ten contributing factors of resilience" including creativity, self-esteem, self-efficacy, internal locus of control, problem solving skills, autonomy, sense of humor, stress coping skills, sense of purpose in life and teacher-student relationship. Scores range from 40 to 200, with students scoring below the median of 120 labeled non-resilient at risk. It was used both to identify non-resilient at-risk students and as the pretest-posttest outcome measure.
requirements: Administered to identify students scoring below the median of 120 as non-resilient at risk
constraints: Developed and validated for this study's secondary-school sample; expert validation was by PhD-holding faculty members in education
target_learners: Non-resilient at-risk 9th and 10th grade secondary students
target_learning_goals: Academic resilience and its ten protective factors
examples: Used as pretest and post-test measure in the three-month intervention experiment; internal consistency Cronbach's α = .87
key_sources: Muhammad Irfan Arif and Munawar S. Mirza. (2017). Effectiveness of an Intervention Program in Fostering Academic Resilience of Students at Risk of Failure at Secondary School Level. Bulletin of Education and Research, 39(1), 251-264. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1210192

article_title: Effects of the Coordination Exercise Program on School Children's Agility: Short-Time Program during School Recess
citation: Tatsuo Yasumitsu, Haruo Nogawa, Yoshiro Hatano. (2012). Effects of the Coordination Exercise Program on School Children's Agility: Short-Time Program during School Recess. Journal of Research, volume 6, issue 2. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Effects+of+the+Coordination+Exercise+Program+on+School+Children%27s+Agility
title: Repetitive side steps test as a measure of children's agility
description: The repetitive side steps test is the agility measure adopted by Japan's Ministry of Education (MECSST) for 6-11 year olds, a Japanese version of the side step test in the California Physical Performance Test. Students side step (not jump) from a center line to touch or cross lines on the right and left for 20 seconds, scoring one point per line passed; the test was administered twice at pretest and twice at posttest with the better score recorded. The article states it "is an accepted way to measure the agility aspect of coordination".
requirements: Students paired to count and record each other's steps per the MECSST guideline
Administration in two lines of seven to eight students, measuring 14-16 students simultaneously
constraints: The test was conducted twice at the pretest and twice at the posttest, with the better score recorded for each
target_learning_goals: Measure the agility aspect of coordination
examples: One point was given for each line passed, so a sequence of right, center, left, center would make four points
key_sources: Tatsuo Yasumitsu, Haruo Nogawa, Yoshiro Hatano. (2012). Effects of the Coordination Exercise Program on School Children's Agility: Short-Time Program during School Recess. Journal of Research, volume 6, issue 2. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ954491

article_title: Effects of the Coordination Exercise Program on School Children's Agility: Short-Time Program during School Recess
citation: Tatsuo Yasumitsu, Haruo Nogawa, Yoshiro Hatano. (2012). Effects of the Coordination Exercise Program on School Children's Agility: Short-Time Program during School Recess. Journal of Research, volume 6, issue 2. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Effects+of+the+Coordination+Exercise+Program+on+School+Children%27s+Agility
title: Use recess time for short coordination interventions without disrupting regular physical education classes
description: The article argues that recess periods can host brief, effective coordination interventions because they require little time and leave regular physical education untouched. The experimental program occupied only two to three of five weekly 20-minute recesses over five weeks and still produced significant agility gains. The authors state that "effective use of the recess time also enables intervention to be carried out without disrupting regular physical education classes and produces significant results".
requirements: A regular daily recess period of about 20 minutes available two to three times per week
School staff support; the home room teacher and principal approved and commented that the program made effective use of time
constraints: Evidence comes from one five-week study with 60 third-grade students at a single public elementary school in Tokyo
target_learning_goals: Improve physical fitness, specifically agility and coordination
examples: The study implemented the intervention across 12 twenty-minute recesses during a regular school semester, with the agility test administered immediately before and after
key_sources: Tatsuo Yasumitsu, Haruo Nogawa, Yoshiro Hatano. (2012). Effects of the Coordination Exercise Program on School Children's Agility: Short-Time Program during School Recess. Journal of Research, volume 6, issue 2. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ954491

article_title: Changes in Reading Habits by Low Literate Adults through Extensive Reading
citation: Rodrigo, V., Greenberg, D., & Segal, D. (2014). Changes in reading habits by low literate adults through extensive reading. Reading in a Foreign Language, 26(1), 73-91. http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl
title: Model for the development of a reading habit through access, enjoyment, attitude, and motivation
description: The article proposes a step model (Figure 1) describing how a reading habit develops in low literate adults. It begins with a healthy library containing a variety of books with easy access and freedom to select, leading to enjoyment and a sense of accomplishment, then a positive reading attitude, then motivation to read more, culminating in a reading habit, independent readers, and language development. The authors present it as "a model with the steps that favor the development of a reading habit", grounded in their finding that only participants with access to books and encouragement developed habits.
requirements: A healthy library containing a variety of books in genre and level, with easy access and freedom to select books
Enjoyment and a sense of accomplishment during reading, in a low-anxiety situation where readers can choose and abandon books
constraints: The model is offered for adults with low reading skills in short-duration literacy programs, based on self-reported data
target_learners: low literate adults reading at grade 3-5.9 levels, native and non-native speakers of English
target_learning_goals: development of a reading habit and positive reading attitude
becoming independent readers and eventual language development
examples: The ER instructional model gave students access to a library with books on different topics and levels, with reading and enjoying the reading experience as the only literacy task
key_sources: Rodrigo, V., Greenberg, D., & Segal, D. (2014). Changes in reading habits by low literate adults through extensive reading. Reading in a Foreign Language, 26(1), 73-91. http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl

article_title: An Investigation into the Impact of Reflective Teaching on EFL Learners' Autonomy and Intrinsic Motivation
citation: Abdolrezapour, P., & Fallah, E. (2015). An investigation into the impact of reflective teaching on EFL learners’ autonomy and intrinsic motivation. Cypriot Journal of Educational Science. 10(4), 305-315. https://doi.org/10.18844/cjes.v10i4.229
title: Reflective teaching as a cyclical process of hypothesising, investigation, reasoning, testing and evaluation
description: Reflective teaching, traced to Dewey (1933), treats teachers as active decision-makers rather than passive curriculum implementers. The article describes it as a process in which "teaching needs to be a process comprising the following components: hypothesi sing, investigation, reasoning, testing and evaluation", leading to adaptations that take account of class dynamics. In the study, the reflective teacher drew on Kumaravadivelu's (2006) principles, analysed problems on the spot, and used both reflection in teaching and reflection on teaching.
requirements: The teacher must actively participate, spot problems, analyse and fix them on the spot, and review their teaching decisions and students' learning
constraints: The study operationalised it through one reflective teacher selected by questionnaire score, so effects are tied to that implementation
target_learning_goals: learner autonomy
intrinsic motivation
examples: The experimental teacher explained the new approach beforehand, analysed possible problems on the spot and fixed them, drawing on reflection in and on teaching
key_sources: Abdolrezapour, P., & Fallah, E. (2015). An investigation into the impact of reflective teaching on EFL learners’ autonomy and intrinsic motivation. Cypriot Journal of Educational Science. 10(4), 305-315. https://doi.org/10.18844/cjes.v10i4.229

article_title: LIT Programme: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Claire Crawford, Amy Skipp. (2014). LIT Programme Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation.
title: Deliver reciprocal-teaching literacy interventions in small groups of 5–6 pupils led by staff experienced in literacy interventions
description: The article's process evaluation found that delivery conditions mattered to perceived success: "groups of 5 –6 children led by qualified teachers or teaching assistants with experience of delivering literacy interventions worked best." This principle captures the implementation conditions under which practitioners judged the programme effective, complementing the null year-group impact finding.
requirements: Staff qualified as teachers or teaching assistants with experience of delivering literacy interventions
Groups of 5–6 children
constraints: Based on practitioner feedback rather than experimentally tested comparisons; the evaluation could not separately identify the contributions of different delivery elements
target_learners: Year 7 pupils with poor literacy skills
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
examples: In the trial, children typically received 3–4 hours of LIT tuition per week for eight months, mostly delivered in small groups
key_sources: Claire Crawford, Amy Skipp. (2014). LIT Programme Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581139

article_title: LIT Programme: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Claire Crawford, Amy Skipp. (2014). LIT Programme Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation.
title: Reciprocal teaching: four comprehension strategies in which pupils 'become the teacher'
description: Reciprocal teaching is "an instructional procedure designed to teach students cognitive strategies that might lead to improved reading comprehension", in which teacher and pupils take turns leading discussion of a text. Pupils are taught four strategies — "summarising, clarifying, questioning, and predicting" — which force them to check understanding, identify problems, and make inferences. The LIT programme packages this approach with staff training and detailed lesson plans.
requirements: Training for staff and detailed lesson plans on the use of reciprocal teaching
constraints: Not felt suitable for the lowest ability pupils who required intensive support; delivery method is not particularly prescriptive, allowing wide variation
target_learners: Year 7 pupils reading below Level 4 at Key Stage 2
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Metacognitive strategy use
examples: Teacher or teaching assistant and pupils take turns to lead a discussion of a text adapted from children's literature
key_sources: Claire Crawford, Amy Skipp. (2014). LIT Programme Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581139

article_title: The Effect of a Disability Camp Program on Attitudes towards the Inclusion of Children with Disabilities in a Summer Sport and Leisure Activity Camp
citation: Papaioannou, C., Evaggelinou, C., & Block, M. (2014). The effect of a disability camp program on attitudes towards the inclusion of children with disabilities in a summer sport and leisure activity camp. International Journal of Special Education, 29(1), 121-127.
title: Recreational camp settings as effective environments for developing positive attitudes toward inclusion
description: The article proposes that summer sport and leisure activity camps, emphasizing less-competitive sports, social interaction, and fun rather than academics or winning, provide a unique experience where children can learn new skills, build friendships, and experience personal growth. In this setting, children get the chance to participate in activities and games with peers on a daily basis, which foster inclusion and develop close relationships. The authors hypothesize that the camp's emphasis on having fun daily and being part of a team rather than competition and winning explains why sport-specific attitudes improved here, contrasting with prior school physical education findings.
requirements: Programs must be structured to structure interaction, encourage extensive personal contact, promote joint participation, facilitate equal status, foster cooperating interdependence, focus on similarities, and develop effective communication
target_learners: children and young people in recreational and educational settings
target_learning_goals: positive attitudes toward individuals with disabilities
examples: The camp setting provides a unique experience emphasizing less-competitive sports, social interaction, and having fun, unlike the school setting which emphasizes academics
key_sources: Papaioannou, C., Evaggelinou, C., & Block, M. (2014). The effect of a disability camp program on attitudes towards the inclusion of children with disabilities in a summer sport and leisure activity camp. International Journal of Special Education, 29(1), 121-127. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1033944

article_title: The Guiding Effects of a Critical Reading Program on the Use of External Reading Strategies When Confronting an Ironical Text
citation: Aysegul Karabay. (2015). The guiding effects of a critical reading program on the use of external reading strategies when confronting an ironical text. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2015.2419
title: Review versus summary as markers of more versus less critical reading of a text
description: The article uses two response formats as diagnostic markers of reading stance: the review evaluates critical reading because it makes students connect with prior knowledge and contains evaluations, while the summary evaluates less critical reading because it involves deleting unimportant knowledge and forming a subject sentence not clearly written in the text. Summarizing was selected because it was "expected to limit critical reading". This pattern let the study classify each essay as a critique or summary with 95% coder agreement.
requirements: Essays coded as critiques if they include participants' opinions about the text-writer's argument and as summaries if they describe only the gist of the argument, coded by an independent coder
constraints: By its nature, summarizing is not appropriate for readers to undertake a critical stance in a summary, per the article
target_learners: Undergraduate pre-service teachers in Elementary Education
target_learning_goals: Distinguishing critical (review) from less critical (summary) engagement with a text
examples: Participants were left free to choose whether to summarize or review the text after reading it
key_sources: Aysegul Karabay. (2015). The guiding effects of a critical reading program on the use of external reading strategies when confronting an ironical text. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2015.2419

article_title: Fostering 21st-Century Evolutionary Reasoning: Teaching Tree Thinking to Introductory Biology Students
citation: Laura R. Novick and Kefyn M. Catley. (2016). Fostering 21st-Century Evolutionary Reasoning: Teaching Tree Thinking to Introductory Biology Students. CBE—Life Sciences Education 15:ar66. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.15-06-0127
title: Research-based phylogenetics laboratory for introductory biology
description: A new 3-hour phylogenetics laboratory developed for the study, consisting of a student laboratory manual, an instructors' guide with answer key, and various specimens. The manual was "an 11-page, six-part booklet" in which students working in small groups examined members of nine major animal groups, mapped character states onto three alternative cladogram topologies, evaluated the topologies using parsimony and resolution, distinguished homologies from homoplasies, and practiced phylogenetic inference. All students in the course completed it, including the business-as-usual condition, and the revised version remains the primary hands-on phylogenetics teaching tool at the authors' institution.
requirements: Specimens, a student manual, an instructors' guide with answer key, and a 3-hour lab period; lab instructors direct the activity
constraints: Lab instructors reported student difficulties with part I due to unfamiliarity with some character states, which slowed completion of the character matrix; the revised version fills in some difficult character states and provides pictures
target_learners: introductory biology students for science majors
target_learning_goals: building and evaluating cladograms from character data; distinguishing homology from homoplasy; phylogenetic inference
examples: Students mapped character states onto three alternative topologies for nine animal groups and evaluated them for parsimony and resolution
key_sources: Laura R. Novick and Kefyn M. Catley. (2016). Fostering 21st-Century Evolutionary Reasoning: Teaching Tree Thinking to Introductory Biology Students. CBE—Life Sciences Education 15:ar66. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.15-06-0127

article_title: The Evaluation of Students' Written Reflection on the Learning of General Chemistry Lab Experiment
citation: Ng Sook Han, Ho Ket Li, Lee Choy Sin, Keng Pei Sin. (2012). The Evaluation of Students' Written Reflection on the Learning of General Chemistry Lab Experiment. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Science, 2(4). http://www.moj-es.net
title: Seven-category rubric for coding students' reflective writing about experimental work
description: The article applies a coding rubric, adapted from Xu and Talanquer (2012), that classifies students' reflective statements into seven categories: "factual knowledge, conceptual knowledge, procedural knowledge, metacognitive knowledge, problem solving, critical thinking and applications". These are grouped into three major types — knowledge, critical thinking and applications — each with specific codes and example extracts from student writing (Table 2). The rubric was used both to evaluate what students achieved in experimental work and to characterize their reflective responses.
requirements: Two panels of experts validated the instrument contents before use
Written prompts adapted from Xu and Talanquer (2012) to elicit the targeted statement types
constraints: Applied to reflective writing about one general chemistry experiment (chloride determination by Volhard's method/titration) with first-semester undergraduates
target_learners: first-semester undergraduate pharmacy and health sciences students
target_learning_goals: knowledge understanding of experimental work
critical thinking
application of concepts learned in the laboratory
examples: Student example coded as procedural knowledge: "I learned the correct titration and weighing method."
key_sources: Ng Sook Han, Ho Ket Li, Lee Choy Sin, Keng Pei Sin. (2012). The Evaluation of Students' Written Reflection on the Learning of General Chemistry Lab Experiment. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Science, 2(4). http://www.moj-es.net

article_title: The Effects of a Grammar Error Correction Session on Language Learners' Success
citation: Fulda Karaazmak. (2018). The Effects of a Grammar Error Correction Session on Language Learners' Success. International Journal of Curriculum and Instruction 10(1), 61–70. http://ijci.wcci-international.org
title: Remedial grammar error correction session based on errors from a written pretest
description: A remedial lesson in which the teacher identifies the most problematic areas of students' knowledge of a grammar structure from errors made on a written grammar test, then delivers explicit oral corrective feedback. The article describes that "the teacher provided oral corrective grammar feedback to the learners and she did it explicitly together with trying to explain the possible reasons of their errors," without naming error owners. In the study it targeted the simple past tense with eleventh-grade EFL students.
requirements: A written grammar test administered beforehand to detect the problematic usages of the target structure
A teacher-led session addressing those detected problematic areas
constraints: The session corrected the most problematic areas without paying attention to the individual students having the errors
Additional practice materials were not prepared due to time limitations
target_learners: eleventh-grade high school EFL students aged 16-17
target_learning_goals: accurate use of the English simple past tense
examples: In the study, errors detected in the pretest concerned verb forms in the past tense, overgeneralization of the -ed ending, and wrong usages of was, were, did, and didn't.
key_sources: Fulda Karaazmak. (2018). The Effects of a Grammar Error Correction Session on Language Learners' Success. International Journal of Curriculum and Instruction 10(1), 61–70. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1207240

article_title: Effects of Reflective Inquiry Instructional Technique on Students' Academic Achievement and Ability Level in Electronic Work Trade in Technical Colleges
citation: Dr (Mrs) T. C. Ogbuanya & Dr A. S. Owodunni. (2015). Effects of Reflective Inquiry Instructional Technique on Students' Academic Achievement and Ability Level in Electronic Work Trade in Technical Colleges. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.7. https://www.iiste.org
title: Reflective inquiry as a constructivist, student-centred instructional technique
description: Reflective inquiry is defined in the article as "a thinking process through which individuals examine their experiences to better understand the assumptions and implications of events and actions". It combines inquiry activities (investigation, hypothesis formulation, data interpretation) with reflective thinking, which the article says prompts students to relate new knowledge to prior understanding and understand their own thinking. In the study it was operationalised through lesson plans using thinking skills, concept mapping, scaffolding graphic organizers, question prompt tactics and interactive journals.
requirements: Requires lesson plans built on reflective instructional strategies and teacher training; the study used a one-week intensive training programme for participating teachers
constraints: The article notes inquiry's complex nature may account for the lack of inquiry teaching in most Nigerian schools and colleges
target_learners: Technical college year-II Electronic Works trade students
target_learning_goals: Electronic Works trade achievement, including diagnosis and repair of radio, television and communication systems
Workplace thinking and problem-solving skills
examples: The experimental group was taught for ten weeks with ten 90-minute reflective inquiry lesson plans, while the control group received conventional lesson plans
key_sources: Dr (Mrs) T. C. Ogbuanya & Dr A. S. Owodunni. (2015). Effects of Reflective Inquiry Instructional Technique on Students' Academic Achievement and Ability Level in Electronic Work Trade in Technical Colleges. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.7. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1083083

article_title: Reflective Blogfolios in the Language Classroom: Impact on EFL Tertiary Students' Argumentative Writing Skills and Ways of Knowing
citation: Ammar, Abdullah Mahmoud Ismial. (2016). Reflective Blogfolios in the Language Classroom: Impact on EFL Tertiary Students' Argumentative Writing Skills and Ways of Knowing. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 7(5). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.5p.247
title: Reflective blogfolios: an online blog-based portfolio framework for a community of arguers in EFL writing classes
description: Reflective blogfolios combine blogging, portfolios, and reflective practice: Ananyeva's blogfolios are "interactive blog-based portfolios used to record students' lear ning progress" over time. In this study they served as "an online instructional framework for establi shing a community of arguers" where students exchange ideas, negotiate controversial topics, refute, and reflect on arguments across a semester. They change blogging from solitary writing into "a collaborative learning platform governed by principles of group authorship, monitoring and reflection, continuous development overtime, and mutual support."
requirements: Each student creates a blog account and shares it so classmates can follow one another and exchange ideas
An argumentative topic is suggested each week for individual writing and posting
Sustained cycles of peer reading, commenting, revision, and reflection across the whole semester
constraints: Field-tested with 51 EFL tertiary students in the Emirati ADU context, all already competent with the university's Blackboard LMS and owning internet-connected smart devices
target_learners: EFL tertiary students in a writing course
target_learning_goals: Argumentative essay writing skills
Ways of knowing (connected and separate)
Collaborative argumentation and negotiation of controversial topics
examples: Students wrote weekly argumentative posts, drafted essays on their blogs, commented on every classmate's draft, debated face-to-face, and compiled best pieces into printed blogfolios with reflective presentations and videotaped reflections by semester end
key_sources: Ammar, Abdullah Mahmoud Ismial. (2016). Reflective Blogfolios in the Language Classroom: Impact on EFL Tertiary Students' Argumentative Writing Skills and Ways of Knowing. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 7(5). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.5p.247

article_title: The Effects of Previewing Questions, Repetition of Input, and Topic Preparation on Listening Comprehension of Iranian EFL Learners
citation: Rouhi, A., Nabavi, S.-M., & Mohebbi, H. (2014). The effects of previewing questions, repetition of input, and topic preparation on listening comprehension of Iranian EFL learners. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research, 2(2), 73-85. https://www.urmia.ac.ir/ijltr
title: Repeat listening input more than once as a classroom support for comprehension
description: Allowing learners to hear a listening text more than once gives them extra processing time and a chance to revise answers. The study's repetition group (two hearings with previewing before each) scored M = 19.77, well above preview and control, and the article states this "pedagogical mediation which can be carried out with convenience in classroom setting is suggested to be practiced to bring about better listening."
requirements: A modified audio recording so texts play once per hearing, with two hearings and an interval between them
Time for learners to take notes, answer items, and change answers after the second hearing
constraints: In this study repetition's advantage over topic preparation was not statistically significant
The comparison covered two hearings only; the article calls for studies comparing once, twice, or more repetitions
target_learners: Iranian high school EFL learners aged 14-17 with 4-6 years of formal English instruction
target_learning_goals: L2 listening comprehension of monologue and dialogue texts
examples: The repetition group heard each text twice, taking notes and answering items after the first hearing and changing answers after the second, with five extra minutes to complete answers
key_sources: Rouhi, A., Nabavi, S.-M., & Mohebbi, H. (2014). The effects of previewing questions, repetition of input, and topic preparation on listening comprehension of Iranian EFL learners. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research, 2(2), 73-85. https://www.urmia.ac.ir/ijltr

article_title: The Transactional Influence of Parents and Children in a Parent-Administered School Readiness Program
citation: Mathis, E. T., & Bierman, K. L. (2014). The Transactional Influence of Parents and Children in a Parent-Administered School Readiness Program. 2014 SREE Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: REDI-Parent (REDI-P) enriched home visiting program
description: REDI-P extends the Head Start REDI classroom program by enriching home visiting services. Beyond usual-practice home visits it "included 10 additional sessions focused on increasing parent involvement in learning activities" such as interactive reading, conversations, and learning games, plus 6 booster sessions after the kindergarten transition. Parents received books, learning activities and games, were coached in dialogic reading and letter and letter-sound recognition games, and reviewed videotapes of their own interactions with their children to highlight supportive parenting strategies.
requirements: Parents must engage in interactive reading, conversations, and learning games with their children at home
Home visitors coach parents using provided books, learning activities, games, and videotape review
constraints: Changes in supportive parenting emerged primarily in parent-child reading and teaching activities and did not appear to generalize more broadly
target_learners: Head Start children transitioning to kindergarten and their parents
target_learning_goals: Child emergent literacy skills
Supportive parenting practices
Child self-regulation skills
examples: In the randomized trial, 210 Head Start families were assigned at the child level to REDI-P or to a control group receiving mail-home learning materials
key_sources: Mathis, E. T., & Bierman, K. L. (2014). The Transactional Influence of Parents and Children in a Parent-Administered School Readiness Program. 2014 SREE Conference Abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562845

article_title: Lesson Study with Mathematical Resources: A Sustainable Model for Locally-Led Teacher Professional Learning
citation: Catherine Lewis & Rebecca Perry. (2014). Lesson Study with Mathematical Resources: A Sustainable Model for Locally-led Teacher Professional Learning. Mathematics Teacher Education and Development. https://www.merga.net.au
title: Assemble resource kits providing mathematical and logistical support for each lesson study phase so local teams can conduct lesson study without outside facilitators
description: The article proposes that a well-designed resource kit can substitute for university-based facilitation, testing "a potentially sustainable form of lesson study that can be conducted without outside facilitators". Kits supply tasks, curriculum and research materials, lesson video and plans, and protocols aligned to each cycle phase, letting local teams manage their own work and connect materials to their local context. The trial found significant teacher knowledge gains under this locally-led model.
requirements: The kit must provide mathematical and logistical support for each phase of the lesson study cycle
constraints: Sites had no personal contact with the project investigators, so all support had to come from the kit and the lesson study process itself
target_learners: locally constituted teams of U.S. educators, most of them elementary teachers
target_learning_goals: teachers' fractions knowledge and fractions instruction in Grades 2-5
examples: Thirteen groups across the USA conducted lesson study guided only by mailed resources, with 87% of participants elementary teachers and 41% new to lesson study
key_sources: Catherine Lewis & Rebecca Perry. (2014). Lesson Study with Mathematical Resources: A Sustainable Model for Locally-led Teacher Professional Learning. Mathematics Teacher Education and Development. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1046670

article_title: Developing Written Text Production Competence Using the Reader-Response Method
citation: Paraschiva Demény. (2012). Developing Written Text Production Competence Using the Reader-Response Method. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 5, Number 3. https://add.econ.ubbcluj.ro
title: Reader-response / transactional reading theory: meaning is created in the transaction between reader and text
description: The article presents reader-response theory, identified with Rosenblatt's transactional reading, as holding that literature only exists when read and that interpretation is creative. Reader and text "intertwine during their interaction", and meaning is born within that transaction, shaped by the reader's prior knowledge, experiences and cultural background. The article grounds the method in hermeneutics (Gadamer, Ingarden), Iser's reception theory, Richards' relative meaning, and sociolinguistic and psycholinguistic accounts, and uses it as the interpretive basis for its process-reading intervention.
requirements: A literary text and an actively interpreting reader whose prior knowledge and experience shape the response
constraints: The article notes literary texts elude precise and unchangeable definition, and that unresolved issues may remain after reader-response processing, to be addressed by traditional analysis-synthesis methods
target_learners: third-grade pupils learning Hungarian language and literature
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension and interpretation
written text production competence
linguistic creativity
examples: The study's interventions were based on process reading of the reader-response method with adapted literary texts from a textbook and children's poems
key_sources: Paraschiva Demény. (2012). Developing Written Text Production Competence Using the Reader-Response Method. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 5, Number 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1054357

article_title: The Impact of Concept Mapping on EFL Learners' Critical Thinking Ability
citation: Khodadady, E., & Ghanizadeh, A. (2011). The Impact of Concept Mapping on EFL Learners' Critical Thinking Ability. English Language Teaching, 4(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v4n4p49
title: Integrate concept mapping regularly in EFL reading classes as a post-reading or brainstorming tool
description: The article's major implication for EFL instructors is "to integrate the concept map strategy in their classes on a regular basis as a brainstorming tool or post-reading strategy". Doing so, teachers can enhance critical thinking and monitor learners' reasoning weaknesses in order to scaffold appropriate learning and thinking activities. The recommendation rests on the study's significant posttest difference and on the argument that critical thinking skills are teachable through classroom techniques.
requirements: Teachers instruct learners to extract main ideas into boxes, connect them with labeled arrows, and organize post-reading activities such as discussion, exercises, and reflective practices based on the maps
constraints: Evidence comes from one small study (36 learners) whose gender and age representation the authors themselves flag as limited
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
evaluating validity of ideas and identifying reasoning fallacies
examples: In the study, the experimental group constructed a concept map of each passage at home and arranged post-reading activities based on those maps over a 20-session interval
key_sources: Khodadady, E., & Ghanizadeh, A. (2011). The Impact of Concept Mapping on EFL Learners' Critical Thinking Ability. English Language Teaching, 4(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v4n4p49

article_title: The Effects of Multimedia Learning on Thai Primary Pupils' Achievement in Size and Depth of Vocabulary Knowledge
citation: Mathukorn Jingjit. (2015). The Effects of Multimedia Learning on Thai Primary Pupils' Achievement in Size and Depth of Vocabulary Knowledge. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.32. https://www.iiste.org
title: Researcher-designed multimedia vocabulary program on CD with text, picture, and sound
description: A multimedia program developed by the researcher, delivered by computer and packed on a CD, presenting learning material in three modes: text, picture, and sound. It contained 52 word items drawn from two English books recommended by the Thai Ministry of Education in 2008, aligned with the Thai basic Curriculum for English and with pupils' identified vocabulary problems. Assessment instruments included a 32-item pretest, weekly picture (12-item) and no-picture (10-item) time-series tests, and a 32-item posttest.
requirements: Computer rooms, computer availability, and competent resources for implementation
constraints: Materials must align with the learning objectives set for the specific semester and grade
target_learning_goals: English vocabulary knowledge
examples: The program was used across 8 weeks with 2 daily learning periods per week and 24 vocabulary test series in total.
key_sources: Mathukorn Jingjit. (2015). The Effects of Multimedia Learning on Thai Primary Pupils' Achievement in Size and Depth of Vocabulary Knowledge. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.32. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1083500

article_title: The Effect of Incorporating the Extensive Reading Approach into Vocabulary Instruction on Learners' Lexical Depth in an EFL Context
citation: Mohsen Jafarpour. (2014). The Effect of Incorporating the Extensive Reading Approach into Vocabulary Instruction on Learners' Lexical Depth in an EFL Context. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.3p.162
title: Read's Word Association Test (WAT) for measuring lexical depth
description: Read's WAT (1993, 1998) is a 40-item multiple-choice instrument measuring lexical depth based on two relationships among words: meaning (pragmatic) and collocation (syntagmatic). Each item presents one stimulus word with a box of four adjectives that are synonyms and a box of four nouns that are collocations, with four correct answers per item. The study used it as the posttest, scored out of 160, administered in 30 minutes with no penalty for guessing.
requirements: Content at a level similar to students' level of study
Two versions with reordered items to avoid cheating
constraints: The test and study were in receptive mode; productive lexical depth was not measured
target_learning_goals: Assessment of receptive lexical depth (synonym and collocation knowledge)
examples: In the study, each student was given a mark out of 160, one score for each correct answer, with a 30-minute time limit.
key_sources: Mohsen Jafarpour. (2014). The Effect of Incorporating the Extensive Reading Approach into Vocabulary Instruction on Learners' Lexical Depth in an EFL Context. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.3p.162

article_title: On Reading Comprehension Teaching for English Majors under Relevance Theory
citation: Ping He. (2018). On Reading Comprehension Teaching for English Majors under Relevance Theory. English Language Teaching, 11(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n1p46
title: Relevance Theory: communication as an ostensive-inferential process governed by optimal relevance
description: Relevance Theory, proposed by Sperber and Wilson in 1986, holds that communication is "a process of ostension-inference rather than one of encoding and decoding". Ostension makes manifest an intention to make something manifest; inference accepts an assumption as true on the strength of other assumptions. The article applies this to reading: the writer creates contextual effects (ostensive titles, topic sentences, relevant contextual or cultural information) and the reader decodes and infers relevant information using prior linguistic knowledge, logic, and cognitive context, seeking the optimal relevance between textual information and the reader's cognition.
requirements: The reader must bring previous linguistic knowledge, logic, and a cognitive context to the text for inference to operate
constraints: Readers with a different culture from the original text face a tougher information process because cognitive and cultural contexts are less shared with the text producer
target_learning_goals: English reading comprehension
inferential capability
examples: The article treats a reading discourse as a fixed system of encoded verbal symbols whose writer still shapes ostensive stimuli such as titles and topic sentences
key_sources: Ping He. (2018). On Reading Comprehension Teaching for English Majors under Relevance Theory. English Language Teaching, 11(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n1p46

article_title: The Effectiveness of Cooperative Learning Activities in Enhancing EFL Learners' Fluency
citation: Hassan Alrayah. (2018). The Effectiveness of Cooperative Learning Activities in Enhancing EFL Learners' Fluency. English Language Teaching, 11(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n4p21
title: Recorded fluency interviews scored on five fluency items
description: The study's measurement instrument is recorded interviews produced as oral answers to pre- and post-tests, with "The recorded data consists of (96) interviews" from 48 first-year students, analyzed with SPSS. Fluency is checked through five specific items: "a. The use of a variety of vocabulary and expressions", variety of grammatical structures, smooth speaking, effective communication, and accurate pronunciation and clear intonation. The same items structure the pre-test and post-test comparison tables.
requirements: Pre- and post-test recorded interviews for each student so fluency items can be compared across the intervention.
constraints: The article does not report reliability or scoring procedures for the interview ratings beyond the percentage and mean-score tables.
target_learning_goals: Assessment of oral fluency of speaking
examples: Table 1 shows both groups started low on the production items: smooth speaking 7.9% (control) and 10.0% (experimental), effective communication 6.5% and 8.0%.
key_sources: Hassan Alrayah. (2018). The Effectiveness of Cooperative Learning Activities in Enhancing EFL Learners' Fluency. English Language Teaching, 11(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n4p21

article_title: Multilevel Mixture Structural Equation Modeling with Propensity Score Weights for Quasi-Experimental Evaluation of Virtual Learning Environments
citation: Walter L. Leite, Zeyuan Jing, Huan Kuang, Dongho Kim & A. Corinne Huggins-Manley (2021). Multilevel Mixture Modeling with Propensity Score Weights for Quasi-Experimental Evaluation of Virtual Learning Environments. Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal, 28:6, 964-982. https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2021.1919895
title: Require students to engage in active practice, such as responding to quiz questions, when implementing a VLE
description: The article's classroom-level results indicate that teacher practices requiring student active practice matter for VLE effectiveness. Classrooms where teachers only showed videos without requiring students to answer questions did as well as low-engagement classrooms, while classrooms with high student and teacher engagement obtained higher mean scores. The article states: "These results indicate the importance of teachers requiring students to engage in active practice through responding to quiz questions in the VLE."
requirements: Teachers must require students to respond to quiz questions in the VLE rather than only presenting videos
constraints: The finding comes from quasi-experimental contrasts of self-selected latent classes, not random assignment
target_learning_goals: Algebra I end-of-course achievement
examples: In D2 classrooms teachers showed videos to the whole class but did not require students to answer questions as homework, lecture warm-up, or formative assessment, and these classrooms did as well as low-engagement classrooms
key_sources: Walter L. Leite, Zeyuan Jing, Huan Kuang, Dongho Kim & A. Corinne Huggins-Manley (2021). Multilevel Mixture Modeling with Propensity Score Weights for Quasi-Experimental Evaluation of Virtual Learning Environments. Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal, 28:6, 964-982. https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2021.1919895

article_title: Agents of Change in Promoting Reflective Abstraction: A Quasi-Experimental, Study on Limits in College Calculus
citation: Cappetta, R.W., and Zollman, A. (2013). Agents of Change in Promoting Reflective Abstraction: A Quasi-Experimental Study on Limits in College Calculus. REDIMAT – Journal of Research in Mathematics Education, 2(3), 343-357. https://doi.org/10.4471/redimat.2013.35
title: Reflective abstraction constructs and agents of change framework
description: The article's framework combines Piaget's reflective abstraction constructs — interiorization, coordination, encapsulation, and generalization — with Dubinsky's added construct of reversal, and pairs them with four agents of change that can initiate reflective abstraction: individual, peer, instructor, and curricular. The article defines each agent, e.g., "Peer: A classmate challenges or questions an individual." It uses this framework to design the experimental calculus curriculum on limits and to code student protocols.
requirements: Curriculum activities, peer group work, instructor debriefing, and individual exercises must each be present so each agent can challenge or question students
constraints: The framework was applied to the concept of limit in first-semester college calculus at a community college
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of the limit concept
examples: The experimental curriculum used the ACE (Activity, Classroom Discussion, Exercise) teaching cycle, with cooperative group activities, instructor-led classroom discussion, and individual exercise sets
key_sources: Cappetta, R.W., and Zollman, A. (2013). Agents of Change in Promoting Reflective Abstraction: A Quasi-Experimental Study on Limits in College Calculus. REDIMAT – Journal of Research in Mathematics Education, 2(3), 343-357. https://doi.org/10.4471/redimat.2013.35

article_title: Pedagogical Experience on Formation of Tolerant and Multicultural Consciousness of Students
citation: Evgeny A. Naumenko, Olga N. Naumenko. (2016). Pedagogical Experience on Formation of Tolerant and Multicultural Consciousness of Students. European Journal of Contemporary Education. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2016.17.335
title: Course «Religions of the region under study»
description: A compulsory specialized discipline introduced for Regional studies students, whose duration was 292 hours, 144 of which were class hours, assessed by final test and exam. Its content integrated the history, culture and religion of the region with direct study of primary religious sources — the Quran, the Torah and the Bible in various interpretations of theologians — and mandatory visits to places of religious purpose and museum collections. Students made multimedia presentations on ethno-confessional topics as a foundation for discussions.
requirements: Obligatory status enforced via the bond «fail the test – fail the exam – expulsion»
Teacher emphasis on common historical roots of religions and on reasons for discrepancies in primary sources
constraints: From a legal point of view the compulsory approach meant a restriction of religious students' rights and their academic and religious freedom, compensated by non-interference in cult and ritual actions
target_learning_goals: Knowledge of history, culture and religion of the region
Confessional tolerance
Critical understanding of religious primary sources
examples: Students visited a mosque, an Orthodox church, a Catholic church, a synagogue, and studied museum collections with exhibits of religious cultures
key_sources: Evgeny A. Naumenko, Olga N. Naumenko. (2016). Pedagogical Experience on Formation of Tolerant and Multicultural Consciousness of Students. European Journal of Contemporary Education. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2016.17.335

article_title: The Effects of Hypertext Gloss on Comprehension and Vocabulary Retention under Incidental and Intentional Learning Conditions
citation: Zandieh, Z., & Jafarigohar, M. (2012). The Effects of Hypertext Gloss on Comprehension and Vocabulary Retention under Incidental and Intentional Learning Conditions. English Language Teaching, 5(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n6p60
title: Reading Toolbox software hypertext gloss task with 38 hyperlinked vocabulary items
description: The study's materials were delivered through the Reading Toolbox software (2003), comprising a demographics questionnaire, an electronically enhanced reading text containing 38 new vocabulary items, an immediate reading comprehension test, and a 38-item multiple-choice vocabulary posttest. Target items were "hyperlinked to the same textual enhancements," with permanently highlighted vocabulary in the intentional condition and temporarily highlighted vocabulary in the incidental condition.
requirements: Computer laboratory facilities for delivery
target_learning_goals: vocabulary retention
reading comprehension of academic text
examples: The reading passage was taken from a standardized TOEFL iBT test
key_sources: Zandieh, Z., & Jafarigohar, M. (2012). The Effects of Hypertext Gloss on Comprehension and Vocabulary Retention under Incidental and Intentional Learning Conditions. English Language Teaching, 5(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n6p60

article_title: Reading, Writing, Math, and Content-Area Interventions for Improving Behavioral and Academic Outcomes of Students with Emotional and Behavioral Disorders
citation: Campbell, A. R., Bowman-Perrott, L., Burke, M. D., & Sallese, M. R. (2018). Reading, Writing, Math, and Content-Area Interventions for Improving Behavioral and Academic Outcomes of Students With Emotional and Behavioral Disorders. Learning Disabilities: A Contemporary Journal, 16(2), 119-138. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1191107
title: Report participant demographics, fidelity, social validity, and intervention duration to enable moderator analyses and practice guidance
description: The article recommends that intervention research with students with or at-risk of EBD consistently report participant demographics, fidelity of implementation, social validity, and intervention duration. It argues these data are needed "to help identify for whom and under what conditions interventions are most effective" and to ensure practices are acceptable and consistently used. Few studies across the included reviews reported these variables.
requirements: Studies must report participant demographics such as age/grade level, fidelity of implementation, and social validity
target_learners: Students with or at-risk of emotional and behavioral disorders in grades K-12
target_learning_goals: Academic outcomes in reading, writing, math, and content areas
examples: The review found few studies reported demographics, fidelity, or social validity, and none of the five meta-analyses reported follow-up, generalization, or maintenance data.
key_sources: Campbell, A. R., Bowman-Perrott, L., Burke, M. D., & Sallese, M. R. (2018). Reading, Writing, Math, and Content-Area Interventions for Improving Behavioral and Academic Outcomes of Students With Emotional and Behavioral Disorders. Learning Disabilities: A Contemporary Journal, 16(2), 119-138. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1194543

article_title: Reading, Writing, Math, and Content-Area Interventions for Improving Behavioral and Academic Outcomes of Students with Emotional and Behavioral Disorders
citation: Campbell, A. R., Bowman-Perrott, L., Burke, M. D., & Sallese, M. R. (2018). Reading, Writing, Math, and Content-Area Interventions for Improving Behavioral and Academic Outcomes of Students With Emotional and Behavioral Disorders. Learning Disabilities: A Contemporary Journal, 16(2), 119-138. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1191107
title: Reciprocal connection between social-emotional/behavioral problems and academic achievement
description: The article presents a reciprocal connection between emotional, social, and behavioral problems and academic achievement: deficits in either domain exacerbate the odds of affecting the other. It cites mounting evidence that "deficits in either the social-emotional or academic domain exacerbate the odds of affecting the other," while noting the causal direction remains unclear. This framework motivates intervening academically to improve behavioral outcomes and vice versa.
constraints: Whether an academic and learning problem directly causes social-emotional and behavioral issues or vice versa is not clear
target_learners: Students with or at-risk of EBD in grades K-12
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement
Behavioral and social-emotional outcomes

Reading, Writing, Math, and Content-Area Interventions for Improving Behavioral and Academic Outcomes of Students With Emotional and Behavioral Disorders.
