article_title: Metacognitive Awareness and the Fluency of Task-Based Oral Output across Planning Conditions: The Case of Iranian TEFL Students
citation: Seifoori, Z. (2016). Metacognitive awareness and the fluency of task-based oral output across planning conditions: The case of Iranian TEFL students. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research, 4(1), 11-26. https://www.urmia.ac.ir/ijltr
title: Repair fluency measure: ratio of repair features to c-units
description: Following Foster and Skehan (1999), fluency was quantified as "the ratio of the sum of repair fluency measures, reformulations, false starts, repetitions, and replacements, to the number of c-units produced by each participant". Two independent experienced raters scored transcribed speech, with inter-rater reliability computed via coefficient alpha at .87 for the pre-test and .93 for the post-test. Lower ratios indicate more fluent speech.
requirements: Transcribed oral data and two independent raters with acceptably high inter-rater reliability
constraints: The study measured only repair fluency, not breakdown fluency, due to the executive difficulty of measuring 114 participants' oral performance
target_learning_goals: measuring oral fluency of task-based speech
examples: Pre-test and post-test picture-strip narratives of at least four sentences per picture were transcribed and scored with this ratio
key_sources: Seifoori, Z. (2016). Metacognitive awareness and the fluency of task-based oral output across planning conditions: The case of Iranian TEFL students. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research, 4(1), 11-26. https://www.urmia.ac.ir/ijltr

article_title: Teaching Interactive Art Lessons with Recycled Waste Materials as Instructional Resources
citation: Rita Yeboah, Eric Appau Asante, Nana Afia Opoku-Asare. (2016). Teaching Interactive Art Lessons with Recycled Waste Materials as Instructional Resources. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.14. https://www.iiste.org
title: Recycled waste-material instructional resources for Art topics
description: The researchers designed and developed instructional resources from paper, plastic and fabric waste for teaching Colour, Perspective, Figure Drawing, Elements and Principles of Design, and Weaving at Primary, Junior and Senior High levels, including a "12-point colour wheel" and perspective and weaving models. The resources were tested by 14 Art teachers in five Kumasi schools, and the article concludes that "waste materials can be recycled to create appropriate instructio nal resources for effective teaching and learning of Art". Teachers who had not been contacted also requested to use them.
requirements: Teachers need the ability to recycle waste materials into the appropriate resources; the article states arousal of interest through resources "is limited only by the ability of teachers to le arn to recycle waste materials".
target_learners: Primary, Junior High and Senior High School Art pupils and students in Ghana
target_learning_goals: Colour and colour mixing
one-, two- and three-point perspective
figure drawing
elements and principles of design
plain and twill weaving
examples: Resources on Colour, Perspective, Figure Drawing, Elements and Principles of Design and Weaving were used to teach lessons at Emena Primary, KNUST Bomso/Emena/Kentinkrono JHS and KNUST SHS
key_sources: Rita Yeboah, Eric Appau Asante, Nana Afia Opoku-Asare. (2016). Teaching Interactive Art Lessons with Recycled Waste Materials as Instructional Resources. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.14. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1102965

article_title: React (Relating, Experiencing, Applying, Cooperative, Transferring) Strategy to Develop Geography Skills
citation: Wiwik Sri Utami, Sumarmi, I Nyoman Ruja, Sugeng Utaya. (2016). React (Relating, Experiencing, Applying, Cooperative, Transferring) Strategy to Develop Geography Skills. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.17. https://www.iiste.org
title: REACT strategy: a contextual learning strategy with five components (Relating, Experiencing, Applying, Cooperating, Transferring)
description: REACT is a contextual learning strategy grounded in constructivism, described via CORD (1999) as five components: Relating places learning "in the context of life experiences"; Experiencing is learning "in the context of exploration, discovery, and invention"; Applying uses concepts "in a useful context" such as occupational activities; Cooperating is learning through "sharing, responding, and communicating with other learners"; and Transferring builds on "what the student already knows". The article implements all five in grade XI geography lessons.
requirements: Teachers must call students' attention to everyday situations and relate them to new information, and organize hands-on activities, group work and communication tasks as outlined in teaching materials
constraints: The article presents REACT within contextual, constructivist learning for competency-based curricula; component descriptions are definitional (CORD, 1999) rather than experimentally isolated
target_learning_goals: geography skills
mastery of competencies through meaningful, contextual learning experiences
examples: In this study REACT was implemented on the material 'distribution of minerals in Indonesia', with map-making assignments, analysis of natural resource data, and paper writing
key_sources: Wiwik Sri Utami, Sumarmi, I Nyoman Ruja, Sugeng Utaya. (2016). React (Relating, Experiencing, Applying, Cooperative, Transferring) Strategy to Develop Geography Skills. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.17. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105313

article_title: English Presentation Skills of Thai Graduate Students
citation: Sukitkanaporn, T., & Phoocharoensil, S. (2014). English Presentation Skills of Thai Graduate Students. English Language Teaching, 7(3). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n3p91
title: Effective Presentations courses should be required for graduate students in English for Careers programs
description: The article argues that a dedicated presentation skills course produces measurable improvements in organization/content, delivery, poise, and visuals, and that "Effective Presentations (CR 752) should be a required course for all graduates studying in the Master Program in English for Careers." The authors view presentation skills as professional competence required by employers.
requirements: A dedicated course focusing on clear, well-designed, professional business presentations in English
constraints: Findings are based on a cross-sectional survey of 26 conference attendees at a single Thai university
target_learners: Graduate students in English for Careers programs
target_learning_goals: English presentation skills
Professional communication competence
examples: The article compared 10 CR 752 students and 28 non-CR 752 students rated on their research paper presentations at a graduate conference.
key_sources: Sukitkanaporn, T., & Phoocharoensil, S. (2014). English Presentation Skills of Thai Graduate Students. English Language Teaching, 7(3). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n3p91

article_title: A Mindful Approach to Teaching Emotional Intelligence to Undergraduate Students Online and in Person
citation: Cotler, J. L., DiTursi, D., Goldstein, I., Yates, J., & DelBelso, D. (2017). A Mindful Approach to Teaching Emotional Intelligence to Undergraduate Students Online and in Person. Information Systems Education Journal, 15(1). http://isedj.org
title: RESET Cycle Model for teaching emotional intelligence online
description: The RESET Cycle Model (Recognizing or regulating Emotions through Social and Emotional Team-based learning supported with mindfulness) is the article's proposed framework for teaching EI online. It begins with face-to-face introduction to team-based learning, mindfulness, and a Myers-Briggs workshop to build a foundation of knowledge. The cycle then alternates between online collaborative content workshops and online collaborative EI workshops, with new mindfulness instruction introduced face-to-face between each workshop. The article offers it as a potential foundation for a program to teach EI skills in higher education and organizational settings.
requirements: Face-to-face introduction to team-based learning and mindfulness at the start
A Myers-Briggs workshop presented face-to-face to set the stage for awareness of self and others
Strong and active instructor presence to create community, collaboration and trust
constraints: Findings may not be generalizable to non-team-based learning settings
Mindfulness practices were only taught by one instructor, so this factor cannot be separated from the instructor
target_learners: undergraduate students in information systems and business programs
target_learning_goals: emotional intelligence skills including self-awareness, empathy, and emotional regulation
examples: The study used a 3x2 factorial quasi-experimental design with 159 students across six course sections, all using team-based learning format
key_sources: Cotler, J. L., DiTursi, D., Goldstein, I., Yates, J., & DelBelso, D. (2017). A Mindful Approach to Teaching Emotional Intelligence to Undergraduate Students Online and in Person. Information Systems Education Journal, 15(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1135358

article_title: Effects of Reflective Thinking in the Process of Designing Software on Students' Learning Performances
citation: Hsieh, P.-H., & Chen, N.-S. (2012). Effects of reflective thinking in the process of designing software on students' learning performances. Computers & Education, 58(1), 419-431. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.021
title: Reflective thinking via weekly weblogs can aid lower achieving students to reach learning performance comparable with higher achieving students in a software design course.
description: The study asks lower achievers to write weekly reflection diaries on weblogs, with freedom to add representative images and pictures to supplement their reflections, during the whole process of software design. This reflective thinking process has the potential to improve performance and unique personal creativity of low achieving students.
requirements: Time for reflective thinking is available during the process of software design
constraints: Even the experimental group's students who adopted learning through reflective thinking demonstrated a lower degree of self-confidence for using packaged software
target_learning_goals: animation software design
design analysis
examples: Seven lower quiz scorers wrote weekly reflection diaries of their weblog activities during the design processes, knowing the activity entailed no extra-credit points
key_sources: Hsieh, P.-H., & Chen, N.-S. (2012). Effects of reflective thinking in the process of designing software on students' learning performances. Computers & Education, 58(1), 419-431. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.021

article_title: Idea Sharing: The Use of Read-Share-Act to Promote Extensive Reading
citation: Charumanee, N. (2014). IDEA SHARING: THE USE OF READ-SHARE-ACT TO PROMOTE EXTENSIVE READING. PASAA, 47. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1079544
title: Read-Share-Act: a three-stage extensive reading pattern of self-selected reading, rotating group sharing, and story performance
description: RSA is a classroom technique integrating extensive reading into an existing reading course through three stages: R (reading a self-selected graded reader outside class), S (sharing the story in three rounds of progressively larger groups with note-taking and journals), and A (acting the nominated story as a play). The article describes it as "a means to perform extensive reading activities". In the study it ran over 15 hours of a 15-week semester with 24 Grade-10 EFL students.
requirements: Students each select a book from a list of graded readers suited to EFL students
Time allocated within normal reading instruction for sharing rounds and play preparation
constraints: Time constraints arose because RSA shared hours with teacher-directed intensive reading; a stand-alone extensive reading course is suggested
Students lacked storytelling skills initially, reading notes aloud instead of telling stories
target_learning_goals: English reading habit
listening, speaking and writing skills
confidence expressing ideas in English
examples: 24 students in 6 groups of 4 shared 10-12 pages weekly for 6 weeks, then re-formed groups to share whole stories, merged into 3 groups of 8, and performed Secret Garden, The Wizard of OZ, and Rapunzel as plays
key_sources: Charumanee, N. (2014). IDEA SHARING: THE USE OF READ-SHARE-ACT TO PROMOTE EXTENSIVE READING. PASAA, 47. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1077997

article_title: Identifying College Students' Multiple Intelligences to Enhance Motivation and Language Proficiency
citation: Magda Madkour & Rafik Ahmed Abdel Moati Mohamed. (2016). Identifying College Students’ Multiple Intelligences to Enhance Motivation and Language Proficiency. English Language Teaching, 9(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n6p92
title: Replace memorization-based grammar drilling with multiple intelligences-based activities to improve language proficiency
description: The article's central design principle is that "ineffective teaching strategies that depended on encouraging learners memorizing language rules hindered students from boosting their language proficiency." Instead, teachers should help students identify their multiple intelligences profiles and use those profiles to design differentiated activities that integrate multiple ability domains. The principle rests on the study's finding that the multiple intelligences group scored 89% versus 44% for the traditional group and that motivation rose from 28% to 91%.
requirements: Teachers must identify students' multiple intelligences profiles before designing activities
constraints: Evidence comes from a single quasi-experimental study at one university with no reported effect sizes
target_learners: College EFL students at higher education
target_learning_goals: English language proficiency and motivation for language learning
examples: The study compared a traditional classroom relying on memorizing grammatical rules with a group studying English after identifying their multiple intelligences profiles
key_sources: Magda Madkour & Rafik Ahmed Abdel Moati Mohamed. (2016). Identifying College Students’ Multiple Intelligences to Enhance Motivation and Language Proficiency. English Language Teaching, 9(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n6p92

article_title: The Effect of Fire Context on the Conceptual Understanding of Students: "Expansion-Contraction"
citation: Sibel Er Nas, Tülay Şenel Çoruhlu and Arzu Kirman Bilgin. (2016). The effect of fire context on the conceptual understanding of students: “expansion-contraction”. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2016.2958
title: Use everyday contexts (like fire) to teach abstract science concepts via the REACT model
description: The article recommends designing instruction around familiar real-world contexts to help students relate scientific concepts to daily life. It states that "contextual learning facilitates the students' relating of their daily life experiences with scientific concepts", supporting the use of contexts like fire alarm systems to teach expansion-contraction.
requirements: Teachers should be provided with information and materials before the intervention, as done in this study.
constraints: The fire context was effective for Turkish 5th graders; generalisation to other topics or age groups is not established.
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of expansion and contraction
examples: The experiment group used fire alarm systems as a context across five 40-minute lessons following the REACT steps of relating, experiencing, applying, cooperating and transferring.
key_sources: Sibel Er Nas, Tülay Şenel Çoruhlu and Arzu Kirman Bilgin. (2016). The effect of fire context on the conceptual understanding of students: “expansion-contraction”. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2016.2958

article_title: An Investigation of Teaching Strategy in the Distance Learning Mathematics Classroom
citation: DePriter, T. (2012). An Investigation of Teaching Strategy in the Distance Learning Mathematics Classroom. Journal of Educators Online, 9(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ975633
title: Researcher-made pretest and posttest instruments for Beginning Algebra
description: Two researcher-made assessments measured mathematics content knowledge before and after the teaching intervention. The pretest consisted of 25 multiple-choice questions; the posttest consisted of 25 multiple-choice questions plus 3 brief constructed response/extended constructed response (BCR/ECR) questions. Both contained "an even distribution of low, medium, and high difficulty problems." Cronbach's alpha was computed as .779 for both the pretest and posttest multiple-choice items, and a content expert assessed content-related evidence of validity.
requirements: Content-expert review to establish content-related evidence of validity
constraints: Reliability of .779 fell below the .80 threshold the article states is considered reliable for research use, though above the .70 level it cites as acceptable for educational research
target_learners: adult distance learners in developmental mathematics
target_learning_goals: measuring mathematics content knowledge
examples: BCR/ECR questions were reserved for the posttest because students were unlikely to have the content knowledge to answer them at the beginning of the semester
key_sources: DePriter, T. (2012). An Investigation of Teaching Strategy in the Distance Learning Mathematics Classroom. Journal of Educators Online, 9(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1020037

article_title: Today's Program Is Brought to You by the Letters--Debit and Credit and by the Number Income
citation: Bush, H. F., & Walsh, V. K. (2011). Today‟s Program Is Brought To You By The Letters – Debit And Credit And By The Number Income. American Journal of Business Education, 4(5). https://clutejournals.com/index.php/AJBE
title: Replace daily homework with frequent low-stakes daily assessments to improve performance
description: The article recommends replacing traditional daily homework assignments with daily assessments, approximately 75 percent open-book, as a structure that provides a "constant task and feedback cycle" aligned with millennial learning preferences. The authors report that this change improved course grades, satisfactory completion rates, and final exam performance on most topics.
requirements: Assessments must be developed to follow along with previously developed lectures
The course structure must otherwise remain constant to isolate the effect of the assessment change
constraints: The study was conducted at a small liberal arts school with 50 to 60 majors per year, one professor, and three sections of approximately 25 students; not every institution has these parameters
Withdrawal rates increased, possibly due to earlier feedback about performance
target_learners: undergraduate business students in principles of financial accounting
target_learning_goals: financial accounting knowledge and retention
examples: Students completed daily assessments, approximately 25 percent closed book and 75 percent open book, in lieu of daily homework in principles of financial accounting
key_sources: Bush, H. F., & Walsh, V. K. (2011). Today‟s Program Is Brought To You By The Letters – Debit And Credit And By The Number Income. American Journal of Business Education, 4(5). https://clutejournals.com/index.php/AJBE

article_title: Improve Knowledge, Beliefs and Behavior of Undergraduate Female Nursing Students in Al-Alzhar University toward Breast Self-Examination Practice
citation: Abd El-Mohsen, A. S., & Abd El-Maksoud, M. M. (2015). Improve Knowledge, Beliefs and Behavior of Undergraduate Female Nursing Students in Al-Alzhar University toward Breast Self-Examination Practice. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.8. https://www.iiste.org
title: Regular interventions are needed to build nursing students' confidence and skills in teaching preventive health behaviors
description: The article recommends ongoing rather than one-off training, stating: "the provision of regular interventions is necessary to increase a nd build up the confidence and skills of nursing st udents in teaching preventive health behaviors including BSE to society and other students as colleagues." This positions nursing students as future health educators who need sustained skill development to teach preventive behaviors to communities and peers.
requirements: Recurring intervention sessions beyond a single training program
target_learning_goals: teaching preventive health behaviors
health education skills
examples: The article recommends further research using a larger sample size with students in other faculties and universities
key_sources: Abd El-Mohsen, A. S., & Abd El-Maksoud, M. M. (2015). Improve Knowledge, Beliefs and Behavior of Undergraduate Female Nursing Students in Al-Alzhar University toward Breast Self-Examination Practice. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.8. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1082729

article_title: CLIL in Galicia: Repercussions on Academic Performance
citation: González Gándara, D. (2015). CLIL in Galicia: Repercussions on academic performance. Latin American Journal of Content and Language Integrated Learning, 8(1), 13-24.
title: Reinforce CLIL programs since no negative effect on native-language academic performance has been demonstrated
description: The article argues that because its longitudinal study found no significant negative effect of CLIL on Galician- or Spanish-language marks, and other studies suggest positive effects on additional-language competence, "it can only be concluded that it is advisable to keep on supporting the development of bilingual programs—and, indeed, CLIL—whenever and wherever possible." The principle addresses fears that three coexisting languages overload primary students.
requirements: Explicit consent of teachers, the Consello escolar, and each affected student family
constraints: The Galician bilingual context's particularities could mitigate the value of the conclusions in application to any other population
target_learners: primary education students in bilingual regions
target_learning_goals: native-language academic performance
additional language competence
examples: The study analysed marks of 747 students from 13 primary schools over two consecutive school years
key_sources: González Gándara, D. (2015). CLIL in Galicia: Repercussions on academic performance. Latin American Journal of Content and Language Integrated Learning, 8(1), 13-24. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1132120

article_title: Red Flags, Red Herrings, and Common Ground: An Expert Study in Response to State Reading Policy
citation: Collet, Vicki S.; Penaflorida, Jennifer; French, Seth; Allred, Jonathan; Greiner, Angelia; and Chen, Jingshu (2021) "Red Flags, Red Herrings, and Common Ground: An Expert Study in Response to State Reading Policy," Educational Considerations: Vol. 47: No. 1. https://doi.org/10.4148/0146-9282.2241
title: Reading policy should be informed by a broad body of research rather than a single meta-analysis or standardized methodology
description: This principle holds that policies governing early reading instruction should draw on the full range of research on early literacy rather than leaning heavily on a single report or imposing a uniform methodology. The article argues that "Consideration of a broad body of reading research suggests that policies that impose a standardized methodology upon teachers and children may be a recipe for failure," citing evidence that the Reading First initiative did not produce a statistically significant impact on reading comprehension despite increasing instructional time on emphasized components. The principle calls for instruction that is responsive to student needs, since no single best method for teaching children to read has been identified.
requirements: Policy development processes that incorporate research from varied perspectives and methodologies, including topics absent from influential meta-analyses such as writing connections, background knowledge, motivation, and classroom organization
constraints: The article notes that some states did experience success with Reading First initiatives, indicating that standardized approaches are not uniformly ineffective
target_learners: policymakers, legislators, and educators designing early reading instruction
target_learning_goals: reducing reading difficulties through responsive instruction
aligning reading policy with the full body of early literacy research
examples: The government's own final report found that although instructional time spent on the components emphasized by the Reading First initiative did increase, it did not produce a statistically significant impact on student reading comprehension test scores
key_sources: Collet, Vicki S.; Penaflorida, Jennifer; French, Seth; Allred, Jonathan; Greiner, Angelia; and Chen, Jingshu (2021) "Red Flags, Red Herrings, and Common Ground: An Expert Study in Response to State Reading Policy," Educational Considerations: Vol. 47: No. 1. https://doi.org/10.4148/0146-9282.2241

article_title: Effects of School Counselors' Cognitive Behavioral Consultation on Irrational and Efficacy Beliefs of Elementary School Teachers
citation: Jeffrey M. Warren, Edwin R. Gerler, Jr. (2013). Effects of School Counselors' Cognitive Behavioral Consultation on Irrational and Efficacy Beliefs of Elementary School Teachers. The Professional Counselor, 3(1), 6-15. https://doi.org/10.15241/jmw.3.1.6
title: Rational emotive-social behavior consultation (RE-SBC) integrates REBT and social cognitive theory to address teachers' irrational and efficacy beliefs
description: RE-SBC is a consultation model that combines rational emotive behavior therapy (REBT) principles with social cognitive theory (SCT) to help school counselors work with teachers. In REBC, school counselors help identify and challenge "irrational beliefs that impede teachers' classroom performance." The model targets irrational beliefs (e.g., self-downing, low frustration tolerance, demandingness) and efficacy beliefs through cognitive, emotive, and behavioral strategies. The article describes its application via face-to-face and asynchronous online group formats across eight weeks.
requirements: School counselors providing consultation must possess adequate knowledge of school and classroom settings and how these environments interact with the social-emotional wellness of teachers and students
constraints: Teachers may be skeptical, experience cognitive dissonance, or simply reject the content of the trainings altogether given that some REBT tenets appear to debunk the typical mindset of teachers
target_learning_goals: reduce irrational beliefs
increase efficacy beliefs
promote positive mental health
examples: Face-to-face groups met weekly for seventy-minute sessions across eight weeks; online groups completed five asynchronous discussion modules across the same period
key_sources: Jeffrey M. Warren, Edwin R. Gerler, Jr. (2013). Effects of School Counselors' Cognitive Behavioral Consultation on Irrational and Efficacy Beliefs of Elementary School Teachers. The Professional Counselor, 3(1), 6-15. https://doi.org/10.15241/jmw.3.1.6

article_title: The Effect of Peer-Assisted Mediation vs. Tutor-Intervention within Dynamic Assessment Framework on Writing Development of Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners
citation: Erfani, S. S., & Nikbin, S. (2015). The Effect of Peer-Assisted Mediation vs. Tutor-Intervention within Dynamic Assessment Framework on Writing Development of Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 8(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n4p128
title: RECIPROCITY rating scale for assessing writing within dynamic assessment.
description: The RECIPROCITY rating scale, devised by Van der Aalsvoort and Lidz (2002), was used to assess writing assignments at each session. It "focuses on bidirectional interaction between mediator and learner" and "signifies the role of documentation which will be revealed by comments and written feedback." Ten scores were assigned for taught points repeated across sessions, since the scale focuses on removing errors during a course of study.
requirements: Requires documentation through comments and written feedback; scores taught points repeatedly across sessions to track error removal.
constraints: The article notes the scale is to some extent qualitative, so it was quantified by assigning ten scores for the posttest.
target_learning_goals: L2 writing development
examples: The rating scale was presented to all participants as a checklist to assess the paragraphs, with ratings based on 1-10.

article_title: The Effectiveness of Training Program Based on the Six Hats Model in Developing Creative Thinking Skills and Academic Achievements in the Arabic Language Course for Gifted and Talented Jordanian Students
citation: Ziadat, A. H., & Al Ziyadat, M. T. (2016). The Effectiveness of Training Program Based on the Six Hats Model in Developing Creative Thinking Skills and Academic Achievements in the Arabic Language Course for Gifted and Talented Jordanian Students. International Education Studies, 9(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n6p150
title: Replace conventional information-storage teaching with active creative thinking techniques for gifted students
description: Based on their findings, the authors "strongly recommend that teachers and educators should be rehabilitated and trained to use and apply the latest educational methods and techniques" such as the Alcorn program, creative problem solving, critical thinking and brainstorming, and "to refrain from the conventional old methods used which commonly focuses on information storage and retaining crammed data, regardless of the active participation of students."
requirements: Teachers and supervisors receive workshops and training programs in the alternative techniques
constraints: Recommendation grounded in a study of gifted seventh-grade Arabic language students in Jordan
target_learning_goals: creative thinking skills
academic achievement
examples: The article recommends extending the Six Hats Model in seventh-grade Arabic teaching in Jordan's Ministry of Education and adding creative thinking tools to Arabic textbooks at various levels

article_title: The Effects of an Experimental Training Program for Teachers of Vocational English Using Concentrated Language Encounter Instructional Processes and Reciprocal Peer Teaching Strategies
citation: Saowalak Rattanavich. (2017). The Effects of an Experimental Training Program for Teachers of Vocational English Using Concentrated Language Encounter Instructional Processes and Reciprocal Peer Teaching Strategies. English Language Teaching, 10(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n12p58
title: Reciprocal peer teaching strategy
description: Reciprocal peer teaching is an instructional strategy for cooperative learning in which students take turns being the teacher and the student, exchanging roles to explain their understanding of the learning content. The article describes a model with "four continuous steps: predicting, questioning, clarifying, and summarizing", supported by scaffolding, and implemented with students in groups of about four to six. Its theoretical framework is Vygotsky's zone of proximal development and social construction activities such as dialog, scaffolding, and learning review.
requirements: The teacher must prepare the learning model for students so they develop precision in their learning
Matching student couples or small groups who take turns teaching each other
target_learning_goals: English communication skills
analytical thinking skills
confidence in language use
examples: In the experiment, students in groups of four took turns being the teacher to check mistakes in reading and writing and to lead language games

The Effects of an Experimental Training Program for Teachers of Vocational English Using Concentrated Language Encounter Instructional Processes and Reciprocal Peer Teaching Strategies. English Language Teaching, 10(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n12p58

article_title: The Curious Case of Centrality Measures: A Large-Scale Empirical Investigation
citation: Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas. (2022). The Curious Case of Centrality Measures: A Large-Scale Empirical Investigation. Journal of Learning Analytics. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2022.7415
title: Researchers in CSCL settings with central collaborative modules should rely on degree and eigenvector centralities as indicators of success
description: Based on meta-analytic findings across 69 course offerings, the authors recommend that "researchers with similar contexts (e.g., CSCL where the collaborative module is central to the course design) rely on degree and eigenvector centralities as indicators for success while exercising caution when using short-path centralities (closeness and betweenness)." This principle is grounded in the consistent positive correlations and reasonable predictive intervals observed for degree and eigenvector measures.
requirements: The setting must be CSCL where the collaborative module is central to the course design
constraints: Short-path centralities (closeness and betweenness) should be used with caution due to uncertain predictive intervals
target_learners: higher education students in problem-based learning courses
target_learning_goals: monitoring collaborative learning engagement
predicting academic success in collaborative settings
examples: The study included 69 course offerings from a healthcare college using PBL curriculum with online collaborative discussions over five years.
key_sources: Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas. (2022). The Curious Case of Centrality Measures: A Large-Scale Empirical Investigation. Journal of Learning Analytics. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2022.7415

article_title: Learning Word Meanings from Teachers' Repeated Story Read-Aloud in EFL Primary Classrooms
citation: Lu-Chun Lin. (2014). Learning Word Meanings from Teachers' Repeated Story Read-Aloud in EFL Primary Classrooms. English Language Teaching, 7(7). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n7p68
title: Incorporate repeated read-aloud with teacher explanations of new words into the EFL elementary curriculum
description: The article recommends that EFL teachers devote class time to reading the same story aloud multiple times while explaining target words, because this "allows teachers to provide richer and more meaningful lexical input" and lets learners "learn words incrementally". It counters the common belief that explicit teaching of preselected textbook words is the major source of vocabulary acquisition, noting that unplanned words in such classrooms receive few vocabulary-teaching treatments.
requirements: At least three presentations of the same story are proposed for improved word learning, with word-meaning explanations provided at first encounters
constraints: Repeated exposure alone did not close the achievement gap between high and low-proficiency groups
target_learners: elementary school EFL children at beginning proficiency levels
target_learning_goals: learning the meanings of novel vocabulary words from listening to stories
examples: Two native English-speaking teachers read a wordless picture book with eight pseudo words to their fourth-grade classes four times, explaining each target word by pointing to a picture, giving a synonym or definition, and acting it out
key_sources: Lu-Chun Lin. (2014). Learning Word Meanings from Teachers' Repeated Story Read-Aloud in EFL Primary Classrooms. English Language Teaching, 7(7). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n7p68

article_title: Teaching to Diversity: Creating Compassionate Learning Communities for Diverse Elementary School Students
citation: Katz, J., & Porath, M. (2011). Teaching to diversity: Creating compassionate learning communities for diverse elementary school students. International Journal of Special Education, 26(2), 29–39. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ966542
title: The Respecting Diversity (RD) program: a nine-lesson SEL curriculum using a multiple intelligences framework
description: The RD program is a theoretically derived social competence program based on the SEL framework of Zins, Bloodworth, Weissberg, and Walberg (2004) and using a multiple intelligences framework derived from Gardner (1983). It consists of nine introductory lessons in which students explore their own learning strengths and challenges and those of others, working individually and in small groups on tasks requiring a variety of intelligences. The final lesson explores disabilities within the context of ability. The program is designed to be differentiated to fit the unique context of each classroom while maintaining particular concepts and skills.
requirements: Teacher training workshop, manual detailing lesson plans and extensions, and weekly consultation and observation meetings
constraints: Teachers expressed frustration with the limited time they had to extend and supplement the curriculum
target_learners: elementary school students in Grades four to seven
target_learning_goals: self-awareness
self-respect
awareness of others
respect for others
positive classroom climate
key_sources: Katz, J., & Porath, M. (2011). Teaching to diversity: Creating compassionate learning communities for diverse elementary school students. International Journal of Special Education, 26(2), 29–39. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ937173

article_title: Effect of Real-time Feedback on the Quality of Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation for Medical Students in Colombia.
citation: Piñeros-Alvarez JL, Portuguez-Jaramillo NE, Urbano-Cano AL. (2026). Effect of Real-time Feedback on the Quality of Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation for Medical Students in Colombia. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.50647
title: Integrate real-time feedback devices into CPR training to optimize skill acquisition
description: The article recommends incorporating real-time audiovisual feedback devices into CPR training because they "allow immediate monitoring of key parameters, facilitating adherence to CPR quality goals in simulation scenarios." The randomized study supports this for compression quality but shows ventilation targets were not met even with feedback. The device used is described as "a cost-effective alternative for low-resource settings."

constraints: Ventilation quality did not improve with feedback in this study
Performance may reflect calibration to the manikin's mechanical compliance rather than real-patient chest stiffness
The simulator is strictly a training tool, not a clinical device
target_learning_goals: high-quality CPR chest compressions meeting rate and depth targets
examples: Fourth-year medical students were randomly assigned to train with a PRESTAN feedback device or without feedback over four four-hour sessions.

article_title: Hybrid simulation approach enhances technical and non-technical skills in therapeutic pharmacology education.
citation: Changuiti O, Mahou FZ, Decormeille G, Koraich N, El Hsaini H. (2026). Hybrid simulation approach enhances technical and non-technical skills in therapeutic pharmacology education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09983-1
title: Repeated simulation sessions with identical scenarios reinforce learning and evaluate skill retention over time
description: The article describes repeating role-playing and hybrid simulation sessions one week after the first sessions, using the same learning objectives, simulation scenarios, and assessment procedures. This repetition aimed to reinforce learning while evaluating knowledge retention and skill application over time, enabling participants to consolidate their pharmacological knowledge and medication administration skills. Significant improvements between the first and second sessions support this design.
requirements: Same learning objectives, scenarios, and assessment procedures across repeated sessions
constraints: Knowledge and performance were assessed only one week after the intervention, providing no information on long-term retention
target_learning_goals: medication administration skills
knowledge retention
examples: Students participated in a second role-playing simulation followed by a second hybrid simulation one week after the first sessions
key_sources: Changuiti O, Mahou FZ, Decormeille G, Koraich N, El Hsaini H. (2026). Hybrid simulation approach enhances technical and non-technical skills in therapeutic pharmacology education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09983-1

article_title: Self-Assessed Restorative Care Competence Among Nursing Professionals in Finland: A Cross-Sectional Study.
citation: Lotvonen S, Parkkila M, Tuomikoski A-M, Kääriäinen M, DiBiasi V, Platani E, Bruno I, Siira H. (2026). Self-Assessed Restorative Care Competence Among Nursing Professionals in Finland: A Cross-Sectional Study. Western Journal of Nursing Research. https://doi.org/10.1177/01939459261478193
title: ReCCA instrument (Restorative Care Competence Assessment)
description: The ReCCA is a self-assessment instrument developed by researchers at a university in Northern Finland to measure the restorative care competence of nursing professionals working in geriatric services. It consists of 5 background questions and 8 subscales rated on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = poorly to 5 = excellently), totalling 48 items. It was developed in 3 phases, including face and content validity evaluation by expert panels with Content Validity Index calculation and construct validity testing via exploratory factor analysis. The article reports subscale Cronbach's alpha values "ranged from 0.86 to 0.96, and the overall alpha for the 48-item instrument was 0.98".
requirements: Respondents must be nursing professionals working in geriatric care services
constraints: Due to its novelty, it has not yet been validated across multiple well-being service counties or in international context
target_learners: Licensed practical nurses and registered nurses in older adults' care
target_learning_goals: Self-assessment of restorative care competence and identification of learning needs
examples: Used for the first time in this study to collect data on nursing professionals' RC competence in older adult care
key_sources: Lotvonen S, Parkkila M, Tuomikoski A-M, Kääriäinen M, DiBiasi V, Platani E, Bruno I, Siira H. (2026). article_title: Research on the student-centered research feedback experimental teaching model to enhance the effectiveness of pharmacology experimental teaching.
citation: Miao C, Chen J, Li Y, Xia A, Song Y, Xu C, Mao Y, Wang X. (2026). Research on the student-centered research feedback experimental teaching model to enhance the effectiveness of pharmacology experimental teaching. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000051199
title: Introduce the college's own scientific research achievements into undergraduate experimental teaching as student-led projects
description: The RFPETM converts faculty research results into a teaching project library of 10 four-hour pharmacology experiments, "closely followed the latest scientific frontiers and research achievements, and added scientific research elements to experimental teaching." Students search literature, design routes and plans, and complete feasibility analysis with teacher review before implementation. The article reports this research-feedback approach improved course scores and student evaluations.
requirements: A teaching project library built from the institution's own research achievements
Supervising teachers who review experimental plans before students implement them
Online resources and virtual simulation projects supporting student self-study
constraints: Evaluated in one institution with integrated traditional Chinese and Western medicine undergraduates; confirmatory experiments were compressed but retained
target_learners: medical undergraduate students in pharmacology experimental courses
target_learning_goals: experimental operation skills
scientific research thinking
innovation ability
examples: Students independently searched research literature, developed experimental routes and plans, and could only start implementing them after the guiding teacher reviewed the experimental plans
key_sources: Miao C, Chen J, Li Y, Xia A, Song Y, Xu C, Mao Y, Wang X. (2026). Research on the student-centered research feedback experimental teaching model to enhance the effectiveness of pharmacology experimental teaching. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000051199

article_title: Large-group virtual anatomy via a smart digital podium: a preliminary cross-sectional study of student perspectives toward remote anatomage teaching in a medical lecture hall.
citation: Punja R, Punja D, Prasad Kamachi Christdoss Ruben. (2026). Large-group virtual anatomy via a smart digital podium: a preliminary cross-sectional study of student perspectives toward remote anatomage teaching in a medical lecture hall. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10019-x
title: Remote Anatomage Teaching (RAT): a three-component model for scaling virtual anatomy to large lecture halls
description: RAT comprises three integrated components: (1) the Anatomage table maintained in active state in the dissection laboratory, (2) a smart digital podium with touchscreen, LAN connectivity, and HDMI output in the lecture theatre, and (3) multimodal lecture delivery integrating blackboard diagrams, PowerPoint slides, and live remote Anatomage navigation. The model streams "the full interactivity of the Anatomage table in real time to a large lecture theatre without requiring either students or the instructor to be physically present at the table," enabling a single faculty member to teach an entire cohort simultaneously.
requirements: An institutional LAN segment dedicated to low-latency streaming between the dissection laboratory and lecture theatre
A smart digital podium with touchscreen, computer, and HDMI output connected to dual projectors
constraints: The projection visibility concern raised by 2/94 students identifies the primary technical limitation, with standard classroom projectors introducing resolution loss and ambient light interference at distance
target_learners: First-year medical (MBBS) students in large-cohort lectures
target_learning_goals: Three-dimensional understanding of neuroanatomical structures such as the basal nuclei
examples: A 47-minute integrated basal nuclei lecture combining blackboard diagrams for cortico-striato-pallido-thalamo-cortical pathways, PowerPoint slides for clinical correlations, and live remote Anatomage navigation for three-dimensional visualization
key_sources: Punja R, Punja D, Prasad Kamachi Christdoss Ruben. (2026). Large-group virtual anatomy via a smart digital podium: a preliminary cross-sectional study of student perspectives toward remote anatomage teaching in a medical lecture hall. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10019-x

article_title: AI is Here to Stay: A Scenario-Based Exploration of Leadership, Followership, and the Impact on Skill Development.
citation: Kugler Maike, Aichroth Laura S. (2026). AI is Here to Stay: A Scenario‐Based Exploration of Leadership, Followership, and the Impact on Skill Development. New Directions for Student Leadership. https://doi.org/10.1002/yd.70067
title: Two standpoints on leadership and followership: reversing the lens and co‐creation
description: The article distinguishes two general standpoints for exploring leadership and followership: "(1) positional through hierarchy: the reversing the lens perspective, or (2) relational, through social interaction: the co‐creation perspective." From the hierarchical standpoint, leadership is influence through positional authority; from the co‐creation perspective, followership is an interaction in which individuals grant each other leader and follower roles. The article applies both standpoints to each AI scenario.
requirements: Both perspectives are included because leader/manager and employee/follower roles are often adopted by the same organizational members but are distinct in origin and skillset
constraints: Most current literature explores the reversing‐the‐lens roles of managers and employees, while the co‐creation perspective remains underexplored
target_learning_goals: understanding positional and relational perspectives on leadership and followership
key_sources: Kugler Maike, Aichroth Laura S. (2026). AI is Here to Stay: A Scenario‐Based Exploration of Leadership, Followership, and the Impact on Skill Development. New Directions for Student Leadership. https://doi.org/10.1002/yd.70067

article_title: Student-teacher relationships as a mediator of children's education-linked genetics: results from the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study.
citation: Austerberry, C., Corfield, E. C., Havdahl, A., Smajlagic, D., Brandlistuen, R. E., Vaage Wang, M., Fish, L., Bernardi, M., van de Grint‐Stoop, J., Bekkhus, M., & Fearon, P. (2026). Student–teacher relationships as a mediator of children's education‐linked genetics: results from the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 67(10), 1729–1740. https://doi.org/10.1111/jcpp.70179
title: Target student–teacher conflict as a potentially modifiable mechanism linking children's characteristics to educational outcomes
description: The article argues that because conflict and positive teacher responses—but not closeness—were evoked by children's genetically influenced characteristics and mediated genetic effects on performance, they are the relationship dimensions most open to change. The authors state the findings "point to student–teacher conflict as being a potentially more promising target than parental/teacher warmth/closeness."
requirements: Interventions would need to operate on relationship dimensions shown to be responsive to child characteristics, i.e., conflict and teacher response positivity
constraints: The mediation pathway is small, accounting for about 10% of the total genetic association; evidence is observational and from a single high-income country
target_learning_goals: reading and mathematics performance
examples: In the MoBa cohort, reduced conflict and positive teacher responses each mediated 10% of the PGSedu–performance association, while closeness did not mediate it

Student–teacher relationships as a mediator of children's education‐linked genetics: results from the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 67(10), 1729–1740. https://doi.org/10.1111/jcpp.70179

article_title: Exploring the Predictive Value of National Residency Matching Program (NRMP) Rank in Residency Outcomes.
citation: Kwon E, Pei M, Xu A, Bahethi RR, Kalyoussef E, Hsueh WD. (2026). Exploring the Predictive Value of National Residency Matching Program (NRMP) Rank in Residency Outcomes. The Annals of Otology, Rhinology, and Laryngology. https://doi.org/10.1177/00034894261436872
title: Restriction of range in highly competitive specialties limits the predictive value of rank order
description: The article proposes that in highly competitive specialties like otolaryngology, the applicant pool is "inherently highly accomplished," so "restriction of range in applicant quality may make it inherently difficult to discern statistically significant differences in future performance based solely on subtle variations in rank order." This account explains why NRMP rank shows inconsistent predictive value across outcomes and specialties, and suggests factors beyond application metrics matter.
requirements: Applies to specialties with highly competitive, homogeneous applicant pools
constraints: The article states this consideration applies especially to outcomes representing general success; it does not quantify the range restriction
target_learning_goals: understanding limits of rank-based selection predictive validity
key_sources: Kwon E, Pei M, Xu A, Bahethi RR, Kalyoussef E, Hsueh WD. (2026). Exploring the Predictive Value of National Residency Matching Program (NRMP) Rank in Residency Outcomes. The Annals of Otology, Rhinology, and Laryngology. https://doi.org/10.1177/00034894261436872

article_title: Exploring the Potential for Smartphone-Based Reflection to Support Socioemotional Competence Development in Student Nurses' Clinical Placement: Mixed Methods Field Trial.
citation: Ivo Bril-Broers, Nick Degens, Joke Fleer. (2026). Exploring the Potential for Smartphone-Based Reflection to Support Socioemotional Competence Development in Student Nurses' Clinical Placement: Mixed Methods Field Trial. JMIR Nursing. https://doi.org/10.2196/91083
title: Reflection apps for clinical placement should remove practical barriers and reduce cognitive load rather than enforce rigid in-app phase-specific activities
description: The article's design lessons hold that "supporting students through the self-regulated learning phases does not require in-app, phase-specific activities" and that "the intensive nature of clinical placement requires reflection apps to reduce the cognitive load of managing one's learning process." Apps should enable self-regulated learning and avoid a rigid process of in-app activities, since students can pass through SRL phases outside the app.
requirements: The app must make the primary task of reflection easy and enjoyable, applying persuasive systems design principles
constraints: Learning cannot be completely scripted in clinical placement learning
target_learning_goals: socioemotional competence development
self-regulated learning
examples: Students asked for a reminder feature after forgetting to use the app following shifts; the authors suggest reminders for daily reflections and goal review
key_sources: Ivo Bril-Broers, Nick Degens, Joke Fleer. (2026). Exploring the Potential for Smartphone-Based Reflection to Support Socioemotional Competence Development in Student Nurses' Clinical Placement: Mixed Methods Field Trial. JMIR Nursing. https://doi.org/10.2196/91083

article_title: Building consensus on the core clinical competencies and outcomes related to effective child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS) crisis team provision: findings from a Delphi study.
citation: Clau N, Tindall L, Sayal K, Holland J, Hewitt CE, Tiffin PA. (2026). Building consensus on the core clinical competencies and outcomes related to effective child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS) crisis team provision: findings from a Delphi study. BMJ Mental Health. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjment-2026-302719
title: Crisis team clinicians should be trained and supported to deliver relationship-based, trauma-informed and culturally responsive care
description: The article's clinical implications state that "crisis team clinicians [should] be trained and supported to deliver care that is relationship-based, trauma-informed and culturally responsive." This follows from the Delphi consensus prioritising relational, validating and personalised approaches over administrative or diagnostic processes. Training programmes should prioritise relational and emotional competencies alongside robust supervision structures.
requirements: Robust supervision structures and staff support to sustain empathic, validating care
constraints: Reductions in inpatient admissions are contingent on a well-supported workforce
target_learning_goals: Therapeutic alliance building
Cultural competency
Validation of distress
Trauma-informed assessment
examples: The findings informed a prototype digital training package for CAMHS crisis teams, with the prototype and manual publicly available

article_title: Poverty Simulations: Are the Learning Outcomes Consistently and Uniformly Positive?
citation: McQuistan, M. R., Young, L. B., & Pendleton, C. (2026). Poverty Simulations: Are the Learning Outcomes Consistently and Uniformly Positive? Journal of Dental Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/jdd.70090
title: Poverty simulations should be reconsidered or supplemented when more than a third of students show worsened attitudes
description: The article argues that instructional initiatives producing poorer outcomes for a substantial minority warrant re-examination. It states "Any instructional initiative which results in poorer scores for more than a third of students should be reconsidered" and recommends identifying student characteristics that predict negative attitudes before participation, or finding alternative instructional methods for students who do not benefit from the simulation.
requirements: Research should identify student characteristics before the simulation that would accurately predict negative attitudes after the simulation.
constraints: The article notes poverty simulations yield substantial benefits for the majority of participants, so the recommendation targets enhancement or supplementation rather than wholesale replacement.
target_learning_goals: understanding of poverty and structural barriers to care
empathy with patients facing socioeconomic barriers
examples: The study found 34.6% of students reported decreased poverty attitudes at T3, and respondents with less favorable post-simulation attitudes were less likely to evaluate the simulation positively.

article_title: Feasibility Evaluation of a Standalone Virtual Reality System for Neonatal Resuscitation Training.
citation: Amari Shoichiro, Eto Masato, Oyama Hiroshi. (2026). Feasibility Evaluation of a Standalone Virtual Reality System for Neonatal Resuscitation Training. Journal of Medical Systems 50:94. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10916-026-02423-z
title: Real-time simulation model with hint-based scaffolding for self-directed resuscitation training
description: The training scene uses a real-time simulation model rather than turn-based interaction: physiological changes continue while awaiting input, so hesitation causes deterioration, approximating real time pressure. When a learner fails to act within a predefined window, the application displays a contextual hint with audio narration—"hint-based scaffolding" intended to prevent learners becoming stuck while preserving self-directed training.
requirements: A predefined time window for triggering hints and a physiological model that deteriorates without appropriate learner action
constraints: Scenario content is based on the Japanese NCPR 2020 guideline; adaptation would be required for regions with different resuscitation algorithms
target_learners: certified neonatal resuscitation providers practicing self-directed VR training
target_learning_goals: experiencing time-critical decision-making and maintaining guideline-based resuscitation performance under pressure
examples: Participants' free-text comments referred to "a sense of tension" and "the time pressure of resuscitation"

article_title: Long-term knowledge and skills retention following Helping Mothers Survive and Helping Babies Survive training in Tanzania: a mixed-methods follow-up study.
citation: Mwilike Beatrice Erastus, Philbert Ruchius, Rimoy Martha, Mabada Lucy, Komba Nicodem, Okade Tom, Mwanga Feddy, Gosse Rashid, Ambikile Joel. (2026). Long-term knowledge and skills retention following Helping Mothers Survive and Helping Babies Survive training in Tanzania: a mixed-methods follow-up study. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1824835
title: Regular refresher training is recommended, particularly for rural providers and those with lower educational qualifications
description: The article recommends structured follow-up strategies to counteract the significant knowledge and skills declines observed after HMS/HBS training. The authors state that "Regular refresher training is recommended, particularly for rural healthcare providers and those with lower educational qualifications." This recommendation responds directly to the study's finding that retention challenges stem from broader health system limitations rather than the passage of time alone.
requirements: Training programs should incorporate structured follow-up and refresher sessions after initial HMS/HBS training
constraints: The study's cross-sectional design and absence of a control group prevent causal inference about training effectiveness
target_learners: Healthcare providers in maternal and newborn care
target_learning_goals: Maintaining knowledge and skills in emergency obstetric and neonatal care over time
examples: The 50,000 Happy Birthdays project implemented HMS and HBS training modules across three Tanzanian regions from 2018 to 2020

article_title: Nutrition-related competencies in undergraduate training of health professionals in Poland: a descriptive analysis of educational standards.
citation: Kupis Robert, Rudzińska Anna, Piotrowicz Karolina. (2026). Nutrition-related competencies in undergraduate training of health professionals in Poland: a descriptive analysis of educational standards. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09284-7
title: Educational standards for health professionals should be revised for accuracy and consistency in nutrition content
description: The article recommends that Polish educational standards for health professional undergraduate programmes be revised to improve the comprehensiveness and consistency of nutrition-related content. Until a dedicated legal framework for dietitians is established, nutrition-related content should be incorporated into programmes in accordance with the needs of the student's field of study. This addresses the finding that current standards produce graduates with limited and varied nutrition training.
requirements: Revision of official ministerial educational standards documents governing health professional programmes
constraints: Applies to the Polish system of nationally standardised health professional education
target_learners: Undergraduate health professional students in Poland
target_learning_goals: Nutrition-related knowledge, skills, and attitudes for patient dietary care
examples: The article analysed educational standards for ten programmes and found nutrition-related learning objectives ranging from 0 to 16
key_sources: Kupis Robert, Rudzińska Anna, Piotrowicz Karolina. (2026). Nutrition-related competencies in undergraduate training of health professionals in Poland: a descriptive analysis of educational standards. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09284-7

article_title: In-Situ Simulation for Enhancing Safety in Outpatient Hysteroscopy: Development and Evaluation of a Crisis Resource Management-Based Training Package.
citation: Warshafsky C, Singh SS, Garber AB. (2026). In-Situ Simulation for Enhancing Safety in Outpatient Hysteroscopy: Development and Evaluation of a Crisis Resource Management-Based Training Package. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11604
title: Regular simulation should be a requirement for setting up and maintaining outpatient procedure centers
description: The authors recommend that "Regular simulations should be a requirement for setting up outpatient procedure centers and maintaining ongoing patient safety." This principle is grounded in their finding that in-situ simulation identifies latent safety threats and improves team preparedness for rare, high-acuity events in settings with fewer resources than hospitals.
requirements: A structured scenario-based simulation curriculum
Trained facilitators and a simulation technician or low-fidelity alternatives
constraints: In-situ simulation must be balanced against the ongoing demand of clinical activities in the space
target_learners: Interprofessional teams in outpatient procedural settings
target_learning_goals: Maintain preparedness for rare, high-acuity emergencies and identify system gaps
examples: The authors state the curriculum "can serve as a continuing quality assurance tool" and that ongoing drills can be incorporated into a regular quality assurance initiative
key_sources: Warshafsky C, Singh SS, Garber AB. (2026). In-Situ Simulation for Enhancing Safety in Outpatient Hysteroscopy: Development and Evaluation of a Crisis Resource Management-Based Training Package. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11604

article_title: Time to Refresh: Design and Evaluation of Refresher Training to Sustain Procedural Teaching Skills.
citation: Mousset RA, de Vos tot Nederveen Cappel WH, Boonstra JJ, Langers AMJ, Brand PLP. (2026). Time to Refresh: Design and Evaluation of Refresher Training to Sustain Procedural Teaching Skills. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.2443
title: Refresher training should be considered an integral component of sustained faculty development rather than a remedial intervention
description: The authors advocate that refresher training should not be considered remedial but as an integral component of sustained faculty development, and they "advocate for its broader implementation and rigorous evaluation across FD initiatives beyond endoscopy." This principle rests on the study's finding that the refresher training demonstrated measurable value even when the initial program had already achieved substantial impact, supporting long-term retention of procedural teaching skills.
requirements: Institutional support and dedicated time for teaching activities
constraints: Optimal timing of reinforcement remains an open question, as the prior study showed continued improvement at 6–9 months without refresher training
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention and transfer of teaching skills
examples: The TCT refresher training was delivered 6–9 months after the initial training, informed by Ebbinghaus' forgetting curve and evidence of cognitive decline after approximately 200 days.

article_title: A novel Z-number based multi-stage assessment framework for problem-based learning in practical courses.
citation: Yu Limin, Chen Zhe, Qin Zeyu. (2026). A novel Z-number based multi-stage assessment framework for problem-based learning in practical courses. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0349114
title: Use reliability-aware multi-criteria aggregation rather than oversimplified averaging for multi-source PBL assessment
description: The article argues that multi-source assessment in PBL lacks mechanisms to reconcile heterogeneous evaluator data, often resulting in 'oversimplified averaging approaches that dilute domain-specific expertise.' It recommends a structured multi-criteria framework using Z-numbers and MABAC to preserve both performance ratings and reliability, producing more transparent and interpretable outcomes than traditional single-dimension subjective evaluation.
requirements: Multiple evaluator groups providing linguistic assessments convertible to Z-numbers
Computational implementation of the Z-MABAC method
constraints: Validated within one course context; broader generalizability requires further validation across cohorts, courses, and institutions
target_learners: undergraduate students in practical PBL courses
target_learning_goals: comprehensive competency assessment including teamwork, problem-solving, and project quality
examples: The article's Table 6 contrasts traditional single-dimension subjective evaluation with the proposed multi-dimension objective method rated high in flexibility, scalability, and diversity
key_sources: Yu Limin, Chen Zhe, Qin Zeyu. (2026). A novel Z-number based multi-stage assessment framework for problem-based learning in practical courses. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0349114

article_title: AI-assisted case-based learning and flipped classroom to improve clinical decision-making: a randomized controlled trial in reproductive medicine.
citation: Wang, Q., Hu, C., Li, Y., Zhang, T., & Zhang, S. (2026). AI-assisted case-based learning and flipped classroom to improve clinical decision-making: a randomized controlled trial in reproductive medicine. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2026.2670047
title: Redistribute cognitive workload to pre-class AI-supported acquisition so in-class time serves higher-order clinical learning
description: The article states that the instructional architecture of the AI-assisted CBL+FC model is predicated on strategic redistribution of cognitive workload: foundational content acquisition is transitioned to the pre-class stage via targeted e-learning and virtual SP engagement, allowing classroom sessions to be dedicated to higher-order learning activities. The authors suggest this time-redistribution effect enhances initial acquisition and retention without increasing total workload, which they identify as a crucial factor for the scalability of this pedagogical approach.
requirements: Pre-class e-learning and virtual SP engagement infrastructure
In-class sessions restructured for collaborative case discussion rather than lecture
constraints: Exact pre-class preparation time was not quantitatively measured in this study
target_learning_goals: clinical decision-making
knowledge retention
efficient mastery of clinical competencies
examples: The AI-assisted group completed pre-class virtual patient interviews and Superstar Learning case analysis, then used class time for small-group discussions, presentations, and instructor clarification of unresolved issues

article_title: Simulation-based mastery learning for nasolacrimal duct probing in ophthalmology residency: a prospective pre-post educational study.
citation: Theerakulpisut Saralee, Tengtrisorn Supaporn, Singha Penny, Rattanalert Narisa. (2026). Simulation-based mastery learning for nasolacrimal duct probing in ophthalmology residency: a prospective pre–post educational study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09213-8
title: Use real-time expert feedback during hands-on simulation practice rather than video-based instruction alone for procedural skill acquisition
description: The article's findings indicate that participants did not experience significant gains from video tutorials alone, and the authors attribute this to extrinsic cognitive load during the pre-practice phase. The trial-and-error process critical to skill acquisition is absent in purely video-based instruction, emphasizing the need for interactive learning experiences. Real-time feedback during hands-on simulation practice reinforced and corrected performance, and confidence significantly improved following hands-on practice and direct feedback.
requirements: Immediate formative feedback from expert supervisors during supervised simulation practice
constraints: Video-based instruction alone produced low baseline confidence and struggled manual techniques despite reviewing the instructional videos
target_learning_goals: procedural skill acquisition
confidence building
examples: Residents completed a video tutorial and MCQ but struggled with manual techniques; confidence and rubric scores improved only after guided simulator practice with expert feedback
key_sources: Theerakulpisut Saralee, Tengtrisorn Supaporn, Singha Penny, Rattanalert Narisa. (2026). Simulation-based mastery learning for nasolacrimal duct probing in ophthalmology residency: a prospective pre–post educational study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09213-8

article_title: Does medical students' perception of team-based learning have an impact on achieving planned learning outcomes?
citation: Jabeen Kauser, Rehman Javeria, Fatima Syeda Sadia, Ahmed Imran, Ghias Kulsoom. (2026). Does medical students’ perception of team-based learning have an impact on achieving planned learning outcomes?. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09185-9
title: Redesign TBL sessions by shortening pre-reading material, right-sizing teams to 5–7, and strengthening peer assessment to improve acceptability without sacrificing learning gains.
description: The authors recommend actionable design levers identified through mixed-methods triangulation: shorter, multi-modal preparatory materials; right-sizing teams to approximately 5–7 members; strengthening peer-assessment processes; and pacing application tasks. These changes aim to "reduce friction while preserving the learning benefits we observed", addressing dissatisfaction drivers without compromising knowledge acquisition.
requirements: Pre-reading material should be short, concise, and relevant, with visual alternatives such as pictorials and tabular readings.
Teams should be sized to 5–7 students to maintain individual contribution visibility.
constraints: Larger teams (9–10 members) limited individual participation and visibility of effort in this study.
Extensive pre-reading material led to learner dissatisfaction and disengagement.
target_learning_goals: Knowledge acquisition in basic sciences
Critical thinking and analytical skills
Teamwork and engagement
examples: Students suggested 1–2 TBL sessions per 6-week module, one at midpoint and one towards the end, and proposed a PBL-TBL hybrid session.
key_sources: Jabeen Kauser, Rehman Javeria, Fatima Syeda Sadia, Ahmed Imran, Ghias Kulsoom. (2026). Does medical students’ perception of team-based learning have an impact on achieving planned learning outcomes?. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09185-9

article_title: Assessment of clinical readiness, knowledge and attitude, regarding Basic Life Support (BLS) and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) skill among dentists practicing in Saudi Arabia.
citation: Khattak Osama, Ehsan Aliya, Khalid Ayesha Akbar, Iqbal Azhar, Chaudhary Farooq Ahmad, Baig Muhammad Nadeem, Alsharari Thani, Memon Muhammad Rizwan. (2026). Assessment of clinical readiness, knowledge and attitude, regarding Basic Life Support (BLS) and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) skill among dentists practicing in Saudi Arabia. PeerJ. https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.21098
title: Provide regular, hands-on BLS/CPR refresher training and simulation-based drills, because recent workshop attendance strongly predicted dentists' knowledge and confidence
description: The article recommends that BLS/CPR training for dentists be renewed through frequent, practical refresher sessions rather than long intervals between recertifications, because recent workshop attendance was the strongest predictor of both knowledge and confidence. The authors state that "Simulation-based training and regular mock drills have been shown to improve retention and performance of emergency skills" and that "short, frequent refresher courses are more effective than long intervals between recertification." The recommendation rests on the survey's regression findings and cited retention literature.

constraints: The supporting evidence is cross-sectional and self-reported, so causal effects of refresher training were not established in this study

article_title: Defect-based scenario simulation teaching in the specialized skills training of nurse anesthetists: a before-after within-subject design.
citation: Ma Yanli, Li Han, Zhang Huan, Gao Fengli, Ma Xiaobei. (2026). Defect-based scenario simulation teaching in the specialized skills training of nurse anesthetists: a before–after within-subject design. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09098-7
title: Repository of Instructional Defects for Defect-Based Scenario Simulation
description: A curated repository of defect-based teaching scripts developed by a seven-member multidisciplinary team (including one N1-level NA, two faculty members, one assistant head nurse, one head nurse and two associate chief physicians averaging 13 years of experience). It was "developed based on the learning objectives and standard operating procedures in the Anesthesia Nursing Manual and typical errors in daily practice", with representative defect-based scripts integrating real clinical cases and teaching goals, produced as micro-videos for the scenario teaching phase.
requirements: Developed from learning objectives, standard operating procedures, and typical errors in daily practice, with scripts produced as micro-videos
constraints: The article states the repository "was not intended to serve as an outcome evaluation instrument"
target_learners: nurse anesthetists in specialized skills training
target_learning_goals: recognition of procedural defects and latent risks
mastery of standard operating procedures
examples: Used in the June–July 2025 DBSS phase, where participants watched instructional videos featuring embedded defects across various surgical anesthesia scenarios

article_title: Assessing the realism and face validity of Fix For Life: an embalmed human cadaver model for high-fidelity laparoscopic training.
citation: Rahimi A. Masie, van Emden Michael, Hardon Sem F., Simons Maarten, Bonjer H. Jaap, Horeman Tim, Daams Freek. (2026). Assessing the realism and face validity of Fix For Life: an embalmed human cadaver model for high-fidelity laparoscopic training. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-025-12550-2
title: Use reusable embalmed cadavers that preserve tissue pliability and color as a bridge between simulators and the operating room
description: The article argues that cadaver training offering realistic tissue manipulation, dissection, and procedure-specific steps should sit between simulator training and live surgery, and that an embalming method preserving pliability enables repeated reuse. It states that "Fix4life provides an alternative to on-the-job training and serves as a bridge between simulators and the operating room". Reuse across different courses adds ethical and financial value compared with single-use fresh frozen specimens.
requirements: An embalming technique that maintains suppleness, elasticity, and tissue color
Realistic anatomy allowing exploration of anatomical variations and pitfalls
constraints: Fresh frozen cadavers allow only one or two uses due to decomposition after defrosting

realistic assessment of procedural skills and feedback
