article_title: Using Recontextualisation Theory to Understand Learning Across Multiple Sites in Simulation-Based Nurse Education.
citation: Allan, H. T., and M. O'Driscoll. (2026). Using Recontextualisation Theory to Understand Learning Across Multiple Sites in Simulation‐Based Nurse Education. Journal of Advanced Nursing 82, no. 5: 5513–5520. https://doi.org/10.1111/jan.70163
title: Recontextualisation theory: knowledge is reworked across contexts of learning and practice
description: Recontextualisation theory (Evans et al. 2009) holds that concepts and practices change as they are used in different settings, so knowledge generated in one context must be recontextualised to be put to work in new contexts. The article describes it as "a multi‐faceted pedagogic practice" drawing on Bernstein's idea that concepts change as they move into curricula and van Oers' observation that concepts are integral to evolving practice. It identifies four sets of practices of recontextualisation: content, pedagogic, workplace and learner. The paper applies it to nurse education to understand learning across university, placements and SBE.
requirements: Understanding the knowledge logics underpinning programme flows and how knowledge changes as it is put to work across universities, colleges and workplaces
constraints: The article notes it has not been used to underpin a curriculum in nursing
target_learners: student nurses in undergraduate professional preparation programmes
target_learning_goals: reworking knowledge across multiple sites of learning
integrating theoretical and practical knowledge
examples: The authors use the theory to interpret their SIMS week evaluation, where students reworked knowledge from clinical practice and university within SBE scenarios, groupwork and debriefing.

article_title: Relative Sense of Belonging and the Academic Achievement of Chinese Adolescents.
citation: Zhao Yushan, Gee Kevin A., Yuan Caleb W. (2025). Relative Sense of Belonging and the Academic Achievement of Chinese Adolescents. Journal of Youth and Adolescence. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10964-025-02287-5
title: Relative sense of belonging: a peer-referenced belonging construct grounded in the belongingness hypothesis, self-determination theory, and social comparison theory
description: Relative sense of belonging is defined as "one's own sense of belonging relative to the average sense of belonging of their surrounding peers in school", operationalized as a student's belonging factor score minus their school's average. The article grounds it in three frameworks: the belongingness hypothesis (belonging as a prerequisite for success), self-determination theory (belonging as a mediator of intrinsic motivation), and social comparison theory, which supplies the comparative layer. It also maps onto the status-based validation pathway of multidimensional belonging, in which individuals feel more connected when they see themselves as standing out compared to others. The measure captures relative standing, not directly reported relative feeling.
requirements: Requires a measure of individual belonging plus the school-level average belonging, so each student's within-school deviation can be computed
constraints: The measure does not capture relative feeling; a direct self-reported comparison measure was not available in the dataset
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement in math, reading, and science
examples: The study computed relative belonging by subtracting each school's average belonging factor score from each student's individual factor score in PISA 2018 data

title: Near-peer instruction by clinically experienced residents is a feasible, low-cost way to teach procedural-adjacent skills like CXR interpretation
description: The article argues that near-peer teaching by intensive care medicine residents offers measurable benefits with "high feasibility and low cost, justifying its curricular adoption". Proposed mechanisms include cognitive and social congruence — near-peers share a similar knowledge structure and learning language with junior learners, which may facilitate clarification, feedback, and psychological safety. The authors note this level of near-peer expertise is likely important for content accuracy and instructional credibility.
requirements: Instructors must have relevant clinical expertise; the residents had completed a dedicated one-month radiology rotation and routinely interpret ICU-relevant CXRs
constraints: Blinding was not feasible and instructors were part of the study team, so subtle differences in delivery or instructor enthusiasm may have introduced performance bias

clinical knowledge acquisition
examples: All 50 participants attended a two-hour lecture delivered by two intensive care medicine residents (third- and fourth-year) as part of an existing undergraduate teaching curriculum

In its validation study, "the 10-item knowledge domain demonstrated acceptable reliability (Cronbach's α ≈ 0.70) and 2-week test–retest agreement (Cohen's κ: fair–moderate)". It was administered via Google Forms as identical pre-test and post-test, scored one mark per correct answer for a maximum of 10.

Application of Mixed Reality for Ophthalmic Clinical Skills and Diagnosis: Prospective Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/71338
title: Design simulations that reproduce consistent clinical signs so every student can deliberately practice a defined, comprehensive set of conditions
description: The article argues that simulation's key pedagogical advantage over opportunistic clinical teaching is standardization: "in the EyelearnMR group, every student was given the opportunity to examine a defined and comprehensive set of conditions." Because the module reproduces the same clinical signs for each learner, it supports deliberate practice with repetition at the student's own pace, which the authors link to better assessment performance. Real and simulated patients in traditional teaching cannot guarantee the same conditions or degree of significant findings across a student cohort.
requirements: A simulation able to reproduce consistent clinical signs across learners; a structured and guided session allowing students to practice at their own pace and repeat specific cases
constraints: The improvement cannot be attributed solely to the software, since the structured session also included guided demonstration, self-paced exploration, and repeated practice with immediate visual feedback; simulated patients may not fully replicate critical clinical signs in all domains
target_learners: undergraduate medical students learning clinical examination skills
target_learning_goals: examination technique consistency
diagnostic competency built from exposure to varied conditions
knowledge retention through deliberate practice
examples: EyelearnMR presented six ocular motility scenarios in a model patient, letting students repeat specific cases during a 2-hour guided session, whereas control students relied on chance clinical encounters with varying physical findings

Research topic–driven curriculum content reform in graduate immunology to strengthen students' research and innovation competence. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08711-z
title: Research topic–driven learning model for graduate immunology grounded in constructive alignment, inquiry-based and active learning
description: The article proposes and implements a "research topic–driven learning" model in which graduate students select research topics aligned with immunological frontiers and, under faculty mentorship, construct their knowledge base around those topics. The design is explicitly grounded in educational theory: "Constructive alignment theory provided the conceptual foundation" and inquiry-based learning informed the course structure as students formulated questions, analyzed evidence and synthesized conclusions from authentic research topics. The model operationalizes the research–teaching nexus in a resource-constrained setting and is presented as a transferable framework for other foundational medical disciplines.
requirements: Faculty mentorship with one-on-one guidance for topic selection, literature selection and iterative feedback
Orientation training in literature searching, data extraction and reference management before the course starts
constraints: Faculty workload increased compared with lecture-based formats, and the article states sustainable implementation will require institutional support such as workload recognition and training in educational methods
target_learners: Graduate (master's and PhD) students in basic medical sciences, specifically immunology
target_learning_goals: Research competence and innovative thinking
Mastery of core immunological theory integrated with frontier developments
Academic communication and self-regulated learning
examples: Students selected topics with mentors, built knowledge frameworks, compiled literature reviews, gave thematic presentations with faculty questioning, and were assessed via presentations, short papers and open-book exams

description: This pattern places learners physically co-located with their team and equipment while a remote instructor shares the same clinical visual context (holographic patient and monitor) and facilitates scenario progression in real time. The authors chose a synchronous format because "many NTS behaviors are expressed and observable only during live team interaction". AR's pass-through feature preserves "interaction with real people and physical equipment", which the authors link to communication, situational observation, and coordination behaviors during crisis simulation.

Holographic clinical elements (patient, monitor, resuscitation equipment) plus onsite standardized team members to elicit observable NTS

target_learning_goals: Non-technical skills (leadership, communication, situational awareness, decision-making) during resuscitation scenarios
examples: Residents in Santiago, Chile were facilitated remotely by Stanford instructors in an NRP-scripted AR scenario, each supported by two standardized actors, followed by a five-minute structured debriefing led by the same instructor

constraints: Applied in this article to a single-institution undergraduate US-PIVC simulation programme, not to other educational settings

target_learning_goals: Procedural competence and confidence in ultrasound-guided peripheral intravenous cannulation
examples: The Evaluation section is explicitly organised under the headings Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation and Maintenance, with focus group themes charted into the framework matrix.

description: The article frames producing health education videos for later dissemination within the theory of learning/engagement based on "3 central ideas: relate-create-donate": learning occurs in a social setting (relate), student work is practical and project-based (create), and the project has a real-world focus or use (donate). Social/collaborative setting for the work
Technology used to support deep and collaborative learning

description: The study used the ResusciAnne QCPR Adult simulator (Laerdal Medical, Norway) mounted on a customized cart designed to the organization's specifications. title: Three-chapter asynchronous digital educational training on red flag screening delivered on Talent-LMS
description: A digital educational training built on the Talent-LMS platform to improve physiotherapists' ability to detect serious pathologies. Content was "separated into three chapters, all asynchronously available": an introduction with five 5-minute videos, three clinical vignette modules (internal medicine, oncology, orthopaedics) each with six parts (background document, vignette, quiz, digital background material, solution, forum), and a feedback chapter. Vignette content came from the authors' previous validated vignette work, and module orders were randomised across six combinations.

constraints: The prefabricated platform fixed the module order once set by researchers, so participants could not change it
Only three clinical vignette modules were prepared, and participants requested more vignettes of varying complexity
target_learning_goals: recognising signs and symptoms of serious pathologies (red flags) in musculoskeletal patients
examples: Each module used a distinct format: internal medicine via video podcast, oncology via recorded lecture-style presentation, and orthopaedics via an animated vignette video

citation: Chen Yuqing, Li Jiawen, Liu Yixin, Jiang Fei. (2025). A Novel Student Engagement Analysis of Real Classroom Teaching Using Unified Body Orientation Estimation. Sensors (Basel, Switzerland). https://doi.org/10.3390/s25206421
title: Reconstructed MEBOW dataset for multi-person body orientation estimation
description: The authors reconstruct and extend the MEBOW body-orientation dataset by restoring challenging human instances from COCO and generating pseudo-orientation labels, supplementing complete bounding-box annotations. The result is a dataset that "comprises 225,912 human instances (216,853 for training and 9059 for testing), suitable for multi-person body orientation estimation tasks". It serves as the training and evaluation benchmark for JointBDOE and, per the authors, a more realistic test bed for in-the-wild HBOE research.
requirements: Pseudo-orientation labels generated via the MEBOW method for restored COCO instances
constraints: Includes severe occlusion and low-resolution samples that cause performance degradation relative to the original dataset
target_learners: Researchers in computer vision and classroom analysis
target_learning_goals: Multi-person body orientation estimation supporting student engagement analysis
examples: Used to train and evaluate JointBDOE across YOLOv5 and YOLOv11 backbones at multiple scales

article_title: The effects of stressors on readiness for clinical practice in novice nursing students: a path analysis.
citation: Ozdemir Nur Guven, Dalcali Berna Kokturk, Berse Soner. (2025). The effects of stressors on readiness for clinical practice in novice nursing students: a path analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08079-6
title: Scale of Readiness for Clinical Practice (31 items, four subscales)
description: The Scale of Readiness for Clinical Practice, developed by Avşar and Yıldız, measures first-year nursing students' perceptions of readiness for clinical practice. It is a 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree) with 31 items across four subscales: "Clinical decision-making and practice skills (13 items)", "Ability to provide safety and effective communication (11 items)", "Basic knowledge and holistic care (4 items)", and "Recognition of the practice area (3 items)". Item-mean scores range from 1 to 5; higher scores indicate greater readiness. In this study its Cronbach's α was 0.99.
requirements: Designed for first-year nursing students; used alongside the SINS-T in a cross-sectional survey
constraints: The authors note the extremely high Cronbach's α may reflect item redundancy and suggest a brief version could be designed to reduce the number of items
target_learning_goals: assessing perceived readiness for clinical practice
examples: Administered to 553 first-year nursing students; total item mean score 3.21 ± 1.14

article_title: The effect of reversed screen orientation versus standard orientation in bedside ultrasound on vascular access skill acquisition: a cadaver study.
citation: Köksal Adem, Aygün Ali, Çaltekin İbrahim, Tomakin Mesut, Sarıbaş Mehmet Seyfettin, Özkay İshak, Tokpinar Adem, Baş Orhan. (2025). The effect of reversed screen orientation versus standard orientation in bedside ultrasound on vascular access skill acquisition: a cadaver study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07899-w
title: Integrate reversed screen orientation into novice ultrasound-guided vascular access training to support early skill acquisition
description: The authors recommend exploring reversed screen techniques—flipping the ultrasound image in the transverse plane via the device's 'reverse' function—as a training aid for novices learning USGVA. They write that "The study supports the integration of reversed screen techniques in US training to improve skill acquisition and reduce complication rates in vascular access procedures." The recommendation targets the early learning phase, not routine clinical use.
requirements: Learners must be novices without prior US experience; the reversed image is produced by activating the 'reverse' function on the ultrasound device in the transverse (short-axis) plane.
Theoretical instruction on both orientations, as delivered in the study's 30-minute WFUMB-based sessions, precedes hands-on practice.
constraints: The article states the reversed orientation "was not intended for use in routine clinical settings" and results "are limited to short-term procedural outcomes and cannot be generalized to clinical practice or long-term skill acquisition."
target_learners: final-year medical students (intern doctors) with no prior ultrasound experience
target_learning_goals: ultrasound-guided vascular access procedural skill acquisition
spatial perception and hand-eye coordination during needle insertion
examples: Participants performed femoral vein needle punctures on a cadaver under US guidance, first with their assigned orientation and then with the other, after 30 minutes of theoretical instruction in groups of five.

article_title: Implementation Outcomes of Reusable Learning Objects in Health Care Education Across Three Malaysian Universities: Evaluation Using the RE-AIM Framework.
citation: Lim HM, Teo CH, Lee YK, et al. (2025). Implementation Outcomes of Reusable Learning Objects in Health Care Education Across Three Malaysian Universities: Evaluation Using the RE-AIM Framework. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/63882
title: RE-AIM framework for evaluating e-learning implementation outcomes
description: RE-AIM (Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance) is an implementation science framework the article applies to e-learning resources. Reach is "the access of RLOs by the users"; effectiveness applies the 4-level Kirkpatrick model (reaction and learning measured, behavior and results not measured); adoption counts institutions using RLOs; implementation measures fidelity via completion and nonbounced users; maintenance measures sustained access after project end. The authors conclude the framework provides a comprehensive, objective evaluation that existing models like Kirkpatrick, CIPP, and ADDIE lack.
requirements: Analytics tools (Google Analytics or Moodle monitoring) to capture access patterns, plus pre-post questionnaires for effectiveness measures
constraints: Behavior and results domains were not measured in this study due to limitations in the study design
target_learners: higher education institutions evaluating e-learning resources
target_learning_goals: systematic evaluation of e-learning implementation outcomes
examples: The study measured reach via user numbers, location, and devices; effectiveness via helpfulness ratings and pre-post knowledge and confidence scores; and maintenance via accesses 4 months post-project.
key_sources: Lim HM, Teo CH, Lee YK, et al. (2025). Implementation Outcomes of Reusable Learning Objects in Health Care Education Across Three Malaysian Universities: Evaluation Using the RE-AIM Framework. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/63882

article_title: Toward cross-disciplinary translation of the testing effect: A systematic replication.
citation: Glodowski, K. R., & Hayashi, Y. (2025). Toward cross‐disciplinary translation of the testing effect: A systematic replication. Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis, 58(3), 653–663. https://doi.org/10.1002/jaba.70012
title: Behavior-analytic account of the testing effect: remembering as discriminative behavior shaped by operant contingencies
description: The article translates the testing effect into behavioral principles by conceptualizing remembering as "discriminative behavior at the time of the retrieval", an instance of delayed stimulus control attenuated by the temporal gap. Initial learning occurs during material presentation; testing sets the occasion for discriminated responding that can contact reinforcement, strengthening remembering as an operant. Repeated studying lacks such opportunities for directly reinforced remembering, contrasting with "direct remembering" (White, 2001, 2022; White & Wixted, 1999).
requirements: Retrieval practice must provide opportunities for discriminated responding that can contact reinforcement from the instructor or self
constraints: The article states none of the covert behaviors during repeated studying are directly reinforced as the target discriminative behavior of remembering; mechanisms underlying improved exam scores still need future research
target_learning_goals: long-term retention and recall of course material
examples: The study operationalized retrieval practice as 5- or 10-question fill-in-the-blank quizzes administered quasirandomly across quiz class periods in an Advanced Conditioning and Learning course.
key_sources: Glodowski, K. R., & Hayashi, Y. (2025). Toward cross‐disciplinary translation of the testing effect: A systematic replication. Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis, 58(3), 653–663. https://doi.org/10.1002/jaba.70012

citation: Greisberger A, Klinger M, Dopona A, Riegler M, Müller V, Wilhelm A, Wess T, Nägele A, Aftenberger H, Kurz K, Seebacher B. (2025). Recommendations for a core assessment set for neurological physiotherapy entry-level education in Austria - a multistage process including a Delphi study. title: RECOGNISING/APPLYING categorisation framework mapping intended level of student engagement with an assessment onto cognitive and psychomotor learning-outcome levels
description: The article adapts the Academy of Neurologic Physical Therapy's two-level framework to the Austrian context: RECOGNISING means "students are familiar with the assessment through exposure", while APPLYING additionally means students "can appropriately select, perform, and interpret the assessment in specific situations". The authors map RECOGNISING to levels 1–2 of Bloom's cognitive taxonomy and APPLYING to Bloom levels 1–4 and levels 1–2 of Dave's psychomotor taxonomy, so the categories anchor learning objectives and their assessment in each programme.
requirements: Assessments must first be assigned to the categories by consensus before learning objectives and evaluation can be aligned
constraints: The framework was tailored to the Austrian entry-level bachelor's context and to the seven defined scope diagnoses
target_learners: entry-level physiotherapy students in bachelor's degree programmes
target_learning_goals: familiarity with standardised assessments
ability to select, perform and interpret standardised assessments
examples: Following implementation in theoretical training, students are evaluated on familiarity with RECOGNISING assessments and on selecting, performing and interpreting APPLYING assessments

citation: Scott IA, Shaw T, Slade C, Wan TT, Barmanray R, Coorey C, Johnson SLJ, Bell L, Herd M, Sullivan CM. (2025). Proposing core competencies for physicians in using artificial intelligence tools in clinical practice. Internal Medicine Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/imj.70112
title: Require and interpret factsheets or model cards before adopting an AI tool, and avoid tools lacking such information
description: The article recommends that physicians request and interpret a factsheet or model card detailing an AI tool's function and context, training datasets, model performance, bias evaluation, failure mode analyses, safety assessment, technical architecture, data storage, prompt engineering, user testing and conditions of use. It states plainly: 'Tools lacking such information should be avoided.' This supports transparency-based appraisal of clinical suitability and Quintuple Aim impact.

Physicians must be able to interpret the performance metrics these documents report
constraints: The article notes standardised appraisal guides for LLMs are yet to be developed
target_learning_goals: critical appraisal of AI tools
procurement decision-making
examples: The article lists what a model card should detail, including bias evaluation, failure mode analyses and conditions of use

article_title: Study on the improvement of image interpretation skill of non-radiology residents based on an image case database in gastroenterology department.
citation: He Xiayin, Li Yangsheng, Gao Chengcheng, Zhu Xiangwen, Xia Qianqian, Han Zhijiang, Zhu Jiying. (2025). Study on the improvement of image interpretation skill of non-radiology residents based on an image case database in gastroenterology department. BMC Medical Education 25:936. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07537-5
title: Pair case-database learning with real-time platform supervision and task deadlines to accelerate and sustain residents' study
description: The article attributes part of the experimental group's advantage to the platform's management backend, which let teachers observe progress in real time and prompted completion of learning tasks. It states that after a prompt from the teaching secretary "the pace of learning tasks for both the experimental and control groups notably increased" and concludes that "an effective supervision and management mechanism was fundamental to enhancing the image interpretation skills of non-radiology residents". The recommendation is grounded in the authors' interpretation and cited literature rather than a directly manipulated factor.
requirements: A database platform with backend progress tracking, assigned task deadlines one week in advance, and a staff member who monitors completion and reminds learners
constraints: The supervision effect is an authors' interpretation of the observed score patterns, not a separately tested condition; backend statistics showed experimental residents logged in 30–45 minutes daily against a 30-minute minimum
target_learners: residents with busy clinical schedules studying in fragmented time
target_learning_goals: sustained daily engagement with image-interpretation practice
examples: The teaching secretary reminded experimental-group residents to complete learning tasks promptly after the mid-term assessment while encouraging control-group residents to study diligently

scientific research ideas
experimental skills

article_title: Acceptability and applicability of using virtual reality for training mass casualty incidents- a mixed method study.
citation: Heldring Sara, Jirwe Maria, Wihlborg Jonas, Lindström Veronica. (2025). Acceptability and applicability of using virtual reality for training mass casualty incidents- a mixed method study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07319-z
title: Critical realism and realist inquiry as a framework for explaining how and why VR training works for MCI preparedness
description: The study adopts critical realism as its theoretical approach, carried out through a realist inquiry approach. As the article states, "Realist inquiry concerns what works for whom, under what conditions, how, and why by focusing on relationships between contexts, mechanisms, and outcomes." Context covers fixed settings like VR equipment and variable human factors such as cultures and trained behaviors; mechanisms operate at a psychological level to explain how and why people respond to interventions; outcomes are the intended and unintended impacts of the intervention. The authors use this framework to structure the discussion of VR's acceptability and applicability for MCI training.
requirements: Multiple data sources (quantitative and qualitative) integrated during discussion, as in the study's embedded mixed-methods design
constraints: The framework's strength, per the article, is explaining how and why interventions work or fail in different contexts and for different people; it does not by itself establish effectiveness
target_learners: healthcare professionals training as first responders to mass casualty incidents
target_learning_goals: understanding how and why VR-based MCI training works, for whom, and under what conditions
examples: The discussion is organized under the realist inquiry headings of context (technical features, realism), mechanisms (satisfaction, feeling safe to make mistakes), and outcomes (preparedness, physical symptoms)
key_sources: Heldring Sara, Jirwe Maria, Wihlborg Jonas, Lindström Veronica. (2025). Acceptability and applicability of using virtual reality for training mass casualty incidents- a mixed method study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07319-z

article_title: Teacher-Student relationships and academic grades in Chinese high schools: the roles of perceived teaching quality and students' mental health symptoms.
citation: Chen Xiao hui, Bailey Richard Peter, Xie Hong bin, Samsudin Nadia. (2025). Teacher–Student relationships and academic grades in Chinese high schools: the roles of perceived teaching quality and students’ mental health symptoms. BMC Psychology, Volume 13, Electronic Location ID 530. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-025-02843-5
title: Integrated conceptual framework linking relational, instructional, and psychological factors to academic grades
description: The article proposes an integrated conceptual framework (Fig. 1) in which teacher–student relationships, students' perceived teaching quality, and mental health symptoms jointly relate to academic grades. Perceived teaching quality is positioned as an indirect pathway linking TSRs to grades, consistent with social cognitive theory's view that relational experiences shape cognitive appraisals of instruction. Mental health symptoms are positioned as a moderator of the teaching quality–grades link. As the article states, "By simultaneously considering relational, instructional, and psychological factors, this study aims to provide preliminary insights into the variables associated with academic grades in high-pressure educational environments."
requirements: Validated self-report measures of TSRs, perceived teaching quality, and mental health symptoms, plus academic grades from official school administrative records
constraints: The cross-sectional design limits the ability to infer causal relationships among the constructs
target_learners: Chinese high school students aged 16–18 in high-stakes academic contexts
target_learning_goals: Understanding factors associated with academic grades in high-pressure educational environments
examples: The framework was tested with SEM on 332 Chinese high school students from a homogeneous disadvantaged subsample, with grades from three monthly tests.
key_sources: Chen Xiao hui, Bailey Richard Peter, Xie Hong bin, Samsudin Nadia. (2025). Teacher–Student relationships and academic grades in Chinese high schools: the roles of perceived teaching quality and students’ mental health symptoms. title: Regional pattern of telesimulation challenges and matching solutions across seven world regions
description: Table 1 of the review organizes challenges to telesimulation in medicine and their solutions by geographical region, pairing each region's obstacles with corresponding remedies. For example, African regions face "Serious financial constraints, poor infrastructure, and a lack of qualified teachers" met by international alliances and mobile simulation units, while South Asia's large student populations, unequal infrastructure development, and cultural resistance are met by targeted teacher training and expandable simulation programs. The table spans African, South Asia, South East Asia, Latin America, Middle East, America, and Europe regions.
requirements: Solutions must be matched to the specific regional challenges identified, such as shared resource centers for South East Asia or public-private cooperation for Latin America
constraints: The pattern is region-specific; the review states each LMIC faces unique obstacles
target_learners: Healthcare professionals and trainees across African, South Asian, South East Asian, Latin American, Middle Eastern, American, and European regions
target_learning_goals: Sustaining simulation-based medical training under regional resource and infrastructure constraints
examples: The review's Table 1 pairs, for instance, Middle Eastern political instability and regulatory variations with regional stability and harmonizing regulations

article_title: The Effect of "Online-Simulation-Bedside" Three-Step Teaching Method in Team Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Skills Training of Emergency Department and Critical Care Nursing Interns-An Analysis Based on Kirkpatrick Model.
citation: Liu Huan, Huang Hui, Li Miaoya, Mao Ping, Zhang Aidi, Sun Yanting, Liu Zhaoxun, Tao Hong, Zhao Sha, Xia Yuting, Zhou Jiandang, Liu Jinxin. (2025). The Effect of “Online–Simulation–Bedside” Three-Step Teaching Method in Team Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Skills Training of Emergency Department and Critical Care Nursing Interns—An Analysis Based on Kirkpatrick Model. Journal of Nursing Management. https://doi.org/10.1155/jonm/8624274
title: Schedule regular team CPR retraining to counter skill decay after initial training
description: Because retention of training effectiveness declines over time, the article recommends that nursing managers conduct periodic retraining. The article states that “in order to promote the retention of CPR skills, nursing managers can regularly conduct team CPR retraining for nursing interns,” citing evidence that reviewing or refresher courses improve CPR skill retention. The article also notes the optimal repetition timing is still unclear, with suggested intervals ranging from monthly to 18–24 months.
requirements: An organizational commitment from nursing management to schedule and deliver periodic retraining sessions
constraints: The article states the optimal timing for repetition is still unclear; suggested retraining intervals in the cited literature range from monthly training to 18–24 months
target_learners: nursing interns in acute and critical care departments
target_learning_goals: retention of team CPR skills
examples: The discussion cites studies using refresher courses, rolling refresher training, and monthly interval training to improve CPR skill retention
key_sources: Liu Huan, Huang Hui, Li Miaoya, Mao Ping, Zhang Aidi, Sun Yanting, Liu Zhaoxun, Tao Hong, Zhao Sha, Xia Yuting, Zhou Jiandang, Liu Jinxin. (2025). The Effect of “Online–Simulation–Bedside” Three-Step Teaching Method in Team Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Skills Training of Emergency Department and Critical Care Nursing Interns—An Analysis Based on Kirkpatrick Model. Journal of Nursing Management. https://doi.org/10.1155/jonm/8624274

article_title: A Standardized Clinical Case-Based Assessment for Evaluating Medical Students' Oral Spanish Communication Skills.
citation: Mai AM, Molina RL, Aguayo-Mazzucato C, Diaz AA, Canenguez K, Cheung HC, Graupera NR, Martel B, Bonilla S. (2025). A Standardized Clinical Case-Based Assessment for Evaluating Medical Students' Oral Spanish Communication Skills. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11518
title: Recruit standardized patients with diverse backgrounds and compensate professional SPs to enhance realism and representativeness
description: Based on the limitation that volunteer SPs were mostly physicians or medical students already serving as teaching assistants, the authors recommend broadening SP recruitment. They state: "we recommend recruiting SPs with more diverse backgrounds and, when possible, compensating professional SPs to enhance the realism and representativeness of the encounters." This principle addresses the gap between the volunteer SP pool and the patient demographics students are likely to encounter in their careers.
requirements: Funding or institutional support for compensating professional standardized patients
Recruitment channels reaching candidates with diverse backgrounds
constraints: The original implementation lacked funding for hiring professional SPs, so volunteers were recruited without compensation or comprehensive training
target_learners: medical and dental students in Medical Spanish courses
target_learning_goals: communication skills with linguistically and culturally diverse patients
examples: The Fall 2021 assessment used seven volunteer native-level Spanish-speaking SPs: five physicians and two medical students, recruited via hospital-wide and university-wide listserv emails
key_sources: Mai AM, Molina RL, Aguayo-Mazzucato C, Diaz AA, Canenguez K, Cheung HC, Graupera NR, Martel B, Bonilla S. (2025). A Standardized Clinical Case-Based Assessment for Evaluating Medical Students' Oral Spanish Communication Skills. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11518

article_title: How a Preschool Intervention Affected High School Outcomes: Longitudinal Pathways in a Randomized-Controlled Trial.
citation: Bierman Karen L., Heinrichs Brenda S., Welsh Janet A., Jones Damon E., Crowley D. Max. (2025). How a Preschool Intervention Affected High School Outcomes: Longitudinal Pathways in a Randomized‐Controlled Trial. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.14235
title: Head Start REDI: a multi-component preschool SEL enrichment program
description: REDI enriched Head Start classrooms with an evidence-based SEL curriculum (Preschool PATHS) providing weekly lessons in emotional understanding, social skills, self-control, and problem-solving; a coordinated interactive reading program using two books per week to extend PATHS themes and strengthen oral language; sound games and alphabet centers for phonemic awareness and print knowledge. Teachers received "4 days of workshop training and weekly mentoring visits", and parents received weekly PATHS handouts and three DVDs. Teachers delivered most planned lessons (M = 86%).
requirements: Requires Head Start classrooms using a whole-child curriculum and teachers receiving workshop training plus weekly mentoring visits to support high-fidelity implementation.
constraints: The intervention is multi-component, limiting attribution of effects to specific components; specific links between program components and intervention gains remain speculative per the authors.
target_learners: Preschool children (mean age 4.49) from low-income families attending Head Start
target_learning_goals: Social-emotional competence, emotion knowledge, oral language, print knowledge, phonemic awareness
examples: In the RCT, 44 Head Start classrooms in 26 centers were stratified and randomized to REDI enhancements or usual practice.
key_sources: Bierman Karen L., Heinrichs Brenda S., Welsh Janet A., Jones Damon E., Crowley D. Max. (2025). How a Preschool Intervention Affected High School Outcomes: Longitudinal Pathways in a Randomized‐Controlled Trial. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.14235

article_title: Evaluation of health care providers' ability to identify patient-ventilator triggering asynchrony in intensive care unit: a translational observational study in China.
citation: Liu Shengjun, Zhao Zhangyi, Chen Xiangyu, Chi Yi, Yuan Siyi, Cai Fuhong, Song Zhangwei, Ma Yue, He Huaiwu, Su Longxiang, Long Yun. (2025). Evaluation of health care providers’ ability to identify patient-ventilator triggering asynchrony in intensive care unit: a translational observational study in China. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06638-5
title: Remote-VentlateView platform for automated identification of patient-ventilator asynchrony
description: A remote mechanical ventilation visualization network system with an automatic recognition algorithm for patient-ventilator asynchrony, developed by the authors' team. The system "can accurately and quickly identify several types of PVA in real time and provide real-time feedback through the cloud platform", using rule-based decision logic on pressure-time, flow-time and volume-time waveforms (e.g., a flow-velocity deflection amplitude above 5 L/min and duration above 0.12 s flags an ineffective trigger). In this study the platform recognized all 8 validated asynchrony waveform sets, and the authors suggest automated assistance and simulation tools may help teach PVA identification skills.
requirements: Ventilator waveform data (pressure-time, flow rate-time, volume-time curves, and esophageal pressure where applicable) streamed to the cloud platform
constraints: Algorithm thresholds (e.g., 5 L/min amplitude, 0.12 s duration) are pre-set values; the article reports platform performance only on the 8 study waveform sets in this paper, with prior reported accuracies of 97%, 89% and 79% attributed to Su and colleagues' earlier study
target_learning_goals: recognizing patient-ventilator triggering asynchrony from ventilator waveforms
examples: In this study the platform recognized all 8 sets of patient-ventilator asynchrony waveforms, while no human participant recognized all 8 sets
key_sources: Liu Shengjun, Zhao Zhangyi, Chen Xiangyu, Chi Yi, Yuan Siyi, Cai Fuhong, Song Zhangwei, Ma Yue, He Huaiwu, Su Longxiang, Long Yun. (2025). Evaluation of health care providers’ ability to identify patient-ventilator triggering asynchrony in intensive care unit: a translational observational study in China. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06638-5

article_title: Understanding Community Health Care Through Problem-Based Learning With Real-Patient Videos: Single-Arm Pre-Post Mixed Methods Study.
citation: Kiyoshi Shikino, Kazuyo Yamauchi, Nobuyuki Araki, Ikuo Shimizu, Hajime Kasai, Tomoko Tsukamoto, Hiroshi Tajima, Yu Li, Misaki Onodera, Shoichi Ito. (2025). Understanding Community Health Care Through Problem-Based Learning With Real-Patient Videos: Single-Arm Pre-Post Mixed Methods Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/68743
title: Real-patient videos depicting community and home health care scenarios
description: Scripted real-patient videos of 3-5 minutes depicting community health care situations, from initial assessments in a community hospital to follow-up in-home visits, produced with medical education experts, community health care professionals, and audiovisual specialists. Real patients participated "under strict ethical guidelines to ensure authenticity and respect for patient privacy." Students viewed the videos collectively on shared screens before facilitated small-group discussion.
requirements: Patient consent obtained for video use; students instructed to adhere to confidentiality guidelines
constraints: Producing high-quality real-patient videos requires substantial time, resources, and collaboration, which may limit the feasibility of widespread adoption
target_learners: fourth-year medical students in a preclerkship/clerkship transition course
target_learning_goals: understanding of community health care systems, home health care, and rural clinician roles
examples: Videos prepared with Multimedia Appendices including a tutor guide, patient information sheets, and tasks; one case involved a patient with diabetes and severe lower leg edema transitioning from acute to chronic care and home visit services
key_sources: Kiyoshi Shikino, Kazuyo Yamauchi, Nobuyuki Araki, Ikuo Shimizu, Hajime Kasai, Tomoko Tsukamoto, Hiroshi Tajima, Yu Li, Misaki Onodera, Shoichi Ito. (2025). Understanding Community Health Care Through Problem-Based Learning With Real-Patient Videos: Single-Arm Pre-Post Mixed Methods Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/68743

article_title: Use of virtual simulation for regenerative endodontic training: randomized controlled trial.
citation: Hu Jia, Wang Xiuqing, Chen Ruonan, Lu Guoying, Zhang Ming, Huang Xiaojing. (2025). Use of virtual simulation for regenerative endodontic training: randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06808-5
title: REPs-VS: a web-deployable virtual simulation teaching platform for regenerative endodontic procedures
description: The REPs-VS platform is a virtual simulation teaching module built with "Unity3D, Visual Studio, ARKit, DirectX, and Figma" that lets students interview a virtual patient, make diagnostic and treatment decisions, and perform interactive virtual REPs operations through a web-based clicking interface. It offers learning and examination modes, is deployable as web pages, standalone executables, or Apps on Windows, Android, and iOS, and a network version is publicly accessible on the National Virtual Simulation Experiment Teaching Center (iLAB-X). An accompanying educational administration platform adds attendance, administration, problem communication, and VS practicing and examination systems.
requirements: Requires the Eclipse development environment and MySQL database for the management platform hosted on the university's internal servers
constraints: Due to the lack of haptic feedback, students are unable to experience differences in hardness between enamel and dentin or interferences from soft tissues, saliva, and patient movements
target_learners: off-campus learners using the iLAB-X network version
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning for regenerative endodontic procedures
REP operative steps and treatment-efficacy evaluation
doctor-patient communication
examples: The treatment protocol script was designed based on the revised 2021 Clinical Considerations for a Regenerative Procedure by the American Association of Endodontics, for a patient with chronic periapical periodontitis and an immature incisor.
key_sources: Hu Jia, Wang Xiuqing, Chen Ruonan, Lu Guoying, Zhang Ming, Huang Xiaojing. (2025). Use of virtual simulation for regenerative endodontic training: randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06808-5

article_title: Youth experiences in gender-sexuality alliances predict academic engagement but not disaffection through social-emotional wellbeing.
citation: Poteat, V. P., Calzo, J. P., Yoshikawa, H., Kellogg, D., Marx, R. A., Richburg, A., & Lipkin, A. (2025). Youth experiences in gender–sexuality alliances predict academic engagement but not disaffection through social–emotional wellbeing. Child Development, 96, 847–864. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.14209
title: Relational developmental systems paradigm as a framework for understanding how settings such as clubs promote positive youth outcomes
description: The article draws on the relational developmental systems (RDS) paradigm as a meta-theory for youth development to explain how settings such as GSAs may promote positive youth outcomes. The article states that "RDS stipulates that youth thrive when they are in environments that provide support and resources that match their needs and strengths." The article applies this framework to argue that GSAs feature provisions that facilitate youth development, including affirming students' diverse identities, providing leadership opportunities, and having adult advisors.
requirements: The framework is applied to settings that provide support and resources matching youth's needs and strengths, such as school clubs with peer support, leadership opportunities, and access to supportive adults.
constraints: The article applies RDS as a conceptual framework rather than testing it directly; the study's findings are consistent with but do not prove the framework.
target_learners: LGBTQ+ youth in secondary school GSAs
target_learning_goals: Social–emotional wellbeing
Academic engagement
key_sources: Poteat, V. P., Calzo, J. P., Yoshikawa, H., Kellogg, D., Marx, R. A., Richburg, A., & Lipkin, A. (2025). Youth experiences in gender–sexuality alliances predict academic engagement but not disaffection through social–emotional wellbeing. Child Development, 96, 847–864. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.14209

article_title: Disputing and challenging academic procrastination behaviors in students using REBT approach.
citation: Amoke CV, Ede MO, Mawila-Chauke D, Obeagu IE. (2025). Disputing and challenging academic procrastination behaviors in students using REBT approach. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000041725
title: Rational emotive behavior therapy (REBT) as a framework for disputing irrational beliefs underlying academic procrastination
description: REBT is an explanatory and therapeutic framework holding that "people contribute to their own psychological issues" through irrational beliefs, and that humans are "born capable of both rational or “straight” thinking and irrational or “crooked” thinking." Its goal is "to dispute and challenge irrational and dysfunctional thoughts and replace them with adaptive and functional thoughts." In this study the framework is operationalized as a six-step ABCDEF group protocol (activating events, beliefs, consequences, disputation, new effective beliefs, feelings) applied to academic procrastination.
requirements: Delivery in therapy sessions following systematic steps, including cognitive, emotive, and behavioral techniques and trained therapists
constraints: The article notes little was known about REBT's impact on procrastination among in-school adolescents prior to this study
target_learning_goals: reducing academic procrastination behaviors
replacing irrational beliefs with rational ones
examples: The study's 12-session program moved students through identifying activating events, disputing beliefs, replacing negative self-statements, and termination.
key_sources: Amoke CV, Ede MO, Mawila-Chauke D, Obeagu IE. (2025). Disputing and challenging academic procrastination behaviors in students using REBT approach. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000041725

article_title: Disputing and challenging academic procrastination behaviors in students using REBT approach.
citation: Amoke CV, Ede MO, Mawila-Chauke D, Obeagu IE. (2025). Disputing and challenging academic procrastination behaviors in students using REBT approach. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000041725
title: Researcher-developed 12-session REBT treatment package for academic procrastination
description: A manualized REBT treatment package created by the researchers "to assist in-school adolescents with academic procrastination." It contains "detailed information about the 6 weeks of intensive treatment, including timeline, procedures, objectives, activities, duration, and evaluation processes," delivered as 40-minute sessions twice weekly for 6 weeks (12 sessions total). Sessions progress from familiarization and identifying procrastination factors, through identifying and disputing irrational beliefs and self-talk, to termination. Techniques include cognitive restructuring, rational emotive imagery, role playing, humor, and direct teaching.
requirements: Certified school counselors trained in REBT application as therapists
A daily hour-long debriefing meeting for 5 days to prepare therapists on the ABCD steps
constraints: Developed and evaluated specifically with secondary-school adolescents in Udenu Education Zone, Nigeria
target_learning_goals: reducing academic procrastination
disputing irrational beliefs about academic tasks
examples: Sessions 8 and 9 trained participants to modify negative self-statements using cognitive reframe, role playing (teaching others), and forceful self-statements.
key_sources: Amoke CV, Ede MO, Mawila-Chauke D, Obeagu IE. (2025). Disputing and challenging academic procrastination behaviors in students using REBT approach. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000041725

article_title: Impact of a change from A–F grading to honors/pass/fail grading on academic performance at Yonsei University College of Medicine in Korea: a cross-sectional serial mediation analysis.
citation: Kim Min-Kyeong, Kim Hae Won. (2024). Impact of a change from A–F grading to honors/pass/fail grading on academic performance at Yonsei University College of Medicine in Korea: a cross-sectional serial mediation analysis. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2024.21.20
title: Reducing the number of grades and eliminating rank-based grading may support a learning environment that sustains intrinsic motivation and performance
description: Based on the observed benefits of moving from a 13-category norm-referenced A–F system to criterion-referenced honors/pass/fail grading, the article concludes that "Reducing the number of grades and eliminating rank-based grading might have created an affirming learning environment that fulfills basic psychological needs and reinforces the intrinsic motivation linked to academic performance." The recommendation is grounded in the serial mediation finding rather than a manipulated test of grading design.
requirements: Assessment should shift to criterion-referenced standards so students are compared against a clear standard rather than against the performance of others
constraints: Evidence comes from one cohort per grading system at a single center; the authors call for further studies on effects on learning and mental health and on long-term effects during clerkship and residency
target_learning_goals: sustaining intrinsic motivation
maintaining academic performance under reduced grading differentiation
examples: Yonsei University College of Medicine changed core mandatory courses to a 3-tiered honors/pass/fail system and elective courses to a 2-tiered pass/fail system in 2014, the first such attempt among 40 medical schools in Korea
key_sources: Kim Min-Kyeong, Kim Hae Won. (2024). Impact of a change from A–F grading to honors/pass/fail grading on academic performance at Yonsei University College of Medicine in Korea: a cross-sectional serial mediation analysis. article_title: The battle of question formats: a comparative study of retrieval practice using very short answer questions and multiple choice questions.
citation: van Wijk EV, de Jonge M, van Blankenstein FM, Janse RJ, Langers AMJ. (2024). The battle of question formats: a comparative study of retrieval practice using very short answer questions and multiple choice questions. BMC Medical Education, 24:1547. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06538-0
title: Retrieval effort hypothesis and transfer-appropriate processing as competing accounts of question-format effects in retrieval practice
description: The article frames two theoretical accounts for why question format might matter. The retrieval effort hypothesis "states that retrieval requiring greater cognitive effort proves more beneficial for learning than easy retrieval with prompts or cues," predicting an advantage for effortful VSAQs. Transfer-appropriate processing holds that "learning and knowledge retention are improved if the type of processing used during retrieval matches the type of processing used during encoding." The study's null interaction challenges TAP, and the null format effect qualifies the retrieval effort account.
requirements: Both accounts presuppose that retrieval practice (testing) itself enhances long-term retention, which the article treats as established by prior research
constraints: The study found no support for a format-matching (TAP) advantage and no significant practice-format effect, so both theories receive only qualified support in this real-life setting without feedback
target_learning_goals: long-term knowledge retention
recall of lecture content
examples: The study tested TAP by giving students congruent and incongruent practice–final test format pairings and assessing the interaction
key_sources: van Wijk EV, de Jonge M, van Blankenstein FM, Janse RJ, Langers AMJ. (2024). The battle of question formats: a comparative study of retrieval practice using very short answer questions and multiple choice questions. BMC Medical Education, 24:1547. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06538-0

article_title: Short-term cognitive learning outcomes in team-based learning: is the permanent team important?
citation: Heber Stefan, Wagner-Menghin Michaela, Volf Ivo, Slak Rupnik Marjan, Schmid Diethart, Marz Richard, Fischer Michael J.M. (2024). Short-term cognitive learning outcomes in team-based learning: is the permanent team important? Medical Education Online, 29(1). https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2024.2397864
title: For knowledge acquisition, TBL team formation can be relaxed rather than strictly controlling team familiarity
description: A practice point drawn from the article's randomized controlled trial: because permanent and temporary teams produced nearly identical domain knowledge test scores, forming TBL groups for knowledge acquisition need not control team familiarity. The authors write that "a more relaxed approach can be applied to the formation of TBL learning groups", while still assigning students rather than letting them self-enroll.
requirements: Team membership is assigned rather than self-chosen; the article states students should not self-enroll.
constraints: Applies to short-term cognitive learning outcomes; the article states team composition may influence outcomes beyond domain knowledge acquisition, which requires further investigation.
target_learners: second-term undergraduate medical students in large-enrollment TBL courses
target_learning_goals: domain knowledge acquisition in TBL sessions
examples: In the trial, five students per group were randomly assigned to permanent teams and five to temporary teams reassembled per problem via a 6 × 6 Latin squares design, and dkTest scores did not differ between arms.
key_sources: Heber Stefan, Wagner-Menghin Michaela, Volf Ivo, Slak Rupnik Marjan, Schmid Diethart, Marz Richard, Fischer Michael J.M. (2024). Short-term cognitive learning outcomes in team-based learning: is the permanent team important? Medical Education Online, 29(1). https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2024.2397864

article_title: A novel step-by-step teaching method improves training outcomes in transvaginal ultrasound for postgraduate reproductive medicine students: an exploratory randomized controlled study.
citation: Li Xin, Li Hao, Zhang HuiXia, Li Gang. (2024). A novel step-by-step teaching method improves training outcomes in transvaginal ultrasound for postgraduate reproductive medicine students: an exploratory randomized controlled study. BMC Medical Education 24:1270. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06257-6
title: Reproductive vaginal ultrasound training questionnaire
description: A questionnaire designed for this study to compare the two groups' evaluations of their teachers and their overall satisfaction with the training. It covers "six aspects—teaching ability, teaching methods, medical ethics, teaching attitude, responsibility to students, and their own theoretical and operational abilities", each scored on a 0 to 10 point scale, with satisfaction responses categorized into very satisfied, generally satisfied, and dissatisfied.
requirements: Administered to postgraduate students in both groups after the training period
constraints: A questionnaire designed for this study, not a validated generic instrument
target_learning_goals: Evaluation of teaching quality and training satisfaction in reproductive ultrasound education
examples: Used to detect significantly higher ratings of teaching ability and teaching methods in the SBS group, and the 96.0% vs. 72.0% satisfaction difference that was not statistically significant.

article_title: Virtual reality-based simulation learning on geriatric oral health care for nursing students: a pilot study.
citation: Lin Pei-Chao, Wung Shu-Fen, Lin Pei-Chen, Lin Yi-Ching, Lin Cheng-Yu, Huang Hsiao-Ling. (2024). Virtual reality-based simulation learning on geriatric oral health care for nursing students: a pilot study. BMC Oral Health 24, Article 627. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-024-04249-y
title: Repeat VR-based oral health training at least twice to improve attitudes and behavioral intention
description: The article concludes that "A single dose of training may be sufficient in improving nursing students' knowledge and self-efficacy of geriatric oral health. However, repeated training at least twice may be minimally required to improve nursing students' attitudes toward geriatric oral health and intention to assist oral health care for older adults." Attitude and intention improvements emerged only after the second round of training delivered two weeks after the first.
requirements: Two VR training sessions scheduled two weeks apart, each with the same training system and teaching content
constraints: In this pilot, attitude and intention effects were not observed after only one round of training
target_learning_goals: positive attitudes toward geriatric oral health care
intention to assist oral health care for older adults
examples: The experimental group received the VR-based simulation training twice, at two weeks and four weeks after baseline, with post-tests after each session

article_title: Self-assessment, and not continuous training, improves basic open suturing skills.
citation: Hillemans Vera, Buyne Otmar, de Blaauw Ivo, Botden Sanne M.B.I., Verhoeven Bas H., Joosten Maja. (2024). Self-assessment, and not continuous training, improves basic open suturing skills. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2024.2374101
title: Use reflection before practice with a self-assessment form before suturing training and tests to raise students' starting skill level
description: This principle holds that studying a self-assessment form before executing a task induces reflection before practice, letting trainees identify and focus on the most important task components. In the study, the self-assessment group "studied a self-assessment form before starting the pre-test resulting in reflection before practice" and completed tasks faster, with shorter distance and higher composite scores at the start of the learning curve. The authors conclude reflection before practice and self-assessment during training "resulted in a higher starting level at the beginning of the learning curve".
requirements: A self-assessment form (in this study a Competency (self-)Assessment Tool with four objective subtasks) must be studied before each training session and before each test, and completed after each session and test.
constraints: The article states the baseline skills level of the self-assessment group was not directly measured, so baseline bias could not be completely excluded.
At the after-test no significant between-group differences remained for three of four tasks, so the benefit is framed as raising the start of the learning curve, not end performance.
target_learners: Medical students before and during an eight-week surgical rotation with basic suturing course experience but fewer than five prior sutures
target_learning_goals: Basic open suturing skills: knot tying by hand, transcutaneous suture, vertical mattress (Donati) suture, continuous intracutaneous suture
examples: Students studied a CAT self-assessment form before each weekly supervised 30-minute training session and before each test, and completed the form after each session and test.
key_sources: Hillemans Vera, Buyne Otmar, de Blaauw Ivo, Botden Sanne M.B.I., Verhoeven Bas H., Joosten Maja. (2024). Self-assessment, and not continuous training, improves basic open suturing skills. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2024.2374101

article_title: Optimizing resident training in obstetrics and gynecology: a new perspective on the refined Peyton four-step teaching method.
citation: Zhang Dandan, Wang Xiaoxue, Chen Xueting, Lou Yingze, Zhou Xin, Zhang Kai. (2024). Optimizing resident training in obstetrics and gynecology: a new perspective on the refined Peyton four-step teaching method. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05851-y
title: Refined Peyton Four-Step Teaching Model combining video demonstration, interactive deconstruction, peer group practice, and PEARLS-based assessment
description: A refinement of the Peyton four-step method (demonstration, deconstruction, comprehension, performance) for OB-GYN basic skill training. The article states its adaptation "incorporates video instruction, peer learning, and Promoting Excellence and Reflective Learning in Simulation (PEARLS) feedback, creating a synergistic and complementary approach". Step one adds pre-course videos for self-paced study, step two adds interactive questioning, step three uses teams of 3–4 residents rotating recitation, demonstration, and scoring roles, and step four adds independent performance with PEARLS feedback and a mastery standard.
requirements: Instructor training conducted prior to implementation, standardizing each skill's specific operation steps and integrating patient communication skills and medical humanities
A standardized teaching process and the Clinical Basic Skill Operation Scoring Form established before delivery
Learning resources such as instructional videos, lecture slides, and clear assessment criteria uploaded to a teaching management platform
constraints: Evaluated only in first-year OB-GYN residents at a single institution; the authors call for multi-center studies across specialties and contexts
target_learning_goals: acquisition and retention of clinical basic procedural skills
patient communication and professional behavior
self-directed learning
examples: The 2022 cohort of 57 residents completed 16 procedures over eight weeks (48 hours total) under the refined four-step process, compared with 59 residents under traditional simulation-based instruction in 2021
key_sources: Zhang Dandan, Wang Xiaoxue, Chen Xueting, Lou Yingze, Zhou Xin, Zhang Kai. (2024). Optimizing resident training in obstetrics and gynecology: a new perspective on the refined Peyton four-step teaching method. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05851-y

article_title: A comparison of rapid cycle deliberate practice and traditional reflective debriefing on interprofessional team performance.
citation: Colman Nora, Wiltrakis Susan M., Holmes Sherita, Hwu Ruth, Iyer Srikant, Goodwin Nandranie, Mathai Claire, Gillespie Scott, Hebbar Kiran B. (2024). A comparison of rapid cycle deliberate practice and traditional reflective debriefing on interprofessional team performance. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05101-1
title: Reflective Deliberate Practice (RDP): a combined debriefing framework pairing deliberate practice with reflective debriefing
description: Reflective Deliberate Practice (RDP) is a proposed synergistic debriefing framework that combines RCDP's focus on the 'what' with TRD's focus on the 'why'. The article proposes it after observing that learners in each arm wanted the alternate approach: TRD learners wanted practice opportunities, while RCDP learners wanted to reflect and challenge assumptions. RDP would let learners "practice in action and reflect; a focus on the 'what' (RCDP) and 'why' (TRD)", with RCDP conducted alongside interval or final cumulative reflective debriefing. It is proposed for future study, not tested in this trial.
requirements: Requires combining RCDP's repetitive practice with immediate feedback and TRD's reflective discussion so learners can both practice in action and reflect
constraints: Not yet empirically tested; the article states additional research comparing single-methodology debriefing versus RDP is necessary, including effects on retention and clinical application
target_learners: Interprofessional emergency department teams including physicians, fellows, nurses, medical technicians, paramedics, and respiratory therapists
target_learning_goals: Teamwork skills such as role clarity, closed loop communication, and shared mental model in resuscitation care
examples: Supplementary Table 2 provides an example of RDP applied as RCDP with interval TRD; the article also cites Eppich et al.'s 'microdebriefing' concept of coupling deliberate learning with feedback and reflection
key_sources: Colman Nora, Wiltrakis Susan M., Holmes Sherita, Hwu Ruth, Iyer Srikant, Goodwin Nandranie, Mathai Claire, Gillespie Scott, Hebbar Kiran B. (2024). article_title: SIMPEDVR: using VR in teaching pediatric emergencies to undergraduate students-a pilot study.
citation: Savino Sandro, Mormando Giulia, Saia Giorgia, Da Dalt Liviana, Chang Todd P., Bressan Silvia. (2023). SIMPEDVR: using VR in teaching pediatric emergencies to undergraduate students—a pilot study. European Journal of Pediatrics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00431-023-05254-z
title: ResuscitationVR pediatric emergency simulation with immersive audio and character interaction
description: ResuscitationVR (i3 Simulations, London, UK) is a VR simulation program, localized to Italian for this pilot, in which the student plays the emergency department physician managing pediatric scenarios. "Immersive audio provides sounds typical of the setting (monitor alarms, patient’s moans, the mother’s vocalizations, and intercom announcements), which adds stress and creates a realistic environment." The student interacts with characters (paramedic, nurse, respiratory therapist, a distraught mother as a potential distraction) and with equipment and medications in response to changing patient states; medication doses or age-based equipment sizing are not required. Sessions ran on Oculus Quest 2 headsets.
requirements: A 15-min introduction on headset use and a software tutorial given beforehand to familiarize students with the headset
A facilitator-centered debriefing after each scenario
constraints: Medication doses or age-based size of equipment are not required in the scenarios
One student felt nauseated and could not complete the VR session
target_learning_goals: ABCDE systematic approach to the assessment and management of pediatric emergencies
examples: In the 2021 pilot, nine VR sessions with 5 students each were staged at the University of Padova; scenarios were an infant with status epilepticus and a child with anaphylaxis

article_title: Application of direct observation of operational skills in nursing skill evaluation of pressure injury: A randomized clinical trial.
citation: Zhang W, Peng Y, Zhuang H, Yu H, Liu Q, Gu Y, Yao J. (2024). Application of direct observation of operational skills in nursing skill evaluation of pressure injury: A randomized clinical trial. Int Wound J. https://doi.org/10.1111/iwj.14498
title: Implement DOPS assessments repeatedly and train assessors before adoption to realize its benefits in specialized nursing skill evaluation
description: The article recommends that implementers use DOPS for assessments repeatedly, because its effectiveness becomes apparent through repeated implementations and may not always be evident in quantitative results from a single round. It also stresses that DOPS requires assessors with ample clinical experience and the ability to provide accurate feedback, so assessors should be identified and trained before implementation. In this trial, assessors underwent standardized training with consensus scoring on operation videos before the assessment.
requirements: Assessors properly identified and trained before implementing DOPS assessments
constraints: The study was single-centre at Shanghai East Hospital; the authors call for larger multi-centre samples, repeated DOPS assessments, and additional outcome measures such as departmental PI occurrence and patient satisfaction
target_learners: Specialized nurses in PI care training programs
target_learning_goals: Specialized nursing skill evaluation and development of critical thinking
examples: In the trial, assessors watched three operation videos twice, scored with the DOPS form, reached consensus, and received additional training when evaluations diverged

article_title: High-stakes examinations during the COVID-19 pandemic: to proceed or not to proceed, that is the question.
citation: Tan Chee-Kiat, Chua Wei-Ling, Vu Charles Kien-Fong, Chang Jason Pik-Eu. (2021). High-stakes examinations during the COVID-19 pandemic: to proceed or not to proceed, that is the question. Postgraduate Medical Journal. https://doi.org/10.1136/postgradmedj-2020-139241
title: Keep the examination format unchanged and provide an equivalent technological environment for all candidates when conducting high-stakes examinations under disruption
description: The article recommends that a high-stakes examination conducted during disruption should keep its established format, since 'It should ideally be the same as previous prepandemic years for the best assurance of validity and maintenance of standards', and that technology introduction must not change the intellectual process or the score achieved. To be equitable, 'there should be an equivalent technological environment for everyone, including candidates with disabilities', and organisers should remain candidate-centric rather than technology-centric.
requirements: Technology used should not cause a significant difference in the intellectual process or in the score achieved
An equivalent technological environment for all candidates, including those with disabilities
constraints: The authors acknowledge it is less challenging to organise an examination without patient-contact components under social distancing rules
target_learning_goals: valid, fair, standards-consistent high-stakes assessment
examples: The authors retained pen-and-paper MCQs and gave all candidates equivalent laptop setups for the remote viva, with comprehensive briefings, live rehearsals a week before, and coexaminers from different hospitals

article_title: Nursing training and retraining on cardiopulmonary resuscitation: a theoretical-practical intervention.
citation: de Araujo Nyagra Ribeiro R, de Araújo Raul Amaral H, Moretti Miguel Antonio A, Chagas Antonio Carlos Palandri C. (2022). Nursing training and retraining on cardiopulmonary resuscitation: a theoretical-practical intervention. Revista da Escola de Enfermagem da USP. https://doi.org/10.1590/1980-220X-REEUSP-2021-0521
title: Maintain regular CPR training with a defined interval of up to twelve months to retain nursing professionals' resuscitation competencies
description: The article argues that CPR competencies decline over time without periodic retraining and that regularity of training is fundamental to retention. It states that for health professionals with greater exposure to cardiac arrest victims, "more frequent training with intervals of up to 12 months is indicated, considering that after this period the skills can already reduce to values close to 70%", and that maintaining regularity and a defined interval between trainings is fundamental for health services.
requirements: Institutional commitment to scheduling periodic in-service training sessions with a defined interval between them
constraints: The article notes health institutions, especially large ones, have difficulty carrying out continuing education with very short time intervals, and that the ideal interval between trainings remains unknown in the literature
target_learners: Nursing professionals working in hospital settings with exposure to cardiopulmonary arrest situations
target_learning_goals: Retention of CPR theoretical knowledge and practical skills over time
examples: The study used a nine-month interval between the two trainings, chosen because its effect is not documented in the literature and skills decline in periods of less than one year

article_title: Effectiveness of rational emotive behavior education (REBE) on computer anxiety among school teachers enrolled in e-learning.
citation: Onah BI, Ede MO, Eze BN, Uzoegwu CR, Mgboji C, Agbo GC, Uzuagu AU, Chiamagu C, Agbo PA, Oneli JO, Ogbueghu SN. (2023). Effectiveness of rational emotive behavior education (REBE) on computer anxiety among school teachers enrolled in e-learning. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000034303
title: E-learning moderator platform with themed 10-minute video clips for reducing computer anxiety
description: The researchers developed and implemented an e-learning moderator platform to moderate anxious schoolteachers' computer use. It relied on "the use of a 10-minute video clip for both synchronous/asynchronous", with each clip addressing computer anxiety-related themes such as dimensions of computer anxiety, attitudes toward computers, self-efficacy, avoidance, and self-perceptions. After viewing, participants reflected, shared experiences, asked questions, and received feedback through an e-learning forum discussion lasting 30 minutes per session, anchored by digital education experts.
requirements: Delivery by digital education experts who anchored each discussion session
An e-learning forum through which participants reflect, share experiences, ask questions, and receive feedback
constraints: The article reports the intervention was delivered to primary school teachers in Southeast Nigeria; the authors state the finding is limited to primary schoolteachers and cannot be generalized to every teacher in Nigeria
target_learners: Primary school teachers enrolled in e-learning with computer anxiety
target_learning_goals: Reducing computer anxiety
Understanding dimensions of computer anxiety and attitudes toward computers
examples: Treatment group participants viewed video clips covering themes such as the use of computers for online/blended learning and the psychological, operational, and sociological dimensions of computer anxiety, followed by 30-minute forum discussions
