article_title: Measuring the Effectiveness of a Multicomponent Program to Manage Academic Stress through a Resilience to Stress Index.
citation: Figueroa Carlos, Ayala Andrés, Trejo Luis A., Ramos Bertha, Briz Clara L., Noriega Isabella, Chávez Alejandro. (2023). Measuring the Effectiveness of a Multicomponent Program to Manage Academic Stress through a Resilience to Stress Index. Sensors. https://doi.org/10.3390/s23052650
title: Resilience to Stress Index (RSI): a physiological recovery metric computed from PCA cluster distances
description: The RSI, proposed by Díaz et al., measures a subject's ability to recover from stress using physiological signals. A psychophysiological stress profile is recorded through nine two-minute stages alternating baseline, stressors, and recovery periods; PCA clusters each stage, and the RSI is computed as RSI=ΔRΔS, where ΔR is the distance between the centroids of the last two stages and ΔS the largest distance between the baseline centroid and other phases. "An RSI close to one indicates that the individual has a high resilience to stress by presenting the ability to recover from stressors and approaching his/her initial baseline."
requirements: A calibration (baseline) stage measured before stressors are applied, per-subject physiological recordings across all stress-profile stages, and PCA-based inter-stage Euclidean distances.
constraints: The baseline and other stages are unique to each participant, so RSI values are individualized comparisons against each person's own calibration stage.
target_learners: University students undergoing psychophysiological stress assessment
target_learning_goals: Measuring resilience to academic stress and changes in autonomic recovery after intervention
examples: Applied at pre-test and post-test in this study to evaluate a multicomponent stress-management program with 38 undergraduates.
key_sources: Figueroa Carlos, Ayala Andrés, Trejo Luis A., Ramos Bertha, Briz Clara L., Noriega Isabella, Chávez Alejandro. (2023). Measuring the Effectiveness of a Multicomponent Program to Manage Academic Stress through a Resilience to Stress Index. Sensors. https://doi.org/10.3390/s23052650

article_title: Nurses experience increased clinical and organisational competence by working with a medical quality register, RevNatus - a qualitative study.
citation: Bjørngaard Hilde, Koksvik Hege Svean, Jakobsen Bente, Grønning Kjersti. (2022). Nurses experience increased clinical and organisational competence by working with a medical quality register, RevNatus – a qualitative study. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-022-08595-x
title: RevNatus: a consent-based nationwide medical quality register for pregnancy and inflammatory rheumatic disease
description: RevNatus is "a consent-based, nationwide medical quality register that collects data on patients with inflammatory rheumatic diseases during pregnancy and one year postpartum". Data are entered in rheumatology outpatient clinics; the register is web-based (earlier versions paper-based) with high national coverage, drawing on 19 of 22 rheumatology units in Norway. Its purpose is to obtain knowledge about the interaction between pregnancy and rheumatic disorders and to ensure high-quality treatment and follow-up.
requirements: Written patient consent and an inflammatory rheumatic disease with a pregnancy-wish are inclusion criteria; training those who register data is crucial to data quality.
constraints: The article reports that insufficient data quality is often associated with healthcare workers' lack of motivation, lack of training, uncertainty regarding variable definitions, or incorrect typing.
target_learners: Nurses and rheumatologists entering and using register data in outpatient clinics
target_learning_goals: Monitoring disease activity, treatment and follow-up during pregnancy and postpartum; building knowledge on pregnancy and rheumatic disease
examples: The register includes data from 19 of the 22 rheumatology units in Norway and data collection is carried out by a nurse or the rheumatologist during outpatient consultations.

Nurses experience increased clinical and organisational competence by working with a medical quality register, RevNatus – a qualitative study. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-022-08595-x

article_title: School of Thrombectomy-A 3-Step Approach to Perform Acute Stroke Treatment with Simulator Training and Virtual Supervision by Remote Streaming Support (RESS).
citation: Paech Daniel, Lehnen Nils, Lakghomi Asadeh, Schievelkamp Arndt, Gronemann Christian, Bode Felix J., Radbruch Alexander, Dorn Franziska. (2022). School of Thrombectomy—A 3-Step Approach to Perform Acute Stroke Treatment with Simulator Training and Virtual Supervision by Remote Streaming Support (RESS). Clinical Neuroradiology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00062-022-01242-2
title: RESS remote streaming supervision system for neurointerventional procedures
description: RESS (remote streaming support) is a teleproctoring setup in the smart angiography suite through which a remote supervisor follows and supports a live thrombectomy. The article describes the Tegus system as "a low-latency, high-resolution solution for streaming live events both visually and auditorily", with a remotely steerable 360°-rotatable, 90°-tiltable HD network camera, hands-free headset communication, account-based access and encrypted ePHI. It was used for step 3 of the curriculum, when the supervisor is no longer physically in the angio suite.
requirements: Requires bidirectional internet audio-video communication infrastructure in the angiography suite, a user account with session invitation, and encrypted handling of electronic protected health information.
constraints: Evaluation is subjective (questionnaires); the article notes criteria for objective assessment of telemedical supervision of neurointerventional procedures are difficult to define.

examples: Five trainees each completed approximately 15 mechanical thrombectomies with RESS after prior on-site supervised procedures; the proctor additionally rated 30 consecutive RESS interventions.

citation: Paech Daniel, Lehnen Nils, Lakghomi Asadeh, Schievelkamp Arndt, Gronemann Christian, Bode Felix J., Radbruch Alexander, Dorn Franziska. (2022). School of Thrombectomy—A 3-Step Approach to Perform Acute Stroke Treatment with Simulator Training and Virtual Supervision by Remote Streaming Support (RESS). title: Use remote audio-video supervision to ease the transition from supervised to independent interventions
description: The article argues that the hardest step in procedural training is moving from supervised procedures, where an experienced colleague can intervene at any time, to fully independent ones that often occur outside working hours. It states that "Telemedical live support can help to simplify this step and increase the level of safety of the treating physician by incorporating audio-video technology and internet connectivity into the angio suite." Trainees agreed the virtual presence and unmediated communication improved their sense of security.
requirements: A low-latency streaming platform with remote camera control and hands-free bidirectional audio between trainee and supervisor.
constraints: Support is framed for the initial independent procedures; reported benefit decays as trainees gain autonomy, so it serves as a transitional scaffold rather than a permanent arrangement.
target_learners: physicians in procedural specialty training performing their first independent interventions
target_learning_goals: safe independent procedural performance during the transition from supervised to autonomous practice
examples: The supervisor followed entire procedures via a steerable camera and audio communication, and a cited monocentric report found no difference in contrast use, fluoroscopy time, or technical success between live and remote supervision.

article_title: REMOTE ASYNCHRONOUS FEEDBACK FOR UNSUPERVISED LAPAROSCOPIC TRAINING: THE "LAPP" PLATFORM.
citation: Ulloa G, Neyem A, Escalona G, Ortiz C, Varas J. (2022). Remote asynchronous feedback for unsupervised laparoscopic training: the "Lapp" platform. ABCD Arq Bras Cir Dig. https://doi.org/10.1590/0102-672020220002e1712
title: Use remote asynchronous personalized expert feedback via technology-enhanced learning to overcome spatiotemporal barriers in skills training
description: The article proposes that technology-enhanced learning with remote asynchronous personalized feedback lets trainees "learn at their own pace... without geographical or time constraints asynchronously", while still receiving direct expert feedback on recorded performance. Because experts' availability is a critical scarce resource, delivering feedback asynchronously through a platform allows training "wherever and whenever they train". The randomized comparison found no competency disadvantage relative to in-person feedback.
requirements: Experts who review recorded trainee performances and add personalized feedback
A platform supporting video upload, review, and audiovisual interactive feedback tools
constraints: The article's evidence comes from a basic laparoscopic skills course; the authors note the elevated drop-out rate should be addressed in future studies
target_learners: Surgical trainees and healthcare professionals learning practical procedural skills
target_learning_goals: Practical skills acquisition through deliberate practice with personalized feedback
examples: In the study, some students received initial instructions and feedback through Lapp while others received them in person in a simulation center, with both groups reaching approval criteria

article_title: Impact of high-fidelity simulation exposure of nursing students with their objective structured clinical examination: A quasi-experimental study.

title: Supplement nursing clinical training with repeated high‐fidelity simulation exposure to enhance OSCE performance
description: The article recommends adding repeated HFS exposure to traditional laboratory and clinical training before high‐stakes practical assessment, reporting that 'The repeated exposure to HFS training offers an advantage and enhances the students' performance in the OSCEs'. HFS‐based training requires students to apply theoretical knowledge in a safe environment that simulates the real clinical setting, developing decision‐making and clinical competency.
requirements: A simulation laboratory with high‐fidelity simulators and trained faculty to run pre‐briefing, scenario and debriefing sessions
Scenarios aligned to course topics with procedural rubrics for assessment
constraints: The supporting evidence is a single‐institution quasi‐experiment limited to female students at one location
The procedural rubrics were not tested for reliability

clinical reasoning, decision‐making and clinical judgement

article_title: Teaching skills for medical residents: are these important? A narrative review of the literature.
citation: Fakhouri Saadallah Azor Filho, Feijó Lorena Pinho, Augusto Kristopherson Lustosa, Nunes Maria do Patrocínio Tenório. (2018). Teaching skills for medical residents: are these important? A narrative review of the literature. São Paulo Medical Journal. https://doi.org/10.1590/1516-3180.2018.0147060818
title: Require pedagogical (teaching-skills) instruction within residency training because demonstrated positive effects support it
description: The review argues, on the strength of the positive effects it synthesizes, that teaching-skills instruction should be a required part of residency: "Considering the positive effects that have been demonstrated, it can be argued that all residency programs should require residents to undergo instruction relating to teaching skills." It grounds this in residents' extensive teaching time, their role in the informal curriculum, and recommendations from the ACGME and LCME, and applies it specifically to Brazil's expanding medical education system.
requirements: Formal instruction time within residency curricula
Qualified instructors, since the review notes expertise to lead instruction is unevenly distributed
constraints: The review states its own susceptibility to selection and reporting bias, and that it only explored RaT program modes that had been introduced
target_learning_goals: teaching skills
clinical teaching of students and peers
examples: The review cites a one-hour One-Minute Preceptor intervention that showed benefits, and a one-day flipped-classroom RaT program with statistically significant pre/post improvements

article_title: Innovative Pedagogical Strategies in Health Professions Education: Active Learning in Dental Materials Science.
citation: Lin Galvin Sim Siang, Tan Wen-Wu, Tan Hung-Jia, Khoo Chia-Wee, Afrashtehfar Kelvin I. (2023). Innovative Pedagogical Strategies in Health Professions Education: Active Learning in Dental Materials Science. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph20032041
title: Revise undergraduate dental materials science curricula to integrate active-learning pedagogical strategies in place of purely didactic lectures
description: The review recommends that dental educators revise current undergraduate dental materials science curricula and integrate more effective, student-centered teaching methods, since didactic lectures promote passive learning and risk cognitive overload. It concludes "students generally showed positive perceptions toward these pedagogical strategies" and that educators should "integrate more effective teaching methods". The recommendation rests on a synthesis of 12 mostly Level 2–3 studies.
requirements: Well-controlled studies addressing teacher perceptions, teaching load, faculty training, availability of learning resources, and students' compliance before full implementation
constraints: Positive perceptions may reflect the Hawthorne effect and should be interpreted as acceptability and appeal, not efficacy

target_learning_goals: Dental materials science knowledge and clinical application of dental materials
examples: The review identified flipped classrooms, clinical-based learning, computer-assisted learning, group discussion, microteaching with BOPPPS, and game-based learning as strategies educators could integrate

The ten aspects range from information check and indication to image optimization, systematic examination, image interpretation, documentation, management, privacy protection and humanistic solicitude. The maximum score was 100 and a passing score was defined as 80; it served as the proctored practical outcome measure.

A proctored administration at the end of the training period

examples: At the end of the 30-day program, residents were graded performing an US examination on volunteer patients using the ten-aspect OSAUS rubric

article_title: Removing the academic framing in student evaluations improves achievement in children with dyslexia: The mediating role of self-judgement of competence.
citation: Rohmer, O., Doignon‐Camus, N., Audusseau, J., Trautmann, S., Chaillou, A.‐C., & Popa‐Roch, M. (2022). Removing the academic framing in student evaluations improves achievement in children with dyslexia: The mediating role of self‐judgement of competence. Dyslexia, 28(3), 309–324. https://doi.org/10.1002/dys.1713
title: Reduce the academic framing of evaluations so students with dyslexia are assessed in less threatening, non-academic task formats
description: The article argues that evaluation contexts function as threat cues for students who have repeatedly associated school with failure, so performance should be assessed in formats that "remove any association with the school environment." The study operationalized this by presenting the same vocabulary and comprehension skills with illustrated response options instead of all-written material, and found the dyslexia performance gap disappeared in this format. The authors conclude that "the present study suggests that in a non‐academic context, students with dyslexia can achieve as much as students without dyslexia," and recommend "less threatening evaluations" as part of training programs.
requirements: Alternative task formats must assess the same literacy skills at equivalent difficulty, as the article states the two task versions "assessed the same literacy skills and were equivalent in difficulty"
constraints: The article notes the non-academic tasks also displayed less written language, and addresses this confound by pointing to the equivalent mathematics result and the similar performance of students without dyslexia across formats
target_learners: middle school students with dyslexia in inclusive mainstream classes
target_learning_goals: literacy (vocabulary and comprehension) and mathematics achievement under evaluation
examples: Speech therapists proposed illustrated versions of the same standardized vocabulary and comprehension tests, with answers presented in picture form instead of all-written form

article_title: Anxiety is associated with extraneous cognitive load during teaching using high-fidelity clinical simulation.
citation: Fredericks Salim, ElSayed Mostafa, Hammad Mustafa, Abumiddain Omneya, Istwani Leila, Rabeea Abdulla, Rashid-Doubell Fiza, Bella Abdelhaleem M.E. (2021). Anxiety is associated with extraneous cognitive load during teaching using high-fidelity clinical simulation. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2021.1994691
title: Measures taken to reduce anxiety during simulation may help minimise extraneous cognitive load
description: Because state-anxiety during simulation is associated with extraneous rather than intrinsic load, the article reasons that "Measures taken to reduce anxiety during simulations may help to minimise ECL." Since it is widely accepted that optimal simulation design should minimise ECL, managing learner anxiety — for example through debriefing — is a design lever for protecting working memory from task-irrelevant processing during high-fidelity simulation teaching.
requirements: Simulation sessions that elicit measurable state-anxiety and are assessed with component-level cognitive load measures
constraints: The study measured no learning outcomes, so the anxiety-ECL link to performance was not tested
Findings come from a single higher educational institution and may not be generalisable to other settings
target_learners: Final-year undergraduate medical students in high-fidelity clinical simulation
target_learning_goals: Clinical competencies in emergency care scenarios, including history taking, examination, management and communication
examples: The study's debriefing segment significantly reduced state-anxiety after the scenario, and high post-scenario state-anxiety was associated with higher ECL ratings
key_sources: Fredericks Salim, ElSayed Mostafa, Hammad Mustafa, Abumiddain Omneya, Istwani Leila, Rabeea Abdulla, Rashid-Doubell Fiza, Bella Abdelhaleem M.E. (2021). title: RESHAPE antistigma training intervention with PhotoVoice recovery narratives and aspirational figure cofacilitation
description: RESHAPE is a stigma-reduction intervention in which people with lived experience of mental illness cofacilitate a 40-hour mhGAP-IG training for primary care practitioners. PWLE "present recovery testimonials through photographic narratives, using a technique known as PhotoVoice," with narratives of about 7 minutes covering life before treatment, the experience of treatment, and life after treatment, followed by question-and-answer sessions. Aspirational figures (PCPs previously trained in mental health care) present a myth-busting session and a clinician-perspective recovery story, and PWLE join structured and unstructured social activities with trainees.
requirements: PWLE must be in recovery from one of four priority disorders as evaluated by a psychiatrist, with PhotoVoice skill-building across 12 sessions over 3 months and psychosocial counselor support during sessions
The cofacilitated training must be time matched to standard training (9 days) so sections are equivalent in duration
constraints: Evaluated as an in-service intervention for certified primary care practitioners with prescribing privileges in Nepal; the article notes evidence-based preservice stigma reduction programs are lacking in LMICs
target_learners: Primary care practitioners (physicians, health assistants, auxiliary health workers) in low-resource settings
target_learning_goals: Reduce explicit and implicit stigma toward people with mental illness
Improve accuracy of mental illness diagnosis
Improve clinical competency in common factors of mental health care
examples: In the pilot trial, 34 primary care facilities were randomized 1:1; RESHAPE PCPs received the mhGAP-IG training with PWLE PhotoVoice narratives and aspirational figure sessions on days 2 through 8 of 9 training days

article_title: Factors Influencing Quality of Team Discussion: Discourse Analysis in an Undergraduate Team-Based Learning Biology Course.
citation: Leupen, S. M., Kephart, K. L., & Hodges, L. C. (2020). Factors Influencing Quality of Team Discussion: Discourse Analysis in an Undergraduate Team-Based Learning Biology Course. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 19(1). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.19-06-0112
title: Preclass readiness assurance appears to be a prerequisite for high-quality conceptual team discussion
description: The authors interpret TBL's readiness assurance process—incentivizing preclass mastery of basic objectives, team discussion of that content, and immediate feedback via scratch-off forms—as a key enabler of the high-quality discussion observed after higher-level questions. They write that this preparation "was likely a necessary prerequisite for the amount and quality of conceptual discussion that occurred in response to higher-level questions". Without baseline knowledge secured beforehand, higher-level questions may not elicit conceptual talk.
requirements: A preclass accountability process that ensures all students hold the basic learning objectives before in-class application questions
constraints: This is the authors' interpretation of why their findings differ from prior studies, not a directly tested manipulation
target_learners: Undergraduate students in flipped, team-based courses
target_learning_goals: Conceptual disciplinary explanations during in-class team work
examples: Students in the study generally did not ask each other about vocabulary or basic definitions, which the authors attribute to readiness assessment having covered them

article_title: Navigating Tensions of Research and Teaching: Biology Graduate Students' Perceptions of the Research-Teaching Nexus within Ecological Contexts.
citation: Reid Joshua W., Gardner Grant E. (2020). Navigating Tensions of Research and Teaching: Biology Graduate Students' Perceptions of the Research–Teaching Nexus within Ecological Contexts. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.19-11-0218
title: The research–teaching ecology (RTE) framework
description: The research–teaching ecology is a conceptual framework adapted from Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory and the research–teaching nexus literature to explain how perceptions of the relationship between research and teaching form during graduate professional development. The article states that "perceptions of the RTN are informed through social and cultural structures that individuals are embedded in during their professional development," organized across four levels: the individual, the microsystem, the exosystem, and the macrosystem. The study uses this framework to structure its survey and interpret where RTN messages originate.
requirements: Survey or interview instruments must attend to multiple ecological levels simultaneously, since the framework treats the levels as interdependent structures that should not be isolated.
constraints: The article limited its scope to research and teaching, excluding the mesosystem, chronosystem, and the service pillar of academic work.
target_learners: Biology graduate students developing academic professional identities
target_learning_goals: Understanding how social and cultural contexts shape graduate students' perceptions of research and teaching roles
examples: The survey was structured with item blocks for the individual, microsystem, exosystem, and macrosystem levels, and results were reported level by level.
key_sources: Reid Joshua W., Gardner Grant E. (2020). Navigating Tensions of Research and Teaching: Biology Graduate Students' Perceptions of the Research–Teaching Nexus within Ecological Contexts. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.19-11-0218

CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.21-01-0012
title: Conduct biology education research across multiple institution types, because institutional context shapes the mechanisms underlying performance gaps
description: The article's central recommendation is that BER should not over-rely on selective institutions. It calls for future research to "not exclusively focus on selective institutions and instead include data across different types of institutions," to systematically examine institutional or classroom characteristics that help or hinder equity, and to design targeted interventions that fit institutional contexts. Its own findings — URM gaps present at inclusive and selective institutions but absent at community colleges, and mediation effects varying by context — demonstrate that interventions effective at one institution type may not transfer.
requirements: Research collaborations and data collection spanning community colleges, inclusive institutions, and selective institutions
constraints: Grouping institutions into broad categories assumes students share similar experiences within a type, which the authors state is a limitation
target_learners: Undergraduate biology students across all institution types, including community colleges
target_learning_goals: Identify and reduce demographic performance gaps in introductory biology
examples: The study collected data from 33 biology courses at seven institutions across three institution types through a research coordination network, and found only 3% of recent BER articles included community college authors or study contexts.

title: Reallocate the cost savings from abridged IMNCI training to training more providers and to supervisory visits
description: A cost-reinvestment principle drawn from the study's economic findings: because the abridged 7-day IMNCI course cost US $525 per participant against US $825 for the standard course, the authors argue the surplus funds "can be reallocated to train more providers or for supervisory visits for previously trained providers", which they state can further improve the quality of care and sustain the quality of skills.
requirements: An abridged training must be adopted in place of the standard 11-day course so that surplus funds are generated for reallocation.
constraints: The article notes that lack of long term supervision has been identified as an important obstacle to the proper implementation of IMCI, so reinvestment must include supervision to sustain skills.

examples: All training sessions were conducted in public sector hospitals, where the article states there were no additional expenses for logistic arrangements.

article_title: Rational emotive education for reducing stress of undergraduate students of religious education program: An experimental study.
citation: Ilechukwu LC, Egenti NT, Aloh HE, Uwakwe RC, Obande-Ogbuinya N, Eke CL, Kalu IA, Ejionueme LK, Iremeka FU. (2021). Rational emotive education for reducing stress of undergraduate students of religious education program: An experimental study. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000026177
title: WhatsApp-delivered REE stress management program: 10 weekly 75-minute virtual sessions with homework and the ABCDE model
description: The treatment condition was a weekly REE series of "duration of 10 weeks which lasted 75 minutes per session," delivered through WhatsApp. It adapted therapeutic techniques from a previous rational emotive stress management program and aimed to aid students "through a sequence of REE virtual exercises geared towards decreasing their stress level." Participants were exposed to therapeutic techniques for managing stress, homework assignments were given at the end of every session, and the ABCDE model of the rational emotive approach was applied to illustrate how students can handle stress.
requirements: Each participant provided a cell phone number linked to WhatsApp and a functional email address; sessions ran weekly for 10 weeks at 75 minutes per session with homework assignments after every therapeutic session
constraints: Evaluated among religious education undergraduates in public universities in Southwest Nigeria who had high stress scores at baseline on the PSS-10
target_learners: undergraduate students of religious education programs with high perceived stress
target_learning_goals: recognizing and managing stress through behavioral, cognitive, and emotive coping skills
examples: The control condition paralleled the format: a weekly WhatsApp group with motivational posts, pictures, and short videos on stress, moderated for 10 weeks and 75 minutes per session

article_title: A quasi-experimental study of ethnic and gender bias in university grading.
citation: Bischoff Carina Saxlund, Ejrnæs Anders, Rubin Olivier. (2021). A quasi-experimental study of ethnic and gender bias in university grading. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0254422
title: Report null findings on grading bias to counter publication bias in the discrimination literature
description: The article argues that studies finding no evidence of grade discrimination should be published because the literature over-represents significant findings. It states that "Reporting on these types of “non-findings” is important to avoid publication bias, where studies with statistically significant or “spectacularly” strong findings are more frequently submitted and published than studies finding weak or no evidence," which risks overstating the evidence for grade discrimination. The article enacts this principle by reporting its own null results with full robustness checks.
requirements: Null results should be accompanied by robustness checks and sensitivity analyses to establish that the null is not an artifact of coding or model choice
constraints: The article notes single-country results face limits on generalization to other contexts, university cultures, and exam formats
target_learning_goals: fair and unbiased assessment of student performance
examples: The article reports its non-significant gender and ethnic interaction terms from OLS, examiner-split, ordered-logit, bootstrap, and coder-agreement analyses
key_sources: Bischoff Carina Saxlund, Ejrnæs Anders, Rubin Olivier. (2021). A quasi-experimental study of ethnic and gender bias in university grading. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0254422

citation: Williams Tremaine B., Prince Latrina Y., Allen Antiño R., Sterba Kristen M., Thomas Billy R., McGehee Robert E. (2021). Performance measures of racially underrepresented Ph.D. students in biomedical sciences: The UAMS IMSD Program Outcomes. PLoS ONE 16(2): e0246683. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0246683
title: Reduce reliance on the GRE in graduate admission decisions and identify psychometrically valid indicators tailored to biomedical career outcomes
description: Based on finding weak, non-significant associations between GRE scores and first-semester Ph.D. GPA, and GRE-outcome correlations that ran counter to admissions expectations, the article recommends admissions reform. It states the need to "1) reduce reliance on the use of the GRE in admission committee decisions, 2) identify psychometrically valid indicators that are tailored to assess outcome variables that are relevant to the careers of biomedical scientists, and 3) ensure the effective use of the tools in making admission decisions." The authors argue these recommendations could strengthen the validity of how racially underrepresented minorities are evaluated for entry and matriculation through doctoral training programs.
requirements: Admission committees currently use GRE scores and GPA as standardized comparison measures; reform requires identifying alternative psychometrically valid indicators tailored to biomedical career outcomes.
constraints: Evidence comes from a single IMSD initiative with a small sample (37 trainees) that the authors state is not generalizable; findings are correlational.
target_learners: Racially underrepresented minority applicants to biomedical science doctoral programs
target_learning_goals: Valid and equitable evaluation of applicants for entry and matriculation through doctoral training in biomedical sciences
examples: The article reports that the removal of Ph.D. programs' GRE requirements indicates a move toward expanded holistic approaches to evaluating UR Ph.D. applicants.

The authors state residents "retained the skill better when they were taught in a repeated training manner with a period of rest between sessions compared to a mass training". article_title: Knowledge acquisition and retention after a high flow training programme in Peru: a quasi-experimental single group pre-post design.
citation: Ellington Laura E, Becerra Rosario, Mallma Gabriela, Tantaleán da Fieno José, Nair Deepthi, Onchiri Frankline, Nielsen Katie R. (2020). Knowledge acquisition and retention after a high flow training programme in Peru: a quasi-experimental single group pre–post design. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-035125
title: Schedule repeat refresher training sessions to achieve and maintain competency after implementing new technology
description: The article's central design recommendation is that a single initial training session is insufficient: scheduled refresher training at follow-up intervals is needed both to restore lost knowledge and to build beyond baseline performance. As the authors state, their findings suggest the importance of repeat training sessions in order to achieve and maintain competency after the implementation of new technology. Refresher sessions at 3 and 12 months raised overall median scores from 78% to 83% and 87%, exceeding the 80% competency threshold after baseline training had failed to reach it.
requirements: Refresher sessions require scheduling around clinical schedules and, ideally, nursing coverage to maximise attendance
constraints: Substantial attrition in refresher attendance (>50% drop-off) limited statistical power and may have introduced selection bias
Refresher sessions did not prevent between-session knowledge decline
target_learners: multidisciplinary PICU staff: attending physicians, fellows, residents, nurses, respiratory therapists, medical technicians
target_learning_goals: safe and competent use of nasal high flow respiratory support
examples: Refresher trainings at 3 and 12 months were performed daily for four consecutive days during clinical hours, incorporating case-based discussion after the didactic lecture based on participant feedback

Staff entered information on a resident's health and abilities, life history, communication style and others' responses; logic-based algorithms generated bio-psychosocial action plans. title: Resilience reconceptualized as protective and vulnerable factors within and outside the individual
description: The article describes a reconceptualization of resilience as a construct associated with the presence of protective and vulnerable factors within and outside the individual that influence adaptation to problems causing a break in homeostasis. This replaces the older linear event-maladjustment account and accommodates the role of emotions, which people value as facilitators of developing resilience capacity. It underpins using the ARS to identify students' coping resources in the academic context.

examples: the study validated the ARS to let educators analyze whether students have sufficient defense mechanisms to adapt to daily difficulties

article_title: Supervision training in healthcare: a realist synthesis.
citation: Rees Charlotte E., Lee Sarah L., Huang Eve, Denniston Charlotte, Edouard Vicki, Pope Kirsty, Sutton Keith, Waller Susan, Ward Bernadette, Palermo Claire. (2019). Supervision training in healthcare: a realist synthesis. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-019-09937-x
title: Realist context-mechanism-outcome program theory of supervision training, differentiated by intervention duration
description: The article develops a modified program theory (MPT) explaining how supervision training works, for whom and in what circumstances, using realist logic in which interventions lead to outcomes through mechanisms operating in contexts. It states: "Interventions are thought to lead to outcomes through the operation of mechanisms, that is, the resources proffered by an intervention and the ways in which this influences participants' reasoning." The theory distinguishes causal pathways for short-duration interventions (pedagogy and supervisor-characteristic mechanisms) from extended-duration interventions (facilitator-characteristic mechanisms), built from 74 final CMOCs identified as demi-regularities across 29 outputs.
requirements: Program theory development and refinement through iterative realist review stages (scope clarification, searching, selection, extraction, synthesis)
constraints: The CMO relationship is not necessarily straightforward or linear; what works for one person might not work for another
target_learners: Supervisors in health and human services
target_learning_goals: Explaining how and why supervision training interventions produce supervisor and supervisee outcomes
examples: The initial program theory was built from three prior non-realist reviews and refined against 29 included outputs

title: The Recognising, Diagnosing and Managing Dementia in General Practice workshop
description: A tailored continuing-medical-education workshop developed by the Wicking Dementia Research and Education Centre in response to the expressed absence of appropriate dementia-related content in GP registrar training. The article states "The GPR workshop consists of a 3-hour face-to-face presentation delivered by medical educators focusing on (1) recognising and diagnosing dementia and (2) managing dementia in general practice"; supervisors attend a 2-hour modified version designed to help them teach registrars this content. It provides a framework for decision-making, tools and resources, a strong focus on lived experience situating people with dementia and their carers as central, and considers diagnosis and management through a biopsychosocial lens.
requirements: Delivered face to face by medical educators at regional training offices, augmenting the apprenticeship-model interaction between supervisors and registrars.
constraints: There is more in-depth coverage of some aspects of dementia diagnosis and management in the registrars' workshop than in the supervisors' workshop.
target_learning_goals: Recognising and diagnosing dementia
Managing dementia in general practice
Supporting timely and supportive engagement with diagnosis
examples: Delivered in 18 workshops across six Australian states between 2014 and 2018, evaluated with a pretest post-test design.

Effect of a dementia education intervention on the confidence and attitudes of general practitioners in Australia: a pretest post-test study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-033218

article_title: Course-based research experience of undergraduate medical students through project-based learning.
citation: Si Jihyun. (2020). Course-based research experience of undergraduate medical students through project-based learning. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2020.152
title: Nine-criterion research skill rubric (levels 1–3) for authentic assessment of research reports
description: A rubric developed from research skill areas classified by Stark et al. and Murdoch-Eaton et al. — research methods, information gathering, critical analysis and review, and data processing — modified for an introductory CRE. It "includes nine research skill criteria, with the level of quality of each criterion ranging from 1 to 3," scored from each group's final research report by two professors with consensus on disagreements. The authors argue that because PBL emphasizes authenticity, assessment also needs to be authentic.
requirements: Two professors scoring reports separately with consensus discussion for disagreements
constraints: The rubric was not disclosed to students at the beginning of the class, which the authors identify as a missed opportunity
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in introductory research courses
target_learning_goals: research skill assessment
authentic performance assessment
examples: Criterion 6, effectively present data, earned the lowest mean score of 1.89±0.60 across groups

title: REACT (Relatives' Education And Coping Toolkit) online self-management toolkit for relatives
description: REACT is a supported self-management toolkit providing accessible evidence-based information and support for relatives of people with psychosis or bipolar. It included "12 psychoeducation modules addressing key questions identified by relatives; peer support through a moderated group forum; a confidential direct messaging service; and a resource directory". Modules contained evidence-based written information, videos of clinical experts and experts by experience, and self-reflection tasks personalising content; a separate instance was set up for each case, with REACT Supporters moderating the forum and responding to messages.
requirements: REACT Supporters identified within the Early Intervention team to moderate the forum, respond to messages and update the resource directory
Staff accounts (IMPART lead, REACT supporter, clinician) with defined access levels to invite and support relatives
constraints: The article reports some content was static and sometimes at odds with current practice, e.g. diagnostic definitions, and the dashboard for creating relatives' accounts was not sufficiently user friendly

article_title: Planning injury prevention training for youth handball players: application of the generalisable six-step intervention development process.
citation: Ageberg E, Bunke S, Nilsen P, Donaldson A. (2020). Planning injury prevention training for youth handball players: application of the generalisable six-step intervention development process. Injury Prevention. https://doi.org/10.1136/injuryprev-2019-043468
title: RE-AIM SSM framework for designing and evaluating implementation outcomes
description: The Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance Sport Setting Matrix (RE-AIM SSM) framework is applied to design and evaluate implementation outcomes at the individual and organisational levels. In step 5 the implementation strategies are reviewed to ensure they address awareness (reach), adoption, implementation and maintenance dimensions at the individual player, coach, club and federation levels, giving the model a social–ecological and evidence-based focus.
requirements: Application across multiple levels of the sports delivery system (player, coach, club, federation)
constraints: Designed for community sport settings
target_learners: coaches and club administrators as implementers
target_learning_goals: widespread, sustained and high-fidelity use of injury prevention training
examples: Anticipated implementation outcomes are that coaches, players and administrators will be aware of the model, deliver the programme and use it as intended

article_title: Testing the "Zero-Sum Game" Hypothesis: An Examination of School Health Policies and Practices and Inequalities in Educational Outcomes.
citation: Long SJ, Littlecott H, Hawkins J, Eccles G, Fletcher A, Hewitt G, Murphy S, Moore GF. (2020). Testing the “Zero‐Sum Game” Hypothesis: An Examination of School Health Policies and Practices and Inequalities in Educational Outcomes. Journal of School Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/josh.12889
title: Do not treat school health improvement as a zero-sum trade-off against academic attainment
description: The article argues against the assumption that focusing resources on health takes resource away from schools' core business of education. Its conclusion states: “The present cross‐sectional study does not support the “zero‐sum game hypothesis,” and in fact, provides evidence to the contrary for KS3 attainment and attendance,” suggesting “health improvement activity may be associated with better educational outcomes, particularly among low‐income schools.” The principle holds that embedding health improvement is compatible with, and in more deprived schools potentially beneficial to, educational outcomes.
requirements: School-level commitment to health improvement activity across curriculum, ethos/environment, and family/community engagement domains
constraints: Evidence is cross-sectional and school-level; confounding cannot be ruled out, and no associations were found for KS4 attainment
target_learners: secondary school students, especially those in more deprived schools
target_learning_goals: academic attainment and attendance without sacrificing health improvement
examples: Regression models across 97 Welsh secondary schools found no negative associations of health improvement variables with attainment, and positive associations with KS3 attainment among high FSM schools
key_sources: Long SJ, Littlecott H, Hawkins J, Eccles G, Fletcher A, Hewitt G, Murphy S, Moore GF. (2020). Testing the “Zero‐Sum Game” Hypothesis: An Examination of School Health Policies and Practices and Inequalities in Educational Outcomes. Journal of School Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/josh.12889

article_title: Long-term retention assessment after simulation-based-training of pediatric procedural skills among adult emergency physicians: a multicenter observational study.
citation: Ansquer Raihei, Mesnier Thomas, Farampour Farnam, Oriot Denis, Ghazali Daniel Aiham. (2019). Long-term retention assessment after simulation-based-training of pediatric procedural skills among adult emergency physicians: a multicenter observational study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1793-6
title: For rarely practiced emergency procedural skills, schedule simulation refresher training about every 2 years and no later than 4 years after the initial course.
description: The article recommends that simulation-based training for rare, low-volume procedural skills be reiterated periodically because retention decays within months and is lost by 4 years. Based on performance evaluation with the TAPAS scale, the authors state that "simulation-based training requires reiteration every 2 years" and, if not, that the course be retaken before 4 years to maintain acceptable performance.
requirements: Baseline simulation training followed by measurable performance assessment, as done with the TAPAS scale in the PEP course
constraints: The optimal repetition interval was not determined and the authors state it "requires further research"; the recommendation derives from a cross-sectional observational comparison, not a prospective cohort test of refresher schedules
target_learning_goals: Retention of rare pediatric emergency procedural skills such as airway and ventilation management
examples: The study compared five groups trained 0.5 to 4+ years prior to assessment plus untrained controls, and only 6.9% (18/262) of course attendees had received any additional simulation training beyond the 6-month PEP course
key_sources: Ansquer Raihei, Mesnier Thomas, Farampour Farnam, Oriot Denis, Ghazali Daniel Aiham. (2019). article_title: Strategic elements of residency training in China: transactional leadership, self-efficacy, and employee-orientation culture.
citation: Deng Guangwei, Zhao Di, Lio Jonathan, Chen Xinyu, Ma Xiaopeng, Liang Liang, Feng Chenpeng. (2019). Strategic elements of residency training in China: transactional leadership, self-efficacy, and employee-orientation culture. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1792-7
title: Resident assessment questionnaire (ReAQ) measuring six ACGME core competencies
description: The ReAQ is a resident performance instrument the article uses to measure training performance. It "consists of 20 items that assess the six core competencies identified by the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education", administered to help assess resident performance during training. In this study it served as the performance measure on the 5-point Likert-type scale (Cronbach's α = 0.92, composite reliability 0.94, AVE 0.50 as printed in Table 1).
requirements: Administered as part of the questionnaire battery with all scales on a 5-point Likert-Type Scale from 1 (very disagree) to 5 (very agree)
target_learners: resident physicians in standardized residency training
target_learning_goals: assessing residents' six core clinical competencies during training
examples: The study used the ReAQ as the dependent measure of training performance for 247 residents across five tertiary hospitals
key_sources: Deng Guangwei, Zhao Di, Lio Jonathan, Chen Xinyu, Ma Xiaopeng, Liang Liang, Feng Chenpeng. (2019). Strategic elements of residency training in China: transactional leadership, self-efficacy, and employee-orientation culture. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1792-7

article_title: Peer Teaching Increases Knowledge and Changes Perceptions about Genetically Modified Crops in Non-Science Major Undergraduates.
citation: Chrispeels H. E., Chapman J. M., Gibson C. L., Muday G. K. (2019). Peer Teaching Increases Knowledge and Changes Perceptions about Genetically Modified Crops in Non–Science Major Undergraduates. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.18-08-0169
title: Repeated cross-age peer teaching with a prepared active-learning lesson as a lesson-level design for attitude and knowledge change
description: The pattern trains older students on a scripted active-learning lesson, then has them teach the same lesson to younger students multiple times in small groups. Students identified the repetitive teaching cycle as central: understanding "only served to increase as I taught over the course of our two teaching labs." The design targets both content mastery and opinion change on a socioscientific issue.
requirements: Undergraduates master the lesson in a faculty-led training week before teaching
Small-group structure (six to 10 younger students per pair) is maintained
The lesson must be written at a level appropriate for the younger students
constraints: Assessed in a single nonmajors biology course at one private liberal arts institution with no control group
target_learning_goals: deepened understanding of taught genetics concepts
informed opinions about socioscientific issues
examples: Students taught the same lesson to high school classes in two sequential weeks; 35% of reflection comments cited repetition of teaching as supporting their understanding
key_sources: Chrispeels H. E., Chapman J. M., Gibson C. L., Muday G. K. (2019). Peer Teaching Increases Knowledge and Changes Perceptions about Genetically Modified Crops in Non–Science Major Undergraduates. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.18-08-0169

article_title: The power of simulation: a large-scale narrative analysis of learners' experiences.
citation: Bearman Margaret, Greenhill Jennene, Nestel Debra. (2019). The power of simulation: a large‐scale narrative analysis of learners’ experiences. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.13747
title: Reframe failure as fallibility in SBE: use facilitated opportunities to examine personal failures so learners come to see things going wrong as part of professional practice
description: The article recommends that, given how often narratives of 'things going wrong' carried learning, "it may be valuable for SBE practitioners to consider how to reframe failure as fallibility and to offer facilitated opportunity to examine the role of personal failures in health care". SBE offers a platform to make mistakes and learn through self-reflection shared with peers and facilitators. The recommendation rests on the study's finding that error and associated emotion and reflection were a key part of learning.
requirements: Facilitated debriefing and an appropriate learning environment so that examining failure is productive rather than damaging
constraints: The article warns that focusing on errors may not always be helpful and suggests balancing attention to 'things going right'
target_learners: Health professionals and trainees participating in simulation-based education
target_learning_goals: Understanding fallibility and error as part of professional health care practice
examples: The 327 narratives frequently revolved around mistakes in scenarios, with debriefing shifting uncomfortable experiences into learning
key_sources: Bearman Margaret, Greenhill Jennene, Nestel Debra. (2019). The power of simulation: a large‐scale narrative analysis of learners’ experiences. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.13747

article_title: The development and use of a pharmacist-specific Mini-CEX for postgraduate year trainees in Taiwan.
citation: Wei Chung-Jen, Lu Tzu-Hsuan, Chien Shu-Chen, Huang Wan-Tsui, Liu Yueh-Ping, Chan Cho-Yu, Chiu Chiung-Hsuan. (2019). The development and use of a pharmacist-specific Mini-CEX for postgraduate year trainees in Taiwan. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1602-2
title: Include social and administrative pharmacy and interprofessional practice as required subjects in postgraduate pharmacy training
description: Because senior trainees significantly outperformed first-year trainees specifically in organization and efficiency and communication skills, the authors suggest these abilities "could be improved with training in multidisciplinary teamwork, as well as social and administrative pharmacy". They recommend that "social and administrative pharmacy, as well as interprofessional practice be listed as required subjects in the Taiwanese PGY training program", noting trainees currently could take such electives only if already performing well after basic training. They further urge policy encouraging teaching hospitals to improve instruction quality in required courses.
requirements: Qualified faculty to provide the courses
Placement within the 24-month PGY program structure
constraints: The recommendation is directed at the Taiwanese PGY training program, based on cross-sectional differences between trainee cohorts
target_learning_goals: Organization and efficiency, communication skills, and multidisciplinary teamwork
examples: The article notes such subjects are required in many pharmacist residency programs in the United States

article_title: The flipped classroom model for an undergraduate epidemiology course.
citation: Sohn Sangho, Lee Young-Mee, Jung Jaehun, Cha Eun Shil, Chun Byung Chul. (2019). The flipped classroom model for an undergraduate epidemiology course. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2019.122
title: Restructure pre-existing curricular components in parallel when introducing a flipped classroom
description: The article concludes that implementing a flipped classroom alone is insufficient where existing curricular structures compete with it. Because the 'practice of epidemiology' course ran in parallel with a lecture-based 'preventive medicine' course whose key concepts were already taught, "this might have discouraged students’ engagement in the pre-class, self-directed learning activities." The authors therefore recommend that institutions "consider restructuring other preexisting curricular components in parallel with implementing a novel instructional method" to encourage self-directed learning and better outcomes.
requirements: Institutional willingness to adjust course scheduling and content beyond the single course being flipped
constraints: Where redundant lectures cover the same key concepts, student engagement with pre-class materials may drop
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in traditional, heavily scheduled curricula
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning
better learning outcomes
examples: The epidemiology course was scheduled in parallel with the 'preventive medicine' course, whose lectures had already taught the key concepts
key_sources: Sohn Sangho, Lee Young-Mee, Jung Jaehun, Cha Eun Shil, Chun Byung Chul. (2019). The flipped classroom model for an undergraduate epidemiology course. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2019.122

article_title: Randomized Controlled Trial of Simulation vs. Standard Training for Teaching Medical Students High-quality Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation.
citation: McCoy C. Eric MD, MPH; Rahman Asif MD; Rendon Juan C. MD; Anderson Craig L. PhD, MPH; Langdorf Mark I. MD, MPHE; Lotfipour Shahram MD, MPH; Chakravarthy Bharath MD, MPH. (2019). Randomized Controlled Trial of Simulation vs. Standard Training for Teaching Medical Students High-quality Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.2018.11.39040
title: Use training manikins that provide real-time feedback on CPR performance metrics when teaching high-quality CPR
description: The article argues that real-time feedback during skills practice is the mechanism behind superior CPR performance: students "get to actually experience what the correct compression rate, depth, recoil and compression fraction feel like," allowing immediate adjustment. This aligns with the AHA guideline statement that "CPR prompt and feedback devices may be useful for training rescuers and may be useful as part of an overall strategy to improve the quality of CPR for actual cardiac arrest."
requirements: Manikins or devices capable of providing real-time feedback on compression rate, depth, and recoil during practice
constraints: The trial showed no measured effect on compression rate or recoil, and results come from simulated rather than actual cardiac arrest scenarios
target_learning_goals: adherence to AHA high-quality CPR guidelines
faster activation of emergency medical services
examples: In the trial, the intervention group received real-time simulator feedback during training while the control group received post-performance feedback, the approach used in standard North American CPR courses with low-fidelity manikins
key_sources: McCoy C. Eric MD, MPH; Rahman Asif MD; Rendon Juan C. MD; Anderson Craig L. PhD, MPH; Langdorf Mark I. MD, MPHE; Lotfipour Shahram MD, MPH; Chakravarthy Bharath MD, MPH. (2019). Randomized Controlled Trial of Simulation vs. Standard Training for Teaching Medical Students High-quality Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.2018.11.39040

article_title: Using an interactive digital calendar with mobile phone reminders by senior people - a focus group study.
citation: Baric, V., Andreassen, M., Öhman, A., & Hemmingsson, H. (2019). Using an interactive digital calendar with mobile phone reminders by senior people - a focus group study. BMC Geriatrics, 19, 116. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12877-019-1128-9
title: RemindMe: interactive digital calendar with active SMS reminders and a self-monitoring feedback system
description: RemindMe is an interactive digital calendar with mobile phone reminders developed to support people in organizing, planning, and executing everyday activities, designed "to reduce complexity, including limiting choice of colours and limiting options for multiple windows". It offers three core functions: scheduling of activities/events and reminders via a user-friendly web-based calendar (which a support person can share), active confirmation of reminders sent by SMS requiring a Yes/No answer, and a feedback system registering self-monitoring information based on the user's interaction with the system. Reminders can be customized in timing, recipient, and location.
requirements: The user needs access to a mobile phone or smartphone able to receive and answer SMS reminders, and may invite a support person to share the digital calendar.
constraints: The article notes some seniors perceived it as signalling aging and dependence, and participants with impaired vision found small displays difficult and reduced fine motor skills made answering SMS difficult.
target_learners: Community-dwelling seniors, ultimately senior people with cognitive impairments
target_learning_goals: Organizing, planning, and executing everyday activities with reminders
examples: In the study, 20 seniors used RemindMe for six weeks after a 30–90 minute introduction course, a written manual, and weekly support phone calls.
key_sources: Baric, V., Andreassen, M., Öhman, A., & Hemmingsson, H. (2019). Using an interactive digital calendar with mobile phone reminders by senior people - a focus group study. BMC Geriatrics, 19, 116. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12877-019-1128-9

article_title: Implication of nurse intervention on engagement with urate-lowering drugs: A qualitative study of participants in a RCT of nurse led care.
citation: Latif Zahira P., Nakafero Georgina, Jenkins Wendy, Doherty Michael, Abhishek Abhishek. (2018). Implication of nurse intervention on engagement with urate-lowering drugs: A qualitative study of participants in a RCT of nurse led care. Joint, Bone, Spine. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbspin.2018.10.008
title: Long-term care packages for gout should include regular review involving discussion of gout status, SU measurement and assessment of lifestyle factors and comorbidities
description: The article recommends that long-term management of gout should not end when an initial treatment phase concludes. Participants interviewed 18–26 months after the RCT reported that monitoring and discussion had lapsed, which the authors read as a care-design gap: "any long-term package of care for gout should include regular review (for example, annually)". The review should cover gout status, serum urate measurement, and adverse lifestyle factors and comorbidities.
requirements: Ongoing access to a healthcare professional able to measure SU levels and discuss treatment continuation
constraints: At the end of the study primary-care practitioners were advised to monitor SU levels annually, but very few did
target_learners: Adults with gout on long-term urate-lowering therapy
target_learning_goals: Sustained engagement and adherence with urate-lowering therapy
examples: Participants interviewed a median of 22 months after the RCT reported no long-term monitoring or discussion of ULT use with their GP

Implication of nurse intervention on engagement with urate-lowering drugs: A qualitative study of participants in a RCT of nurse led care. Joint, Bone, Spine. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbspin.2018.10.008

article_title: Multi-institutional study of GRE scores as predictors of STEM PhD degree completion: GRE gets a low mark.
citation: Petersen Sandra L., Erenrich Evelyn S., Levine Dovev L., Vigoreaux Jim, Gile Krista. (2018). Multi-institutional study of GRE scores as predictors of STEM PhD degree completion: GRE gets a low mark. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0206570
title: Reconsider the role of GRE scores in STEM doctoral admissions and develop more inclusive and predictive selection processes
description: The article recommends that STEM doctoral programs reexamine heavy reliance on GRE scores and cut-offs in admissions, because the study found GRE scores were not predictive of completion and GRE Q acted as a negative predictor for men. It states that "it seems prudent to reconsider the role of GRE scores in the STEM PhD selection process" and urges identifying the characteristics that led committees to admit low-scoring men who completed at high rates, to build more inclusive admissions assessments.
requirements: Programs currently using GRE scores or cut-offs in admissions decisions, as the article describes for most U.S. universities.
constraints: The study covers U.S. citizens and Permanent Residents entering STEM PhD programs at four state flagship institutions between 2000 and 2005, using pre-2011 GRE scores; race/ethnicity data could not be used due to small sample size.
target_learning_goals: fair and predictive selection of doctoral students who will complete STEM PhD programs
increasing diversity and inclusion in STEM doctoral admissions
examples: The four institutions admitted students across the full GRE Q range, producing a lowest-quartile male group that completed at 74.0%, above all higher quartiles.
key_sources: Petersen Sandra L., Erenrich Evelyn S., Levine Dovev L., Vigoreaux Jim, Gile Krista. (2018). Multi-institutional study of GRE scores as predictors of STEM PhD degree completion: GRE gets a low mark. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0206570

article_title: Dynamic changes of brain functional states during surgical skill acquisition.
citation: Shafiei Somayeh B., Hussein Ahmed Aly, Guru Khurshid A. (2018). Dynamic changes of brain functional states during surgical skill acquisition. PLoS ONE 13(10): e0204836. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0204836
title: Schedule regular, continuous practice in RAS training because brain-function gains deteriorate with long practice gaps
description: The principle holds that robot-assisted surgery trainees should practice regularly and continuously rather than with long gaps, because the dynamic architecture of brain functioning was not permanent and was affected by gap in practice. The authors write that "for a shorter RAS learning curve, trainees need to practice regularly and continuously" and that deterioration of brain functioning changes should be considered in the RAS learning curve. This rests on the finding that longer practice gaps reduced motor and visual module recruitment.
requirements: Monitoring via EEG-derived recruitment and integration features of motor and visual modules to detect deterioration from practice gaps.
constraints: Recordings in this study were limited to 6 sessions, so deterioration and recovery rates for individual subjects could not be quantified.
target_learners: Medical students training in robot-assisted surgery
target_learning_goals: Human-machine interface skills of robot-assisted surgery
examples: The study recorded EEG across six sessions over one year with unequal gaps between practice sessions and correlated recruitment with average practice gap.

article_title: The Relative Effect of Team-Based Learning on Motivation and Learning: A Self-Determination Theory Perspective.
citation: Jeno Lucas M., Raaheim Arild, Kristensen Sara Madeleine, Kristensen Kjell Daniel, Hole Torstein Nielsen, Haugland Mildrid J., Mæland Silje. (2017). The Relative Effect of Team-Based Learning on Motivation and Learning: A Self-Determination Theory Perspective. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.17-03-0055
title: Incorporate team-based learning into higher education teaching to support autonomous motivation, competence, and engagement
description: The article recommends that teachers incorporate active-learning approaches, specifically TBL, into their teaching because students perceived teachers as more autonomy supportive under TBL and because TBL showed positive motivational effects on intrinsic motivation, perceived competence, and engagement. It further recommends teachers evaluate teaching activities in light of motivational consequences and autonomy-supportive contexts, and nurture students' needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness "by providing choice, structure, and caring" to reduce feelings of external regulation.
requirements: Teachers should provide rationales, structure, and challenging tasks, and support students' basic psychological needs in an autonomy-supportive way
constraints: The evidence base is a quasi-experimental one-group pretest–posttest study with no causal inferences; some controlling aspects of TBL enhanced external regulation
target_learning_goals: autonomous motivation, perceived competence, engagement, and perceived learning
examples: The authors recommend teachers incorporate TBL in higher education due to the positive motivational effects found in the physiotherapy course study

article_title: Exploratory Application of Augmented Reality/Mixed Reality Devices for Acute Care Procedure Training.
citation: Kobayashi L, Zhang XC, Collins SA, Karim N, Merck DL. (2018). Exploratory Application of Augmented Reality/Mixed Reality Devices for Acute Care Procedure Training. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.2017.10.35026
title: Registered holoimage overlay of patient anatomy onto physical task trainers for blind insertion procedural training
description: A session-level instructional design in which rendered holoimages of key cervical and thoracic structures are manually scaled and registered onto physical task trainers using surface anatomy landmarks such as the sternal notch, laryngeal prominence, and rib spaces. This provides learners "the equivalent of a 'visible human'" conveying locations, shapes, sizes, and juxtapositions of internal structures, and "permitted the stable overlay of task-relevant anatomy ... for training with enhanced visual cues and haptic feedback." It was applied to central venous catheter and tube thoracostomy insertion training on a CVL task trainer and a SimMan 3G manikin.
requirements: Requires AR/MR headset devices, pre-rendered patient holoimages, and physical task trainers compatible with landmark-based registration.
constraints: Registration is manual; spatial alignment between holoimage and task trainer was intermittently lost and required adjustments.

target_learning_goals: blind insertion invasive procedural skills (central venous line, tube thoracostomy)

article_title: Differences in opinions of occupational physicians on the required competencies by field of practice: results of an international Delphi study.
citation: Demou Evangelia, Lalloo Drushca, Macdonald Ewan B. (2018). Differences in opinions of occupational physicians on the required competencies by field of practice: results of an international Delphi study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1139-9
title: Those defining and developing competency standards should recognise perspective differences among practitioner groups, particularly when academics largely define the skills
description: The article argues that because competency standards are largely defined by academics, differences of opinion between fields of practice must be recognised by those developing standards. It states that "Recognition of these perspective differences by OP professional group is important for those directly involved in defining and developing competency standards, particularly if these tasks continue to a large extent to be undertaken by academics." The Delphi comparison showed the Academic/Physician group deviated the most from the other two groups.
requirements: Competency standard developers with access to opinion data from multiple field-of-practice groups
constraints: Evidence base is a Delphi survey with a relatively low response rate and categorisation based on self-reported job titles
target_learners: Occupational physicians across clinical, managerial, and academic fields of practice
target_learning_goals: Alignment of competency standards and training curricula with the perspectives of practitioners in different roles
examples: The study compared ratings and rankings of 12 principal domains across Physician, Manager/Physician, and Academic/Physician groups drawn from an international Delphi survey

article_title: Computerized Sign Language-Based Literacy Training for Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Children.
citation: Holmer Emil, Heimann Mikael, Rudner Mary. (2017). Computerized Sign Language-Based Literacy Training for Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Children. The Journal of Deaf Studies and Deaf Education. https://doi.org/10.1093/deafed/enx023
title: Design multimedia literacy training to reduce working memory load through individualized starting level, contiguity, visual filtering, and recasting of meaning across modalities
description: The article holds that "There are several aspects of the design of Omega-is-d2 that are likely to reduce working memory load and thus release cognitive resources for learning." These include starting training at the participant's appropriate linguistic level, presenting sign equivalents and target written words in close proximity, a visual filter that "overshadows extraneous visual information" when a word is selected, simultaneous animation with the written sentence so the learner need not hold content in working memory to compare them, and recasting — repeating meaning in written language, sign language, and animation within a short period. The cited multimedia-learning rationale (Mayer & Moreno, 2003) is that reducing extraneous processing and segmenting frees resources for connecting language forms and meaning.
requirements: An individualized starting level determined by test performance
Proximity of sign equivalents and target written words on screen
Animations containing only target-relevant information
Recasting of meaning in several forms within a short time period
constraints: The article notes situations exist in multimedia learning when static depiction is preferable to dynamic animation
target_learners: DHH signing children learning to read
Beginning readers with weak representations in the language of instruction
target_learning_goals: Mapping written language forms to meaning
Reduced cognitive load during literacy practice
examples: In the Create exercises the participant sets the pace of sentence construction and the program inserts a short time lag before presenting the corresponding sign
key_sources: Holmer Emil, Heimann Mikael, Rudner Mary. (2017). Computerized Sign Language-Based Literacy Training for Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Children. The Journal of Deaf Studies and Deaf Education. https://doi.org/10.1093/deafed/enx023
